Think of Iraq and Afghanistan - their crystal ball is often as muddy as yours or mine. While the 2010 Strategic Defence Security Review (SDSR) did identify terrorism and international military crises as high level (tier 1) threats, there was no specific mention of Russia and so-called Islamic State (IS) did not exist in anything like its present form. The 2015 SDSR will identify both IS and Russia as tier 1 threats, but they may not be the same threat five years hence. They say that armies train to fight the last war they fought and military plans don't survive the first contact with the enemy. "In 2010 it was rather assumed the armed forces would get out of Afghanistan and take a bit of a breather," says Michael Clarke, director of the defence think tank Rusi. Instead "the world has shown us the armed forces won't be getting a holiday," he says. First, the government should be commended on its commitment to carry out a defence review every five years. Before, defence reviews were done ad hoc. But ministers will still have to overcome a high degree of scepticism as to whether this latest SDSR is genuinely "strategic" or if it matches Britain's global ambitions with the resources needed. SDSR 2010 may have been strategic in name but it'll be remembered for the savage cuts that followed. It wasn't just the scrapping of iconic names, it left gaping holes in Britain's defences - with no aircraft carriers for the Royal Navy and no maritime patrol aircraft to hunt down Russian submarines. Full document The Royal Navy also lost thousands of personnel and is now having to recruit marine engineers from foreign navies. In order to man its two new aircraft carriers it'll need another 2,000 sailors but they'll have to manage with fewer, which could mean mothballing other warships. The armed forces are still licking the wounds inflicted by the 2010 review. Defence Secretary Michael Fallon admits it involved "painful" decisions. But this week he told me: "We're now able to expand the defence budget again.... to enhance the capabilities of our armed forces to deal with the increased threats we face." Key to this, he says, has been the commitment to meet the Nato target of spending 2 of the nation's wealth (GDP) on defence. It means there'll be a modest increase in the defence budget over the next five years. Mr Clarke says while the armed forces might be in a better place this time round "it'll still find it difficult to meet all the commitments the government wants it to meet." New maritime patrol aircraft will be top of the shopping list. Over the past five years Britain has had to call on the help of the US, Canada and France to hunt for suspected Russian submarines near UK waters. RAF crews have already been training on the US Boeing P8 Poseidon - but it's expensive. Other defence contractors are offering cheaper alternatives. Britain needs new aircraft now, but it has to work out what it can afford. The RAF will also be looking for more frontline fast-jet squadrons. It now has seven squadrons but would like more than a dozen. In the fight against IS it's still having to rely on the ageing Tornado. The life of some of the early Typhoons is likely to be extended to add a few more squadrons, but still probably fewer than the RAF would like. One key decision will be how many of the new F-35s Britain will buy. The aircraft, also known as the Joint Strike Fighter, is already the most expensive defence project ever undertaken by the Pentagon. The UK had originally planned to buy 138, but each jet will cost about PS100m. The decision on F-35s is also important for the Royal Navy and its two new aircraft carriers from which they will fly, as are new anti-submarine frigates needed to protect the carriers. The Navy wants 13 of the new Type 26 frigate. If it has to settle for less that would have a knock-on effect on shipbuilding jobs on the Clyde. The government will also signal its push to renew the fleet of Vanguard submarines which carry the Trident nuclear systems. The cost of building four new submarines will be updated from around PS20bn to more than PS30bn. The Army will be looking at how many new armoured "scout" vehicles they'll be getting and new Apache attack helicopters. Although the Army has become less likely to engage in any large-scale conflict on its own, it still needs a range of capabilities to deploy alongside its key ally - the US. The Army also hopes this SDSR will help change public perceptions - that it's not just there to deploy en masse. The Army now sends small teams to trouble spots all over the world to help train and assist fragile states with conflict prevention. The number of regular troops is shrinking, from 163,000 in 1978 to 102,000 in 2010 and 82,000 in 2020 The government has said it does not want whole regiments to be scrapped; some will be merged, others face "salami slicing." The Army will become more reliant on part-time soldiers; the number of reservists will double from 15,000 to 30,000 by 2020 The government says Britain will have an effective, well-equipped fighting force, integrating regulars and reserves Analysts say the Army will have resources for only one major operation at a time and there will be swingeing cuts to support units such as logistics and engineers More on the Army reorganisation In fact, this SDSR will signal a significant break with the past. Mr Clarke says: "What we are seeing is a shift of resources away from fighting major wars towards using the forces in more intelligence-led, cyber-led, Special Forces-led ways for specific operations." The armed forces still want and need their big ticket items like warplanes and warships, but recent events have underlined the shift. In the wake of the Paris attacks, ministers have said the security services will get another 1,900 personnel while there'll be an extra PS1.9bn for cybersecurity and another PS2bn for Special Forces. The RAF will see the size of its drone fleet double to 20. It's a sign the military will be involved in more intelligence-led counter-terrorism operations and an indication that, post-Iraq and Afghanistan, politicians are increasingly reluctant to put "boots on the ground." After the brutal cuts of the last SDSR, ministers hope this one will be a positive story. While the Ministry of Defence is still having to make efficiency savings, it's not being asked to make cuts right across the board like many other government departments. But more important than how the review is regarded by the public, or the armed forces themselves, is how it's interpreted by Britain's allies and enemies.

First, the most extreme type - Tetragametic chimerism Tetra four Gametic relating to eggs and sperm. A woman is pregnant with twins, two of her eggs (ova) have been fertilised with two of her partner's sperm. These fertilised eggs are called zygotes. Normally we would expect these zygotes to develop separately as two individuals, but instead the zygotes merge to become one individual embryo. Hence tetragametic 1 sperm1 sperm 1 egg 1 egg four gametes This can also happen at the blastocyst stage when the developing infant is still only about 100 cells big. This embryo will have some cells with DNA from twin A and some with DNA from twin B. That is to say, genetic testing will reveal that this one person was once two people. That's the most extreme type and incidences of it in humans recorded in the medical literature are very, very rare, but it's likely that cases aren't detected unless there is occasion for a person to undergo genetic testing. Even then it can be missed as whole organs may have the DNA from just one twin, whilst DNA of the other twin resides elsewhere in the body. A less extreme type is microchimerism where you have some cells with DNA from another individual. Most people have some cells with DNA from their mother during childhood, these were cells that migrated through the placenta and became part of the developing infant. Marmosets (a cute little monkey) are usually born as fraternal (non identical) twin pairs (sisters or brothers) and it is normal for each to have some organ tissue or blood cells or gametes with the DNA of their twin, because they share a blood supply during development stem cells can migrate easily from one to the other. Detecting cases of Chimerism where identical twins were fused is very tricky - so the vast majority of cases in the literature, whether looking at humans or animals, are about fraternal twins - simply because they are genetically distinct enough that the differences in their cells stands out.

The annotation of biological entities with concepts from various bio-ontologies has led to the creation of extensive and expanding repositories of ontology-based annotated data containing implicit connections between different ontologies. The development of effective data mining techniques and evaluation metrics for these relationships has not kept up with the increasing volume of annotation data. In this research, we introduce a data mining approach that employs ontology-guided generalization to uncover relationships across ontologies, alongside a novel interestingness metric grounded in information theory. We apply our methodology and metrics to datasets from the Mouse Genome Informatics Gene Expression Database to explore relationships between developmental stages in the mouse anatomy ontology and Gene Ontology terms (biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components). Furthermore, we compare our interestingness metric with four existing ones. Ontology-based annotation datasets serve as a crucial resource for discovering cross-ontology relationships. Utilizing efficient data mining methods and suitable interestingness metrics facilitates the identification of high-quality relationships.

A synapse fires which creates a chemical connection to another synapse. When a specific set of synapses fire across these connections in a specific order, that sequence is how your brain remembers the word'banana'. The more you repeat something, the stronger these connections become, so if I gave you a 10 digit number right now, you might remember it for few minutes, but because it's a new connection and the connection is newly formed and weak, it breaks down easily, so you forget it easily. This is why if you're trying to remember a phone number while looking for a pen to write it down, repeating it over and over to yourself makes it easy to remember...you're keeping the connections that represents that number active. When you learn something, those connections become permanent, making that memory much easier to recall. So how does this relate to dreaming? Well, MRI images show that when you sleep, your synapses fire randomly...so the connections that are most likely to fire are the ones with the strongest most'established' connections. It's basically electricity following the path of least resistance So, if you've spent all day thinking about a particular thing, you're more likely to dream about it....so you're creating a feedback loop. You have these dreams, so you think about them a lot, which makes you more likely to dream about them, each time making those connections stronger and the dreams more likely (and possibly more vivid). Now, that could all be 100 complete and total crap, but it's the theory that makes most sense to me.," "Is there objective meaning (eternal or universal truths)? Intrinsic dimensionality (ID) is one of the most fundamental characteristics of multi-dimensional data point clouds. Knowing ID is crucial to choose the appropriate machine learning approach as well as to understand its behavior and validate it. ID can be computed globally for the whole data point distribution, or computed locally in different regions of the data space. In this paper, we introduce new local estimators of ID based on linear separability of multi-dimensional data point clouds, which is one of the manifestations of concentration of measure. We empirically study the properties of these estimators and compare them with other recently introduced ID estimators exploiting various effects of measure concentration. Observed differences between estimators can be used to anticipate their behaviour in practical applications.

In this paper, we propose a hybrid parallel programming approach for a numerical solution of a two-dimensional acoustic wave equation using an implicit difference scheme for a single computer. The calculations are carried out in an implicit finite difference scheme. First, we transform the differential equation into an implicit finite-difference equation and then using the ADI method, we split the equation into two sub-equations. Using the cyclic reduction algorithm, we calculate an approximate solution. Finally, we change this algorithm to parallelize on GPU, GPUOpenMP, and Hybrid (GPUOpenMPMPI) computing platforms. The special focus is on improving the performance of the parallel algorithms to calculate the acceleration based on the execution time. We show that the code that runs on the hybrid approach gives the expected results by comparing our results to those obtained by running the same simulation on a classical processor core, CUDA, and CUDAOpenMP implementations.

Arthur and the lads were crouched in the alley, looking out at the wharf. They were nervous, sweating, but their eyes were steady, keeping close watch to the ships. Sam Adams and his boys were going to be ready in just a moment and we needed to be ready. Timing would be everything. I looked at the boys again. They were so damned young. About a dozen total, and not one among them deserved to be involved in any of this. I took a deep breath, and addressed them one final time. "Boys..... no. No, today you aren't boys any longer. Men, I know you're scared. Hell, I've been in actual wars, charging damned savages and I wasn't as scared as this. It's been a long time coming and the moment of truth is here. We, good loyal British subjects, are about to commit a treasonous act of terrorism." Some of them shivered visibly at that. Spot on, lads. Spot on. "We've come too far to back out now. It's been months of planning to spark this event. First, Arthur used his connections at the Philadelphia Inquirer and we all know how that turned out. Seems like overnight people were mad about the "Stamp Tax." Arthur spoke up on that, incredulous, "Can't believe that worked. Stamp Tax is the first new tax in decades, and England's never collected from the American Colonies anyway. We pay less than any colony in the Empire." I allowed myself a wry smirk. Never bet against man's distaste for taxes. "But it did work. Then we used that Mistress friend of Luke's to place the idea in ol'Sam Adams' head that a monopoly on Tea was just like a tax, by a different name. Boy, Adams couldn't wait to bite at that one." Luke grin took a decided mischievous look. "He's lucky he didn't just sign over the deed to his house. When Sally hooks a man, he's practically under witchcraft, that damned Jezebel." I decided to power through that one. I can't say I approved of Luke's affiliations. "And then I used my connections at the Governor's office to have the Darmouth held up in the harbour. Which took some doing, let me tell you. But things are finally coming together. Fitz is out there, right now, rallying up the Sons of Liberty. He'll work them up into a damned lather, and then before you know, they'll be aboard the ships rioting, burning, looting and generally creating all sorts of havoc." Arthur fidgeted and said, "Apparently there's more tea on the Eleanor too. Should be a hell of a mess." "That'll work fine for our purposes. But remember, we're after the Beaver. She's on that wharf. That's where they're keeping the drug." The men visibly steeled themselves. That's what this was all about. The abomination that was the drug. The drug, I believe, was actually called Decreacies by the monsters who made it. It's terrible purpose, originally, was the subjugate negros more easily. It turned a man's mind to mush. Made him suggestible, placid, docile. It was made from a tree flower found in the heart of the Dark Continent. It was goddamn crime against God's creation and those heartless bastards, those "natural philosophers" meant to use it for profit. We meant to destroy their entire supply, under the chaos of the riot tonight. That's when we saw the first signs of the mob. "Act quick boys. And remember, what we do now may yet have us hung, but we do it for the honor and respect of God and Country." We snuck aboard the Beaver easily enough. All around us the riot raged. Sam Adams and his boys knew how to carry on, and Fitz seemed to have enraged them to an incredible degree. Since learning of the damnable drug and it's journey from Africa, the boys and I had had ample time to plan. In the months since, it seemed we'd all become masters of the Great Game. Manipulation, deceit and provocation were our weapons, and anonymity our calling cards. We'd become monsters to fight monsters, but I had long resolved that if any of us we're going to stop this terrible "science," it would not be with our souls intact. After light waves hit the receptors in your eye, the receptors activate small electrical signals in the optic nerve. The optic nerve is basically a wire, carrying the signals further back into the brain. Once the signals reach the optical center in your brain, your brain starts trying to recognize patterns. Broadly speaking, it compares the signals it is getting now, to its memories of other signals it has gotten before, and the decisions that have been made based on them. This is done by electrical signals bouncing around everywhere. I'm going to anthropomorphize. Your optical center uses a complex network of associations, to notice where there is a large amount of any given color grouped together, and seperates everything out into objects. It compares apparent sizes of objects, and color intensities, and a thousand other little cues, and decides what is near and far, and big and small. A pattern-recognition part of your brain then tries to match the objects it has recognized in the sensory input to things in your memory: What have you seen before that may be similar to what you are seeing now? It primes any memories that are similar to this pattern of information, so that those memories are easier for your brain to find, and are ready to be triggered on a moment's notice. This is a long process, and involves a lot of logical leaps going from direct observations like "that is a blob of green" to decisions like "that is a blob of green shaped like a dress, therefore that might be a dress." When you recognize shapes in clouds, this is your brain making patterns out of nothing. Now that a selection of memories are ready to be triggered and you've recognized loosely what is going on, the patterns you've noticed are fed to the thinky part of your brain in an extremely summarized format. Instead of the entire long process of "Oh. That's a human. That's a green dress. The green dress is closer than the human. The green dress overlaps the human. The green dress moves when the human moves. The human is wearing the green dress. The human has red hair. The human is smiling. The human is familiar. The human has been seen before. The human's face is familiar. The human is Sarah." you just get "Sarah is wearing a green dress and smiling." There is a lot of data lost along the way: 99 of it is not important. As long as none of it was wrong. Sometimes this summary process means that you don't notice minor things that are in the background, because you haven't focused on them enough for your brain to process exactly what it is you're looking at. It's still stuck at the "There is a blob of color in the background" stage, rather than recognizing "There is someone in a horse mask behind her.,'To be honest, the processes inside the brain that go from, "Hmm, here is the light patterns the eyes received" to "Woah! this is my 2nd cousin patrick that I haven't seen in 6 years!" isn't all that well understood. We have theories with big gaps. [Visual Cortex] (URL0) is the part of the brain where [Visual Processing] (URL1) happens. Our current understanding of visual processing is called [Two-Streams Processing] (URL2).

A new method for estimating the relative positions of location-unaware nodes from the location-aware nodes and the received signal strength (RSS) between the nodes, in a wireless sensor network (WSN), is proposed. In the method, a regularization term is incorporated in the optimization problem leading to significant improvement in the estimation accuracy even in the presence of position errors of the location-aware nodes and distance errors between the nodes. The regularization term is appropriated weighted on the basis of the degree of connectivity between the nodes in the network. The method is formulated as a convex optimization problem using the semidefinite relaxation approach. Experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art competing methods show that the proposed method yields node positions that are much more accurate even in the presence of measurement errors.

In this paper, we introduce a regularized mean-field game and study learning of this game under an infinite-horizon discounted reward function. The game is defined by adding a regularization function to the one-stage reward function in the classical mean-field game model. We establish a value iteration based learning algorithm to this regularized mean-field game using fitted Q-learning. This regularization term in general makes reinforcement learning algorithm more robust with improved exploration. Moreover, it enables us to establish error analysis of the learning algorithm without imposing restrictive convexity assumptions on the system components, which are needed in the absence of a regularization term.

In this work, we explain the working mechanism of MixUp in terms of adversarial training. We introduce a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training, or DAT. In a nutshell, a DAT scheme perturbs a training example in the direction of another example but keeps its original label as the training target. We prove that MixUp is equivalent to a special subclass of DAT, in that it has the same expected loss function and corresponds to the same optimization problem asymptotically. This understanding not only serves to explain the effectiveness of MixUp, but also reveals a more general family of MixUp schemes, which we call Untied MixUp. We prove that the family of Untied MixUp schemes is equivalent to the entire class of DAT schemes. We establish empirically the existence of Untied Mixup schemes which improve upon MixUp.

Touchscreen devices have rapidly become one of the most popular technologies in the world. Tablets and smartphones have revolutionized the way people interact with technology, offering a more intuitive and engaging experience. However, there is one common problem that affects most touchscreen devices - smears from the oils and sweat on our fingers. The issue with fingerprints on touchscreen devices is multifaceted. Not only do these smudges look unsightly, but they can also impair the performance of the device. The oils from our fingers can interfere with touch detection, causing the device to misinterpret our commands. Moreover, persistent smearing can damage the touch-sensitive coating on the screen, ultimately reducing the lifespan of the device. However, despite the significant drawbacks of finger smears, most people continue to use their devices without regular screen cleaning. According to a survey, only 9 of smartphone users clean their screens daily, with the majority admitting that they only clean their screens once a week or less. This reluctance to clean devices regularly is surprising considering that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends cleaning phones and tablets daily, considering them a potential source of viral transmission. To help tackle the problem of finger smears, device makers have come up with various solutions. One of the most effective is the oleophobic coating, a thin layer applied to the screen that repels the oils on our fingers. This works to a certain extent, but it can wear off over time and with regular cleaning. Moreover, the effectiveness of the coating varies between devices, with some performing better than others, depending on the manufacturer. Another solution is the use of multi-touch displays that can detect touches from a stylus or other object, rather than just fingers. This can be very helpful for people who struggle with smudging screens or who require greater precision in their work, but it doesn't solve the problem entirely. Not everyone wants to use a stylus, and sometimes fingers are simply the most convenient option. Other tips for reducing the appearance of fingerprints on a device's screen include keeping your hands clean and avoiding touching the screen too much, keeping the device out of direct sunlight, and using a microfiber cloth or screen protector to wipe away the smudges. In conclusion, touchscreen devices have transformed our lives and brought a world of convenience to our fingertips, but they do come with their own unique challenges. While finger smears may seem like a minor problem, they can affect the function and lifespan of our devices. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help keep our screens smudge-free, but it's up to us as users to take responsibility for our devices and ensure that they perform to the best of their capabilities.

The earliest references to "democracy" was Athens in about the 6th century BC, where all male citizens over the age of 20 were part of the legislative assembly, and so had the right to take part in the lawmaking process. But it's very likely that some form of democracy must have existed long before then; for example, through the appointment of ordinary citizens to city councils. Our modern European-style democracy wasn't so much "invented" as "evolved" over a long period of time, from the Middle Ages on. If you're American, you've almost certainly heard of the Magna Carta. This was a treaty that the unpopular King John of England was forced to sign in the 13th century, and which granted the barons certain freedoms and privileges, the aim being to curb the king's powers and make him more answerable to the rest of the aristocracy. King John actually simply ignored the Magna Carta, but later monarchs revived it, and it was an important event in the long, slow road to a modern democracy. (Americans are usually given the impression in history classes that it was the single most important stage in the process, but this is actually not true: many other steps were necessary, and the 1689 English Bill of Rights was actually far more important.) In other European countries, though, the process needed to be helped along with the occasional revolution, such as the famous French Revolution, although not all of them were really successful (the Russian Revolution, for example, replaced a despotic monarchy with a despotic government). Germany had a particularly unfortunate experience: after one attempt at a revolution had failed, the First World War basically finished off the monarchy and paved the way for the Weimar Republic; but the young democracy was swiftly subverted by the Nazi Party and it took another devastating war to get things back on track and even then it resulted in the partition of the country.

In this paper, we introduce a new method for generating an object image from text attributes on a desired location, when the base image is given. One step further to the existing studies on text-to-image generation mainly focusing on the object's appearance, the proposed method aims to generate an object image preserving the given background information, which is the first attempt in this field. To tackle the problem, we propose a multi-conditional GAN (MC-GAN) which controls both the object and background information jointly. We introduce a Las Vegas variant of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for estimating Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). We refer to this approach as Markov Chain Las Vegas (MCLV). MCLV provides statistical assurances at the cost of potentially random computation times. It employs a stopping set derived from the training data and features a maximum number of Markov chain iterations, denoted as K (MCLV-K). We present a MCLV-K gradient estimator (LVS-K) for RBMs and examine the relationship and distinctions between LVS-K and Contrastive Divergence (CD-K), demonstrating that LVS-K achieves superior performance in training RBMs on the MNIST dataset compared to CD-K, suggesting that MCLV is a viable path toward learning generative models.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) has been phenomenally successful on various pattern recognition tasks. However, the design of neural networks rely heavily on the experience and intuitions of individual developers. In this paper we propose an approach to model ANNs that can learn from data automatically by unsupervised methods without any domain knowledge or prior human intervention. The proposed system is based on: a deep learning framework for training and complexifying layers in order to meet global constraints; and constraint-based reinforcement learning techniques to optimize topology using locally differentiable loss functions. We tested our method with several experiments where it outperforms its baselines consistently across multiple datasets as well as cross validation tests.

It hit 55 MPH in a 50 MPH zone, proving that we're not that far away from a fully autonomous fleet. The truck was equipped with an array of cameras and radar systems, but the bulk of its controls came from a remote human driver located in the driver's seat. They used a joystick to communicate with the truck and use their peripheral vision to make sure that they could predict what the truck was doing. The truck used an array of cameras and radar to move around other traffic. The truck is also equipped with a variety of sensors that can detect blind spots. This makes it less likely that the truck would accidentally hit another car, truck, or pedestrian. What's really impressive is that the truck is designed to handle long hauls and heavy loads. It's still not safe for the truck to hit speeds of 75 MPH. This would be too fast to be comfortable for the drivers controlling the truck and too fast for another vehicle to avoid a collision. Even with these safety protocols, the truck will have to be more advanced before it can be trusted to drive on public roads.

When I refer to "bigger," I mean an actual increase in the number of congressional members and women in the House of Representatives. Before the early 20th century, Congress often expanded the size of the house to ensure that each representative's district was small enough to allow them to genuinely represent their constituents. This approach was discontinued to weaken city power and address anti-immigrant concerns, but it has resulted in some representatives serving over six-figure populations while others manage five-figure ones, with no significant difference in their influence. I believe smaller districts would encourage politicians to focus more on local communities rather than just re-elections, and it would reduce the impact of extreme, densely populated areas that contribute to the "tyranny of the minority." I propose adopting the idea from this op-ed with a 1-to-60,000 ratio for representation, which would greatly expand the size of Congress, but the main challenge lies in implementing this change. Would we enlarge the Capitol? Find a reliable online voting system? It's difficult, but I think these issues are less critical than the broader advantages of improved representation. When political dysfunction is as widespread as it currently is in the U.S., I tend to examine systemic issues—where do these problems originate? My perspective is that they stem from the disproportionate representation of citizens' views. However, imagining this physically feels absurd to me, so I wish to be challenged.

Once at Golgotha, Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall to drink. Matthew's and Mark's Gospels record that he refused this. He was then crucified and hung between two convicted thieves. According to some translations from the original Greek, the thieves may have been bandits or Jewish rebels. According to Mark's Gospel, he endured the torment of crucifixion for some six hours from the third hour, at approximately 9 am, until his death at the ninth hour, corresponding to about 3 pm. The soldiers affixed a sign above his head stating "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" in three languages, divided his garments and cast lots for his seamless robe. The Roman soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, as they did to the other two men crucified (breaking the legs hastened the crucifixion process), as Jesus was dead already. Each gospel has its own account of Jesus' last words, seven statements altogether. In the Synoptic Gospels, various supernatural events accompany the crucifixion, including darkness, an earthquake, and (in Matthew) the resurrection of saints. Following Jesus' death, his body was removed from the cross by Joseph of Arimathea and buried in a rock-hewn tomb, with Nicodemus assisting.

I sat there, staring at the clock, waiting for the clock the hit 18:56- the exact time of my birth. On my lap sat a phone, my phone to be specific, which displayed the countdown to my birth time. No major realization dawned upon me, no deep insight was gained- instead, I sat there, feeling a little silly for having waited for this moment for so long. But then I realized that sometimes, waiting for certain moments or milestones can give us a sense of hope and purpose. It can help us to focus on what we want to achieve or what we want to happen in our lives. And even if nothing significant happens at that exact moment, it doesn't mean that the waiting was wasted. So, I put down the phone and went about my day, feeling a little lighter and with a renewed sense of hope in my heart.

It gave the band their first real experience of international success, and was a hit on both sides of the Atlantic. The album experimented with a variety of musical genres, including British music hall, heavy metal, ballads, ragtime, and Caribbean. At this point, Queen started to move away from the progressive tendencies of their first two releases into a more radio-friendly, song-orientated style. Sheer Heart Attack introduced new sound and melody patterns that would be refined on their next album, A Night at the Opera.

Quorum systems are useful tools for implementing consistent and available storage in the presence of failures. These systems usually comprise a static set of servers that provide a fault-tolerant readwrite register accessed by a set of clients. We consider a dynamic variant of these systems and propose FreeStore , a set of fault-tolerant protocols that emulates a register in dynamic asynchronous systems in which processes are able to joinleave the servers set during the execution. These protocols use a new abstraction called view generators , that captures the agreement requirements of reconfiguration and can be implemented in different system models with different properties. Particularly interesting, we present a reconfiguration protocol that is modular, efficient, consensus-free and loosely coupled with readwrite protocols, improving the overall system performance.

Sure, you could technically broadcast 1080p without giving the channel a higher bitrate than it had at 720p, but this would lead to a drastic increase in compression artifacts, because you now have twice as many pixels but not twice as much "space" to send them in, so you have to compress them twice as much. If a satellite is maxed out at 400 720p channels, switching all channels to 1080p without compressing them way more would mean you'd only be able to fit 200 channels on the satellite. That means you're either going to charge more for the channels, or make less money. For 4k, we're talking about 4x as many pixels as 1080p again, or 8 times more than 720p. For each 4k channel broadcast, there's likely 6-8 720p channels that can't be broadcast due to bandwidth constraints. The radio frequency spectrum is a limited resource, and you can't just start broadcasting on additional frequencies just because you want to, as it could interfere with other people or businesses that use those frequencies. Imagine if a TV station suddenly decided to broadcast TV on the frequencies you use to receive phone calls. There would be so much interference that your phone wouldn't be able to operate. It's often easier to "broadcast" super high def video over the internet, because the internet is not a broadcast technology. Broadcasts have all channels sent out to everyone at the same time, which uses a lot of bandwidth, but makes reception less complicated. That's not to say you're forever stuck with with the same quality on TV broadcasts, as there are advances in signaling technology as well, allowing for more bits to be expressed with the same amount of frequency spectrum. New video compression techniques are constantly being developed as well. h265 is for example able to express the same quality as h264 while using substantially fewer bits. It does however require a lot more processing power both on the sending and receiving end, so it likely requires new equipment, and that takes time before it becomes common. Can somebody explain to me how supernovas can "explode" given that space is a vacuum? A conventional explosion is generally an expansion of gas caused by a chemical reaction, something that would not be possible in a vacuum. The explosion is inside the star, not in the vacuum. One way to look at it is this: a star is a very hot ball of gas, millions of degrees. It's hard to imagine, but that means that the gas is ionized: instead of the atoms being neutral (1 electron) they're mostly in a plasma state (free electrons and nuclei). Inside the star, the outward pressure of the gas is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. If the star collapses, the pressure will increase. The gas will heat up more, and the nuclei will start to fuse, releasing energy. If the fusion proceeds fast enough, it can counteract the gravitational collapse, and the star will stabilize. However, if it doesn't, the star will continue to collapse, and the pressure will increase even more. The gas will get hotter and hotter, and will fuse more and more, and the star will explode. The fusion reactions are not chemical reactions, they are nuclear reactions, and they don't depend on an atmosphere to propagate. Actually, a supernova is the explosion of the star, not the implosion. A supernova is the end result of a massive star that has run out of fuel (fusing hydrogen into helium, helium into carbon, carbon into iron, etc). When there is no more fuel, the outward pressure of the core is no longer enough to counterbalance the inward pull of gravity, so the core collapses. This collapse raises the temperature and pressure of the core, and the star explodes. This may sound like a contradiction, but it's not. Imagine a balloon. If the balloon is full, it will expand outward because of the pressure of the air inside. But if you let out all of the air, the balloon will collapse inward, because the pressure of the air outside is now greater than the pressure of the air inside. This is similar to the way a star works. The outward pressure of the core is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. But if the core runs out of fuel, the pressure will drop, and the star will collapse, just like a balloon that has no air inside. The collapse raises the temperature, and the star explodes. Supernovae and Novae: The distinction between supernovae and novae is the mass of the star that explodes. When a white dwarf star accretes matter from its companion, it can reach a mass of 1.4 solar masses (called the Chandrasekhar limit) and explode as a type Ia supernova. Supernovae of this type are useful because they always explode with the same mass, and so have the same intrinsic brightness. Novae are produced by the explosion of a white dwarf which is part of a binary system. The white dwarf accretes matter from its companion until it reaches a mass of 1.4 solar masses, the Chandrasekhar limit. At this point, the star can no longer support its mass and it collapses. The collapse heats up the material inside the star and ignites a runaway fusion reaction. The fusion releases energy, but not enough to unbind the white dwarf. Instead, the outer layers of the star are blasted off, leaving behind a dense, hot core. This core can continue to fuse and release energy for weeks or even months after the explosion, causing the nova to gradually fade away. Novae are much less luminous than supernovae and can take months to fade. I've seen a few answers saying that it's not a chemical explosion but a nuclear one. This is incorrect - it is a chemical explosion. A chemical explosion is defined as a reaction that releases energy in a very short time. As such, it is independent of the medium it is in. A nuclear reaction is also a chemical reaction. The reason that supernovae explode is because fusion produces energy. Fusion requires pressure and temperature, but it is not dependent on a medium. Thus, when the pressure and temperature is high enough, fusion can occur. The outward force produced by the energy released in the fusion is much larger than the inward force of gravity. The reason that the pressure and temperature are high enough is because of the collapse of the star. So, the collapse of the star is not caused by the lack of fusion

The immune system protects organisms from infection with layered defenses of increasing specificity. In simple terms, physical barriers prevent pathogens such as bacteria and viruses from entering the organism. If a bacterium infects another cell or organ first, it usually means that the key to survival is retained; but if bacteria and viruses enter other cells, then the immune system can attack them. So what happens when these new types of immunity have been discovered? In the small intestine, there are two kinds of antibodies: one is an antibody called antigens, which is made up of an enzyme called lipids called polypeptides, which is found in complex molecules of food. This type of antibody binds to the active site on the surface of the cell that causes infection. But the problem is that bacterial cells don't always stay coated in this protective net against infections. Instead, they get released into the bloodstream. So when new forms of immunity emerge, those will need medicine - and some drugs. But none of this was possible without the help of antibiotics. When the immune system attacks specific proteins, or "guts" by going near specific receptors, its immunity is weakened. That means the immune system won't still be able to fight off infection. Even when antibiotic-resistant strains are introduced, only a few cells survive. That doesn't mean antibiotics alone aren't effective at preventing disease. It just means that most people who develop severe infections come out the other side of the hospital with no symptoms. Scientists estimate that between 1 and 5 of patients suffer from serious illnesses during their treatment for "infective" disease. (You may want to read a recent article about an American doctor getting sick because he used a secret drug.) Antibiotics can also keep viruses away from the body's non-pathogenic parts, like the liver and kidneys. But the human immune system has different strategies for keeping virus molecules inside the body. The simplest way to protect yourself is with a bacterial poison. Just as in the case of humans, colon cancer kills off all the good bacteria we had been making. However, researchers believe that a controlling agent, such as oral antibiotics, could also work. Both X.25 and Frame Relay provide connection-oriented operations. But X.25 does it at the network layer of the OSI Model. Frame Relay does it at level two, the data link layer. Another difference between X.25 and Frame Relay is their error correction process. X.25 uses a complex error correction protocol that ensures data integrity, while Frame Relay does not have this feature. Additionally, X.25 provides support for virtual circuits, while Frame Relay uses permanent virtual circuits to establish a connection between endpoints. Finally, Frame Relay is generally considered to be faster and more efficient than X.25 due to its simpler protocol and lack of error correction.

Here’s what I discovered on Wikipedia: In many situations, the interaction between the two alleles at a particular genetic location can be categorized as dominant or recessive, depending on which of the two homozygous phenotypes the heterozygous individual most closely resembles. Let me simplify this. When two individuals reproduce—such as a man and a woman having a child, or two plants producing offspring—their genes combine to form the child’s genotype. One gene comes from the father, the other from the mother. The "genetic interactions" referred to are essentially the combination of the mother's and father's genes to create the baby's genetic makeup. Alleles are various versions of the same gene, representing differences in traits among individuals. They are the characteristics that distinguish one person from another, yet remain part of being human. When the genes from the mother and father merge to form the child's genome, their alleles combine to create a heterozygous genotype. After explaining all that, the answer to your question is clear: the factor that determines dominance is which homozygous phenotype (the parent gene) the heterozygous genotype (the baby's gene) most resembles. Essentially, when the square allele from the mother combines with the octagonal allele from the father, does the resulting baby's allele appear more square or octagonal? If it appears more square, then the mother's allele is dominant, and the baby inherits the mother's trait. It's important to note that dominance isn't always straightforward; sometimes a "square" allele paired with a "circle" allele results in a square appearance without any indication of the circle. Other times, it may resemble the square slightly more than the circle. In general, the intensity and pattern of dominance vary. Additionally, dominance can be cyclical—there isn’t always a strict hierarchy from top to bottom. A trait might be dominant over another, which is dominant over a third, but the third could dominate back over the first, creating a loop. This is just an overview. I hope this clarifies things!  
This is grounded in the biological reality behind the trait. For instance, eye color is naturally either blue or green.

At midnight UTC 14 on August 28, 2014, the world suddenly went dark. In an instant, all internet connectivity was disabled across the globe. People scrambled to figure out what had happened, but it soon became apparent that no one knew why or how it had occurred. Governments scrambled to find a solution, but their attempts were in vain. Without the internet, communication between countries and international business came to a standstill. Panic spread as people feared for their safety and the safety of their families. As time passed, some people began to adapt to the new reality, relying more heavily on local communication networks and resources. But most people felt lost without the internet. They missed being able to stay connected with friends and family around the world, access information at their fingertips, and be entertained with their favorite shows and movies. Days turned into weeks, and after 2 months of darkness, there was still no sign of the internet coming back. Many had given up hope and resigned themselves to living without it, while others held onto a shred of optimism that the internet would eventually come back online. It was then, on October 28th, 2014 - two months to the day since the internet had gone down - that people around the world suddenly heard a sound emanating from their computers, signaling the return of the internet. People rejoiced at the news and quickly logged on to check up on their loved ones. The cause of the blackout was never officially determined, but the global pandemic of 2020 brought forth theories linking the incident to a cyber attack by a secret organization. Whatever the reason, the world was thankful for the return of the internet, which had become so deeply entrenched in everyday life.

A key challenge in visual storytelling lies in creating methods that preserve the narrative context across extended sequences of events, enabling the generation of human-like stories. This paper introduces a hierarchical deep learning framework built upon encoder-decoder networks to tackle this issue. To enhance the network's ability to retain context while producing lengthy and varied sentences, we integrate natural language image descriptions alongside the images themselves to construct each story sentence. Our approach is tested on the Visual Storytelling (VIST) dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art solutions across multiple automated evaluation criteria. Experimental results highlight the necessity of various components within our architecture and validate its efficacy in facilitating visual storytelling.

My mother is a neurologist. I recently asked her about this, and she explained that when you're hungover, you might still be slightly drunk, which is the primary reason behind some of the effects. The second factor involves dehydration and a severe headache, which can cause the brain's usual protective mechanisms to fail. For instance, you wouldn't typically hit someone every time you feel angry or consume an entire cake before eating a gourmet meal. This is because your brain recognizes the consequences of such actions. These are examples of the brain's compensatory responses. When these systems fail, you may become more emotionally unstable. I thought I was the only one who felt this way. After drinking heavily, I usually say, "If I'm crabby, you know why." It happens almost immediately. We introduce LETO, a novel hybrid Lagrangian-Eulerian approach for topology optimization. At its core is a hybrid particle-grid Material Point Method (MPM) designed to address elastic force equilibrium. LETO transfers density data from mobile Lagrangian particles to a fixed set of Eulerian quadrature points. These points function as MPM particles within a coarser grid, enabling high-resolution analysis of complex structures while reducing computational costs. By considering both particle densities and positions as optimization variables, LETO redefines the Eulerian solution space in a Lagrangian perspective. It also integrates consistent handling of both linear and nonlinear elastic materials. In nonlinear deformations, the method accommodates significant strain and buckling phenomena. Furthermore, LETO incorporates a fictitious domain-based contact model into the static equilibrium solver, facilitating the identification of innovative structures. Extensive testing shows that LETO outperforms a standard Eulerian method by approximately 20% (up to 40%) in 3D and 2% (up to 12%) in 2D. Qualitatively, it reveals advanced nonlinear functional configurations and enables self-contact-aware design exploration.

It seems others haven't grasped the key idea that what you're looking for isn't being addressed. As mentioned by other contributors, your red blood cells actually transport oxygen to your muscles and remove carbon dioxide from them. Let's imagine we're returning to the lungs. The blood cells contain CO2, and as the blood flows through the arterioles—small blood vessels that are numerous and have a low volume-to-surface-area ratio—the CO2 is exchanged for oxygen. Why? Because oxygen is more concentrated near the lungs than in the muscles, and the molecules naturally move toward an equilibrium. This process is simply diffusion and osmosis through the vessel walls. The oxygen-rich blood moves to the muscular arterioles, where the high CO2 levels cause the oxygen to be swapped again. Your muscles then have oxygen to use, which is converted into CO2 during cellular respiration. However, the blood now has less oxygen and more CO2, bringing us back to the start. The only nutrient a healthy red blood cell transports to peripheral cells is oxygen. It carries oxygen within a large container called hemoglobin. When the RBC reaches the capillaries—small blood vessels—the container opens, allowing oxygen to diffuse out and into the surrounding blood, then into nearby cells. The process is complex, but the reasons behind it involve various factors affecting the tightness or looseness of the hemoglobin container. In the periphery, where capillaries are located, this allows RBCs to efficiently release oxygen to the cells.

The corpus has been collected over time-span of over 8 years and includes over 2 million tweets entailed with additional useful data. Oxygen is the most abundant chemical element by mass in the Earth's biosphere, air, sea and land. Oxygen is the third most abundant chemical element in the universe, after hydrogen and helium. Oxygen makes up 20.8 of the Earth's atmosphere, as well as 89 of water. It is found in nearly all organic molecules and is essential for life. All known forms of life require oxygen to survive. Oxygen is the most important element for the functioning of cells, because it is required for respiration and energy production. Oxygen is used by cells to create ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is the main source of energy for the body. Oxygen is also necessary for cell growth and repair. Without adequate amounts of oxygen, cells cannot function properly and can die. In addition, oxygen is also necessary for proper immune system functioning, as it helps to fight off bacteria and other pathogens.

We propose and study a task we name panoptic segmentation (PS). Panoptic segmentation unifies the typically distinct tasks of semantic segmentation (assign a class label to each pixel) and instance segmentation (detect and segment each object instance). The proposed task requires generating a coherent scene segmentation that is rich and complete, an important step toward real-world vision systems. While early work in computer vision addressed related imagescene parsing tasks, these are not currently popular, possibly due to lack of appropriate metrics or associated recognition challenges. To address this, we propose a novel panoptic quality (PQ) metric that captures performance for all classes (stuff and things) in an interpretable and unified manner. Using the proposed metric, we perform a rigorous study of both human and machine performance for PS on three existing datasets, revealing interesting insights about the task. The aim of our work is to revive the interest of the community in a more unified view of image segmentation.

An r-identifying code in a graph G(V, E) is a subset C of V such that for every vertex u ∈ V, the intersection of C with the ball of radius r centered at u is both non-empty and unique. Earlier research on r-identifying codes focused on various grid structures. Specifically, it was demonstrated that there exists a 2-identifying code in the hexagonal grid with a density of 4/19, and no 2-identifying code can have a density less than 2/11. Most recently, the lower bound for this problem was refined to 1/5 by Martin and Stanton (2010). In this study, we show that the 2-identifying code with density 4/19 is optimal, meaning no 2-identifying code in the hexagonal grid can have a lower density.

Thermal imagers are electronic devices highly sensitive to infrared wavelengths. After processing, the data is displayed as an image that humans can view. Under a longstanding agreement with the city of New York, the museum must accept whatever patrons offer to pay. But signs at cashier desks appear to demand full price, the suit contends. The museum says its "recommended" policy has been place for 40 years and it makes no effort to deceive visitors. The lawsuit, filed in New York City on behalf of former patrons, contends that the world famous museum, which receives six million visitors a year, uses misleading marketing and cashier training to deceive unwary visitors. Lawyers say the signs in the lobby listing the price of admission with the word "recommended" below in smaller type violate a 1893 law mandating the public be admitted free of charge at least five days and two evenings per week in exchange for monetary grants and rent-free use of city-owned land. The suit, which lawyers hope will eventually represent a broad class of people who have visited the museum in recent years, seeks a change in the admissions policy and reimbursement for those who they say were misled. Confusion over whether visitors were required to pay the full 25 is "an issue with tourists travelling to the US from a foreign country," Michael Hiller, a lawyer for those who brought the suit, told the BBC. "They are violating the statute, plainly and simply," Mr Hiller said, referring to the 1893 law. "The museum was designed to make art accessible to the public." A former employee of the Met is expected to testify, Mr Hiller said. The witness, who trained cashiers from 2007-2011, alleges that signage was changed from "suggested" to "recommended" because administrators believed it would encourage people to pay more, Mr Hiller said. Harold Holzer, a spokesman for the museum, said the 1893 law had been superseded. New York City agreed to the museum's request in 1970 to charge an admission fee - so long as the amount was left up to individuals and the signage reflected that. About 40 of visitors pay full price, Mr Holzer said. He said gate proceeds allowed the Met to offer free admission to special exhibitions. About 11 of the museum's operating expenses were covered by admissions last year. As a non-profit organisation, the museum pays no income taxes. It is one of the wealthiest museums in the world, with a 2bn investment portfolio. Mr Holzer estimated the museum would receive 15-20 of its operating budget from the fees this year, with 11 coming from city grants. The Met believes its policy "guarantees access for people regardless of their ability to pay," Mr Holzer said. He noted other New York City museums charge steep admission fees. Entrance fees for prominent New York City art museums such as the Whitney, the Museum of Modern Art and the Guggenheim range from 18 to 25. Mr Hiller demands the museum stop charging entirely for admission and remove the cashier desks. "You have got to eliminate any effort to charge people," he said.

We present an approach to inferring such information that applies a link-analysis ranking algorithm at different levels of time granularity. In addition, a voting scheme is employed for obtaining the hierarchical relations. The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms more traditional approaches to inferring hierarchical relations from social networks.

John treated the interdict as "the equivalent of a papal declaration of war." He responded by attempting to punish Innocent personally and to drive a wedge between those English clergy that might support him and those allying themselves firmly with the authorities in Rome. John seized the lands of those clergy unwilling to conduct services, as well as those estates linked to Innocent himself; he arrested the illicit concubines that many clerics kept during the period, only releasing them after the payment of fines; he seized the lands of members of the church who had fled England, and he promised protection for those clergy willing to remain loyal to him. In many cases, individual institutions were able to negotiate terms for managing their own properties and keeping the produce of their estates. By 1209 the situation showed no signs of resolution, and Innocent threatened to excommunicate John if he did not acquiesce to Langton's appointment. When this threat failed, Innocent excommunicated the king in November 1209. Although theoretically a significant blow to John's legitimacy, this did not appear to greatly worry the king. Two of John's close allies, Emperor Otto IV and Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, had already suffered the same punishment themselves, and the significance of excommunication had been somewhat devalued. John simply tightened his existing measures and accrued significant sums from the income of vacant sees and abbeys: one 1213 estimate, for example, suggested the church had lost an estimated 100,000 marks (equivalent to 66,666 at the time) to John. Official figures suggest that around 14 of annual income from the English church was being appropriated by John each year.

A floor stone dedicated to Larkin - who died in 1985 - will join the names of the country's best-loved poets including WH Auden, TS Eliot and William Wordsworth. It will be unveiled on 2 December 2016, the 31st anniversary of Larkin's death. The last poet to be honoured was Ted Hughes in 2011. With poems like The Whitsun Weddings and This Be The Verse - which contains his famous musings on "your mum and dad" - Larkin is widely regarded as one of Britain's finest 20th Century poets. The decision to honour him was made by the Dean of Westminster, the Very Rev Dr John Hall. "Philip Larkin is one of the great poets of the 20th Century in English and it's been pressed on me by a number of his colleagues and friends that it's the right time to memorialise him," Dr Hall told the BBC. Prof Edwin Dawes, who chairs the Philip Larkin Society, said Larkin's words were quoted more frequently than those of any of his poetic contemporaries. "The memorialisation of Philip Larkin in Poets' Corner will be warmly welcomed by his many admirers in all walks of life," he said. "We are delighted that in 2016 Larkin will take his place at the very cultural heart of the nation, in Westminster Abbey amongst Britain's greatest writers." Born in Coventry in 1922, Larkin studied at Oxford and had his first poems published in 1940. He took up the position of librarian at the University of Hull in 1955 and, in the same year, published his acclaimed collection The Less Deceived. His last collection High Windows was published in 1974. In December 1984, a year before his death from cancer, he was offered the chance to succeed Sir John Betjeman as Poet Laureate but declined, being unwilling to accept the post's high public profile. The posthumous publication of Larkin's letters gave an often unflattering insight into his inner life and led to accusations of racism and misogyny. Despite the dent to his reputation, in 2003 Larkin was chosen as the nation's best-loved poet of the last 50 years, in a survey by the Poetry Book Society. Poets' Corner became established at Westminster Abbey after Geoffrey Chaucer's remains were interred in a tomb there in 1556.

As in Brazil, the mandolin has played an important role in the Music of Venezuela. It has enjoyed a privileged position as the main melodic instrument in several different regions of the country. Specifically, the eastern states of Sucre, Nueva Esparta, Anzoategui and Monagas have made the mandolin the main instrument in their versions of Joropo as well as Puntos, Jotas, Polos, Fulias, Merengues and Malaguenas. Also, in the west of the country the sound of the mandolin is intrinsically associated with the regional genres of the Venezuelan Andes: Bambucos, Pasillos, Pasodobles, and Waltzes. In the western city of Maracaibo the Mandolin has been played in Decimas, Danzas and Contradanzas Zulianas; in the capital, Caracas, the Merengue Rucaneao, Pasodobles and Waltzes have also been played with mandolin for almost a century. Today, Venezuelan mandolists include an important group of virtuoso players and ensembles such as Alberto Valderrama, Jesus Rengel, Ricardo Sandoval, Saul Vera, and Cristobal Soto.

UKIP is looking for a new leader following the shock resignation of Diane James, who had succeeded Nigel Farage after the EU referendum. MEP Steven Woolfe, who had been seen as the frontrunner, quit the party on Monday. He had been hospitalised after a "scuffle" with fellow MEP Mike Hookem. Speaking to the BBC's Good Morning Scotland programme, Mr Coburn denied Mr Woolfe's claim that UKIP was in a "death spiral" and had become ungovernable. He said the incident between Mr Woolfe and Mr Hookem had been "regrettable" but had involved only two people rather than the whole party. Mr Woolfe has stood by his claim that he "received a blow" from Mr Hookem, though this has been denied by Mr Hookem. Mr Coburn said: "I keep saying it is country, party and self last. It is ideas that count, not individuals. What we are looking for is an agenda for the future, we are publishing it now and that is how we are moving forward. "Can I lead the party? Well, if I were asked by colleagues then of course I would do my best. But the thing is it is not about who is governing, it is to do with getting a group of people together, a collegiate group of people, who are going to run the thing." Mr Coburn said the party's libertarian politics meant people "can't be told what to do" but called on party members to "govern their own emotions and govern their own behaviour." He added: "What has happened is that we have had a charismatic leader for many years, who has kept a lid on things. "Now what you have got is you've got to choose a new leader. In that, you've lifted the lid off things a bit and it bubbles over." Mr Coburn, who is UKIP's only elected representative in Scotland, insisted there was still a reason for the party to exist despite achieving its core aim of having the UK leave the EU. He said he wanted to ensure the country was run "in the interests of the people not in the interests of big business or trade unions" and that he had joined UKIP because he wanted "radical change" to the way the country was governed, not just because he wanted to leave the EU. And he said he would "certainly not" be supporting First Minister Nicola Sturgeon's attempts to keep Scotland in the EU single market after Brexit. Mr Coburn insisted: "We decided during the Scottish referendum on independence that we are part of the United Kingdom and in terms of that we voted in the European referendum, that was as a United Kingdom. "We entered as a United Kingdom, we leave as a United Kingdom. We voted as a United Kingdom, everybody knew that beforehand." Nominations to replace Ms James as UKIP leader close on 31 October, with the new leader announced on 28 November.

Semantic grasping is the problem of selecting stable grasps that are functionally suitable for specific object manipulation tasks. In order for robots to effectively perform object manipulation, a broad sense of contexts, including object and task constraints, needs to be accounted for. We introduce the Context-Aware Grasping Engine, which combines a novel semantic representation of grasp contexts with a neural network structure based on the Wide Deep model, capable of capturing complex reasoning patterns. We quantitatively validate our approach against three prior methods on a novel dataset consisting of 14,000 semantic grasps for 44 objects, 7 tasks, and 6 different object states. Our approach outperformed all baselines by statistically significant margins, producing new insights into the importance of balancing memorization and generalization of contexts for semantic grasping. The negative aspect is the maintenance and short life problems caused by the commutator. Such motors are used in devices such as food mixers and power tools which are used only intermittently, and often have high starting-torque demands. Multiple taps on the field coil provide (imprecise) stepped speed control. Household blenders that advertise many speeds frequently combine a field coil with several taps and a diode that can be inserted in series with the motor (causing the motor to run on half-wave rectified AC). Universal motors also lend themselves to electronic speed control and, as such, are an ideal choice for devices like domestic washing machines. The motor can be used to agitate the drum (both forwards and in reverse) by switching the field winding with respect to the armature.

If a problem X is in C and hard for C, then X is said to be complete for C. This means that X is the hardest problem in C. The most famous example of this idea was given by Euler when he wrote down his formula for the first time: V I A cdot B vc, x where V is the solution in C, I is the initial value (that's why it's called a commutative matrix), A is some vector that determines if we are at zero or one, and B is our hardcode. So now we can easily compute this from other information available about how well we solved the original problem. It wasn't until much later, after many years, that the construction became widely popularized as solvers were built on top of it and parallel algorithm implementations proliferated. Right now you probably know enough algebraic geometry to solve any problem in C; but have no clue what all those vectors meant just five minutes ago! In fact, there seems to be quite a bit more going on under the hood than just arithmetic operations, such as encryption algorithms, that haven't even been invented yet! Hopefully, someday soon the magic will come out so we can truly implement these things against such problems. Still, it makes me happy knowing that my work might be used as a prototype for new applications - whether they're useful or not remains to see...

The image created by night vision is blackwhite. Human eyes are most sensitive to green light. Since you're in the dark and it takes your eyes time to adjust to lightdark, you only want to make the image as bright as necessary. So the image is given in green to make it more comfortable to view in the dark, possibly for long periods.,The human eye is most sensitive to green light. This is why the Bayer pattern used in many cameras has two green pixels, one red pixel, and one blue pixel per quad. Night Vision Goggles amplify low light to appear green so that the user can distinguish as much detail as possible while keeping the luminous flux (light intensity) as low as possible as to preserve their actual night vision.

In this letter we propose the Rao test as a simpler alternative to the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) for multisensor fusion. We consider sensors observing an unknown deterministic parameter at one and same time, followed by a modulus distribution of the composite signal. The difference between the two tests is significant: on average, the non-invariant noise reduction in the composite signal has significantly reduced the errors obtained with the GLRT tests compared with the GLRT tests. This results strongly indicate that both tests can be used as basis for characterization of various hybrid distributions. The Rao test is a basic, well-known set of Ergion-like predictions which rely on a predetermined information to predict future behavior trends in a system. These predictions are then coupled with numerical computing techniques such as the pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). In some cases, such predictions could be applied to multiple systems using the Ergion-type prediction model. For example, a political prediction may be made based on Lorentz statistics or RSI equations. Other methods include the Huffman approximation method, and bounds-based axial projections. However, these methods do not have the advantage over the Ergion-type prediction model because their assumptions require more computations than the Ergion type prediction models. Furthermore, though they use random numbers instead of linear algorithms, they do not allow for generalization that does not depend on probability distribution estimation. We therefore want to show that the Rao test is reliable when applying the ERGion-type prediction model to multiple systems, whereas the ERGion-type prediction model is unreliable when using it only to several sites. We currently experimentally evaluate the Rao test against the ERGion-type prediction model in our simulation experiments. A simulation system is described in which different signals are measured simultaneously from different locations. Both types of measurement devices are used to measure motion, and no error was observed during measurement. By comparison, the Rao test performs better if the universe is composed of objects on a larger scale. However, the Rao test cannot be used to estimate the amplitude of any one component of an object due to the fact that the sizes of the components correspond to each other. Therefore we decided to provide a simple Routine Analysis of the Rao test that optimizes the accuracy of averaging. Specifically, the Rao test generates a prediction which is rated based on the mean value of all components of the object on which the Rao test measures the variance of the predicted value. Only after calculating the absolute values of all components of the object will the Rao test demonstrate the efficacy of averaging, thereby avoiding the risk in predicting the magnitude of other components of the object upon comparing them. Since only a small percentage of unknowns exist in a system with the Rao test, we are forced to reduce the Rao test to just one set of estimators. Due to the high cost associated with the Rao test, the Rao test should be able to obtain similar performance without compromising its efficiency. Furthermore, we intend to compare the Rao test against the ERGion-type prediction model to determine whether the Rao test achieves equal performance with either model. Finally, we plan to find an appropriate algorithm for performing the calculation of the Rao test. RESULTS Rao Test Results A Rao test represents two sets of data; the first set contains the most common components, and the second set contains the most advanced features. The Rao test produces a relatively accurate result because of the existence of a large amount of features which are not necessarily present in the original Rao test. Because of the greater number of possible effects of the Rao test compared with the OLP, we did not design the Rao test with the assumption that there would be any appreciable effect of the Rao test for every system. To ensure that the Rao test achieves optimal results, we tested the Rao test against the OLP using computer simulations in which subjects were asked to answer questions about the Rao test, and perceived changes in their perceptions of the Rao test's findings. As a result of this, we designed the Rao test to simulate what would happen if one of the participants performed a test that placed a higher emphasis on the laws of thermodynamics.

The young seaman tugged at my sleeve, "Captain look! Out there! To starboard!" I took the binoculars hanging on my neck and glassed the waters, calm seas, except for what looked to be a single white mass, kind of like a wave. "Do you see it sir?" "Well..... I think so. Is that a rogue wave?" A tower of foam spurt through the water, and the "white mass" was what looked like a gargantuan white tail that lifted into the air, and then disappeared into the water. But that couldn't be..... "Jesus Christ, what was that? " , I screamed. "Sir, that looks like Moby Dick!" "What? " "Moby Dick, Captain!" "I heard you the first time. How on God's green planet do you figure that is Moby Dick?" "I figured it out from the tail..... the white tail, Captain." I raised the binoculars to the waters again, but any sign of this "Moby Dick" was gone. Whatever it was, it had disappeared. I heard the seaman cough behind me, "Ahem..... Sir..... You do know how to fight Moby, right?" "Jesus Christ son, there's no such thing as Moby Dick." His eyes widened as his face became very Moby Dick-colored-like, "Begging your pardon Sir..... But yes there is. Didn't you ever read the book in your training?" "You mean that book by uhh.... what's his name..... umm..... Charles Dick..... Charles Dickinson?" He pinched his nose with his fingers, "Oh my God." I laughed, "Is this some sort of joke? Seriously? Like, some sort of'Oh hey, we have a new Captain, so let's fuck with him' kind of thing?" "N-no..... Sir. All sea captains are required to read Moby Dick by Herman Melville before taking command of a ship." "You're starting to piss me off now son. Moby Dick is a fucking novel." Another young seaman's voice sounded on the horn, "Captain! We've detected a large mass below us on SONAR. It's Moby Dick! No submarine can move as fast as what we're picking up! " As sarcastically as I could humanly muster, with as much animation in my hands as possible, I laughed, "Well all hands to battle stations then!" " ALL HANDS TO BATTLE STATIONS! ALL HANDS TO BATTLE STATIONS! THIS IS NOT A DRILL! I REPEAT, THIS IS NOT A DRILL! " The ship's siren blared, and strobe lights hanging on the ceiling and on the deck that I didn't even know existed started panickly spinning about, shining their red lights all over the walls. Sailors sprinted about, down below I saw the Chief screaming orders, and my 1st Officer ran up on deck. He was breathless, and the look of unadulterated terror was in his eyes. "Captain, what's our next move?!" "Jesus Christ, am I the only one who isn't fucking crazy? There's no such thing as Moby Dick!" The 1st Officer looked at me and blinked. "Now is not the time for games sir!" The seaman chimed in, "The Captain is being serious, sir." "Captain, please tell me you've read Moby Dick." "What? I read like a third of it in High School, but that's it! It was a fucking boring book!" "Captain! Half that book is about how to kill whales!" "I know, that's why it was so goddamn fucking boring!" The 1st Officer was now jumping up and down, his fingers pulling out his hair, "How the hell do you expect to kill Moby Dick, if you've never read Moby Dick?" "BECAUSE IT WAS A FUCKING NOVEL! " A huge, vibrating, animalistic roar shook the entire ship. I rushed to the window and much to my horror and disbelief, out of the water, a colossal white whale launched itself into the air, easily two times the size of our old frigate. A diety, spawn of Poseidon. The very definition of behomoth itself. It soared out of the water, mouth agape, and its shadow covered the entire ship. Before it landed on top of us, the very last thought I had before being snuffed off the face of this planet was, I wish I hadn't smoked so much pot in high school.
