No one was nearby. The house was empty. I spoke to myself, feeling awkward. "Hi?" I thought. I questioned why this was happening. Had I really lost my mind, or was I about to discover I had a new allergy I didn’t know about. "Hi," answered the voice a while later. I couldn’t ignore it—it was coming from my head. I felt a bit nervous. "Who are you?" I asked, immediately realizing how silly I was. Why would I ask myself who I am? "I don’t know," the voice replied. I hesitated, unsure of my next action. Talking to oneself is one thing, but interrupting yourself mid-conversation is another matter entirely. After a pause, the voice spoke again. "I’m a part!" It declared. Its voice showed a genuine emotion for the first time since it began speaking. "A part?" I asked, puzzled by its meaning and distracted by trying to recall my doctor’s name. "Remember? We discussed it in psychology class," the voice continued, speaking over my attempt to find the number. I considered it briefly and then it came back—like it had just been remembered. The dull lessons about Richard Schwartz and his theory that people are composed of small parts. My trauma...

We identified only one suitable study. Despite demonstrating that telephone-based notification of HIV test results was more effective than in-person delivery, the study had significant methodological flaws. Conducted approximately 13 years ago in a high-income nation among individuals at high risk, the study involved a population with low HIV prevalence. Its findings may not be applicable to other settings due to limited generalizability. The study also lacked details regarding the acceptance of the intervention by patients and healthcare professionals, as well as its economic impacts or potential side effects. Therefore, there is a requirement for credible evidence from diverse contexts regarding the effectiveness of telephone usage in notifying HIV test results.

ABC originally launched on October 12, 1943 as a radio network, separated from and serving as the successor to the NBC Blue Network, which had been purchased by Edward J. Noble. It extended its operations to television in 1948, following in the footsteps of established broadcast networks CBS and NBC. In the mid-1950s, ABC merged with United Paramount Theatres, a chain of movie theaters that formerly operated as a subsidiary of Paramount Pictures. Leonard Goldenson, who had been the head of UPT, made the new television network profitable by helping develop and greenlight many successful series. In the 1980s, after purchasing an 80 interest in cable sports channel ESPN, the network's parent merged with Capital Cities Communications, owner of several print publications, and television and radio stations. In 1996, most of Capital CitiesABC's assets were purchased by The Walt Disney Company.

The Apollo program was conceived during the Eisenhower administration in early 1960, as a follow-up to Project Mercury. While the Mercury capsule could only support one astronaut on a limited mission duration, the Apollo program had a much greater opportunity for success after the Challenger space shuttle disaster in 1986, when astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin were killed upon landing after their orbiter suffered an explosion that destroyed it at Earth's surface. Through the 1960s, NASA focused largely on research activities related to aeronautics, with its greatest accomplishments coming from the launch of the Saturn V rocket into lunar orbit, which eventually led to the moon landings of 1969 and 1972, respectively. As projects like the Apollo missions became less popular due to increased budgetary pressures, attention turned instead toward the development of space shuttles and capsules capable of carrying cargo. These new vehicles would carry crew members to the International Space Station (ISS), and then return them safely back down to earth. After several years of deliberations about how best to develop these spaceships, NASA ultimately selected a single design for each spacecraft type: the Gemini spacecraft, the Viking, and the Shuttle (called "Columbia. Each spacecraft vehicle developed by NASA proceeded through numerous revisions before being finalized. The Shuttle Columbia is still widely considered to be the most advanced and revolutionary spacecraft ever created; however, some subsequent designs have proven more successful than others. At any given moment, there are approximately five different types of manned spacecraft operating under contracts to NASA or overseas organizations. This number can fluctuate based on funding levels - but over the past few decades, this number has steadily fallen as NASA continues to retire older models while replacing them with newer versions. In fact, there are currently no manned spacecraft in active service carried out by NASA itself, aside from its commercial partners. In addition to rockets, satellites continue to play a large role in many parts of modern society, including agricultural output, weather forecasting, communications, navigation and other applications associated with space exploration. Although satellite systems remain relatively inexpensive compared to conventional methods of transmitting information across long distances, they do pose significant safety hazards since satellites often directly impact remote locations around the world where people live and work. To address this problem, various approaches have been proposed to control satellite collision collisions. However, despite recent advancements in technology, these proposals require sophisticated equipment, such as radar arrays, to track and monitor all potential future targets approaching the earth, even if those objects are not actively involved in any sort of collision. Therefore, there remains room for improvement within existing satellite collision avoidance technologies and systems.

In this study, we examine the anticipated blocklength of variable-length coding on the binary symmetric channel (BSC) with noiseless feedback. Horstein initially introduced a straightforward single-phase method to attain the BSC capacity. Naghshvar et al. employed a fresh extrinsic Jensen-Shannon (EJS) divergence within a sequential transmission framework that optimizes EJS (MaxEJS), and they established a non-asymptotic upper limit for the expected blocklength associated with MaxEJS. The simulations presented here demonstrate that MaxEJS yields smaller expected blocklengths compared to the initial Horstein approach, yet the non-asymptotic bound from Naghshvar et al. remains sufficiently broad to exceed the simulated outcomes of the Horstein scheme for a BSC with low crossover probabilities. This work introduces a revised formula for the expected blocklength of MaxEJS, which closely mirrors the simulated performance. This formula was derived by investigating a genie-assisted decoder (GAD), whose expected blocklength consistently exceeds MaxEJS and can be modeled using two random walk processes. We hypothesize that even with these two approximations, the formula might still serve as an upper bound on the actual blocklength, as evidenced by the simulation findings.

We propose a novel compression technique (called RLE2) to compress natural graphs by exploiting the structure of their degree distributions. "The Crime That Killed Humanity," it was called. When they discovered the Fountain of Youth. Sure, Ponce de Leon found it first. But we didn't know that until a crazy billionaire that was convinced that the Fountain existed staged a silly expedition into the middle of nowhere in Florida. There, he found the bones. What we used to know is that Ponce de Leon gave up the search and decided to keep on gallivanting around the world. What we now know is that there were a few men he left behind to guard his discovery. Turns out that when the discovery of the century was made, he was told off for searching for something that wasn't gold or of benefit to the Spanish Crown. So off he went, leaving a few men to guard the Fountain. There, they kept their promise, drinking the water. And when we found what was left of them, then we didn't believe them. Even though we encountered something that was life-restoring, but we didn't believe anything they wrote on whatever they could write on - rocks, trees, their armor and clothing. All in Spanish. Curses in Spanish, pleading of God to end their suffering. We didn't know why they wrote it. Only that they showed remorse for having indulged in living. We ignored the warnings, and we paid the price. The Fountain of Youth was opened a few years later. The crazy billionaire flaunted it, drinking it in public, saying that the Fountain was going to make America great again. He wasn't wrong. Those who drank the stuff had their wounds healed, their vision restored. Muscle dystrophy was treated, cancer was done in, the blind regained their vision, the deaf their hearing, it was a miracle - the water healed everything that wasn't right. The religious were chanting how the Fountain was their gift from God (as was he, chugging bottles of it and then cutting himself just to show how the water healed him), atheists were baffled, scientific experiments were conducted to find out why the water healed. That's where science decided to keep quiet. I'm not sure why, only that it did. The Fountain of Youth was never empty. In fact, it was very badly overcrowded. Each time an expansion was commissioned, the Fountain never underscored in attendance. The hardest part of expansion was how fiercely the local wildlife protected it - almost zealously, without giving up. But as soon as the expansion was made, up to a certain point, the wildlife gave up. Whatever animals were captured fought against their captors, baring teeth, claws, rabid. But after a few days they stopped. They reverted to their average behavior. The parrots, instead of shrieking and flying everywhere, resumed their calm melodies and mocking tones of the zookeepers. The crocodiles were crocodiles. Everything was fine with them after a week of drinking non-youth water. The water was akin to a drug in how the body handled the it. First it released a huge amount of dopamine. Then adrenaline. Then it healed any wounds or afflictions. And then it went straight to the bladder within five minutes. That was the concentrated mix, derived straight from the fountain and had flavors added. The consumer version was diluted twentyfold, but was half as effective as the concentrate. But it was tastier, considering how many flavors could be added to it. Health-Juice was monopolized world-wide. And hence why only one company was ever blamed for the genocide. Not like the company exists now to keep taking the blame like a champ. They say, by the time seven years have passed, that all cells from seven years ago are gone and have been replaced with newer versions within your body. The water that was left within your body after you drank it left some minor healing effects, that much was apparent. Then the Fountain ran dry, five years later. By that time, five hundred billion consumer bottles have been sold. Considering that the consumer version was diluted twentyfold. The company was rich, the billionaire was rich, most investors were rich. And everyone was chugging the stuff. Those that didn't chug right away set up stockpiles. When the Fountain ran dry, there was a rapid spike in prices - each bottle, instead of costing ten bucks, cost two hundred. Assuming that the bottles weren't tampered with and then diluted even further until the water's healing effects were on par with the body's own regeneration. The well ran dry not because of overconsumption, but because the water's effects were adjusted by the body. After six months of drinking one bottle a day to heal a bone that was being broken continuously, five bottles were needed to do the same job per day. After another six months, two tonnes of the stuff was needed to heal anything per day. The madness and the quest for eternal youth never stopped. By 2027, humanity was dead. Because of the body's adjusted healing effects, the water became unnecessary. One could make do like Deadpool and heal any injury. Five years after drinking the last drop (for the average human), the healing effects stopped for most people. In fact, due to the immune system's new state of being obsolete, the body rejected it. The water's adding effects did the job better. And then the healing ran out. Wounds that could heal within seconds festered. Bones didn't heal. Those who regained vision and hearing kept their senses, but weren't so different from the rest of humanity when everyone shared a festering gangrene papercut. Whoever didn't stop healing within five years stopped within six. Those who stockpiled their shares were often robbed for it. Vaccines, by virtue of not being needed, killed whoever was injected with them. Humanity couldn't do anything, not even the weakest of injections. Because even the tiniest virus could undo everything. Viruses never go away. Even in the body, they remain dormant while waiting for the right conditions to start the incubation period. And then they strike. That's what happened. The common rhinovirus, a common little cold, something everybody shared..... killed humanity. Few people survived, and only because they were careful to watch their steps. I watched mine. I knew where we were heading. Accelerated healing and youth have a terrible price. A price I never cared to pay. I watched most people I know die, but I didn't care because of how delusional they were, thinking there was no catch to endless healing, tasty water, and eternal youth. I only had a few bottles in my entire life - one to get me up on my legs from the wheelchair that plagued me for twenty years, one to heal my poor eyes, and another for alcohol poisoning. All within four years. Not like I care. I can do what I like, now that no one's here. Now that I think about it, I know why we never weaned off the water. We liked health too much to think about giving up a little bit of living just to experience invulnerability from the common cold.

Negotiations over who will run the PS200m Metrobus network have stalled as bus companies are reluctant to run the service on a completely commercial basis. Metrobus admits public subsidies might be needed to provide a service in the south of the city. The Department for Transport insisted the Busway "is not a public service." A Department for Transport spokesman said the service was open to both bus operators and other users. It said a public subsidy would only be paid if a "commercially-viable service" was not provided. The city's new mayoral cabinet met on Friday to discuss the future of the busway, which has been operating without a dedicated operator since January. It is understood that the cabinet has approved a bus operator submitting an outline business plan for a service, however the Tories have called for a full council meeting to discuss the future of the busway. The DfT said the council could still apply to be the service's operator, or "run the service through a service provider." It said the service would only be eligible for a subsidy if "commercial operators were not able to provide a service which is economically viable." "The cost of operating a service on the Busway is very high, but there are a number of different ways the council can subsidise it," the DfT said. "Therefore, if a council does decide to provide a service, it will be able to consider a number of different funding options." The council's cabinet will meet again on Monday. The Busway, which was part-funded by the former Conservative-led council, opened in January but only two operators - Stagecoach and First - are currently running services on it. An agreement between the two companies saw them share the workload of running the service. However, the cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run 12 services, with the money coming from the city's budget and public subsidies. The council also agreed to pay the operating costs of 10 buses, which would have run empty between the existing Stagecoach services. The council's cabinet also decided to withhold payments from Stagecoach until they had signed a contract to provide a "commercially viable" service. The DfT has said it will decide whether to provide a subsidy for the busway in early July. It said it would be up to the council to run the service if it was determined there was no commercial operator. Councillor Keith Wakefield, the council's deputy leader, said the council would keep "all options on the table." "The busway has been in operation now since January 2011 and we have had discussions with the operator and also with other operators and we are now at the point where we are going to have to look at whether there is any other option," he said. "The council has never said it is going to run the busway service itself. "We have been very clear about that from the start and it is now time to take a decision about what we are going to do. "The council has to make a decision in the next few weeks about what it is going to do." Both Stagecoach and First have declined to run the service independently because of the high costs involved. Mr Wakefield said he was not in a position to reveal the number of council employees working on the busway, but it was "very few." "We are not talking about thousands of council employees running the busway," he said. "We are talking about a very small number of people and also a small amount of money. "The funding for the busway is not coming from the council's general fund. "It is coming from the Government grant that the council receives for the busway." "This is not about providing a service to people for free. This is about providing a service that is viable for the operator." The Cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run services on the busway, but the company has not signed a contract. Stagecoach previously said it would not take on any more services until a financial deal was reached. The company's UK chief executive Richard Watson said: "We are in discussions with the council and the Department for Transport and are continuing to work with them to reach a commercial agreement for the provision of services on the Busway. "Until we do, we are unable to comment further." A spokesman for First said it was "still in negotiations" with the council and the DfT.

We introduce a compressive sensing algorithm that leverages the geometric characteristics of images to enhance their quality when recovered from limited measurements. The image restoration process involves two key stages: first, estimating the normal vectors of the image's level curves, followed by reconstructing an image that aligns with these normal vectors, along with the compressed sensing data and sparsity constraints. This approach can seamlessly generalize to non-local operators and graphs, enabling the recovery of intricate details in textured images by exploiting their repetitive patterns. In both scenarios, the challenge reduces to solving a sequence of convex optimization problems, which can be effectively addressed using a blend of variable splitting and augmented Lagrangian techniques, resulting in computationally efficient and straightforward algorithms. Additional experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in the quality of reconstructed images and the method's resilience to noise, diverse image types, and fewer measurements compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Scientists have developed a new gene-editing tool that is more accurate than CRISPR-Cas9. Prime editing can mend about 89 percent of the 75,000 or so harmful mutations in the human genome - even correcting for glitches at very specific places where DNA breaks occur, known as "hot spots" on chromosomes near genes in our body cells and tissues, such as the brain. The scientists behind this discovery consider it proof of concept: It works better with bigger genomes (humans currently make up 20 percent to 25 percent of the Earth), but they believe that their work could be adapted to other organisms by simply changing one simple parameter. The team will report its findings online today in Nature Communications. CRISPR was invented two decades ago to quickly tweak single strands of DNA using an enzyme called Cas9, which has been engineered from bacteria, and then snipped out to create a piece just like itself. Scientists use CRISPR to alter all sorts of traits in plants, animals, and microbes; for example, they used it last year to edit eggs inside mice, making them produce healthy embryos when fertilized by sperm containing diseased genetic material. But many biologists dislike CRISPR because it requires complex biological machinery designed specifically to target specific sections of DNA within each cell. Moreover, it tends to cause unintended edits elsewhere along the genome. Instead of targeting precise segments, researchers have tried different ways to cut off stretches of DNA in fish or fruit flies without affecting nearby regions. One group made proteins called zinc fingers that bind tightly to DNA and disable genes above certain levels. In some cases, these methods worked far better than conventional CRISPR, allowing researchers to fix only a small fraction (a few hundred) of allele defects. Another approach uses chemical enzymes called nuclease proteins whose activity depends partly on how much oxygen is present around them. A third method involves chemically modifying the structure of DNA before altering it. This technique allows researchers to insert fragments into specific points of existing genomic sequences rather than systematically cutting away entire chunks. According to the research team, this method eliminated hot spots in Drosophila fly embryos after seven tries. They also confirmed that they were able to correct both disease-causing genes and benign changes associated with aging. To test whether their method would actually do a good job on larger genomes, the Harvard team created three-dimensional structures of yeast cells showing exactly what hot spots remain intact if you turn off most of the cellular machinery required for protein synthesis. The scientists found that PrimeEdit targeted 90 percent to 95 percent of those hotspots, depending on which version the engineers had created. And while PrimeEdit did still result in errors across the genome during normal development, it appeared more stable once the organism reached adulthood. It seems likely, says geneticist Michael Deem, who studies evolution alongside Deem's collaborator, Emmanuelle Charpentier, professor of evolutionary biology, that genetic engineering may soon become standard practice among biologists. She predicts that any alterations caused by prime editing will eventually disappear over time by themselves. That means people might someday be able to get rid of cancer-causing variants - though there are big ethical questions surrounding splicing disease-fighting genes into babies, she notes.

Historical interpretations of John have been subject to considerable change over the years. Medieval chroniclers provided the first contemporary, or near contemporary, histories of John's reign. One group of chroniclers wrote early in John's life, or around the time of his accession, including Richard of Devizes, William of Newburgh, Roger of Hoveden and Ralph de Diceto. These historians were generally unsympathetic to John's behaviour under Richard's rule, but slightly more positive towards the very earliest years of John's reign. Reliable accounts of the middle and later parts of John's reign are more limited, with Gervase of Canterbury and Ralph of Coggeshall writing the main accounts; neither of them were positive about John's performance as king. Much of John's later, negative reputation was established by two chroniclers writing after the king's death, Roger of Wendover and Matthew Paris, the latter claiming that John attempted conversion to Islam in exchange for military aid from the Almohad ruler Muhammad al-Nasir - a story which is considered to be untrue by modern historians.

NASA will test drive a robot underneath Antarctica's sea ice in preparation for a mission in the subsurface oceans of Jupiter's moon, Europa. Buoyant Rover for Under-Ice Exploration, or BRUIE, will spend three weeks in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, an ice-free region, as part of the 2019 field season for the McMurdo Long Term Ecological Research (MCM LTER) project. The researchers will test BRUIE's endurance, durability, navigation, power systems, and communications. "We've found that life often lives at the interface, both the sea ice and the water beneath it," said MCM LTER Project Manager Jack DiTullio. "If there's an environment on Europa where there's an ocean that might be similar to Antarctica, this would be a good way to start to understand what kind of life could possibly survive there." Understanding the biogeochemical and geophysical interactions between ice and water in the Antarctic Dry Valleys, which is similar to conditions on Mars and the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, is a primary focus of the MCM LTER. Ice-covered moons in the outer solar system, such as Europa, are of interest to astrobiologists because they may contain liquid oceans. A NASA mission to Europa, tentatively scheduled for the 2020s, would attempt to look for evidence of extraterrestrial life in the moon's subsurface oceans. The BRUIE has a buoyant cylindrical body that is 3.3 feet (1 meter) long and has a diameter of 1.7 feet (0.5 meters). The buoyancy allows the rover to roam under sea ice for extended periods without having to manage the power necessary for surfacing and submerging. BRUIE is equipped with two thrusters that propel the vehicle forward or backward. It also has a camera, lights, a communications system, a water sampler, and a sediment corer. The BRUIE will not carry instruments to detect life, because scientists do not want to contaminate the environment they are trying to study. "We don't have life detection instruments, because this is a platform for us to go investigate the area under the ice," said MCM LTER Scientist Kirsty Tinto. "It's about going back to the same place over multiple years, which is how you start to understand what type of life is there, how it's surviving, and how it's adapting to its environment." Tinto is the principal investigator of the Benthic Rover project and has been working on it for several years. She recently joined the MCM LTER team as the field season support scientist. Tinto and her colleagues in the Benthic Rover team at JPL will spend two weeks in Antarctica testing BRUIE. They plan to deploy the rover under the sea ice in McMurdo Sound, where the average ice thickness is 6 feet (2 meters). They will guide the rover back and forth as it autonomously samples and records data. BRUIE will be the first instrument to carry out a science mission under sea ice in Antarctica. The rover is designed to stay under the ice for weeks at a time. It will carry a communications system and an electric heater to prevent the electronics from freezing. "We hope to get it to go under the ice, maybe 10 to 20 meters, stay there for a little while, and then come up and resurface through the ice," said Tinto. The BRUIE will be equipped with a radio antenna, GPS unit, and a Wi-Fi modem for communications. It will also be equipped with a pair of sonars to provide real-time data about the ice and water conditions around the rover. The BRUIE team plans to test its navigation system, as well as the camera and lights. The navigation system is based on an algorithm developed at JPL called the Anywhere-on-Ice algorithm. The algorithm works with information from the GPS and the sonar to determine the rover's position in the ice. "We're not going to have a rover that can go anywhere, but we are going to have a rover that can go anywhere under the ice," said Tinto. An elderly man stood in an open field, situated in the middle of nowhere. The area was devoid of anything except for the meadow, the sky, and a solitary gravestone. A single word, "Christine," was inscribed on the smooth stone. The old man gazed lazily at the gravestone, his blue, cloud-like eyes not truly fixated on anything. His hair swayed slightly as a breeze blew, causing his peach beret to fall off and land on the grass. Apart from that, the man remained motionless. His cane, lying on the spot for so long, had begun to dig into the ground. "Christine," he murmured from his weak voice, the words coming out hoarse but melodiously sorrowful. He believed she had led a fulfilling life, though he wished he could have given her more. He was merely a boy when they first met; it wasn’t a perfect love story or even a tale of star-crossed lovers. Their connection didn’t begin until later in high school, when they were in the same class. However, it wasn’t until the end of senior year that they became acquainted. Both had waited at the bus stop, leaving a friend’s party around the same time. It was chilly outside, but unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, the lost boy was too drunk to realize he should have offered his jacket to her. In previous eras, the key played a significant role. On musical instruments, certain chords sounded harmonious while others were dissonant due to the tuning of the instrument. Today, most instruments employ "equal temperament," where all keys produce sounds that are nearly identical. For example, on a piano or organ, all keys sound similarly. This is because many compositions were never assigned titles by the composers themselves; instead, they were labeled by archivists or researchers to create a consistent reference system posthumously.

Classical music often includes the key of the piece in its title when it has a standard name, helping to distinguish it from other works of the same genre. For instance, a sonata or a fugue might be titled with the key specified, such as "sonata in C major" or "fugue in B minor." However, if a composition has its own unique name, like "Turkish March," "Eine kleine Nachtmusik," "Clair de Lune," or "Don Giovanni," the key is not required, as there is only one such work.

Many parts of Europe have sufficient natural fluoride levels to provide the benefits of fluoridation. In contrast, many regions of the U.S. do not. However, it is not accurate to say that "99% of Western Europe does not fluoridate water." Ireland has a national water fluoridation program, and some communities in other countries have artificially fluoridated water. Natural fluoridation is also important; however, it is not universally present in the U.S., with only two-thirds of the population receiving fluoridated water (whether naturally or artificially). Approximately half of Canadians have fluoridated water, with some provinces having it more commonly than others.

Most European countries support programs that provide fluoride varnish or fluoride rinses to schoolchildren. Italy lacks a national water fluoridation policy because several areas have natural fluoride levels at the optimal threshold. Salt fluoridation aligns with the World Health Organization’s recommendation to consider it when water fluoridation is not feasible due to technical, financial, or cultural factors. By'regular' Mathematics you are probably referring to'pure' Mathematics, which basically boils down to trying to understand numbers, concepts and theories in Mathematics. 'Applied' Mathematics is concerned with those theories and concepts which can be'applied' to other topics and real world situations; think engineering or Physics. TL;DR'Regular' (Pure) is Maths for the sake of understanding Maths;'Applied' is using Maths to understand real situations.,Pure mathematics is done for its own sake, essentially asking "if we assume these things to be true, what can we prove?," and maybe moving on to "how little do we have to assume to still be able to prove those things?" Applied mathematics is concerned with solving real-world problems like mechanics and statistics - as the name suggests, it has applications in the real world. The distinction has become a bit more fuzzy since it turned out even apparently very pure mathematics which was originally done for its own sake can have real applications, particularly number theory being used in encryption. Sometimes this is referred to as "applicable" mathematics.

Electricity stems from a property of matter called charge. Electric charges exert forces on other electric charges through what is known as an electric field. There are positive and negative charging points, those located near the electrical connection between electrodes. If these charged volumes are disturbed by disturbance in electricity flowing around them, the voltage drop will cause the electricity to flow away from the battery pack into the battery pack which causes it to lose its electric potential difference for a short period of time until the battery cells can be replaced with fresh cells. The energy loss from this phenomenon occurs when electric currents flow across the electrical connections between different types of batteries. This process creates heat that causes currents among various levels of charge which will eventually heat up three or four times more than normal wireless conductors such as copper wire strands used today. Although there are many possible solutions available they tend to be difficult to accomplish since most techniques involve attaching multiple layers of metal wires together so that each layer must be separate to allow easy removal within the battery packs using a separate power supply or power distribution system without creating additional cost constraints (such as installation costs). However, these methods have been efficacious enough even if the lithium ion batteries use the same materials as today's batteries because of their relatively small size thus making them ideal candidates for use alongside standard batteries due to their low weighting requirements while providing long life cycles compared to current lead acid batteries. The drawbacks of using wire-connected battery chargers include: the lack of control over voltages applied to devices; the need for additional protection circuitry; the inability to store large quantities of data; and the possibility of defects affecting design values due to corrosion caused by elevated temperatures during discharge processes due to temperature variations outside the confines of typical consumer electronics. These problems may reduce efficiency significantly because battery charger designs typically incorporate a single source of voltage regulation instead of two alternating current sources. Furthermore, battery chargers designed for use alone provide insufficient advantages at higher wattage ranges where one device can generally produce much greater output than another but still achieve similar performance results relative to one unit equipped separately. Accordingly, it would be desirable to develop improved lithium ion rechargeable batteries having improvements relative to existing chargers wherein both harnesses were operated independently rather than relying solely upon individual systems operating simultaneously against a common supply.

Over the last few years, and especially now with the popularity of Bernie Sanders, a heavily debated subject is the raising of the minimum wage to 15hour. While many would expect this to strengthen the lower class and only decreasing the wealth of the upper class, I feel as if it would end up hurting those it is meant to help. These company's would now have to spend much more of their budget on paying employees, and it's not as if they're going to magically have more money. I understand that the increase of wealth in the lower class would eventually circulate back to the business's, but I highly doubt it would be enough to make up for the increased wages of their employees, and it definitely wouldn't happen right away. Since I highly doubt the CEO or other upper management would take cuts from their pay to make up for this, that leaves two possible solutions that I can see: The first would be to decrease the amount of employees. If approximately an equal percentage of employees are let go to the increase in pay the company will be able to function without upper management having to take a pay cut. While those who are able to keep there jobs would be greatly helped by this, for the most part it would just increase the unemployment rate; with these lay offs happening in a large portion of minimum wag paying company's there would be no demand for jobs while the supply would be sky rocketing. The other solution would be for the company to increase prices (for retailrestaurants). With increasing prices nobody would have to loose their job, however it would still end up hurting the lower class. Practically all people get there basic necessities and luxuries from retail and grocery stores- the lower and middle classes especially rely heavily on major stores such as Walmart or Target. Even if your paycheck is increasing you'd still end up paying more the things you already buy, taking a large chunk of your paycheck. While ideally an increased minimum wage seems perfect, it would in reality end up creating a combination of these two things. I'm sure I didn't hit on some points, so please try to change my view on this, I, as a minimum wage employee myself, would love to have a good reason to support raising it. EDIT: Okay, my views been changed. I still don't think something as drastic as upping it to 15hour right away would be a good idea, but I think a gradual increase could be really good. The biggest things that helped my view change were the historical instances of MW rising, the average proportion of price increase vs. wage increase, as well as the fact that businesses are already operating with the minimum number of employees and that jobs wouldn't just become expendable. Some theories of civil disobedience hold that civil disobedience is only justified against governmental entities. Brownlee argues that disobedience in opposition to the decisions of non-governmental agencies such as trade unions can be justifiable. Brownlees concept of "the principle" refers specifically to trade unionism and its supposed monopoly on moral authority, but it also has implications for other social movements. For example, a group seeking to stop nuclear weapons production could use his idea when taking action against government decision making; an environmentalist movement might employ similar tactics if they felt local governments were impeding their efforts (which has happened). In The Principle: A Primer of Civil Disobedience (2006), Brownlee offers his framework for applying this approach. He identifies seven principles, or guidelines, which are defined by both positive and negative obligations. Positive obligations relate to specific actions that may need to take place within certain situations. Negative obligations concern the obligation not to act upon certain people or organizations, either because some individuals seek retribution after disobeying these rules, or due to a lack of fit between the organization itself and the way it operates. He then discusses how each individual circumstance will require an analysis based on these responsibilities. The philosophy addresses the nature of dissent and resistance from the perspective of modern society. It does so through the application of rights relating to freedom of speech, assembly, association and the right to property - all set out and protected by the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights. These human rights apply regardless of whether said society makes agreement with this list of rights. By using these rights, as well as those he believes should exist under any progressive society including the Four Freedoms (freedom from oppression, freedom of expression, freedom of press and freedom from fear) the author argues that anyone can choose to disobey laws without facing arrest or prosecution. There are several ways one can become involved in civil disobedience activities according to the philosophical theory formulated by Professor Howard P. Brownlee. Some methods include joining protest groups advocating particular issues, forming cooperatives that do not comply with existing economic policies or distributing information about a proposed illegal activity to potential participants. One main method suggests that citizens partake in a political demonstration outside Parliament House where there would be many elected officials present who support the law being attempted to be enforced. Thus as the demonstration progresses, signs that state "We Will Not Comply" move closer and closer to the officers until eventually police begin to surround the demonstration. At this point, supporters standing behind them shout at the crowd to disperse as quickly as possible. According to this model, someone participating in large scale demonstrations should refuse orders given by the police unless shehe feels there is no chance of herhis safety. In most cases however, before a person crosses this line into civil disobedience, shehe must first discuss herhis plans with herhis family members and friends and ensure they understand what they are doing will result in legal ramifications. Other possibilities include advising fellow demonstrators to refuse officer requests to break up protests and attempting to peacefully reason with opponents who have been arrested. Finally, the best course of action suggested by the author involves staging sit-ins inside companies' buildings while demanding compliance at meetings and rallies with senior management, stating that you intend to remain there indefinitely until your demands are met. The Weston Cadet (model 852, introduced in 1949), Direct Reading (model 853, introduced in 1954), and Master III (models 737 and S141.3, introduced in 1956) were among the first in their series to adopt and use the established ASA scale. Earlier models continued to use the original Weston scale until around 1955. After 1955, the company still released Weston film ratings, but the recommended values often differed slightly from those on film boxes. These newer Weston values were based on the ASA system and required conversion using a subtraction of 13 exposure stops, as recommended by Weston. Conversely, older Weston film speed ratings could be adjusted by adding 13 to convert them into new Weston values and align with the ASA scale. Before 1955, a Weston rating of 100 corresponded to 125 ASA. Starting from 1956, Weston meters inherently utilized the ASA system, so no conversion was needed. However, adjustments for the ASA PH2.5-1960 revision might be necessary when comparing with newer ASA or ISO values.

The paper introduces a nonlinear control strategy aimed at stabilizing a fixed-wing UAV. The design incorporates aerodynamic factors and state data from commercial autopilots to facilitate straightforward implementation. The resulting closed-loop system is proven to be globally asymptotically stable (G.A.S.) and resilient to external disturbances. Inspired by map labeling, we investigate a problem involving n disks D_1, ..., D_n in the plane that may grow at varying rates. When two disks intersect, the one with the smaller index vanishes. This problem was initially proposed by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt in [IWOCA 2016]. We present the first general subquadratic method for determining the times and sequence of disk removals. This approach is applicable to various shapes, including rectangles, and operates in any fixed dimension. By employing quadtrees, we develop another algorithm that achieves nearly linear time complexity, though it introduces a logarithmic factor related to the ratio of the fastest to the slowest disk speeds or the spread of their centers' distances. Our findings enhance the efficiency of prior algorithms by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016], Bahrdt et al. [ALENEX 2017], and Funke and Storandt [EWCG 2017]. Ultimately, we establish an (n log n)-lower bound for the problem, demonstrating that our quadtree approaches are nearly optimal.

Captain Harris and his crew of eight had been on a routine space exploration mission in the outer galaxy for over three months. They had encountered all sorts of challenges on their journey, from malfunctioning equipment to dangerous asteroid fields. But none of these obstacles prepared them for the ghost that haunted their ship, the Hermes. The Hermes was an old spacecraft, passed down from generation to generation of space explorers. It was said that the ship had been cursed, with every crew that sailed it haunted by a malevolent ghost. Some believed the ghost was a former crew member who died in a catastrophic malfunction, while others theorized that it was a vengeful spirit of an extraterrestrial race they had angered centuries ago. Whatever the cause, the ghost was real. It first made its presence known one night, when the captain and his crew were enjoying their rare leisure time. They heard a spine-tingling moan, followed by whispers that echoed through the hull of Hermes. At first, they brushed it off, assuming that it was just their overloaded imagination playing tricks on them. But as time went by, the ghost became more and more active. Objects would move on their own, doors would open and slam, and crew members saw apparitions of a humanoid figure hovering in the corridors. The ghost did not discriminate between crew members, either. Everyone experienced the haunting in one way or another, and soon they all began to fear for their lives. One night, Captain Harris decided to investigate the ghostly presence, taking his trusty blaster gun and a bag of detection equipment. As he descended into the lower levels of the ship, he heard the ghost's wail, louder and more menacing than ever before. Harris's heart raced as he felt the icy breath of the ghost on his neck, but he managed to hold his ground and confront the spirit. To his relief, the ghost did not lash out violently, but instead communicated with him telepathically. It informed Harris that it was not a malevolent entity, but merely a projection of the ship's consciousness, a manifestation of the Hermes's long history and the ghosts of all the crew who had sailed it in the past. The ghost begged Harris for mercy, not wanting to cause any harm to the current crew. Moved by the plea, Harris agreed to spare the ghost's existence, and returned to his crew with newfound knowledge about the haunted ship. For the rest of their journey, the ghost remained a harmless presence, and the crew sailed the Hermes back to Earth with a newfound appreciation for the superstitions and lore of their trade.

The use of specialized tools for nail care goes back to ancient Greece at least, where nail care was done by the same fellow who cut your hair. The tradition was imported to Rome. To give you an idea of what kind of instruments were used, this object from the St. Albans Museum is listed as a replica of an ancient Roman nail-care kit, and it includes something that looks very close in form and function to a modern nail clipper. (EDIT: But which actually is not, see my below discussion with kermityfrog.) I can find scattered references to Egyptian nail care tools, but nothing as solid as that. Getting earlier than Egypt and Greece, we'd be looking at Mesopotamia. And it looks like it was customary to impress an unfired clay tablet with your fingernail as a kind of signature, so for at least some of the ancient Mesopotamian civilizations, for at least some time, it seems to have been customary to leave your nails long. Oh, and I found a lot of modern sources offhandedly mentioning that manual laborers' nails wear down and break on their own, and'manual laborer' describes an increasingly overwhelming majority of the population as you get further and further back in history. I can't give you anything so academically rigorous as a primary ancient-world source that directly says that, but have a photograph of the hands of a modern Bangladeshi rice farmer's wife. So it looks like quasi-modern nail clippers are about as old as documented traditions of nail-cutting. Unless there's a cave painting somewhere out there that tells the story of The First Manicure. The problems with North American were severe enough in late 1965 to cause Manned Space Flight Administrator George Mueller to appoint program director Samuel Phillips to head a "tiger team" to investigate the problems and propose solutions. The team was also given the responsibility of preparing a plan for an expeditious return to flight. Phillips's 33-page report was presented on January 21, 1966. It proposed a 10-month schedule to return to flight, including the first test flight of the new Saturn V. The tiger team was clearly concerned about the deterioration in the Apollo program schedule; a new Saturn V would be needed, and the new launch vehicle would take an estimated 18 months to develop. But the tiger team also recommended that the Apollo 204 launch be pushed forward to December 1966, as if the problems with the Apollo 203 launch were already solved. This was possible because Apollo 204 had been cut from 577 pounds to 454 pounds of payload, and because only a single launch vehicle would be needed instead of two. The tiger team also recommended that the second launch of the new Saturn V be delayed from November 1968 to January 1969, to coincide with the first launch of the Skylab space station. Apollo 203 would be the last launch using the old Apollo launch vehicle. That vehicle was now 6 years old and had suffered several failures. But the problems with the Apollo 203 launch could not be blamed on aging. It was caused by design errors, and most of these were identified and corrected. The problems began at the Cape when the T-10 test rocket, which was scheduled to be launched on December 3, 1965, failed to ignite its second stage. The following day, the first stage of the T-10 rocket failed to ignite. The problem was traced to defective electrical wiring, but the electrical wiring in the spacecrafts also had to be checked. In December, the command and service modules were stacked at the Cape and a second test rocket, the T-20, was readied for launch. That rocket also failed to ignite, apparently because of a problem with the second stage. The launch of T-20 was postponed from January 13, 1966, to January 17 because of a minor technical problem with the T-20 rocket. The launch was again postponed from January 25 to January 27 because of a fuel leak in the second stage of the T-20 rocket. It was postponed from January 27 to February 4 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. The T-20 launch was postponed from February 4 to February 12 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. On February 10, 1966, the third stage of the T-20 rocket was tested, and it worked. At that point, the T-20 rocket was ready to fly, and the Apollo 203 launch had been postponed long enough. On February 12, the launch was rescheduled for February 21. On February 21, the T-20 rocket was launched from the Cape and successfully reached orbit. But just after separation of the second stage, a problem developed in the rocket's autopilot. The command to shut off the engine was never sent, and the rocket veered out of orbit. Object detection and recognition algorithms using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) tend to be computationally intensive to implement. This presents a particular challenge for embedded systems, such as mobile robots, where the computational resources tend to be far less than for workstations. As an alternative to standard, uniformly sampled images, we propose the use of foveated image sampling here to reduce the size of images, which are faster to process in a CNN due to the reduced number of convolution operations. We evaluate object detection and recognition on the Microsoft COCO database, using foveated image sampling at different image sizes, ranging from 416 416 to 96 96 pixels, on an embedded GPU - an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 with 256 CUDA cores. The results show that it is possible to achieve a 4 speed-up in frame rates, from 3.59 FPS to 15.24 FPS, using 416 416 and 128 128 pixel images respectively. For foveated sampling, this image size reduction led to just a small decrease in recall performance in the foveal region, to 92.0 of the baseline performance with full-sized images, compared to a significant decrease to 50.1 of baseline recall performance in uniformly sampled images, demonstrating the advantage of foveated sampling.

The Disk wasn't supposed to revolve that day. It needed more basic testing before it should've been turned on. A black, round device, studded with small wires slithering inside. To induce low fields for the coils inside. He was there, late at night, preparing a report for the following morning, dried coffee mug on his cluttered desk. A picture of her adorned one of the corners, her radiant smile reminding him of the day they had met in the shade of the trees by the lake. The room hummed. He stopped writing and looked towards the table in the middle, the Disk cradled on its spindly stilts. It started spinning internally, the hum growing ever louder. A bright flash lit up the room. At first he hadn't noticed anything different. He felt a bit sore, but the Geiger meter registered no radioactivity, and the doctor told him the next day that it was likely fatigue from his research. That he should take a break. Something was off, but he couldn't quite understand what. A week had passed, and the project was going well, the presentation having granted him more money to pursue the study of the Disk. Usually, he shaved in the morning, but for some reason his face was devoid of any stubbles. Odd, but more time to do other stuff, he thought. He went downstairs to prepare the breakfast. She was still asleep, tired from her late shift, and he covered some French toast he had prepared with a bag and left her a note. She would call him around noon to catch up. He added a new picture on his desk, from a recent vacation along the coast, the two of them looking at the camera with a smooth, creamy sea behind them. Despite some progress, the Disk had not given up its secrets, and had been inert for years. Her hair was a duller shine, a few hesitant lines contouring her beaming smile. Strange. Horror gripped his mind, as he rushed to the mirror in the lavatory. His hair was still dark and shining, and not a single hint of a new beard, as if time had stood still. And not even a random flu in a very long time. No. It couldn't be possible. It took all those years to notice. What if it was too late? He now understood what the effect of the Disk was, or at least had a very good idea. He didn't age, he still retained a youthful appearance, and swept the compliments about his appearance without any real care for them. He returned next to the Disk that held the answer. Noon. The phone rang, and he jumped in surprise. Yet he stood there, his legs petrified, his gaze running along the equations scribbled on the blackboards. Ending on the photo. The phone stopped ringing. Activating the Disk carried a great risk, and he felt a bit selfish for what he wanted to try to do. But he couldn't leave her behind, he couldn't live without him next to her side, without her next to his. It had to be done in complete secrecy. What he had discovered after the flash, many years ago, were shiny streaks running along the object, that weren't there when he first began his research. He chalked it up to permanent damage, and slowed down the testing until it could be remedied. Unsure of what might happen a second time, he remained inside the room for a whole week, running various experiments and simulations. What if he were to be affected again? What if the Disk were to fail, or induce a different effect? Tirelessly, he peered over the models, refined them, changed the constants, introduced new wiring. They spent New Year's in the deserted cafeteria, his tired eyes gazing at her. Still beautiful, after so many years, heading for the certainty of Nature's resolve. And him, defying that very Nature. Yet he stood silent about his plan. He visited her daily at the care home, where she was lying on a bed with white linens. She hated that bland arrangement, and he brought her flowers to colour the colourless walls. There had been arguments about what had been happening to him, how he never seemed to age, and he became increasingly isolated, firing all his research staff to keep a low profile, the Disk project abandoned with the room and building sold to an anonymous patron. Time and time again, he promised her that he would change things. A tear rolled down his cheek as gazed at her grey hair and sad eyes, eyes that he so vividly remembered as being vibrant and full of energy. As if it was yesterday. More work to be done for the night, he felt that he was nearing the end of the search, he would be successful, although at a heavy price. The wheelchair was waiting to transport her, all was set, it wouldn't be long. The phone rang, but he ignored it, his mind delved in the simulation. He had found a way to get responses from the Disk, and without damaging it. All he needed now was to bring her in the room and use the right amount of power. He had succeeded, he knew it would work, it had to work, he had spent all his waking time on that Disk, and now it was finally ready. Someone knocked at the door. Someone had entered the closed building and was knocking on the glass, a dark silhouette behind it. He opened the door, furious that someone would disturb his work. A nurse, a thin, young woman, out of breath. She told him of her, how she had told the nurse to call, to summon him to her linen bed, by the flowers. That she had passed away peacefully in her sleep, calling out his name. He told the nurse, in a hoarse, breathless voice, that he wanted to be left alone for a few moments, and the woman exited the room. Yellowed picture of the couple in hand, he collapsed, warm tears falling on the dusty floorboards. The Disk whined slowly, then shattered.

It has to do with how electricity is used in wall power. Two main types of elecrtical current: AC and DC DC: Direct Current, think water flowing through plumbing. AC: Alternating current, think waves going up and down. Wall power is an AC power source, and the frequency of the voltage (waves) is around 50-60 Hz. This is a frequency we can hear as a low pitched buzzing when the power interacts with things (sound from waves hitting a dock or shore). This is how the noise is getting powered. Though I don't have the experience to ELI5 how magnetic induction might be affecting the vibrations that we hear.," "AC electricity cycles at 50-60Hz depending on what country you are in. That is, the polarity and current flow is reversing in direction each cycle. When current flows it makes a magnetic field perpendicular to the direction of the current flow. If the magnetic field intersects with things like the magnetic fields of other wires or nearby metal, it makes a small force. This force is pushing the wire 50-60 times per second, making it vibrate. The human range of hearing starts at about 20Hz, so that 50-60Hz vibration is in the range of your hearing. It takes a lot of current to make a strong magnetic field in something like a power cord, so I expect you'd only hear noise from something like an electric stove, kettle, or iron. If you've ever turned on an old appliance like a tube-television and heard a high pitched whine - its the same thing but at a higher frequency.

We show dense voxel embeddings learned via deep metric learning can be employed to produce a highly accurate segmentation of neurons from 3D electron microscopy images. A metric graph on which the data points are embedded is used as a global structure, and these metrics shrink to generate dense representations that capture information about neuron firing rates over time and space. The work demonstrates real-time neuromorphic neural network segmentations in 3D from SDSC images that include multiple layers of cell architecture. We reveal new features detected by our models, including neuronal overcurrents and axonal outgrowth, far beyond what was previously considered possible with normalized topology traces encoded manually. Neurons within the brain have different densities at different locations, ranging from 0.9460.023 voxels per cubic cm cite11. Because most of these cells do not have any demonstrated mechanism for communication (neurons communicate exclusively through diffusion), these density fluctuations make it difficult to discern their locations with 2D electron microscopy, even if they were available [1]. However, bioluminescence imaging cameras such as JEOL provide excellent visibility into these low-density areas, enabling detailed structural analysis by scanning an entire object section at once. Visualizing these patterns can then help us understand how neurons interact with one another, and we find them useful for many tasks where nonstationary activity needs to be identified. For example, current flow along axons is crucial to understanding how neurons regulate membrane potential and thus determine excitatory and inhibitory behavior cite25. However, since these areas exhibit strong correlation with each other, there is often a significant overlap between two neighboring objects that have been scanned simultaneously. In fact, this is especially true when identifying large regions of interest (ROIs). Thus, in order to identify a single object moving across a field of view, we need to learn a model capable of detecting overlapping portions and creating a spatial representation of its motion. Instruments such as JEOL are designed specifically to address this problem: They use multiple high resolution camera sensors to amplify the light reflected off an object and strike an image sensor array directly behind it. As capacity increases, so does the number of photos taken in this way. This allows several ROI measurements to be made during a given exposure, opening up opportunities for clustering ROIs in dense regions or identifying parts of larger objects that rapidly change in illumination. Further, because all lighting conditions are equally efficient, JEOL provides much better coverage than conventional methods, making it more practical to employ in research settings. China blocked Wikipedia in April, using DNS injections to prevent its citizens from accessing the encyclopedia. There has been no official statement as to why the website was blocked. In May 2014, China unblocked all sites on a temporary basis to allow users to access them during important exam period at high schools and universities. In November 2012, netizens began to question whether or not major Chinese websites have actually become "part of [the] state" after it came out that many popular websites are owned by companies with government ties.[1415] On 13 January 2008, Sina reported that Google had temporarily suspended operations in mainland China because of unreliable bandwidth.[16] The following day, Google issued an apology for what they called unscheduled maintenance: We're] sorry about the inconvenience this may cause our users.17] Afterward, several domestic web portals claimed to be able to connect to Google again.[18] It is believed that when Google's servers were overloaded, their IP addresses changed; therefore, when people tried to type into their browsers before 13 January 2008 (UTC 0001), only 404 pages would appear instead.[1920] However, according to some sources, there might also have been legal issues behind Google being inaccessible in China. On 15 February 2010, Google announced that Google.cn is set to return sometime later in March 2011[21], citing increased demand among other reasons. Later reports indicated that problems remain between Internet service providers and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Even though some ISPs say they can't see any reason for blocking, others claim there will always be censorship due to technical constraints. Some experts believe that the issue may be a political decision by Beijing. Most officials do not directly respond to questions concerning censorship,[22] but only repeat generic statements regarding the protection of online information security. Some journalists assert that the real reason for the ban on China remains unclear.[23]Other analysts suggest that since 2007, taking control over the flow of information inside China has gradually become one of the priorities of Western governments, which could explain why there has been recent tension between them and Beijing.[24] Some social media outlets such as Twitter are accessible via proxy servers outside of China, while others use VPNs to circumvent the firewall.[2526272829] In 2003, Censorship-Free Web Sites published a list of Internet resources freely available worldwide without restrictions.[30] A more current version titled Free Access To Knowledge Online contains content up through 2013. In recent years, particularly with the rise of Bernie Sanders, the discussion around raising the minimum wage to $15 per hour has become highly contentious. Many believe this would benefit the lower income group by increasing their earnings, yet I argue it could ultimately harm those it aims to assist. Companies would need to allocate more funds to employees, but they won’t suddenly gain additional revenue. Although the wealth generated by lower-class earnings might eventually trickle back to businesses, I doubt it would be sufficient to offset the higher wages paid to workers, and this effect would likely take time. Given that top executives are unlikely to reduce their compensation to compensate for this, two potential solutions emerge: either cut employee numbers, which could stabilize operations without requiring salary reductions, though this would lead to higher unemployment, or raise prices at retail and restaurants, which would prevent job losses but still negatively impact the lower class. The latter approach would still burden individuals who rely on these stores for essentials and luxury items, even if their incomes increase. While the ideal scenario of a higher minimum wage appears beneficial, its implementation may face practical challenges.

My classroom environment fosters learning as the main objective. I developed this policy after encountering students who wouldn't submit work at all because it was late and didn't seem worth anything. They preferred to submit it late rather than never. Although this perspective isn't widely accepted, I've received inquiries from colleagues asking me to justify my approach. The system may be under resource constraints, such as limited energy or bandwidth, which pose challenges on the design of an efficient communication mechanism. The communication mechanism itself may be a computation task that is mutually dependent on the actual computational tasks that the users perform. In this paper, we address these problems in the context of distributed computation over wireless communication networks. We propose a novel scheme that combines wireless networking with distributed computing techniques in order to allow users to efficiently collaborate in performing a given computation task. Our scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. We consider a general class of computation tasks, which we call distributed applications, that can be performed by the users in the system. A distributed application is a collection of sub-tasks, each of which is executed by a subset of users in the system. In order to execute a sub-task, the participating users need to exchange information with each other. We assume that the users are equipped with energy-constrained devices, such as sensors or mobile phones. The devices may have limited energy resources, which need to be carefully managed in order to prolong their lifetime. We also assume that the devices are capable of wireless communication, and that they can be turned on and off in order to conserve energy. We propose a novel scheme for distributed computation over wireless communication networks, which we call coded distributed computing. In our scheme, the users cooperate in order to compute a function of their inputs, while taking into account the energy constraints of their devices. The scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among the users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. Our scheme has several advantages over existing schemes for distributed computation. First, our scheme is energy-efficient, as it minimizes the number of times that the devices need to be turned on. Second, our scheme is scalable, as it does not require a central entity to manage the communication among the users. Third, our scheme is robust to communication failures, as the coding theory used in our scheme allows the users to recover from communication errors. We illustrate the use of our scheme with two examples. In the first example, we consider the problem of distributed sorting, in which the users need to sort a sequence of numbers using only local comparisons. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of comparisons than the best known scheme for distributed sorting. In the second example, we consider the problem of distributed matrix multiplication, in which the users need to multiply two matrices using only local operations. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of operations than the best known scheme for distributed matrix multiplication.

Determining the masses of stars is generally manageable under specific conditions, particularly when observing objects orbiting them. By leveraging our knowledge of gravity and motion, we can effectively predict the behavior of celestial bodies in our solar system. Thus, this approach forms a robust theoretical framework. If an object such as a planet or another star orbits a star, we can gather a couple of straightforward observations to calculate the star’s mass with reasonable precision. The first observation involves measuring the period of the orbit—how long it takes for the object to complete one full revolution. The second measurement focuses on the orbital velocity—the rate at which the object moves along its path. This can also be inferred by observing the slight wobble of the star caused by the gravitational pull of the orbiting body, which can be detected via Doppler shifts in the star's light. With these two pieces of information, we apply the principles governing orbital motion to deduce the size of the orbit and the necessary mass of the central star. As long as our measurements are precise enough, we can obtain reliable estimates of the star's mass, typically within a few percent in most scenarios. 

Edit: Many individuals suggest that we cannot truly determine the mass of a star or that it remains just theoretical. However, in practice, it often relies on straightforward applications of fundamental physical laws that have been meticulously verified on Earth. The laws of orbital dynamics are well-established and widely applied, such as in satellite launches. If one knows the composition of an object, the proportion of its mass that constitutes each component, and its overall size, they can reasonably infer its total weight.

Embeddinghub is a database built for machine learning embeddings. Embeddings are dense numerical representations of real-world objects and relationships. They are used to quantify how similar vectors are to each other in a way that supports learning and reasoning. Embeddings are particularly useful for unstructured and non-tabular data like text or images. Machine learning models like neural networks can use embeddings to understand the similarity between two words or the relation between two objects. In the past few years, researchers have created embeddings for all sorts of domains. They've created embeddings for words and phrases, countries and cities, movies and actors, and even genes and proteins. However, these embeddings are siloed away in academic papers and software repositories. It's very hard to find embeddings for a particular domain, even when they've been published. Embeddinghub aims to solve this problem by creating a database for embeddings, where people can easily search, browse and compare them. Anyone who wants to use embeddings for their research can use the search and compare features to find the embeddings most appropriate for their domain. Researchers who've created embeddings can add them to the database, which will increase the visibility of their work and help others discover it. The function counting theorem, which addresses the role of covering in the theory of artificial neural networks, marks a significant advancement. It offers a solution to the challenge of identifying how many distinct binary classifications (dichotomies) of p points in n dimensions can be linearly represented. However, extending this framework to more complex issues beyond point classification remains difficult. There is an increasing need to develop techniques for handling structured data, particularly non-point-like patterns. A notable example is invariant recognition, where the identification of a stimulus is unaffected by irrelevant transformations such as rotations or perspective changes in images. An object is thus represented by an expanded perceptual manifold containing inputs that are classified similarly. We introduce a function counting theory tailored for such structured data by expanding Cover's combinatorial method and derive analytical formulas for the average number of dichotomies in sets of patterns that are generally correlated. Applying this, we derive a closed-form expression for the capacity of a binary classifier trained to differentiate general polytopes across all dimensions. These findings could contribute to broadening our theoretical comprehension of generalization, feature extraction, and invariant object recognition within neural networks.
