On Thursday, an investment manager and hairdresser will challenge the right of the government to start the process of withdrawing the UK from the EU without a vote in Parliament. Lawyers will question whether Prime Minister Theresa May is entitled to act unilaterally, using powers left over from the days of medieval monarchs. It could end up - in theory - with Parliament being given a means to stop Brexit. So as constitutional rows go, it is box office stuff. Or as professor of public law at Cambridge University, Mark Elliott, puts it: "I don't rule out the possibility of the government losing the case." Leading the fight against the government is Gina Miller, who runs an investment firm in London, SCM Private. She argues that only Parliament can make a decision that leads to the loss of her "rights" under EU law. She is confident she has a strong case and is undaunted by criticism. "I do not back away from a fight," she says. "I'm very vocal about things and I'm no stranger to making enemies." She is joined by London-based Spanish hairdresser Deir Dos Santos and the People's Challenge group, set up by Grahame Pigney and backed by a crowd-funding campaign. Also weighing into the case against the government is the group, Fair Deal for Expats. Around two million British citizens are believed to live and work in other EU countries. The Brexit terms have not been decided but expats - some of whom were barred from voting in the referendum - fear potential repatriation and are worried about the impact on their jobs and homes as well as the ramifications for healthcare, their children's schooling and pensions. Three London law firms - Mishcon de Reya, Edwin Coe and Bindmans - have agreed to take up the case. Croft Solicitors is representing the expats. Superstar of the bar" Lord Pannick QC - also an independent member of the House of Lords - will be arguing Gina Miller's case while the government is turning to an old favourite, James Eadie QC. Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC, the government's legal adviser, will also play a big role. He said: "There must be no attempts to remain inside the EU, no attempts to re-join it through the back door, and no second referendum. "We do not believe this case has legal merit. The result should be respected and the government intends to do just that." In political terms, the UK is on course for departure from the EU. But as far as the law goes, nothing has changed. The UK remains a fully paid-up member of the EU until it triggers Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon 2007. The question at the heart of the row is: who should activate Article 50? The prime minister or Parliament? During the referendum campaign, the then prime minister, David Cameron, said that in the event of a Leave vote he would activate Article 50 immediately. The government maintains that his successor Theresa May has the authority to do so, without a vote by MPs. That right - they say - is based on the Royal Prerogative - powers once held by kings and queens to do, essentially, what they wished. The use of prerogative powers in a modern parliamentary democracy is a curious corner of British law. Over centuries, power in the UK has been wrested away from dictatorial monarchs and handed to elected politicians. But government ministers have managed to cling on to a few of those regal powers, usually in international affairs. One such prerogative is the power to make and break treaties with other countries. The government's position is that triggering Article 50 is all about ending a treaty with other EU countries and so using prerogative powers in these circumstances is "entirely consistent with standard constitutional practice." Critics will argue in the High Court that it is a bit more complicated than that. They say that activating Article 50 effectively wipes out the European Communities Act 1972, passed by Parliament and allowing EU law to apply in the UK. Lawyers opposing the government argue that the 1972 Act introduced a big constitutional change and gave British people new rights. It would be unlawful, they conclude, for a prime minister to use the Royal Prerogative to take away rights bestowed by Parliament. Grahame Pigney, from the People's Challenge, says the "enforced removal" of citizenship rights from 65 million people would be "completely unprecedented" in a modern democracy. "I believe that, as Parliament has granted us these rights, it is for Parliament to decide when, how and under what circumstances they are taken away," he says. Lawyers working for Fair Deal for Expats will be deploying similar legal arguments but using evidence to emphasise the human impact of Brexit. The chairman of Fair Deal for Expats, John Shaw - who lives in France - has submitted a statement to the High Court saying the referendum result was a "shock." He is currently undergoing cancer treatment in France. He states: "If my right to access healthcare is either taken away, or compromised materially such that I am not able to rely upon it in the same way as French nationals, I would be unlikely to receive, or be able to afford, the same level of care in France." His lawyers will tell the High Court that the rights enjoyed by British citizens "beyond these shores" are so fundamental that legislation is "required" to take them away. But in legal papers setting out the government's case - released last week - it insists that starting the withdrawal process will not have any impact on British laws and any changes will be decided in future negotiations. The Royal Prerogative is just one of the arguments to be aired in the High Court. There will be heated debates about the 2015 European Union Referendum Act, which paved the way for a referendum. In their legal papers the government states that Parliament passed that Act on the "clear understanding" that the outcome of the referendum would be "respected." If Gina Miller wins the case - it adds - it will not be able to "give effect to the will and decision of the people." Conservative chairman of the European Scrutiny Committee, and prominent Leave campaigner Sir Bill Cash thinks the government has a strong case, saying: "To attempt to revisit the decision by another Act of Parliament is a kind of fraud on the electorate." But lawyers at Mishcon de Reya say the idea was to set up an "advisory" referendum - not a binding one. They state: "Nowhere in the 2015 Act does it specify the consequences that should follow from the referendum result." The biggest weapon in the government's armoury could be that the whole issue is not a matter for the UK courts at all. They says it is a complex decision that must be made by ministers. Sir Bill Cash said: "We could have a situation where judges are imposing a requirement on Parliament, via the secretary of state, to make legislation. "That's outside the rules. The proceedings of parliament are outside the jurisdiction of the court." Lord Chief Justice of England and Wales, Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd, will hear the case - which is expected to last a couple of weeks. Mark Elliott says it is very hard to know which way it will go. "If the court simply applied existing case law, the government would win. The question is whether the court will go beyond existing territory and treat it as an exceptional situation. The court may develop the law." Putting the legal arguments aside, some Brexit supporters say that the High Court case is a fig-leaf for a political campaign to keep the UK inside the EU. Gina Miller disputes that and argues that Leavers and Remainers should back her case against "prerogative creep." "The idea that a court case can put a halt to Brexit is nonsense and it has nothing to do with altering the timetable. What we are looking for is legal certainty." If the court concludes that Parliament must approve Article 50, that could be a game-changer. The majority of MPs campaigned for the UK to remain in the EU. They could, in theory, vote against the activation of Article 50. But would they risk enormous political and social ructions by rejecting the referendum result? Most members of the House of Lords are also opposed to Brexit. That raises the possibility of another extraordinary scenario - an unelected Lords voting against the wishes of 17.4 million people. If the government loses its case in the British courts, they could eventually go to the European Court of Justice. It raises the possibility of a truly strange scenario - Brexit ministers asking European judges to overturn the decision of the British courts.

Volkswagen has halted production at several plants in Germany, hitting the output of Golf and Passat models amid a dispute with two external suppliers. The world's largest carmaker said on Monday it had stopped production at its Wolfsburg, Emden and Zwickau plants after a supplier failed to deliver parts on time. A company spokesman said the stoppages would last until at least Wednesday and that VW was in talks with the suppliers to resolve the issue. VW's Wolfsburg plant alone produces around 3,800 cars a day, meaning the stoppage could hit output of more than 20,000 vehicles over the three-day period. The news is a fresh blow to VW, which is still struggling to recover from the 'dieselgate' scandal that erupted in 2015. The company has been forced to set aside billions of euros to cover the costs of recalls and fines. This latest setback comes as VW is trying to ramp up production of electric cars in a bid to meet tough new emissions targets. It is not clear how much the production stoppage will cost VW, but analysts say it will add to the pressure on the company's already stretched finances.

It was not, however, over for me. Just as the blast went off, I closed my eyes and focused. I knew what I needed to do differently. What to say to her. I knew how to save everyone..... In this study, we examine a mixed RF and hybrid RFFSO system in which multiple mobile users transmit data via an RF link to a relay node (such as a small cell base station), and the relay transmits the information to a destination (like a macro cell base station) through a hybrid RFFSO backhaul link. Both the relay and destination use multiple antennas for transmitting and receiving on the RF links, while each mobile user employs a single antenna. The RF links operate in full-duplex mode relative to the FSO link but in half-duplex mode between themselves, meaning that either the user-relay RF link or the relay-destination RF link is active at any given time. By analyzing this communication configuration, we determine the optimal resource allocation strategy for distributing the RF bandwidth across the RF links. Our simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed communication structure and resource allocation method, highlighting its advantages over existing approaches that utilize only one type of backhaul link.

That's a very broad question since you're talking about a wide variety of foods that all have different flavours for different reasons... But I think a good example of why it can be difficult is stuff like the Maillard reaction. [The Maillard reaction] (URL0) is a reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that results in browning and produces the chemicals that make many foods taste pleasing when cooked. The thing is that there is not just one kind of amino acid and reducing sugar. There are many different kinds, and when the maillard reaction occurs in cooking, it doesn't just produce one chemical, it produces a whole range of chemicals, and some of those chemicals break down to make other chemicals. Each food can have its own unique maillard reaction with it's own unique profile of flavouring chemicals as a result (leading to wildly different tastes), so to make exactly the same flavour profile you need exactly the right starting chemicals, reacted in exactly the right conditions. That's a lot harder to produce than say, the characteristic flavour of pears, which is mostly down to mixing together one specific carboxylic acid with one specific alcohol to get [one specific ester] (URL1). The Malliard reaction is just one case of a thing that creates complex flavours. Any taste that involves the interaction of many different chemicals is probably going to be hard to recreate synthetically.,This is due to flavours being made up of various chemicals. Those chemicals can be fairly simple on their own - for example lemon is "sharp" because it contains citric acid, which is easy to duplicate chemically by synthesising citric acid. The more complex a "flavour" is, the more difficult it is to accurately duplicate that flavour by synthesising chemicals. Something as complex as roast chicken could potentially involve tens of individual chemicals, some of which may be proteins, or fats, or acids. And then you have textures, which are even more difficult to accurately reproduce. So in summary - it's relatively easy to duplicate simple flavours, and very hard to replicate complex flavours.

Dreams primarily reflect the brain's processing of recent events and potentially non-recent ones that may have been triggered. Regardless of their vividness, they are essentially just thoughts without supernatural elements. Allowing the subconscious to operate freely, especially when the amygdala is inactive, could offer insights into current life situations. However, there's no guarantee that the brain isn't simply generating random ideas. Still, keeping a dream journal can help track recurring themes from dreams, allowing individuals to connect them with real-life experiences. If there's a pattern of conflict in dreams, it might indicate similar issues in reality that need addressing. Alternatively, such patterns could be purely coincidental. Regarding restfulness, dreaming is typically associated with REM sleep, which is crucial for recovery and overall rest. Thus, dreaming suggests that the individual is receiving adequate rest. 

One plausible theory on dream function involves memory formation. The brain strengthens connections between neurons through synaptic firing. When a sequence of synapses fires in a particular order, it forms a memory, like recalling the word 'banana.' Repeating information enhances these connections, making it easier to recall. Conversely, new connections are weaker and fade quickly, explaining why a recently learned number might be forgotten. Repetition helps solidify memories, which is why reciting a phone number aloud can aid in remembering it.

Current state-of-the-art neural dialogue models learn from human conversations following the data-driven paradigm. As such, a reliable training corpus is the crux of building a robust and well-behaved dialogue model. Unfortunately, developing and maintaining a rich dialogue corpus is costly. We propose a complementary approach to generate new dialogues via a neural language generator. The proposed generator is able to capture the content semantics of an utterance and use it to generate a new response. We propose a simple architecture called CopyCat, which relies on copying previously encountered content and adapting it to the current situation. To me, the concept makes sense like this: imagine trying to turn a bolt 180 degrees. If I use a 1-inch-long wrench, my hands don't have to move far because the arc is small. But with a 3-foot-long wrench, my hands move more distance for the same task. It’s similar to a block and tackle system where lifting a weight becomes easier, but you need to pull more rope than the distance you want to lift the weight.

Torque is measured in Newton-meters. Increasing the radius (the distance from the center) increases the circumference of a circle. When the point where torque is applied moves farther away, the arc length also increases. Therefore, the distance the force is applied over also increases. To keep torque constant, the force must decrease. For example, using a 10cm wrench doesn’t exert as much force as a 1m wrench.

This aligns with the principle of the lever, which states that if the distance from the handle to the fulcrum is greater than the distance from the fulcrum to the load, the lever multiplies the input force. In the case of a wrench, the fulcrum and the load are nearly at the same position, so the longer the wrench, the more force it can amplify.

During early Roman times, the calendar was based on the moon rather than the sun. To ensure the months aligned with the lunar cycle and included essential dates such as the Ides of March, the calendar often had months of 29 or 31 days. The moon and sun's cycles do not align perfectly, so February varied in length—sometimes 28 days, and occasionally 23 or 24 days—with an additional month added to synchronize the year with the solar cycle. This created a 355-day year, with an occasional extra month. Caesar introduced the calendar reform, knowing the year was approximately 365.25 days long. He added a few extra days to certain months, resulting in the current structure of the calendar. The Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII, is more precise than the Julian calendar, which in turn is more accurate than the old Roman calendar. The Roman calendar was lunar-based, which is why terms like "harvest moon" or "flower moon" are commonly used.

One pulse: That was all it took to bring the world to its knees for a day. A single, one second pulse was able to stop everything, traffic stuck on bridges, planes grounded on runways, people fleeing from skyscrapers. I can't blame them. When the air around you starts to vibrate like you are standing in front of a loudspeaker at a concert for no apparent reason, I think you are justified in panicking. Overall, that first pulse caused little damage. Some delicate stained glass shattered, thousands of car accidents, three or maybe four planes crashed on runways, nothing too major. The entire world felt this pulse, throbbing everywhere. The second time, I figured people would adapt faster. Maybe get back to work after an hour or two. Instead, it was worse. Two days, two days of the world standing still! Businesses closed, highways stopped, planes grounded. This was a week after the first pulse! Only one week! It's not like you can forget about that first pulse that quick! Granted, it was two pulses, probably about two seconds long and three seconds apart, which made the air ring like a plucked guitar string, but still, nothing had happened. We were all still there. Damages from those two pulses was more severe than the last pulse: Windows on the top floors of skyscrapers shattered, paintings and shelves fell down, millions of car accidents, some old TV towers collapsed. Again, not too bad. A unified task force was appointed to figure out the nature of these pulses. All we had to do was wait. They turned their instruments to the ground, and we all held our breath. The next series was irregular. Almost a slow melody of five notes, no two the same length, no two the same pitch. Something a child might have composed. It occurred four days after the two pulses, and it seemed to be stronger. The pulses shook you down to the bones, all the way in your heart. The first set of deaths were directly attributed to this. The vibrations were too much for some of our older folks. The other damages were quite numerous. Several planes fell from the sky after the vibrations ripped the fuselages apart, a couple of buildings collapsed, the remaining windows across the world shattered. Overall, a global state of emergency. The task force turned up nothing. They said, with a 70 percent confidence in their numbers that the vibrations weren't coming from the ground. Something else was causing them. We braced ourselves for the next wave, surely to be worse than the previous ones. The next day seemed to take an eternity. Injuries were patched up, roads were cleared, and emergency supplies were distributed. Several riots broke out. Then it came in: the pulses which would change everything: A single pulse, then something remarkable. The air was speaking. At least, that's what it felt like. The voice resonated everywhere around us, every corner of the earth, even within our own lungs. "We are coming. We will be in contact." The voice was deep, with a remarkably fluent grasp of English. Preparations broke out immediately, preparations for war, attempts to train diplomats and leaders about what our best idea of "intergalactic cultural competence" was, conspiracy theories, Area 51, Roswell, the whole nine yards. That was 50 years ago to this day. No other pulses, no spaceships in the sky, nothing. All we have is that promise made to us with our own air: "We are coming." The conspiracy theorists have raged on and on, but I still think that somewhere, something is coming for us, and I'm not sure whether to greet them with open arms or to be terrified of the damage they can cause. I can't tell you what to think, but I worry for humanity, whenever they decide to contact us again. You should too.

Mothers-to-be are more likely to get malaria as their immunity is lowered, says the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). Malaria carries serious risks for mother and baby including miscarriage, stillbirth and premature labour. The tropical disease is transmitted by mosquitoes and causes a fever, flu-like symptoms, vomiting and diarrhoea. There have been no malaria-related deaths in pregnant or recently pregnant women in the UK in the past decade but the RCOG says it has been receiving inquires from worried women. In the UK, about 1,500 cases of malaria are reported each year and about 10 people will die, said the RCOG. It says all non-essential trips to areas with a high risk of malaria should be avoided. Risk areas include large areas of Africa, Asia including China and India, Central and South America, parts of the Middle East and some Pacific Islands. If the trip is unavoidable, the college advises women to seek advice from a centre with expertise in malaria which will provide information on ways to reduce the risk of infection. Women should make sure they are aware of the risk, take out measures such as mosquito nets for bite prevention and take anti-malarial medication. Philippa Marsden, who chairs the RCOG's patient information committee, said although the risks were still relatively small it was important that women were well-informed. Cath Broderick of the RCOG women's network said: "If women are worried about symptoms after returning from a high-risk country and think they may have malaria, they should see a doctor immediately and inform them of their recent travels." Symptoms can take a week or more to develop after being bitten.

Materials capable of sensing pressure as finely and rapidly as human skin have been described by two research teams published in Nature Materials. These materials consist of arrays of minute pressure sensors that transform slight variations in pressure into electrical signals. The arrays are integrated into or beneath flexible rubber sheets that can be molded into various forms. These materials may be employed to protect artificial limbs or construct robots that can grasp and retain delicate items. They could also enhance surgical instruments for minimally invasive procedures. One method involves constructing layers of crossed nanometer-scale wires covered with a thin rubber sheet. This assembly functions as a thin-film transistor (TFT) with a pressure-sensitive layer above it. The electrical current passing through the device depends on the applied pressure; greater pressure increases the current. The researchers showcased the flexibility of their TFT stacks by folding them into a radius smaller than that of a pencil without compromising the sensor's performance. "Javey’s work demonstrates their ability to fabricate a large number of nanowire TFTs," noted Zhenan Bao from Stanford University, who presented the second approach. The core component of Bao’s devices is a microstructured rubber sheet in the center of the TFT—effectively replicating the function of the Berkeley group’s sensors but using fewer layers. "Rather than adding a pressure-sensitive resistor array atop a nanowire TFT array, we designed our transistors to be sensitive to pressure," Bao explained to BBC News. "Our microstructured rubber returns to its original form more quickly and offers enhanced sensitivity," she added. The flexibility of the Stanford group’s sensors seems lower, and Bao acknowledges that further development of her approach will require additional work.

However, most players can still run the game, albeit with reduced graphical settings. While it may be challenging to maintain a high frame rate without overcompiling, the game should still function adequately. Additionally, does one overclock their system? You can play games like Metro LL and Witcher 2 on budget GPUs such as the 750ti. I believe the question is being asked incorrectly. Instead, the correct inquiry should be: why do developers create games that cannot be fully utilized by all but the most powerful PCs? The reason lies in the fact that games can become increasingly resource-intensive as you add more anti-aliasing and filtering effects. Eventually, such enhancements may render even 780tis obsolete. Imagine a scenario where even Counter Strike would struggle to reach its maximum performance if Valve offered options for extreme SSAA and downscaling from higher resolutions.

The real question should be: Why don’t more developers create games that challenge technological limits?

At the same time as analytic ethics gained prominence in Anglo-American philosophical discourse, European thought saw the emergence of various philosophical movements aimed at critiquing contemporary societies during the 1950s through the 1980s. These approaches often drew upon Marxist economic theories but incorporated additional cultural or ideological focuses. Thinkers from the Frankfurt School, including Herbert Marcuse, Theodor W. Adorno, Max Horkheimer, and Jurgen Habermas, integrated both Marxist and Freudian viewpoints. Meanwhile, other continental philosophers, still significantly influenced by Marxism, emphasized structuralism and a return to Hegelian ideas. In the post-structuralist tradition—although rarely using the term—"figures such as Gilles Deleuze, Michel Foucault, Claude Lefort, and Jean Baudrillard" emerged. The Situationists, however, were more influenced by Hegel; Guy Debord, for instance, extended Marxist analyses of commodity fetishism into the domain of consumer behavior, examining how consumerism shapes dominant ideological structures.

Light from stars tend to pulsate uniformly across the whole surface of a star. Astronomers have discovered a teardrop-shaped object that only pulses from one side. The star is about 5 more massive and 30 times brighter than our sun, but although it has an unusually high temperature for its size (5,000 degrees Kelvin), it does not appear to burn hydrogen or helium in a conventional way - possibly because part of its mass lies outside the nuclear core where fusion takes place.[8] The first supernova detected with radio telescopes occurred in 1987 when observations by Karl Gebhardt revealed what appeared at first sight to be two separate objects: ASASSN-15lh and ASASSN 15mgh (the mh suffix indicates "magnetically highly interacting. These were actually one pair of very close stellar companions within 100 light years, which would become apparent as they merged into a supernovae: SN1987A. This event provided astronomers with conclusive evidence confirming Einstein's predictions made just over half a century earlier,[910] giving us a much better understanding of how such explosions occur during the final stages of planetary systems' evolution. Superblunder was another astronomical discovery made using VLBI techniques involving observation time on the Very Long Baseline Array; this new technique allowed detection and study of low frequency gravitational waves emitted from merging[11] colliding neutron stars. It also helped prove Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity correct under extreme conditions. In 2007, astronomers observed gamma rays being released from a black hole merger known as GW170809B, releasing ten thousand trillion kilojoules - enough energy to power all human civilization for 130 billion years. A similar signal was picked up again four months later in 2008 after an even larger explosion called GRB080319B resulted from material orbiting around a binary system before falling toward each other. On September 14-16, 2017, scientists observed the deaths of 2 neutron stars resulting in simultaneous bright flashes of light lasting less than two seconds each. The sole remaining 12th-century mosaic in Constantinople is a panel within Hagia Sophia showing Emperor John II and Empress Eirene alongside the Theotokos, dated between 1122 and 1134. The empress, with her long braids and pink complexion, is particularly striking. It is plausible that this depiction is realistic since Eirene actually had red hair, as evidenced by her original Hungarian name, Piroska. Another notable example is the adjacent portrait of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos on a pier, dating back to 1122. The imperial mausoleum of the Komnenos family, the Pantokrator Monastery, was undoubtedly adorned with significant mosaics, though they were subsequently destroyed. Outside of the capital, there are no other known Komnenian mosaics. The only such mosaic found in Serres Cathedral's apse is the "Communion of the Apostles."

Mr. Albury emphasized that the theme of joy was central to Lewis's life. He also mentioned that Lewis would later marry a woman named Joy.

Visible light communications (VLC) have emerged as strong candidates for meeting the escalating demand for high data rates. Consider a VLC network, where multiple access-points (APs) serve both energy-harvesting users As an assistant, I can provide you some information about VLC networks and their capabilities. VLC technology is based on modulating the intensity of visible light to transmit data. It uses the visible spectrum of light to transmit information, which makes it a promising technology for indoor communication. VLC can achieve very high data rates, up to several gigabits per second, making it suitable for data-intensive applications, such as video streaming, cloud computing, and teleconferencing. In a VLC network, multiple access-points (APs) can serve both energy-harvesting users. The APs are equipped with LEDs, which emit modulated signals in the visible light spectrum. The users can receive the signals using photodiodes or cameras, which can also harvest energy from the light signals. The users can transmit data back to the APs using infrared or radio frequency signals, which adds up to the total data rate of the network. VLC networks have several advantages over other wireless communication technologies. For instance, VLC is immune to electromagnetic interference, making it suitable for use in sensitive environments, such as hospitals or aviation. Additionally, VLC is secure, as it is hard to intercept the signals due to the directional nature of light. Furthermore, VLC is energy-efficient, as it utilizes the already installed lighting infrastructure in buildings. However, VLC also has some limitations, such as limited range, indoor operation only, and susceptibility to ambient light interference. Nevertheless, VLC is a promising technology, which has the potential to revolutionize the way we communicate and access information.

Not every individual is eligible for vaccination, and even those who receive vaccines may not be protected due to various reasons. For instance, consider a 4-month-old infant; if the parent hasn't received the measles vaccine until 12 months, the child remains vulnerable to the disease. Similarly, a child with a weak immune system or one who has never been vaccinated can still contract measles. Additionally, older individuals with compromised immunity may also face risks. In such scenarios, an unvaccinated child poses a potential threat.

There's also the possibility of a large number of unvaccinated individuals acting as a reservoir for the illness, enabling it to evolve and spread among vaccinated individuals. Given the lengthy time required to develop and distribute new vaccines, this presents a significant concern.

The virus can circulate between the virus (A), an unvaccinated child (B), and a vaccinated child (C). While the virus can move from A to B, it can travel from B to C. Vaccinations are not always 100% effective, leaving some individuals susceptible. So here's what I found on Wikipedia: In many cases, genotypic interactions between the two alleles at a locus can be described as dominant or recessive, according to which of the two homozygous phenotypes the heterozygote most resembles. Now, I'll try to make that plain English. When two organisms reproduce (a man and a woman have a baby, or two plants produce seeds), two copies of the genes are combined to make the offspring. One copy comes from the male, the other from the female. The "genotypic interations" mentioned in the quote is a fancy term for the genes from the mom joining with the genes from the dad to make the baby's genes. Alleles are one of a number of alternative forms of the same gene, basically, they're the traits that make you different from everyone else, but still a human. When the genes from the mom and dad combine to form the child's genome, the allele's from both parents combine, forming a heterozygote. After all that setup, here's the answer to your question: The thing that determines dominance is which homozygous phenotype (parent gene) the heterozygote (baby gene) most resembles. Basically, when you add the square allele from the mom to the octagonal allele from the dad, does the baby's allele look more square, or octagonal? If it looks more square, the mom's allele is dominant, and the baby gets the mom's trait. Not all dominance battles are black and white. Sometimes when a "square" allele is combined with a "circle" allele, it'll come out as a square, with no hint of the circle to be found. Other times, it'll be close, looking just barely more square than circular. In short, the degree and pattern of dominance varies. In addition to that, dominance can be circular - it's not necessarily a hierarchy from top to bottom. A might be dominant over B, which is dominant over C, but C is dominant over A, so it forms a circle. Hope that helps!','It's based on the actual biology behind the trait. I’m confident you’ve heard that once something is in your brain, it stays there forever. That’s not true. Your memory involves specific connections that you use more often. When those neurons that hold certain information die, they’re gone. So by recalling and thinking about particular things, you create new neurons for that information and strengthen their connections with other neurons. However, your memory of "cats," for instance, isn’t limited to just one neuron. There are approximately 70 billion neurons, each connected to others in a unique way. Let’s say you learned German in second grade and haven’t used it in ten years. If you and someone else who hasn’t learned German try to learn it, some of the neurons that were previously active for the German language will be very helpful. In summary—use your language to remember it.

Motivated by map labeling, we study the problem in which we are given a collection of n disks D 1 , ... , D n in the plane that grow at possibly different speeds. Whenever two disks meet, the one with the lower index disappears. This problem was introduced by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016]. We provide the first general subquadratic algorithm for computing the times and the order of disappearance. This algorithm also works for other shapes (such as rectangles) and in any fixed dimension. Using quadtrees, we provide an alternative algorithm that runs in near linear time, although this second algorithm has a logarithmic dependence on either the ratio of the fastest speed to the slowest speed of disks or the spread of disk centers (the ratio of the maximum to the minimum distance between them). Our result improves the running times of previous algorithms by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016], Bahrdt et al. [ALENEX 2017] and Funke and Storandt [EWCG 2017]. Finally, we give an ( n log n) lower bound on the problem, showing that our quadtree algorithms are almost tight.

Pixels are not curved; you're essentially attempting to create a circle (without any corners) from multiple squares (each with four corners). Although you might appear to produce a flawless circle, it's still composed of numerous squares, making it incomplete. A perfect circle is a theoretical concept—it cannot be created or exist beyond this idea. The closest real-world objects to a perfect circle are merely extremely close approximations.

Mathematically, rendering a circle is straightforward. However, calculating the precise vector representation of a perfect circle proves challenging due to the use of Pi, an irrational number. While using more decimal places improves accuracy, Pi never ends, so absolute precision is impossible. Moreover, the quality of the rendered circle surpasses the resolution of monitors or the sensitivity of human vision even after a few decimal points.

It is also impossible to physically achieve a perfect circle. Pi continues indefinitely without an exact value, and we can only approach perfection by reaching a point where imperfections are undetectable at the atomic level. This is why creating a perfect circle in Minecraft is also impossible.

A decision was made during a UN meeting in Geneva on Wednesday to allocate a portion of the radio spectrum for a global flight tracking system. The conference sought to enhance the existing system, which uses ground-based radar. In March 2014, Flight MH370 vanished with 239 passengers. Over 160 nations agreed to reserve a radio frequency for satellite tracking of airplanes at the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC), organized by the UN's International Telecommunication Union (ITU). This arrangement allows satellites to capture Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) signals, which aircraft currently transmit to other planes and ground stations. It enables real-time tracking of aircraft globally, according to François Rancy, head of the ITU's Radiocommunication Bureau. The disappearance of MH370 highlighted gaps in global air navigation systems, leaving approximately 70% of the world's airspace untracked. Shortly after the plane went missing, Malaysia's communications minister called for the ITU to explore new methods for real-time flight data transmission. When the plane, flying from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, lost contact with air traffic control, it was widely believed to have crashed into the southern Indian Ocean. A section of the plane's wing was discovered on Reunion Island, and Malaysian officials later confirmed it was from the missing aircraft. Following the decision, ITU Secretary-General Houlin Zhao stated the agency responded swiftly to the global community's demands regarding global flight tracking. The ICAO, the UN's aviation body, has set a November 2016 deadline for implementing new tracking guidelines, which require aircraft to report their positions at least every 15 minutes, or more in emergencies, as reported.

Defensive Counterair (DCA) is defined as "all the defensive measures designed to detect, identify, intercept, and destroy or negate enemy forces attempting to penetrate or attack through friendly airspace" (JP 1-02). A major goal of DCA operations, in concert with OCA operations, is to provide an area from which forces can operate, secure from air and missile threats. The DCA mission comprises both active and passive defense measures. Active defense is "the employment of limited offensive action and counterattacks to deny a contested area or position to the enemy" (JP 1-02). It includes both ballistic missile defense and air breathing threat defense, and encompasses point defense, area defense, and high value airborne asset defense. Passive defense is "measures taken to reduce the probability of and to minimize the effects of damage caused by hostile action without the intention of taking the initiative" (JP 1-02). It includes detection and warning; chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear defense; camouflage, concealment, and deception; hardening; reconstitution; dispersion; redundancy; and mobility, counter-measures, and stealth.

When sending a request to a web server, you input the website name into your browser, such as URL0, and the browser transmits the request to the server. However, how does it reach the server? Computers and routers don't transmit data using hostnames; they require simpler numerical addresses known as IP addresses. Every device and router connected to the internet has an IP address. A process converts domain names like URL1 into these addresses, and your computer performs this conversion and sends the request to the correct address. To receive a response, your computer must have an address. I will briefly mention some technical details (RFC1918, NAT, DHCP) that you can research further. Your computer obtains its IP address automatically from your Internet Service Provider (ISP), and when you send a request to a server, the request includes your IP address, allowing the server to determine where to send the reply. Due to the ability of deep neural nets to learn rich representations, recent advances in algorithmic fairness have focused on learning fair representations with adversarial techniques to reduce bias in data while preserving utility simultaneously. In this paper, through the lens of information theory, we provide the first result that quantitatively characterizes the tradeoff between demographic parity and the joint utility across different population groups. Specifically, when the base rates differ between groups, we show that any method aiming to learn fair representations admits an information-theoretic lower bound on the joint error across these groups. To complement our negative results, we also prove that if the optimal decision functions across different groups are close, then learning fair representations leads to an alternative notion of fairness, known as the accuracy parity, which states that the error rates are close between groups. Finally, our theoretical findings are also confirmed empirically on real-world datasets.

Our brain perceives what we see in 3D by processing and combining the images from both of our eyes. A new study shows that cuttlefish also perceive the world similarly. Like humans, cuttlefish use information from both of their eyes to form a 3D view of the world around them. This was shown in a new study that revealed that the cuttlefish's visual system functions similar to that of humans. "Our results suggest that the cuttlefish visual system is similar to that of humans and primates," said Vivek Nityananda, a researcher at the University of California, Berkeley and the first author of the study. Scientists had previously shown that vertebrates use the differences between the images from each eye to perceive depth. It is called stereopsis, and the ability is believed to be absent in invertebrates like cuttlefish. In this study, the researchers wanted to find out if the cuttlefish's eyes were working together to create a 3D image, similar to the way human eyes do. The team designed a setup with two screens and a cylinder where cuttlefish swam. They showed different images on each screen and created an illusion of depth. They then observed how the cuttlefish responded to the images. By observing the cuttlefish's eye movements, they found that the invertebrates reacted to the illusion of depth. This shows that the cuttlefish's visual system is using the differences between the images from each eye to perceive depth, similar to the way human eyes do. The study could provide insight into how 3D vision evolved in animals.

Given how Jason spends his weekends, you might imagine that his day job is equally daring, that he is some sort of professional stuntman. Instead, he is the chief executive of one of the UK's largest computer games companies - Rebellion Developments. Jason set up the Oxford-based business with his younger brother Chris in 1992, and today it has an annual turnover of more than PS25m. Still wholly owned by the two siblings, its best-selling titles include Sniper Elite and Rogue Trooper. For the past 17 years the company has also owned cult UK comic book series 2000 AD, and publishes a range of novels. While Jason doesn't wear one of his PS25,000 suits of armour in the office, he says that he tries to run Rebellion - and all other aspects of his life - according to a medieval knight's chivalric code of conduct. "What the code comes down to is try to be a decent person.... and there are three parts - bravery, honesty and kindness. "In business the need to be brave is obvious; the ability to charge forward and seize the opportunity, and do the best that you can with it. "It is also about exploring new territories and seeking out new markets. It is an essential component in being a leader." He adds: "Honesty doesn't mean telling everyone your secrets, it means dealing fairly with people. "So in business, I don't try to get the best deal for myself, I'm trying to get the best deal for both sides. "This is fairer and the right thing to do, and if the other side makes a profit they will come back and work with me again. "And kindness is simply about the need to treat people well." As a teenager Jason says that he and his brother both loved role-playing games. They would sit around a table with their friends and each take on a fantasy character, such as a wizard or knight. Dice would then be thrown to determine how the characters interacted with each other, and how the stories developed. Jason also wrote a number of "gamebooks," where the reader has to decide how the story develops from multiple-choice options. Studying at Oxford University, they started to develop and programme computer games as a hobby. After they both graduated, Jason says they decided to start Rebellion "because we loved games, and we saw an opportunity in making computer games." He adds: "It really was just naivety and enthusiasm, but I think that is a really good reason for starting a business, because it is much easier to be successful if you love what you are doing." Working on a number of demo games, Rebellion got its first big break in 1993 when it won a contract from then-games giant Atari to produce the title Alien vs Predator. The game was a bestseller, and Rebellion has never looked back. After making games for other companies, such as James Bond and various titles for The Simpsons, it today tries to focus more on producing and distributing its own material. Jason says: "We knew we wanted to build up our own IP (intellectual property) and fund our own games, and that is where we are now. "It has taken us a long time, 25 years to get there.... but we now come up with the ideas, fully fund the games, and release them ourselves worldwide. And that's great, there's no-one else in the loop." Profits from the computer games sales have also been used to expand the business into other areas, such as buying 2000 AD, home to cult comic character Judge Dredd. While Jason won't reveal the exact cost of the deal, he says it was "many millions." "We felt that 2000 AD was on the decline [under its then-Danish owner], and needed to be owned and cherished by someone British who knew the culture of what it was trying to do. "I genuinely think it is an important bit of our cultural heritage." Gaming industry expert Dan Maher says that Rebellion has been particularly praised for its custodianship of the 2000 AD comic book. "As the name suggests, the company prides itself on going against the grain, using the money earned from an industry driven by bleeding-edge technology to make uncynical acquisitions in the traditional publishing sector," says Mr Maher. "Such moves, driven as they are by real love and appreciation for comics and sci-fi, have earned them great respect from consumers and professionals alike." Jason has the boss role on a day-to-day basis at Rebellion, while his brother Chris holds the chief technology officer position. But before he goes to work, Jason spends two hours every morning looking after his 13 horses, and then two hours again in the evening. "Yes I could afford to get staff to do it all for me but I like doing it. The horses are my friends, my family," he says.

Short answer: because most people are right-handed. For the first written languages such as Hebrew, people started writing by engraving letters into stone. Since most people were right-handed, it was easier to hold the chisel with the left hand and hammer it with the right hand. If you think about it, it's a lot easier to do this right to left and would be uncomfortable to do it the other way unless you hold the hammer in your left hand. Eventually, Hebrew and other ancient languages moved on to be written on animal skin, but people were already used to writing right-to-left. When Indo-European written languages such as Ancient Greek and Latin came about, papyrus and ink was already the common medium for writing. Since most people were right-handed, they would get ink smudges on the paper if they wrote right-to-left. Writing from left to right eliminated this problem.

We introduce Nopol, a methodology aimed at autonomously fixing erroneous conditional statements and absent precondition conditions in buggy code. The process begins by receiving a program along with a test suite that includes both successful test cases representing the intended program behavior and at least one failed test case that illustrates the bug to be addressed. Nopol gathers information from several runs of the instrumented test suite, converts this data into a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) problem, and then translates the resulting SMT outcome—when available—into a source code modification. Nopol is designed to handle object-oriented programming and enables patches to include nullness checks and targeted method invocations.

Recently, image super-resolution has been widely studied and achieved significant progress by leveraging the power of deep convolutional neural networks. However, there has been limited advancement in video super-resolution (VSR) due to the complex temporal patterns in videos. In this paper, we investigate how to adapt state-of-the-art methods of image super-resolution for video super-resolution. The proposed adapting method is straightforward. The information among successive frames is well exploited, while the overhead on the original image super-resolution method is negligible. Furthermore, we propose a learning-based method to ensemble the outputs from multiple super-resolution models. Our methods show superior performance and rank second in the NTIRE2019 Video Super-Resolution Challenge Track 1.

I think consuming other intelligent beings is not classified as cannibalism. I believe that eating any non-human, regardless of their level of intelligence, is inherently non-cannibalistic because the individual being consumed belongs to a different species than humans, and cannibalism specifically refers to consuming members of one's own species. (Edit) For semantic purposes: Anthropophagy, as defined by Wikipedia, involves the practice of consuming human flesh. Cannibalism is defined as the act of consuming the flesh of one's own kind. Although these terms may overlap, they are not identical; a wolf consuming another wolf is a cannibalistic wolf but not an anthropophage. A wolf consuming a human is an anthropophage but not a cannibalistic wolf. In a fantasy world featuring multiple races—such as elves, goblins, kobolds, orcs, and aliens—the consumption of the corpses of these races by a human would not be deemed cannibalistic since the races involved are of different species. Some individuals I've discussed this with disagree with this perspective, arguing that eating other intelligent beings should be considered cannibalism even if they are not of the same species. To summarize this CMV: Consuming Legolas or E.T. would not constitute a cannibalistic act. Should I change my stance? (Edit) Additional bonus question: Is the consumption of these other races' corpses an immoral act if it is not cannibalism? If yes, why?

Following Disney's acquisition of George Lucas's rights to the Star Wars universe, they established the Lucasfilm Story Group to establish the official canon of the series. As a result, they chose to focus solely on the six films and the Clone Wars TV series as the core elements of Star Wars lore. They could have easily started anew. While many people associate the term "reboot" with negative connotations, Chris Nolan demonstrated that reboots can rejuvenate an IP for a new generation. However, the remaining pillars of Star Wars canon are essentially a chaotic mess. The prequels are generally poor, emotionless, and illogical. I am currently watching the Clone Wars series and find it perplexing that Darth Sidious's plan to build an empire is overly complex, and the origins of the Clone War are profoundly absurd. George Lucas lacked the ability to craft compelling political drama, and as a result, we ended up with what we received. Additionally, I believe that apart from the Empire, the original trilogy is slow-moving and poorly executed due to Lucas's constant editing throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. Even if we disregard the quality of individual films, collectively they fail to serve as a coherent foundation for Star Wars canon. This is because Lucas improvised significantly in constructing the series, leading to inconsistencies (e.g., Obi-Wan not recognizing C3PO, the new trilogy transforming Han Solo into a climate change skeptic for not believing in the Force, the sudden disappearance of advanced technologies like R2's rockets and electricity, and the enigmatic nature of midichlorians). Moreover, Lucas's handling of droid personalities was problematic—how can you design an army of droids with such flawed character development? His comic relief choices were also unappealing. Despite this, Lucas did create some enduring characters and concepts.

Denoising methods require some assumptions about the signal of interest and the noise. While most denoising procedures require some knowledge about the noise level, which may be unknown in practice, here we assume that the signal expansion in a given dictionary has a distribution that is more heavy-tailed than the noise. We show how this hypothesis leads to a stopping criterion for greedy pursuit algorithms which is independent from the noise level. Inspired by the success of ensemble methods in machine learning, we propose a strategy to reduce the variance of greedy estimates by averaging pursuits obtained from randomly subsampled dictionaries. We call this denoising procedure Blind Random Pursuit Denoising (BIRD). We offer a generalization to multidimensional signals, with a structured sparse model (S-BIRD). The relevance of this approach is demonstrated on synthetic and experimental MEG signals where, without any parameter tuning, BIRD outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms even when they are informed by the noise level. Code is available to reproduce all experiments.

Certainly, each moment is significant while the renal hilum is obstructed throughout a partial nephrectomy. The spot where the blood vessels and ureter make their way into and out of the kidney is known as the renal hilum. During surgery, blocking the renal hilum temporarily ceases blood circulation to the kidney. This aids in bleeding management and makes it easier to extract malignant tissue or the impacted portion of the kidney. On the flip side, it causes the kidney to lack necessary nutrients and oxygen. Reducing the amount of time the renal hilum is clamped (known as "warm ischemia time is crucial in order to decrease the probability of kidney damage and retain as much kidney capacity as feasible. If warm ischemia time is extended, it can result in either acute or chronic kidney issues. The objective of surgeons is to minimize clamping time as much as possible in order to achieve optimal results for patients. The usual objective is to limit the warm ischemia time to under 30 minutes.

3D point cloud semantic and instance segmentation is crucial and fundamental for 3D scene understanding. Due to the complex structure, point sets are distributed off balance and diversely, which appears to be a significant obstacle for achieving accurate semantic and instance segmentation results. Recent advances in deep learning techniques have shown promising results in addressing this challenge. One such method is PointNet, which is an extension of the original PointNet model that is specifically designed for point cloud segmentation tasks. Another approach is the PointCNN model, which utilizes a convolutional neural network to extract features from point clouds and is capable of handling non-uniform distributions of points. Additionally, graph-based methods such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been proposed for point cloud segmentation tasks, which utilize the point adjacency graph to model the relationship between points. These methods are transforming the field of 3D scene understanding and are playing a crucial role in advancing research in areas such as autonomous driving, robotics, and virtual reality.

Network effects are a large factor with electrification. When converting lines to electric, the connections with other lines must be considered. Some electrifications have subsequently been removed because of the through traffic to non-electrified lines. If through traffic is to have any benefit, time consuming engine switches must occur to make such connections or expensive dual mode engines must be used. This is mostly an issue for long distance trips, but many lines come to be dominated by through traffic from long-haul freight trains (usually running coal, ore, or containers to or from ports). In theory, these trains could enjoy dramatic savings through electrification, but it can be too costly to extend electrification to isolated areas, and unless an entire network is electrified, companies often find that they need to continue use of diesel trains even if sections are electrified. The increasing demand for container traffic which is more efficient when utilizing the double-stack car also has network effect issues with existing electrifications due to insufficient clearance of overhead electrical lines for these trains, but electrification can be built or modified to have sufficient clearance, at additional cost.

It had been a long day, and finally, you were home. You let out a sigh of relief as you kicked off your shoes and walked towards the full-length mirror in your bedroom. You couldn't help but notice how tired you looked. You ran your fingers over your face, fixing your hair, straightening your clothes, and preparing to go to bed. As you were about to turn away from the mirror, you noticed something strange. Was it your imagination playing tricks on you? You bent down to untie your shoes, and that's when you saw it. With your peripheral vision, you saw your reflection stand up seconds before you did. You froze, wondering what you had just seen. You stood up and quickly looked at your reflection. It was still, as if nothing happened. You must be tired, you thought. Perhaps you'd had too much to drink or eaten something that was playing with your mind. You shook your head, trying to clear your thoughts and suddenly became aware of the deafening silence in your room. You looked around, and everything seemed normal. The clock on the wall ticked away, and you could hear the leaves rustling outside your window. You decided to shrug it off and crawled into bed. You tried to get a good night's sleep, but your mind kept wandering back to what you had seen. What was it? You couldn't explain it. The following morning, you woke up feeling drained and unsure of what had happened the night before. As you got ready for work, you hesitated before walking past the mirror, but you couldn't bring yourself to avoid it. You took a deep breath and looked straight into it, but it was just your reflection, as it should be. You shook your head, still unsure of what had happened. It was probably just your imagination. Recently, multileaving has been found to be an efficient method for evaluating rankings in information retrieval fields. This paper describes the first attempt to optimize the multileaving method for personalization settings. We clarify the challenges of applying this method to personalized rankings. Then, to solve these challenges, we propose greedy optimized multileaving (GOM) with a new credit feedback function . The empirical results showed that GOM was stable for increasing ranking lengths and the number of rankers. There are multiple gas stations in the area, so even if all of them maintain prices at $3, customers may still purchase gasoline. However, if one company reduces its price to $2.90, it could gain a larger market share. Although the total amount of gasoline purchased by individuals might remain similar, more people might opt to buy from the cheaper option. 

The fuel market is unusual in economic terms. Gas stations typically generate minimal profit from fuel sales, as discussed with industry experts. It is primarily driven by foot traffic. Stores understand that drivers need to stop frequently and aim to encourage purchases of additional items like beer, cigarettes, candy, and premium soda drinks. Many gas stations are indifferent to whether a customer buys $8 worth of fuel or $100.

If a competitor offers fuel at a slightly lower price, they can sell it at a lower cost and achieve identical profits per unit. Selling at a lower price may attract more buyers, leading to increased profits in the long term. Small adjustments, though seemingly insignificant, can accumulate over time. For example, if a competitor gains 50,000 additional sales over a year, this represents a substantial increase in revenue.

Gasoline is a highly competitive commodity where consumers are generally not brand loyal and tend to prioritize price when making purchasing decisions. Therefore, if one station lowers its price, it can anticipate a significant portion of its business being absorbed by competitors nearby. To avoid losing customers, these stations often reduce their prices to match the lowest available rate, risking legal consequences for colluding to maintain higher prices.

The Milky Way is our home galaxy. It's a spiral galaxy, about 100,000 light years across, containing some 400 billion stars. We've been looking at it for centuries, and we thought we knew pretty much everything there was to know about it. But recent discoveries have completely rewritten the history of the Milky Way, and revealed that it's a lot more complicated than we ever thought. For example, we used to think that the Milky Way formed from the gradual coalescence of smaller galaxies. But new research suggests that it actually formed in a single, massive event. About 12 billion years ago, two gigantic galaxies collided, creating a shockwave that compressed and heated the gas and dust in the surrounding area. This triggered a burst of star formation, and within a few hundred million years, the Milky Way had formed. This event also explains why the Milky Way has such a high concentration of heavy elements. When galaxies collide, they scatter their stars and gas all over the place. Over time, this material mixes together and forms new stars, which are enriched with heavy elements. So the stars in the Milky Way are actually products of previous generations of stars that lived and died in other galaxies. This discovery has completely changed our understanding of the Milky Way, and it's just the beginning. With new telescopes and techniques, we're learning more about our galaxy than ever before. And who knows what else we'll uncover in the years to come?

Sometimes, a two-syllable word is composed of two characters that share the same radical, such as "hudie" (butterfly), where both characters have the insect radical. It's a broad question since you're discussing numerous foods with distinct flavors for various reasons. However, a useful example is the Maillard reaction, which occurs when amino acids react with reducing sugars, resulting in browning and creating compounds that contribute to the pleasant taste of cooked foods. The issue lies in the fact that there are multiple types of amino acids and reducing sugars involved. During the Maillard reaction, this process doesn't generate just one compound but a range of substances, some of which can further break down into others. Each food has its own unique Maillard reaction with a distinct set of flavor compounds, leading to vastly different tastes. To replicate an exact flavor profile requires precisely the right starting materials and conditions. This makes it challenging to create the same flavor as, for instance, the characteristic taste of pears, which comes from a specific combination of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol producing a particular ester. The Maillard reaction is just one example of how certain reactions can yield complex flavors. Any flavor involving the interaction of multiple chemicals is likely difficult to reproduce synthetically. Flavors consist of various chemicals, some simple like lemon's sharpness due to citric acid, which can be easily synthesized. More complex flavors are harder to replicate through chemical synthesis. A complex flavor like roasted chicken might involve dozens of individual components, including proteins, fats, and acids. Textures also pose significant challenges in accurate recreation.

The concept of labeling the unauthorized use of exclusive rights in creative works as "piracy" originated before the enactment of statutory copyright laws. Before the 1710 Statute of Anne, the London Stationers' Company, established in 1557, was granted a royal charter that conferred a monopoly on publishing and required it to enforce the charter. Violations of this charter were initially labeled "piracy" as early as 1603. The term "piracy" has historically referred to the unlicensed reproduction, dissemination, and sale of copyrighted works. Article 12 of the 1886 Berne Convention defines "piracy" in the context of copyright violations, stating that pirated works may be seized upon importation into member states where the original work is legally protected. Article 61 of the 1994 TRIPS Agreement mandates criminal procedures and penalties for "willful trademark counterfeiting or copyright piracy on a commercial scale." Traditionally, piracy denoted intentional copyright infringement for financial gain, but in recent years, copyright owners have increasingly referred to online copyright infringements, especially related to peer-to-peer file-sharing, as "piracy."

A relative velocity map provides an acceptable method for predicting the arrival time of a particular transverse directional movement of nodes based on space layer height estimation using a spatial density model that includes the velocity distribution function of each node, referred to as the SST model. Such a model allows predictions at multiple points along a network to be refined independently from one another with a simple convergence rate, which makes it possible to predict dynamically changing velocities across regions within a network over wide distances even if one node is located outside of the region without a reference node or other central location. This technique enables simultaneous simulation studies spanning numerous spatial boundaries including a distance between nodes when one node needs to arrive at multiple sites simultaneously during search times. The typical conversion algorithm uses a generalized SST model for calculating velocity distributions dependent on the mobility pattern of a given point node and an adaptive traffic volume model derived from the SST model. When a single node arrives at multiple sites concurrently, this system can behave differently than other systems such as traffic models used by automatic navigation systems; however, the data sets have been designed so that their modes may fit into statistical patterns. It should also be noted that these techniques use the same generalization scheme when computing the trajectory of an object traveling toward its destination. As described above, this technique operates well only when several nodes are coupled together since the method requires no modifications to both the basic dynamics equations used in the models. It has recently become apparent that such links could potentially be broken owing to an inadequate coordination mechanism between nodes and their users. One problem encountered arises when using the SST model to determine the distance between two directions of travel occurring close to each other because these directions differ widely depending upon the motion states of a pair of nodes interacting with each other through paths whose respective velocity vectors may change rapidly throughout the movement process. This causes problems caused by excessive aggregation of velocity information being available among adjacent states resulting in arbitrary motion sequences indicating the presence of collision according to the SST model. These movements also occur frequently and may result in unnatural motions involving the bending of objects such as links between nodes along paths not considered suitable for normal transport. Such movements results in distortions caused by kinetic energy being transferred between adjacent vectors relating to normal locomotion via mesh lifting mechanisms known as gravitational lift effects occurring primarily at low speeds. These motions cause distortions evident prior to the actual collisions but appear before any collisions occurred thus permitting inadvertent movement experiments to be carried out during the calculation period. Another problem occurs when attempting to calculate velocity distributions around similar positions within a network regardless of whether neighboring nodes exist within the network. Further, when two nodes interact together allowing for collisions with other nodes based either independently or jointly, the computation area increases exponentially particularly when the different velocity measurements represent real conditions leading to aggregated motion estimates multiplied by an error signal resulting in unwanted distortions. Statistical calculations performed under this condition require further processing compared to standard methods intended solely to estimate the moving velocity distributions surrounding a stationary proximity perspective. In addition, the method is subjectively affected by the external environment and changes in the center line velocity characteristics of the nodes. For example, with each observer having differing backcrossing or line speed and angle values while observing motion associated with a fixed node causing the variables to increase significantly when observers move closer together. New regulations take effect on 1 January, reducing individual compensation to PS75,000 per institution. Previously, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) offered protection of up to PS85,000 per account. Joint accounts will now have protection lowered to PS150,000. The EU-wide maximum compensation is set at EUR100,000, but the UK level has been adjusted due to the pound's stronger value against the euro. The exact amount was established on 3 July 2015. A senior Tory MP criticized the change as "defective." While 95% of savers remain protected, up to 2.5 million individuals might lose coverage, according to the FSCS. The scheme advises those with over PS75,000 in a single account or institution to transfer funds if needed. Additional savings in other institutions may not be covered if the banks share a license. For instance, if someone has PS75,000 in HSBC, any extra savings in First Direct would not be protected since both banks hold the same license. Similarly, users of Bank of Scotland and Halifax face the same issue. However, RBS and NatWest, though sister banks, are registered separately, allowing savers to protect up to PS75,000 in accounts with both institutions. "Despite the simplicity, the complexity arises because FSCS coverage is shared among banks operating under the same license," said Hannah Maundrell, editor-in-chief of money.co.uk. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) maintains a comprehensive list of registered banks and their associated brands. Under the new rules, savers with up to PS1m in accounts, temporarily, such as after selling a home or losing employment, are also protected. To qualify for compensation, the cash must not have been in the account for more than six months. An additional caution applies to certain foreign banks.

You're pretty much right. When breathing without making sound, the vocal cords (or vocal folds) sit out of the way. When speaking, the folds tighten and move toward the middle of your airway. When they vibrate, the air moving through them responds to that like it would with any other sound source, transmitting that vibration out of your mouth as a sound. Your voice is pretty much an advanced, nuanced biological oboe.

Since the 2005 revival, the Doctor generally travels with a primary female companion, who occupies a larger narrative role. Steven Moffat described the companion as the main character of the series in 2008 and 2009.[7] The Tenth Doctor's first companion was Amy Pond,[89] the Eleventh and Thirteenth Doctors' companions were River Song[101112] and Jodie Whittaker respectively; however, for Peter Capaldi's final season (2017-2018), he would be accompanied by a different companion each episode until his regeneration at the end of Series 12, after which she will never be seen again on screen, or in any media beyond unseen footage from the set via YouTube.[13], showing that the concept is shifting away somewhat from previous incarnations. In its early years, the show had two male companions, one played by Jon Pertwee, another played by Colin Baker. The Doctor has been portrayed by actor David Tennant since 2006 when he took over from Matt Smith. He was succeeded as the Twelfth Doctor by Chris Chibnall, who replaced him following his departure from the programme during the second half of 2017.[14] It has also featured actress Jenna Coleman playing Clara Oswald for many seasons starting from Series 4 onward, preceded by her debut performance under the pseudonym Sybill Trelawney. She was promoted to her true character upon Tennant's exit due to scheduling conflicts between filming commitments and television production. Claire Ferguson took over from Coleman throughout the run of Series 8, while Jenna Coleman departed permanently at the conclusion of Series 9.[15] The Eleventh Doctor's successor was Broadchurch starJody Houser, who initially auditioned remotely but later travelled to Cardiff to try out for the part,[16] replacing Karen Gillan after her maternity leave ended well before the start of production on Series 11. The Ninth Doctor's next companion was Pearl Mackie, who joined the cast midway through Series 5-6. Doctor Who returned in 2018 with BBC American doctor Jodie Whittaker taking over for Coleman as the thirteenth Doctor. Whittaker announced her departure earlier than expected leaving the writing team scrambling to find a replacement before casting Paul McGann was confirmed for the Fourth Doctor part; this marked the first time an actor other than Tom Baker had appeared alongside Patrick Troughton in the title role. However, it was not intended to be the last time Troughton made an appearance in the role: In January 2019, rumours emerged of "a spectacular revelation" in Baker's story arc, leading to speculation about whether or not the fourth Doctor might return to face off against the Fifth Doctor - who was regenerating into Christopher Eccleston.[17] In May 2019, it was officially revealed that both the Fourth and Fifth doctors would appear in upcoming episodes airing shortly prior to Christmas.

A floor stone commemorating Philip Larkin, who passed away in 1985, will be placed alongside the names of Britain's most beloved poets, such as WH Auden, TS Eliot, and William Wordsworth. The tribute will be unveiled on 2 December 2016, marking the 31st anniversary since his death. The last poet honored was Ted Hughes in 2011. Larkin’s works, including "The Whitsun Weddings" and "This Be The Verse," which features his well-known reflections on "your mum and dad," have earned him recognition as one of Britain’s top 20th-century poets. The honor was decided by the Dean of Westminster, the Reverend John Hall. "Philip Larkin is among the greatest English poets of the 20th century, and I’ve been urged by several of his colleagues and friends to memorialize him," Hall stated to the BBC. Professor Edwin Dawes, leader of the Philip Larkin Society, noted that Larkin’s poetry was cited more frequently than that of any other contemporary poet. "The memorialization of Philip Larkin in Poets’ Corner will be enthusiastically received by his admirers across all fields," he said. "We are pleased to see Larkin joining the cultural center of the nation in Westminster Abbey, alongside Britain’s most influential writers." Born in Coventry in 1922, Larkin attended Oxford and published his first poems in 1940. He became the university librarian at Hull in 1955 and released "The Less Deceived" that year. His final collection, "High Windows," appeared in 1974. In December 1984, a month before his death from cancer, he was offered the role of Poet Laureate but refused, citing the high public visibility of the position. The release of Larkin’s letters provided a controversial glimpse into his private life, leading to allegations of racism and misogyny. Although this affected his reputation, in 2003, he was recognized as the nation’s most loved poet in the past half-century.

By the late 1980s, Estonians viewed their population shifts as a national crisis. This situation stemmed from the Soviet Nationalization Program's migration policies, which included the Russification of Estonia through both administrative and military immigration of non-Estonians from the USSR, alongside the forced relocation of Estonians back to the USSR.
