" Hello Mrs. President. " " Hello Mr. - " Hillary glanced at her calendar " Smith ." His appointment was for 2 whole hours. This gentleman must be quite important to occupy so much of her time. " Have you become accustomed to your new chair yet? " he asked with a smile " Well, it's only been a week and I've spent the entire time getting filled in on all sorts of issues, now that my security clearance has been upgraded. " she said, hoping she did not come across as too complaining. " I'm afraid this is another one of such meetings. " Mr. Smith said apologetically. " Oh, I'm sure it's not too bad. Most of what happens in here is really just the continuations of old problems my husband used to tell me about. " " He wouldn't have heard about this issue, as we didn't know about it before 2002. " he said. " Also, I should remind you that this subject is on a strictly need-to-know basis, so you might not want to discuss it with your husband. " Hillary almost chuckled at his little cliche, but something told her that this was serious. The man before her was very well composed and obviously experienced. He did not seem to be impressed with meeting the president for the first time. " So what is this about? My calender only mentions your name and that you are a scientist of some unspecified sort. " she said. " Well, that is true, although I would put more on my business card, if I had one. I am the director of a research institution that was founded in late 2002 to examine an object of alien origin. " he said. Hillary knew that many scientists mused about the possibility of aliens, but she had never been interested in that discussion. She knew she should probably be excited about the fact that alien life was apparently confirmed, but she had gotten used to the president-routine now and quickly got on with the practical details. " Okay. Interesting. How expensive is it and what results have you come up with? " she asked bluntly. " It is very expensive. Currently we are using about 100 billion dollars annually, and it used to be higher. " he said. He looked down for a short moment and then continued. " And as for the results, we are only working on containment, and it is successfully being contained. ." That was a large number. She should have noticed such an amount of money in the budgets. " I am pretty familiar with the government finances. How do you manage to get that amount of money? I'm pretty sure I haven't seen'Alien research' on any of the budget proposals. " she said with a smile. " We get it through the military spending of the State Department. " he said. Well the State Department spending did go up 350 billion between 2002 and 2010 but.... " But how did you get it while the war in Iraq was going on? " she inquired. " The war wasn't as expensive as reported. So we just got the extra overhead. " he replied. Hillery hoped this wasn't the only reason they had gone to Iraq. " Okay. You said you were working on containment only? What kind of object is this? " " Yes, " he said " The object is a perfect cube about 1 meter across. We discovered it in the middle of a meteor crater surrounded by a 5 meter thick spherical shield. The inner part of the shield was made of gold and the outer part was made of a very heat resistant and durable alloy. " Hillary didn't care much for the technical aspects, but it seemed well rehearsed, so she didn't interrupt. " But although the shield was very resistant against blunt force impact, it was easy enough to cut open. So in 2004, we did. We accounted for everything, and prepared for the worst. Even if the cube had been made out of antimatter, the bunker would have contained the explosion. At first, after we opened the sphere, it was rather anticlimactic. Just a black cube, covered in a slimy substance. After a few minutes our initial analysis showed that the substance contained an acid, perfect for dissolving the explosion-proof container we had made. We quickly encapsulated it in a plastic container, that the acid should have been inert to, but after a few minutes the substance changed properties and started dissolving the plastic. " he explained. Mr. Smith shrugged his shoulders and continued. " We ended up placing it inside the original gold container again. " That did sound anticlimactic. " So I guess that accounts for the expenses up to 2004. What did you do afterwards? " Hillary asked. " Well, after we had closed up the gold shell, we detected an extremely small vibration from inside. It turns out, that the substance contained micro machinery which was drilling through the gold. This seemed strange since it could have done that before we brought it in. However, it became clear that this object was harvesting energy from the environment and using this to break down the gold. We discovered it because it drilled far less in the gold after we turned off the lights when replacing the shield. " Mr Smith explained. " Soon after it completely stopped drilling. We hoped that it meant that it had run out of energy, which could perhaps allow us to do more experiments on it. But after a few months of being in the same container, it suddenly started making its microscopic holes in the gold like it was drilling through butter. We just barely avoided a containment breach, and afterwards we found out, that it had probably harvested energy from combination of two things. A small thermal gradient, and vibration energy from a motor running nearby. " " A thermal gradient? " Hillary asked with one eyebrow raised. Now she had let him talk uninterrupted for long enough. Scientists often seemed to have a habit of sliding into an overly technical jargon when they had been talking for too long. " Sorry, it's when there are two different temperatures on each side of an object. It can be used to generate energy, but it's usually in so tiny amounts that - " " Okay ," Hillary interrupted before he could get going again. " So it seems like it wants to escape, and you are trying to contain it, although it's proving to be difficult. " " Yes, but the fact that it suddenly started storing its energy instead of constantly drilling, implies that it understands, that it is being contained and it is getting smarter about escaping. This caused us to ramp up the security. There now are quite a lot of layers of different protection mechanisms in place. " Mr. Smith clarified. Hillary could see the difficulties, but it did not seem to make sense. Why was it trying to escape? " Have you tried communicating with it? " She asked. " Well, we have tried. We drill small holes in the gold shield to interact with the object and send in signals. Mostly low power, low frequency communication, as we don't want to give it energy. So far the only response we have gotten is dissolving equipment. " he said while shrugging his shoulders again. " We don't know what it's for or why it's here on earth. We do have some ideas, and they seem to universally conclude that keeping the object isolated from its surroundings is the best course of action. " " Can you elaborate on the ideas? How can you possibly conclude anything from an object that doesn't communicate? " Hillary asked sceptically. " Well, we know it was sent to earth in a shell that isolated the object. So someone, somewhere thought that sending it without a prison was a bad idea. The question is, why not just throw it into the sun, if they didn't want it to be free? Until the early 1980s, industry was a major source of water pollution. Although many plants and factories can be found along the Rhine up into Switzerland, it is along the Allee des Neues Darmstadt in Germany that most of this septic waste goes down stream to the sea. The river is also heavily polluted with the solid waste generated by people who live or work near the river banks such as manure, excrement and a variety of garden products. The industrial sector has developed very rapidly since the early 1990's when new technologies were introduced which made it possible for large industries to operate in areas lacking adequate sewage treatment systems. Results from municipal sewerage studies show that in Berlin there are approximately 3 million residents living within 1 kilometer of a major wastewater treatment plant while in Munich over 2 million reside close enough to the wastewater plant to have significant environmental impacts from seepages and overflows. Industrial effluents flow directly off site through sewers into storm drains and will eventually continue their journey through the environment at an accelerated rate. Industrial waste contains about 70 percent dissolved organic matter (DO) which poses serious health risks to humans, animals and aquatic life if not processed prior to discharge. If untreated these pollutants may cause harmful effects to rivers, lakes and oceans. The majority of industrial activities occur on riverbanks where people spend much time during the day due to the proximity to waterways. Overfishing, loss of habitat and other social problems associated with human activity around water bodies create pollution challenges. The River Severn is marked by the presence of numerous industrial sites including chemical production facilities, textile mills, paper mills, glass manufacturing units and power stations. Defensive Counterair (DCA) refers to all the defensive strategies aimed at detecting, identifying, intercepting, and neutralizing enemy forces that attempt to infiltrate or attack friendly airspace (JP 1-02). A key objective of DCA, when combined with Offensive Counterarea (OCA) operations, is to establish a safe zone where friendly forces can operate and remain protected from aerial and missile threats. The DCA mission integrates both active and passive defense mechanisms. Active defense involves the use of limited offensive actions and counterattacks to prevent the enemy from controlling a specific area or position (JP 1-02). This includes ballistic missile defense, air-breathing threat mitigation, and protection against point, area, and high-value airborne asset threats. Passive defense focuses on reducing the likelihood and minimizing the impact of harm caused by hostile actions without aiming for a proactive advantage. It includes measures such as detection and warning systems, chemical, biological, radioactive, and nuclear defense, camouflage, concealment, and deception, hardening, reconstitution, dispersion, redundancy, and mobility, countermeasures, and stealth.

Researchers have discovered a new Linux backdoor called Symbiote that uses novel evasion techniques to conceal its presence. It is able to scrub any sign of infection from the file system when it is running and also uses steganography to hide its malicious code inside .PNG image files. The Symbiote malware was discovered by researchers from security firm ESET. It is designed to inject its code into legitimate processes on a compromised machine. The malware consists of a backdoor module that runs in the background and a dropper module that injects its code into a legitimate process, in this case, the xrdp process that is used to allow remote desktop access. The xrdp process is run as root and is designed to interact with the xrdp daemon using the D-Bus inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism. "After being injected, the malware hooks into the D-Bus interface for the Xrdp process. This allows the malware to control the xrdp daemon," the ESET researchers said in a report. The malware communicates with a command-and-control (CC) server over a non-standard HTTPS port. Symbiote doesn't use any polymorphic code obfuscation techniques, but its steganographic capabilities and the fact that it can scrub all signs of its presence from the file system might make it difficult for users and security products to detect. "One of the main reasons this malware is hard to detect is that it hides its presence in the file system," the ESET researchers said. "During the infection process, the malware creates a tmpfs (RAM-based) file system in the runuser1000gvfs directory." The malware creates a file called .cache on this RAM-based file system. The contents of the .cache file are encrypted with AES-256-CBC, but this is done to hide the malware's configuration data and not the malicious code itself. "The malware code is executed directly from this tmpfs file system," the researchers said. "It also stores all the log files generated by the malware in the runuser1000gvfs directory." When the malware is done executing, it wipes the contents of this directory and unmounts the tmpfs file system. This effectively removes all traces of its presence in the file system. ESET malware researcher Lukas Stefanko believes that the malware is most likely used in highly targeted attacks. He noted that the CC server identified so far is only reachable from IP addresses in Brazil. "However, the malware is not 'Brazil-exclusive, he said. "It can be easily adapted to attack any region in the world." In a blog post, Stefanko also noted that the xrdp RDP server is enabled by default on many Linux distributions, making it an attractive attack vector for malware writers. Symbiote is not the first malware to use steganography to conceal its data. A malware program called DarkHotel used this technique to hide its code inside images. Another piece of malware that was distributed through a similar supply-chain attack was the recently patched Drupal flaw. A mountain range stretching across the eastern coastline, known as the Great Dividing Range, facilitates the lifting of moist air from the ocean. As this air rises, it cools and condenses, resulting in rainfall on the windward side of the range. This process supports the development of forests on the coastal side. On the leeward side, the region experiences a rain shadow effect, receiving significantly less precipitation. The western coast lacks such a mountain range, leading to minimal rainfall. Additionally, factors like temperature, geological composition, and soil conditions contribute to the absence of forests in the west. While there is a small area near Perth, the southern part of Western Australia, with the Darling Scarp, receives some rainfall, supporting limited forest growth. However, most of western and northern Australia experiences seasonal monsoons, causing intense rainfall followed by prolonged droughts, which are not suitable for long-term forest development.

John viewed the interdict as comparable to a papal declaration of war. He sought to punish Innocent personally and create division among English clergy who might support him versus those aligned with Roman authorities. John confiscated the property of clergy who refused to perform services, as well as estates tied to Innocent himself. He detained the illegitimate wives of many clergymen and released them only after paying fines. He also seized land held by church members who had left England and offered protection to those who remained loyal to him. Many religious institutions negotiated ways to manage their properties and retain their estate revenues. By 1209, the situation remained unresolved, and Innocent threatened to excommunicate John if he did not accept Langton's appointment. When this threat fell flat, Innocent excommunicated the king in November 1209. While this was a significant challenge to John’s legitimacy, it did not deeply concern him. Two of his key supporters, Emperor Otto IV and Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, had already faced similar punishment, and the impact of excommunication had diminished. John intensified his existing policies and collected substantial funds from vacant churches and monasteries, including an estimate from 1213 suggesting the church had lost approximately 100,000 marks (about 66,666 at the time) to John. Official records indicate that around 14 percent of the annual income from the English church was being taken by John each year.

The Treaties and Regulations may have direct effect if they are clear, unconditional, and immediate, whereas Directives typically do not grant individuals (rather than member states) the right to bring legal actions against other individuals. This is due to Article 288 of the TFEU, which stipulates that Directives are directed at member states and usually allow national authorities to choose how and when to implement them. This reflects that many Directives establish minimum standards, with member states able to impose stricter requirements. For instance, the Working Time Directive mandates at least four weeks of paid leave annually, yet many member states enforce more than 28 days in their domestic legislation. However, according to the current stance of the Court of Justice, citizens can challenge national laws that implement Directives, but not the Directives themselves in isolation. Directives lack what is termed "horizontal" direct effect—meaning they cannot be enforced between non-state entities. This interpretation sparked significant controversy, and in the early 1990s, three Advocates General advocated for Directives to create rights and obligations for all citizens. The Court rejected this proposal, though there are five major exceptions to this rule.

After 1900 some forms of utopian socialism became popular, especially in the United States. See E. L. Godkin, Utopian Socialism (1884, repr. 1969). The term utopian socialism was first used in 1840 by the English socialist John Stuart Mill to describe what he saw as the extreme and impractical proposals of Robert Owen and other thinkers of the early 19th cent. Utopian socialism refers to a wide range of works and proposals, all of which have one thing in common: their authors look to the future and offer their vision of a perfect society. The term utopian socialism is usually used to describe a number of different doctrines and proposals in the socialist tradition. Utopian socialism can be broken into three broad categories: religious utopianism, scientific utopianism, and literary utopianism. Religious utopianism involves the creation of a society in which moral perfection can be attained. Many writers of this period felt that the society of their time was a corrupt and broken one. This corruption and decay was due to the fact that most people were too selfish to pursue moral and social ideals. The task of creating a perfect society would require the destruction of the old society, the creation of a new one, and the reeducation of the people in that new society. To accomplish this, a number of different plans were offered. A number of authors even proposed a violent overthrow of the old society. Religious utopianism was not a major part of the utopian socialist movement. It did, however, have a significant influence in the thought of such writers as William Morris and Edward Bellamy. Morris, in his utopian novel News from Nowhere, takes a strong stand against capitalism and considers the creation of a religious utopian society to be a natural result. Bellamy, in Looking Backward , proposes a society in which the means of production are owned and controlled by the government. Scientific utopianism involves the creation of a society that is based on the discoveries of science. Writers of this period believed that the world was progressing and that science and technology would eventually solve all human problems. The task of creating a perfect society would be the application of science and technology to social problems. The creation of scientific utopian societies would bring about the complete control of nature, the complete mastery of the universe, and the elimination of human suffering. As for the general question of why these locations have such arbitrary names, I assume you're American. Like many older European towns, these areas didn't have clear planning and evolved over time without formal naming conventions. In the early days, people simply described what they saw. For example, a street with a high court of chancery was called Chancery Lane, a street inhabited mainly by Jews was known as Old Jewry, and a specific market might have been called Cloth Fair or Haymarket. If a street had a significant number of prostitutes or brothels, it could be named Cock Lane or Gropecunt Lane. People were straightforward about it—just what they observed.

The Elephant and Castle name originates from a pub recorded in the oldest local documents. According to Wikipedia, the name "Elephant and Castle" comes from a coaching inn. The earliest surviving reference to this name in the area appears in the Court Leet Book of the Manor of Walworth, dated March 21, 1765, when the meeting was held at "Elephant and Castle, Newington." Before that, the location was occupied by a blacksmith and cutler, whose coat of arms featured an elephant with a castle (possibly representing a howdah) on its back, likely due to the use of elephant ivory in their tools.

Blackfriars refers to the area behind Ludgate Hill. It is believed to derive from Dominican monks who relocated their monastery to the area in the 13th century. They wore black caps, and the title for a monk was "brother." The term "frère" (French for brother) eventually became "Friar," and the name spread to the order. Another theory suggests it was named because it's located near the old Ludgate, the eastern continuation of Fleet Street. The exact origin of Ludgate remains uncertain; it may stem from a flood gate or a fleet gate, or from Old English terms like hlidgeat or ludgeat, meaning a postern, swinging gate, or black gate.

Commons Leader Chris Grayling said the change, also applying in some cases to Welsh MPs, would bring "real fairness to our constitutional arrangements." SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon called the plan "staggering in the extent.... of its hypocrisy and incoherence." Labour said it was an "outrage" that ministers wanted to rush into making "profound constitutional change." Shadow Commons leader Angela Eagle said the plans risked creating two classes of MPs and accused the Conservatives of a "cynical" attempt to "manufacture itself a very much larger" majority in the Commons. Under the proposals, all MPs would continue to vote on all key stages of legislation. But English MPs - and in some cases English and Welsh MPs - will have a veto in Westminster when debating matters that have been devolved to the devolved administrations. MPs will debate the changes on 15 July, Mr Grayling said, and the system will be changed using the rules - known as standing orders - that dictate how Parliament conducts its business. With more powers set to be devolved to the Scottish Parliament after September's independence referendum, Tory MPs have said it is not right that MPs representing Scottish constituencies can continue to determine laws affecting England only. Mr Grayling told MPs that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland were getting a "stronger voice" and that it was "only fair" to do the same for England. The Speaker will be asked to certify which bills or parts of bills relate to England or England and Wales only, he said. There will be no changes in the House of Lords, Mr Grayling said. But where Lords amendments are certified as England or England and Wales only, a "double majority" system applies, meaning it will need a majority of both the whole House of Commons and MPs representing English or English and Welsh constituencies. Tablet computers will be used to count MPs' votes as they walk through the voting lobbies so officials can instantly register whether they have used their veto in votes where the "double majority" rule applies. To jeers from opposition benches, Mr Grayling said "Today we are answering the West Lothian Question," a reference to the constitutional anomaly that lets Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland MP at Westminster vote on measures that only apply in England. English votes: What's going on? The SNP's Pete Wishart described the English votes policy as a "cobbled together unworkable mess," and said it was "totally unacceptable." He said this policy showed that the Tories were doing their best to ensure Scotland would become an independent country. His party leader Nicola Sturgeon said: "The Tories have produced a constitutional shambles - staggering in the extent of its hypocrisy and incoherence. "Under these plans - which are all about cutting Scottish MPs out of votes which impact on Scotland and our budget - the Tories are proposing an'English veto' and'double majority'. "I have been very clear that, at least in part, the level of support for independence will be determined by what the Tory government at Westminster does, as well as what the SNP Government does. And there is no question that the great disrespect shown to Scotland in these proposals is likely to have more people asking whether Westminster is capable of representing Scotland's interests at all." Labour's Sir Gerald Kaufman, the father of the house, said the title of the motion, English votes for English laws, "sounds racist." He added: "This government is undermining the whole basis of British democracy, right through from when the Magna Carta was signed."

Drive A functions as the primary floppy drive, while Drive B serves as the secondary one. Drive C is typically the primary hard drive, and Drives D through Z are additional hard drives. Disc drives, such as CD-ROMs, also fall under these categories. The drive labeled A and B were historically used as floppy drives, like on the IBM PC XT from around 1983. This subject is incredibly intriguing. It revolves around scale, efficiency, and an additional dimension. Size indeed influences heart rate. Mice, anatomically speaking, are miniature elephants. Their hearts grow proportionally with their bodies, which leads to the question: why doesn’t their heart rate remain constant? And why does it actually decrease as size increases? To make the concept even more engaging, I can forecast the heart rate of a species as large as a whale or a wombat based on its weight before measuring it. Heart rate follows a 1:1 ratio with weight, or approximately 14th power. This exponent is important to remember. It’s not merely heart rate; weight can also be used to estimate other factors such as metabolism, lifespan, brain size relative to intelligence, oxygen requirements, and reproductive rates over a lifetime. These predictions apply to the typical animal of a given size. The principle isn’t limited to animals alone—it also applies to trees, organizational structures like ant colonies or public companies, and even cities. Life progresses faster in larger urban areas, and you can estimate a company’s lifespan based on its organizational size. Both trends exhibit exponential growth on average. 

To address the question, what causes this phenomenon? What connects mice, elephants, humans, trees, and even cities on a fundamental level? They all require resources to reach every part of their structure. As mass increases, delivering blood (oxygen and nutrients) to each individual cell becomes essential. Once a cardiovascular system develops, there must be a network of tubes reaching every cell—similarly, roads must extend to every address. Each road, including driveways, must connect to a house. This forms a fractal pattern, where the same structural principles repeat at every scale, akin to the branching of tree limbs.

Make bedtime routine for them and make sure they're in bed at the same time each night. [substeps] Include extracurriculars like soccer and dance class in this schedule, as well. 2) Schedule naps. Your children need to spend time on their own during the day - the more time you give them alone without an adult watching over them, the better. This will let kids get rid of pent-up energy before nighttime comes around again. If your child is particularly needy or cranky in the early hours after a nap, try putting him down earlier than usual so he's still tired when it gets dark outside. Keep sleep schedules consistent throughout the week (if possible), which allows older teenagers to begin relaxing into a normal pattern, too. [substeps] Napping helps kids focus and play effectively later on, because both those things are important factors in academic success. 3) Get exercise! For most teens, getting enough physical activity is easier said than done; some students find it fun but others never want to go out with friends or do sports themselves unless it involves working up a sweat and sweating off any extra calories. Try making a point of walking together regularly while shopping, cooking dinner or going to school. Being active can help improve mood, decrease stress levels and even boost workout motivation. Even just 15 minutes of light exercise daily could have long-term benefits for teens. [substeps] Getting plenty of movement boosts cognitive performance and prevents infections from viruses that thrive on sedentary lifestyles. It also makes your teen less likely to develop chronic illnesses such as diabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, all known risk factors for heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes. 4) Establish healthy eating habits. A lot of parents think having a meal plan, menu card or grocery list means that kid's meals come out perfect every single day. But if everyone follows these basic guidelines, your kids' diets won't be filled with junk food: Avoid added sugar. Sugar spikes insulin production in our bodies a couple times per hour, leaving us feeling hungry longer afterward. Studies show sugary drinks contribute nearly 20 percent of total calorie intake among U.S. adolescents aged 12-17 years old.[substeps] Cutting back on soda pop and other sweetened beverages will not only make your kids healthier but save money by preventing weight gain. Make lunchtime supervision optional. Kids who don't feel controlled by adults tend to eat junkier foods and skip breakfast. And research suggests teens learn how much food they should consume from what they see at restaurants.[substeps] So turning away from school lunches altogether may encourage healthier choices. And helping kids prepare their own lunches might increase nutritional value since they'll know exactly what goes inside the sandwich. [substeps] 5) Teach responsibility. Don't expect your teen to take care of everything in his life right now. Instead ask him to pitch in around the house. Give him chores that are small enough to keep him busy yet big enough to teach responsibility. Quiz him on math problems before giving him dishes to wash, then settle scores over dinner. These kinds of assignments foster independence in teens and support family dynamics. 6) Make bedtime routines specific to your child. At first glance, establishing a strict bedtime isn't necessarily helpful. In fact, many studies suggest that kids whose parents impose rigid rules about when they must fall asleep wind up sleeping worse. However, individualized bedtimes that meet your teen's needs work best. Some families choose to ban television at bedtime in favor of reading books. Others stick strictly to age-appropriate bedtimes. The key here is to create routines that correspond closely to your child's development stage. You don't want to force a child to start sleeping through the night until grade school age, just to make him too sleepy in college. [substeps] If your teenager doesn't mind staying up late playing video games, read him a book instead to make sure you've set aside sufficient time for relaxation after homework has been finished. Or maybe turn off computers 30 minutes before bedtime instead of relying solely on "screen timeout" programs that promise nothing more than unplugging a device temporarily. 7) Be supportive. Teens often struggle with balance between home responsibilities and social obligations; setting boundaries and enforcing discipline becomes increasingly difficult once a person reaches adolescence. Helping young people maintain challenging routines is essential for reaching maturity. Plus, there's no reason why you shouldn't enjoy your teen's accomplishments alongside her!

Pregnant women are more prone to malaria due to weakened immunity, according to the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). Malaria poses significant risks to both the mother and fetus, including miscarriage, stillbirth, and preterm labor. This tropical illness is spread by mosquitoes and leads to fever, flu-like symptoms, vomiting, and diarrhea. While there have been no malaria-related deaths among pregnant or recently pregnant women in the UK in the past ten years, the RCOG reports concerns from anxious patients. Approximately 1,500 malaria cases are reported annually in the UK, with around 10 fatalities, according to the RCOG. The college recommends avoiding non-essential travel to regions with high malaria risk. High-risk zones encompass much of Africa, Asia—including China and India—Central and South America, parts of the Middle East, and certain Pacific islands. If travel is necessary, the RCOG suggests consulting a center specializing in malaria for guidance on preventive measures. Pregnant women should be informed of the risk, use mosquito nets for protection, and take antimalarial medication. Philippa Marsden, chair of the RCOG’s patient information committee, emphasized that while the risks remain low, it is crucial for women to stay well-informed. Cath Broderick of the RCOG women’s network noted that if women experience symptoms after returning from a high-risk area and suspect malaria, they should seek medical attention promptly and disclose their recent travel history. Symptoms may manifest within a week or longer after being bitten.

Today's Reed Dance is not an ancient ritual but a modern evolution of the older "umchwasho" tradition. In "umchwasho," all young girls were grouped into a female military unit. If a girl became pregnant outside of marriage, her family had to pay a fine of one cow to the local chief. After several years, when the girls were ready for marriage, they performed labor duties for the Queen Mother, concluding with dancing and celebration. The practice of "umchwasho" remained in place in the region until August 19, 2005.

It's been a bit of an annus horribilis for the internet and all of us who frequent it. In the past year, the world wide web has faced several challenges that have impacted our daily lives, from cybersecurity threats to misinformation and online censorship. One of the biggest threats to the internet this year has been the rise of cyberattacks. In just the first six months of 2021, there were several high-profile hacks that affected millions of people around the world. From the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack to the Microsoft Exchange Server breach, these cybersecurity incidents have caused disruptions in supply chains, energy systems, and governments, and have highlighted the need for stronger online security measures. Misinformation has also been a major problem on the internet this year. The COVID-19 pandemic sparked a deluge of fake news, conspiracy theories, and hoaxes that have been widely shared on social media platforms. This information can be dangerous, as it can influence people's perceptions and behavior, and can harm public health efforts. Social media companies are struggling to keep up with this onslaught, and are being pressed to increase their content moderation practices. Another issue affecting the internet, particularly in countries with authoritarian regimes, is online censorship. Governments in countries like China, Russia, and Iran have increasingly used the internet to control information and suppress dissent. This has led to the blocking of websites, censorship of social media platforms, and even the arrest of online users who criticize their governments. Despite these challenges, there have been efforts to make the internet a better place. Online activism and social movements have gained widespread attention through platforms like Twitter and Instagram. Advocacy groups are working to protect users' privacy rights and push for responsible tech policies. And tech companies are developing new tools and approaches to combat online harms such as misinformation and cybercrimes. As we approach the end of 2021, it's clear that the internet remains an essential part of our lives, but one that we must continue to monitor and safeguard. By holding tech companies accountable and demanding responsible policies from our leaders, we can help ensure a safer and more secure online world for all.

Huge amounts of digital videos are being produced and broadcast every day, leading to giant media archives. Effective techniques are needed to make such data accessible further. Automatic meta-data labelling of broadcast media is an essential task for multimedia indexing, where it is standard to use multi-modal input for such purposes. This paper describes a novel method for automatic detection of media genre and show identities using acoustic features, textual features or a combination thereof. Furthermore the inclusion of available meta-data, such as time of broadcast, is shown to lead to very high performance. Latent Dirichlet Allocation is used to model both acoustics and text, yielding fixed dimensional representations of media recordings that can then be used in Support Vector Machines based classification. Experiments are conducted on more than 1200 hours of TV broadcasts from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), where the task is to categorise the broadcasts into 8 genres or 133 show identities. On a 200-hour test set, accuracies of 98.6 and 85.7 were achieved for genre and show identification respectively, using a combination of acoustic and textual features with meta-data.

It takes more time and research to maximize smaller engines than just build a larger engine.,Almost every answer on here is wrong. Some more than others. Internal combustion engines are very complex and giving a simplified ELI5 answer really doesn't do it justice. Remember that when a manufacturer reports horsepower, they are reporting peak horsepower, meaning the most power the engine makes over it's rev range. To avoid getting too heavily into technical terms, imagine this.... Try flooring your car at 1500rpm, then try it again at 4000rpm, since your car most likely has a power curve that makes more power at higher RPM's, you will accelerate more quickly when you floor it at 4000rpm. That is because your engine is making less power at 1500 rpm. Saying that two cars make "300hp" is not very telling if one makes 300hp at all revs, and the other produces 300hp at a very high rev and doesn't make much power at other times. There are many reasons why some manufacturers choose to use large displacement engines. One of the best reasons is what we just went over, often times a large displacement engine can produce a more even power curve. This is not always true, but it is easier to make an engine with a large displacement have a balanced power curve. This is great for all kinds of driving because being able to accelerate quickly from a low rpm is useful for road driving and racing. Another reason is simplicity and weight. Weight? What? I thought that bigger displacement meant heavier! Not quite. Smaller displacement engines often use turbo chargers to help boost their power and efficiency. This is good, but turbo chargers add their own weight, take up space, and usually come with supporting units like inter coolers that take up more weight and space and will affect the car's center of gravity as well as a host of other driving characteristics. The third reason why large displacement engines are used is because they usually place less stress on components. Without diving into the combustion process, understand that making a small displacement engine produce the same horsepower as a large displacement engine makes it more "high strung." Components are exposed to higher pressures and higher stresses. This with the added complexity of turbo chargers means that they can wear out more quickly (2.0L turbo charged Mitsubishi Evolutions are a good example of this) and be less susceptible to adverse conditions. Since the components are less stressed in a large displacement engine, they can also be made cheaper, making service cheaper. Furthermore, a relatively unstressed engine is easier to modify to produce more power while an already high strung engine might be at the peak of its abilities without heavily sacrificing reliability. Large displacement engines have drawbacks, they often use more fuel and produce more emissions. A turbocharger that they might lack increases efficiency. However, do not confuse large displacement with exterior weight or size. There is much more to this. Notice that I try to use "usually" as much as possibly because there are very many exceptions. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is a scientific intergovernmental body under the auspices of the United Nations, set up at the request of member governments. It was first formed as an independent organization in 1990 and re-established in 1997 after a period of internal turmoil within its membership. On January 1st 2007 the IPCC expanded to include the European Union's climate services following the launch by the executive body of the European Commission of the "Climate Action Plan." On April 21st 2011, the IPCC met for the third time since forming, with most countries signing onto the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (policies formulated by 194 governments, which were adopted in December 2015). The meeting agreed that a new assessment of emissions must be issued every five years from now until 2028; this will indicate whether global warming has slowed or sped up, according to scientists' estimates.

This study presents a hybrid parallel computation strategy aimed at solving a two-dimensional acoustic wave equation numerically using an implicit finite difference method on a single machine. The computations are performed within an implicit finite difference framework. Initially, the differential equation is converted into an implicit finite difference form, followed by the application of the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method to decompose the equation into two separate sub-equations. These sub-equations are solved using the cyclic reduction algorithm to obtain an approximate solution. Subsequently, the algorithm is adapted for parallel execution across GPU, GPUOpenMP, and Hybrid (GPUOpenMPMPI) architectures. The primary objective is to enhance the efficiency of the parallel algorithms by optimizing their execution speed. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid implementation yields accurate outcomes, as verified by comparing its results with those from traditional CPU, CUDA, and CUDAOpenMP simulations.

The 1080p format demands twice the bandwidth compared to 720p. In broadcast systems like cable, satellite, and terrestrial signals, the available bandwidth is constrained by the frequency range permitted. While theoretically possible to transmit 1080p without increasing the bitrate beyond 720p, this would result in significant compression artifacts. With double the pixels but no corresponding doubling of space for transmission, the data must be compressed twice as much. If a satellite is already operating at 400 720p channels, shifting all to 1080p without substantial compression would limit capacity to 200 channels. This would require raising channel prices or reducing revenue. Similar challenges apply to cable and terrestrial broadcasts. For 4K, the pixel count increases fourfold compared to 1080p, or eightfold over 720p. Each 4K channel may necessitate excluding six to eight 720p channels due to bandwidth limitations. The radio frequency spectrum is a finite resource; additional frequencies cannot be allocated arbitrarily as they might cause interference. Imagine a TV station broadcasting on the same frequencies used for phone calls—there would be severe interference, rendering phones unusable. It’s simpler to stream ultra-high-definition video via the internet since the internet isn’t a broadcast medium. Broadcasts transmit all channels simultaneously, consuming substantial bandwidth but simplifying reception. Internet TV, however, uses minimal bandwidth as only the specific channel being watched is transmitted.

" Oh, what a lovely balloon! " Aenea exclaimed. " I've never seen one like that before. Did you make it? " Christopher beamed; " Yep! " He was very proud of his balloon. It was very pretty; red, and blue, and sparkling inside. " It's so... big! " she said. " You must have a very deep breath! " Christopher nodded vigorously, and continued on his way. He had to find father, and quickly. His balloon was quite big, to be sure. But, he'd not breathed that much life into it. No more than the last one. He kept it hidden, most of the time. Father had warned him not to show anyone. At least, once he'd been convinced there was something odd about it. That in and of itself had taken some time. " Some balloons grow, " his father had said. " It's perfectly normal. Don't worry. They all stop after a few million years. " Except it hadn't stopped. Not even a little. If anything it was gaining momentum. And it was getting heavier. It still floated, of course, but occasionally, the string seemed to tug at his hand, as if it were trying to escape. He hadn't told his father about this yet. He'd already had to hide his balloon where he could only see it once in a while. He didn't want to risk losing it forever. Suddenly, a hideous sound ripped through space and time. It was coming from the balloon. " Ack! " Christoper gasped, and rushed to find the new leak. He pored carefully over every tiny surface, slowly, intently. All the while the hiss of escaping dimensions expanding assaulted his ears. They weren't meant to interact this way. " Huh! " Christopher found the problem, and the solution, together. Upon his discovery, the hissing ceased, and the balloon adopted its much more pleasant, silent, tone. His father was not going to be happy. The leaks were a recent development. He would ask father if, once balloons reached a certain age, they leaked to maintain their size. But he already knew what the answer would be. Sure, balloons grow. Balloons change colour. Balloons do some wonderful things. But no balloon had ever leaked before. And Christopher knew what it meant. It meant he was in trouble. " Father! Father! " Christopher cried. " What is it, Ch...- oh. What are you doing with that thing again? I thought I told you to hide it. " " I did hide it! I just, you know, went to check up on it. " " Is it still growing? It looks pretty big now, " his father said, flatly. " Well, yes, I think so. But, um, I think we sh....- " Christopher was saved from having to explain the situation by a new leak appearing, suddenly and violently. " Ugh! " His father said. " What is that sound?! " Immediately Christopher went to work, studying carefully, trying to find the new piece of knowledge that had appeared inside the balloon. It never took him long. The sound subsided, and Christopher stood, looking at his father, looking at him. " What. was that? " his father asked. " Yeah... that's what I wanted to show you. There's been lots of those. " " Lots? " " That I've seen. There could have been more when I wasn't around. Somewhere the balloon opens up, and if I find out why, then it closes. I think it's gotten too big. " His father looked perplexed. " If you... find out why? That doesn't make any sense. " " I know! Except, it keeps happening, and, I was wondering if maybe..... - " " What did you find out? " " Just... you know... some stuff about light and time, " Christopher said, cringing. His father abhorred light. He'd told him not to put it in his balloon. " Sure, it'll be pretty, " he had said, " but light's a troublemaker. Always doing strange things, never behaves the way it ought to. " Christopher had ignored him, of course. And when his balloon had started sparkling, and shining red and blue, his father had been convinced to allow his son to keep it, despite his own misgivings. " They're related, you know. " His father stared. " Yes, " he said, after a time, " I know. What happens if you don't find out? " " No idea, " Christopher said. " I've never let it go. The sound's too horrible. " His father sat in silence, thinking. " Well, it can't hurt to let it shrink a little bit at least. " The same thought had occurred to Christopher. It must have happened, while he wasn't there. Which meant that it must have stopped, eventually. No balloons had ever opened up before, not after being made. Christopher wondered what might have come out. He wondered how big his balloon might have been, if it hadn't started leaking. " I suppose it can't hurt to give it a try then, " his father said, and the two of them moved far away, to where no one would notice them, and they sat peacefully, for only a short amount of time, waiting for the next leak. Despite their intent, it was every bit as startling as the others when it appeared. A loud, jarring hiss, of folding probabilities and diverging fates. So offensive was it, that Christopher automatically went right back to work, trying to find out why. " No, stop! Let it go! " his father said. Christopher did. He let it go, and go, and go. It went for a long time. And under the cacophony, through all the roaring chaos, they suddenly noticed. The balloon wasn't shrinking at all. It was growing. Eventually it stopped, every bit as quickly and violently as it had began. The balloon wasn't noticeably larger. But it HAD grown. Of that they were both quite sure. Father and son looked at each other, staring quietly. Finally, his father said; " I think we're in trouble. "

Many of today's machine learning (ML) systems are built by reusing an array of, often pre-trained, primitive models, each fulfilling distinct functionality (e.g., feature extraction). The increasing use of primitive models significantly simplifies and expedites the development cycles of ML systems. Yet, because most of such models are contributed and maintained by untrusted sources, their lack of standardization or regulation entails profound security implications, about which little is known thus far. In this paper, we demonstrate that malicious primitive models pose immense threats to the security of ML systems. We present a broad class of model-reuse attacks wherein maliciously crafted models trigger host ML systems to misbehave on targeted inputs in a highly predictable manner. By empirically studying four deep learning systems (including both individual and ensemble systems) used in skin cancer screening, speech recognition, face verification, and autonomous steering, we show that such attacks are (i) effective - the host systems misbehave on the targeted inputs as desired by the adversary with high probability, (ii) evasive - the malicious models function indistinguishably from their benign counterparts on non-targeted inputs, (iii) elastic - the malicious models remain effective regardless of various system design choices and tuning strategies, and (iv) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data used for system tuning or inference. We provide analytical justification for the effectiveness of model-reuse attacks, which points to the unprecedented complexity of today's primitive models. This issue thus seems fundamental to many ML systems. We further discuss potential countermeasures and their challenges, which lead to several promising research directions.

The Command Module (CM) was the conical crew cabin, designed to carry three astronauts from launch to lunar orbit and back to an Earth ocean landing. It was the only component of the Apollo spacecraft to survive without major configuration changes as the program evolved from the early Apollo study designs. Its exterior was covered with an ablative heat shield, and had its own reaction control system (RCS) engines to control its attitude and steer its atmospheric entry path. Parachutes were carried to slow its descent to splashdown. The module was 11.42 feet (3.48 m) tall, 12.83 feet (3.91 m) in diameter, and weighed approximately 12,250 pounds (5,560 kg).

Calculating the masses of stars is actually fairly straightforward under certain circumstances, mainly that we can observe something orbiting around those stars. We know from our understanding of gravity and motion how orbits works, and we can predict very well the orbits of things in our solar system, so it's a very solid theory. So if we have something like a planet (or even a 2nd star) orbiting a star, we can make a few straightforward measurements that let us determine the mass of the star fairly accurately. The first measurement is the timing: how long does it take for the planet to make one complete orbit. The second measurement is the orbital speed: how fast the planet is moving (or, equivalently and easier to measure, the star will wobble slightly because of the planet's gravity, so how fast is it wobbling?). This can be measured straightforwardly through Doppler shift measurements on the light coming from the star. So with these two measurements, we can use the equations that describe the orbit, and turn them around. We know the timing and the speed, so we can determine the size of the orbit and how heavy the central star must be. As long as our measurements are accurate (and they can be done very accurately these days), our estimate of the star's mass can be quite accurate as well, within a few percent in many cases. Edit: A lot of people like the say that we can't really know, or that it's'just theory'. But all it is, in many cases, is simple applications of basic laws of physics that we have tested very very thoroughly on Earth. The laws of orbital mechanics are very well understood; we use them every time we launch a satellite.,If you know what its made out of and how much of what its made out of weighs AND you know how big it is then you know the weight!

You can spend several hours being jostled by French camera crews, squashed by Italian snappers, or shoved unceremoniously out of the way by any one of 27 other countries' journalists as the leaders of the European Union arrive one by one, and we frantically try to grab a word with them as they rush past. There'll be sharp elbows in the press pen, craning of necks and stretching of microphones, as David Cameron arrives at this summit, which could define not just his leadership, but the future of his party and his country's place in the world. But how on earth did the man who once accused the Conservatives of being out of touch for "banging on about Europe," get himself into a position where he has already been "banging on about Europe" for months and months, and will spend the next four months still doing precisely that? Since he made that claim in his first season as party leader in 2006, appearing in front of a huge video screen tastefully projected with a giant tree, there have been three big changes, linked, that have got him to this juncture, which of course ultimately is a product of his own political calculation. Most simply, as the years have passed, his party has changed. Since the Maastricht rebels failed to get a public vote in 1993 on the treaty that created the modern version of the European Union, there has been a rump of Conservatives deeply passionate about the cause, significantly concerned that the EU's laws, not Britain's own, are more important - the question of sovereignty that's a big part of the current talks. But their concerns, while shared by many Conservative Party members, were not considered mainstream in the parliamentary party - balanced, if not squeezed out, by heavyweight Europhile voices. But as the EU expanded, and generations of MPs came and went, a soft scepticism towards the European project, neither full-throated support, nor hardcore opposition, became more common, and sympathy for the idea of a referendum spread from the margins. The eurozone financial crisis, and the EU's stumbling approach to sorting it out, gave a fresh energy to eurosceptic MPs who wanted to campaign to leave. In part that apathy, if not downright dislike, towards the EU spread because of the enormous rise in the numbers of people from around the Union who came to live and work in the UK. Numbers that took the political establishment completely by surprise began to arrive from the moment new countries like Poland joined the EU in 2004. There is a complicated, and emotional debate about the impact of the numbers, but few can dispute that the effect has been very significant in some parts of the country, with figures this week showing the numbers still rising, standing at more than two million now. For many people, that very visible impact of our membership of the EU has given them pause for thought. And it was that steep rise in EU immigration that gave David Cameron his most pressing political reason for - in the end - promising a referendum. UKIP's appeal grew alongside the rise in immigration. By 2012, they were greedily nibbling at the Conservative vote with a record performance in the local elections and a leader who in some moments seemed to appeal to swathes of the public for his plain speaking, in a style that also alienated many others. A drive to address the threat from UKIP and satisfy growing internal demands for the promise of a referendum led eventually to Mr Cameron's commitment in the 2013 speech to give the public a vote on whether to stay or go. It's worth remembering that, perhaps strangely, the 2013 speech in which he made his promise to hold a vote made no mention of immigration. But add a general election and increasing public concern to the mix and three years later, his hopes of limiting benefits for migrants are the centrepiece of his renegotiation. The prime minister is not a politician who is known for getting hung up on the past, his seemingly bomb-proof - if maybe sometimes misplaced - confidence in his own abilities tends to lead him to look forward. He is not a prisoner of his record. But as he arrives in Brussels on Thursday, and gets out of the shiny black limousine to sweep past the journalists clamouring to ask a question, will he consider even, for a moment, the irony that he may be risking it all for something he once more or less dismissed as a fringe concern?

Scientists have grown plants in lunar soil using samples collected during the Apollo missions to the moon. The scientists grew thale cress, a small flowering plant that is attractive to fungi and mammals such as rabbits and squirrels The study was published on Thursday in Science Advances. 'It's exciting because it shows we can grow crops on another world,' said lead author Jason Spindler of Ohio State University. 'We just need to find out how well they will do.' Researchers used two different methods for growing plants inside these artificial soils: one method called microgravity-induced root growth (MIGR), which involves a liquid medium containing nutrients, and the other known as cryopreservation - freezing at subzero temperatures so that seeds don't die when planted outside. First the researchers plopped about 20 grams or less of seed into each of three separate plastic containers. Then they placed them in an incubator where the temperature reached around minus 300 degrees Fahrenheit. After a few weeks, all four containers were frozen. These are then taken back up to Earth to be rehydrated before being tested again with seeds from a variety of plants including lettuce, spinach, mustard greens, broccoli, melons, onions, potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, carrots, peas and strawberries In this image made available by the Planetary Society, Jason Spindler holds seeds he helped cultivate in Lunar Lab Zero Two in December 2020 When night time came, tens of thousands of microbes started grazing in the soil - helping to break down the nutrients already present within the container. Finally, after a month, the team ran tests to see if any of the seeds had germinated. That way they could tell whether the plants actually survived after landing on Mars in the hopes of finding a permanent home there someday. All but seven of the 100 sent in for testing sprouted. But only 19 percent of those discovered viable pieces of thale cress, even though it supposedly grows well on the Red Planet. Only 10 potted plants did not survive after planting. There may also still be some issues ironing out how best to feed Martian plants once astronauts arrive on the planet, the authors noted. Mars has no atmosphere like the ones found on our own planet, meaning carbon dioxide for photosynthesis cannot reach the surface. So scientists might use different types of food, perhaps produced on board the spacecraft itself rather than brought in from earth.

The new administration would experience little or no support from Montreal until after his death on April 20, 1755. By that time, two important events had occurred: an attempt at Count Frontenac's succession and a political crisis within the colony itself. When Jean Talon became administrator for Louis XV (1715-23) he did not believe that Quebec City should be used as headquarters. He wanted all government personnel sent there instead. In fact, it took him almost five years before he went himself. As early as June 23, 1714, Jean Talon made elaborate plans with the intendant, Francois Dollier de Cassagnolles, for sending most administrative staff to Canada. These included both officials who held civil posts directly under provincial governors, such as Claude Le Normand Destouches and Nicolas Duguay Legare, and those given ordinary "governor" rank, like Gilles Hocquart Dufresny and Denis Gendre. They also included every other kind of clerk necessary for running the office. For example, Enemond Masseau, son of one of Talon's aides de camp, was appointed commissaire generale du service des affaires courantes et extraordinaires; while Pierre Babineau was named secretary cabantier [acting chief engineer]. All this meant far more than simply moving some offices out into the field people were being detached and sent away permanently. Even individuals whose position was only temporary could now find themselves uprooted to distant locations. Note that none of these persons ever returned to replace their predecessors once they left. It is safe to assume that the exodus deprived the Crown of its best officers as well as the colony of much needed help. There are many reasons why colonial administrators might become disgruntled, but the very nature of the job seems especially difficult when compared to present day conditions. Most administrative services can easily come back home if possible, but these men were professional employees they knew what they were doing! And then even a simple request for a promotion or appointment may have been refused outright. Thus, it must have seemed impossible to move them: their families lived somewhere else; perhaps they had already found jobs elsewhere... After leaving office they remained officially unemployed. To make matters worse, the loss of business to competitors abroad increased competition among colonial traders. This was particularly true in naval stores trading where several French colonies competed with each other. If a ship let us say British ran aground off Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, her cargo would go straight through the hands of Canadian merchants who paid duty when passing through French ports. On returning to port, if her cargo contained goods which could not be sold in a landlocked area, she too lost money. Ships bound for markets further east carried supplies intended chiefly for foreign consumption sugar, tobacco, rum, etc., rather than local needs. The current system worked reasonably well in wartime situations, when military supply ships brought large quantities of foodstuffs or equipment essential to the war effort. During peacetime, however, the same vessels transported goods grown in local agriculture suitable mainly for domestic purposes. Finally, the weight of taxes levied in France forced prices up so high that market forces ceased to operate effectively. A good deal of commerce came to depend upon royal licences to export particular products, or on governmental monopolies established specifically for industry. While commercial interests naturally attempted to secure favourable regulations, they often clashed with agricultural interests because few farmers produced enough profitably to justify large enterprises. By contrast, maritime trade required a steady supply of cheap labour and capital investment. Since much of the available work force consisted of women, husbands, sons and fathers seldom joined merchant fleets unless their own occupation was seasonal or malarial in character. Trade thus depended heavily upon the goodwill of successive governments. However, the purchase of raw materials, tools, building material and machinery often required considerable credit extended against future sales. Here again the Crown played an active role. When all components of a federation hold equal power, it is referred to as "symmetric federalism." In contrast, "asymmetric federalism" occurs when states are granted differing levels of authority, with some possessing greater autonomy than others. This often arises due to the presence of distinct cultural identities within a region. In Spain, the Basques, Catalans, and Galicians played a key role in advocating for the recognition of their unique national characteristics, leading to the formation of "historical communities" such as Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. These communities enjoy more powers than the later expansion of administrative arrangements for other Spanish regions, or the "coffee for everyone" system, which grants equal powers to all autonomous communities. This setup aims to address their separate identities and accommodate peripheral nationalist sentiments, while also respecting historical rights they once possessed. However, technically, Spain is not a federal system but rather a decentralized administrative structure of the state.

Ann Arbor operates under a council-manager system. The city council consists of 11 voting officials: the mayor and 10 council members. Two council members are elected from each of the city's five districts. The mayor is elected throughout the city. The mayor serves as the chair of the City Council and holds authority to appoint all council committee members, board, and commission members, with the council's approval. The current mayor of Ann Arbor is Christopher Taylor, a Democrat who was elected in 2014. Daily city operations are handled by a city administrator selected by the city council.

Most fast food operations operate pretty much identical, be it Burger King, Taco Bell, or Jollibee. The cost of their ingredients, workers, and everything needed to keep the store going is about the same. It's safe to assume that they all have about the same mark-up on the food that they sell. So then, if that's the case, why does Jollibee's 1 piece chicken meal cost P90.00, while Burger King's Whopper Value Meal cost P158.00? I believe that the answer to that question lies in how Jollibee sells their meals. Jollibee sells their meals in sets. You can buy a 1 piece chicken meal, or a 2 piece chicken meal. For an extra P20, you can get an additional drink, and for another P20, you can get an additional chicken pie. What this does is limit the number of items a customer can buy and the combinations they can make. Now, Burger King does have combos, but they are all Value Meals. You cannot buy a Whopper on it's own. You can only buy it as a Value Meal, which, in Burger King, means the meal must come with fries and a drink. This limits the number of items a customer can buy, but not the combinations. By limiting the combinations, Jollibee also limits the number of items a customer can buy, thereby forcing them to buy the more expensive items. This is why, when you buy a burger from Burger King, you can also buy a chicken, and a piece of cake, and a hotdog, and whatever else. The price of those items may be higher than a Jollibee value meal, but you can always save by buying just what you need. The same thing happens with apples and oranges. Both are fruit, but apples are much more expensive than oranges. And they're not as sweet. If I had my way, I'd pick oranges over apples any day. The next time you're in a restaurant, take a look at how they sell their food. The menu may look complicated, but the underlying principle is the same for each. Those long menus are just there to make you think you have a lot of choices. The truth is, there aren't that many. As a point of interest, my favorite Jollibee value meal is the spaghetti. A large one costs P88.00, and it comes with a drink and a piece of cake. It's filling, and it's just about the right amount of sweet. If you want more stories pm me: I stood in the cold of the morning before the house, looking at the old shack, where my Grandpa used to live the last years. My good old man lived far away from civilisation in the forests of Blackburn Mountain, Alaska. Our whole family never understood his decision to not stay with us in Detroit. Some even called him a madman. I never did. While I pushed the heavy door open, my nose was greeted by a thick aroma of vanilla tobacco and paper. Memories flooded my brain. Gramps always used to smell like this. He raised me for a big portion of my live, until I was fifteen I believe. While he once worked as a clerk for insurance companies, which I thought of to be a very very boring profession, he never quite seemed like an accountant clerk to me. I still remember him making me dinner, mostly porridge and then telling me a bedtime story. Even after he left I told stories to myself, dreaming of adventures. I closed the door. The interior of the shack, it was only one big room, was as cold as outside. There were three windows, one at the front and two at the sides, which all shed light on one Bed, which stood right next to a tile stove at the back of the room. The other significant parts of this little home of him were one wardrobe, one very old worktable with a chair, and one shelf with a few books. It all just seemed so empty. After I put down my clothes on the bed and tried to create a fire in the stove, I remembered how the funeral was. The people in the village nearby didn't really know him. He just came in the morning, stayed there at a restaurant for the rest of the day eating and writing and then left when the sun was about to set. I was the only person at his burial. My parents didn't have the time to drop by. They never developed a good relationship with him. I think the main reason of this conflict was that my mother was raised alone without him and blamed him for the rest of his life because of that. Even my older sister didn't come. Just me, fresh out of college, with no job, and not knowing what I want to do with my life. The fire started burning and I felt how everything around me got warmer and more comfy. I didn't know what I was searching for when I started looking around. The books on the shelf were mainly philosophical books. Nothing interesting. His wardrobe on the other hand was exceptional. I never saw as many pieces of pricy clothing at once. He even had coats and weirder stuff like traditional African clothing. That was very weird. Why would he need those Pieces, and how came he to acquire them? I never thought he had enough money. I found myself suddenly being very excited about this. I don't know why, but little things like that make my imagination fly like an eagle. I remember how most of my friends called me a dreamer. Never disagreed on that part. The other parts of his wardrobe were, to my disappointment, pretty normal. Maybe he just liked to collect this stuff, I told myself. Then I sat down at the work desk. The desk was pretty empty, there was only one ballpoint pen and a few empty sheets of paper. I tried pulling out the drawer of the desk. Closed. I tried pulling again. Closed. I started pulling with all my might. Tightly shut. There had to be a key. I started searching for it. Most people never cared about such things, but his wardrobe piqued my interest what more I could find, and now I was a wolf searching for his prey. I don't know how long I searched, but the sun was already way over the zenith when I found the key. It was hanging at the wall, right next to the desk. I'm an idiot. The drawer opened slowly, probably was already frozen. Inside I found a journal, a book titled "The Seven Points," probably about Business Administration, and a letter. It was addressed to me. I teared it apart and started reading, anxious to see what was inside. Why was it addressed to me? Did he know I would come? What if I wouldn't even have found it? "Dear Grandson, I hope you will read this letter as soon as possible. I feared you wouldn't find the one I put in my desks drawer, so I also gave one to my lawyer." I did find this one, I thought. Though I didn't quite understand why he would address a letter only to me, and why he would put so much effort in multiplying those, when he just could have sent it to my home. "Even though I may be not alive anymore when you read those lines, I just wanted to thank you for the time I had with you. It was great seeing you grow up and struggle through life. This time you gifted me, was time I never had with your mother. She probably still hates me for that. Sadly I found myself unable to apologise or explain. That's why I had to leave the family before our conflict would start to tear everyone apart." At this point, I already felt myself touched by the carefully selected words he used. My teacher in elementary school once called him a real gentleman. I kind of picked that up and started imitating him. My mother always hated that part of me. "The reason why I wrote this letter is not only to thank you, my dear, but also to give you counsel." I already started rolling my eyes, that anyone else would have feared they would fall out of my eye sockets. I didn't need more advice. All my life my parents told me to start making money. My sister really picked up on that and worked as a manager at the company of my father. I didn't. You could call me the black sheep of the family. But I still was curios and continued reading. "I know you should probably pursue your job. Should probably start making money and start living the good life." Yup, that's wat they told me. "But in lack of a better phrase; Fuck it." Now this was new to me, I thought, Gramps rarely used such words. "You have to chase your dreams. You have to make your own decisions. My life was not that what you think it was. I never was an accountant clerk. That was a not so very well crafted lie of mine, because well, you know, I suck at maths." I chuckled. That was my old man. "I also lived the live of a commoner, or normal person. When I was young I dreamed of adventure, but also didn't really put any effort into pursuing those dreams. But when my daughter was born, your mother, and the single good thing I did in my life, I needed money. At this time I was basically penniless and didn't have any work. Your mother was just so unexpected, and even if I loved your Grandma, I told her I had work to do." What did you work then, I asked him, even though I knew he couldn't hear me. "I fled from my responsibility as a father, my biggest mistake, and started working overseas. I can't count what I did, just to not be at home. I worked on an oil rig, hunted elephants, and even worked for more shady organisations. All this while sending letters with money to my family, which never truly was mine. You can see already that I never worked in London as a clerk for my whole life. I lived my life all over the place. It was my gravest mistake leaving your mother, but my best decision to live the way I did." I felt many confusing feelings at the same time. Anger at his mistakes, confused about why he never told us, but then I realised, no one would have believed his stories. "But now I want to give you something, that I didn't give your mother. I want to give you a choice. In Alaska, in the very shack that I live, you'll find a journal which is completely empty and a book filled with useful Information like contacts of mine in the drawer of my desk. Furthermore you will find a suitcase under my bed with a purse in it, which should have a respectable sum of money in different currencies. Take what you need from my home, if you want to travel, if you want to live a life, that is adventurous. The choice is yours. Love, Gramps." I felt a tear in my eye. It wasn't the fact that I was a crybaby, but his honesty and his last gift touched me like nothing ever did before. I felt angry at him. My mother didn't deserve this. But the more I thought about it, the more sense it made. My Gramps probably was not the person to raise a child. And he tried to make that up with me. Now I had a choice. I didn't need to be a manager. I could just realise what my dreams were made of. Far untouched landscapes before me. Not a computer desk. The fire I made already burned down like the sun outside and I started freezing when I made my decision. I was at Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport in Alaska when I called my Dad. "Son? When are you coming back? I have a job interview organised for you." He asked in his hounded tone that he always used. "Sorry Father. I won't come back to America." I told him reluctantly. My father was quite dominant. "What do you mean? You'll have to work when you want to live the good life!" He said irritated. "I'm doing a vacation. Sorry my flight to Singapore is about to start. I need to go. Say hi to mom from me." I said as fast as I could. "Wait a sec Click. I turned off my phone and started heading into the future. My name doesn't matter, because we all have a choice.

Semantic grasping involves identifying stable grasps that align with specific object manipulation objectives. For robots to efficiently handle object manipulation, it is essential to consider a wide range of contextual factors, such as object and task-related constraints. We propose the Context-Aware Grasping Engine, which integrates a unique semantic framework for representing grasp contexts with a neural network architecture inspired by the Wide Deep model, enabling the capture of intricate reasoning processes. Our method is evaluated on a new dataset containing 14,000 semantic grasps across 44 objects, 7 tasks, and 6 object states. Our approach significantly outperforms existing techniques, demonstrating enhanced performance and offering new perspectives on the balance between memory retention and generalization in semantic grasping. Additionally, we showcase the efficacy of our approach through robotic experiments, where the model successfully attained 31 out of 32 appropriate grasps. We introduce filling as a novel spatial partitioning issue linked to coverage and packing. Filling focuses on optimally positioning overlapping objects fully contained within an arbitrary shape to maximize the covered internal volume. In n-dimensional space, when dealing with polydisperse n-balls, our findings demonstrate that solutions align with sets of maximal n-balls, reducing the solution space to the medial axis of a shape.
