When you install a program it may make other changes than just copy files to your harddrive. If you just delete the files then those changes won't be undone. For example, the installer may create desktop shortcuts, and it may create a variety of entries in the system registry, perhaps registering the application as a handler for certain filetypes (for example, indicating that this application should be launched when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file), and much more. The uninstaller will remove these entries as well as deleting the files. Simply deleting the files won't perform this cleanup. So if the installer made the above registrations then Windows will still try (and fail) to launch the application when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file. And you'll have a shortcut on your desktop which no longer works. Plus whatever other changes the installer made, which you chose not to undo. In short, you've turned your computer into a bit of a mess where some features have suddenly become broken.," "Often times, programs will write new keys to your Registry on your computer. These won't be removed simply by deleting the files. Usually an installer will remove them. Also, some programs have cache and other files located in many various locations around your computer. Unless you know all of these locations, you probably can't find all of them to be sure you've removed 100. But something important to note, installers and uninstallers are both created by the developer. So if they didn't program the uninstaller to remove everything properly, then it won't. There's nothing to enforce the uninstaller doing what it should do. This is why, even with using uninstallers, you will often still have files, settings and registry keys left over from your programs.

Dynamic equilibrium was first described by Galileo who noticed that certain assumptions of Aristotelian physics were contradicted by observations and logic. Galileo realized that simple velocity addition demands that the general case must be true, but at a point in space distant from all other points there is no motion where there should have been. Thus it appears that either the assumption that everything moves has to be modified or the world does not move as predicted. If one assumes uniformity (or simplicity) then such an anomaly doesn't arise because velocities are additive across any spatial distance for equal masses. The idea works well up until very high speeds when relativity comes into play - Newton's laws predict different behavior than Galilean mechanics depending on whether you're moving close to light speed; this led Einstein to come up with special relativity. In contrast, if bodies follow elliptical orbits around each others' centers then even though objects could appear stationary relative to one another they would still exhibit orbital motions regardless of their physical masses due to Kepler's third law. When combined with Plato's dictum "all things tend toward perfect circles," classical celestial dynamics usually leads to circular orbits which preserve invariance under translation. Once Special Relativity became established, the problem of distinguishing between planetary geometries based solely upon mass arose after it was discovered that Saturn had rings. From an abstract geometric perspective these don't seem like something that can physically exist: If we assume conservation of angular momentum then how do we account for the fact that Rings aren't actually just flat planes? This phenomenon challenged many aspects of Newtonian gravity along with observational evidence regarding Kepler's Laws. However attempts to model them initially left behind what some might consider an undesirable property known as static stability - the most extreme example being presented here wherein every aspect of gravitational theory falls apart once planets enter the picture due to deviations from prescribed elliptic paths. Classical Planets successfully addresses both problems while preserving time-honored thinking about why orbits look the way they do without resorting to adding new penalties whenever you try doing more complicated stuff within the orbitals themselves!

This paper provides a comparative analysis of impedance models for power electronic converters and systems for the purpose of stability investigations. Such models can be divided into either decoupled models or coupled models and the paper provides an overview of how to derive and implement these two different approaches. The analysis is carried out for three different converter topologies: the full bridge converter (VSC), the half bridge converter (HSC), and the single phase inverter. The emphasis is on the design principles for the impedance models and the derivation of the different components, as well as on the comparison between different models. The paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Section III describes the decoupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. Section IV presents the coupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. The paper is concluded in Section V. A power electronic converter is essentially an energy transformation device. The input energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current, is transformed to another energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current. Power electronic converters are used in almost all fields of technology, e.g., for electrical energy production, electrical energy storage, and electrical energy distribution. In all these fields, the stability of the converters is crucial and, hence, a good understanding of the stability is of utmost importance. A general description of power electronic converters and stability investigations can be found in . In stability investigations, the main objective is to analyze the stability of the power electronic system. The first step is to describe the system by means of an equivalent circuit. This circuit is generally based on the concept of impedances and its design requires a detailed knowledge of the converter and the system it is used in. An overview of the different modeling approaches for the impedance model can be found in . This paper focuses on the modeling of impedances for the analysis of power electronic converters. The impedance model can be divided into two different classes: (1) a decoupled model, and (2) a coupled model. The decoupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter can be treated separately. It can be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling, nonlinear current-dependent modeling, or both, and the different modeling techniques are explained in Section III. The coupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter interact and, thus, it cannot be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling. The different modeling techniques are explained in Section IV. The decoupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is not influenced by the other components. For instance, the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage of a DC-DC converter are independent of the output load, which is assumed to be resistive or capacitive, and the decoupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. The coupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is influenced by the other components. For instance, the output inductance of a DC-DC converter influences the dynamics of the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage, and, thus, the coupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. This paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Section III describes the decoupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. Section IV presents the coupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. The paper is concluded in Section V. Power electronic converters can be divided into four different groups, depending on the operation mode: (1) the DC-DC converter, (2) the DC-AC converter, (3) the AC-AC converter, and (4) the AC-DC converter. The presented analysis applies to all these groups, but for the sake of simplicity, the analysis is only presented for the DC-DC converter. A DC-DC converter consists of an input stage, e.g., a boost converter, and an output stage, e.g., a buck converter, and it is shown in Figure 1. The input stage takes the input energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current, and transforms it to another energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current. The output stage takes the input energy and transforms it to the output energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current

Quantum stabilizer codes (QSCs) suffer from a low quantum coding rate, since they have to recover the quantum bits (qubits) in the face of both bit-flip and phase-flip errors. In addition, QSCs have a limited distance, meaning they can only correct a certain number of errors before the code fails. This can make them less suitable for applications that require high error tolerance, such as quantum communication or fault-tolerant quantum computing. Despite these limitations, QSCs are still useful for some applications, particularly when the noise is dominated by one type of error (either bit-flip or phase-flip), or when the number of errors is low. QSCs can also be combined with other error-correcting techniques to improve their performance, such as the use of concatenated codes or the implementation of topological codes. Overall, while QSCs may have limitations, they are an important tool in the field of quantum error correction and have played a significant role in the development of quantum technologies.

This paper presents a regularized mean-field game and examines the learning process of this game under an infinite-horizon discounted reward framework. The game is constructed by incorporating a regularization function into the one-step reward function of the standard mean-field game model. A value iteration-based learning method is proposed for this regularized game using fitted Q-learning. The inclusion of the regularization term generally enhances the robustness of reinforcement learning algorithms and improves their ability to explore. Furthermore, it allows for the derivation of error analyses of the learning algorithm without requiring stringent convexity conditions on the system's components, which are typically necessary when no regularization is applied.

The most unsettling aspect of Aurora's daily life was witnessing her reflection in the mirror. Over time, she had become used to seeing the same faces of people who lived each day. This began many years ago when customers visited a supermarket with varied appearances, hands, and skin tones, spending time searching for perfect fruits like bananas or tomatoes. Scientists spent hours developing ways to make these moments less stressful by creating fruits that appeared identical in appearance. Similarly, they worked on making bananas look the same. Soon, people started wanting their own faces and their children's to be treated the same way. As time passed, the natural wear and tear of aging caused the older faces to fade completely. Everyone now looked alike, and that was supposed to be the final stage. Occasionally, an unforeseen event would occur—such as a child being born with a distinctive freckle or eyes that were green, resembling a rare type of sour apple. For Aurora, one of the most remarkable differences was evident from the moment she was born. She had typical blue eyes and blond hair, but her skin was dark brown, like the earth beneath the surface. Her parents, with their identical peach-like faces, seemed to stare at each other like someone lost in a mirror. They filled out forms just like other parents, aware of the risks involved in altering the genetic makeup of their child. Raising a unique child once posed challenges, but with the museum opening and growing public interest in such conditions, couples could potentially earn substantial income from selling their child. This was preferable to raising the issue themselves, and many chose to reinvest the money into another attempt, hoping the genes would not cause the desired identical appearance.

The term can be found used in an October 1845 Massachusetts Circuit Court ruling in the patent case Davoll et al. v. Brown., in which Justice Charles L. Woodbury wrote that "only in this way can we protect intellectual property, the labors of the mind, productions and interests are as much a man's own...as the wheat he cultivates, or the flocks he rears." The statement that "discoveries are...property" goes back earlier. Section 1 of the French law of 1791 stated, "All new discoveries are the property of the author; to assure the inventor the property and temporary enjoyment of his discovery, there shall be delivered to him a patent for five, ten or fifteen years." In Europe, French author A. Nion mentioned propriete intellectuelle in his Droits civils des auteurs, artistes et inventeurs, published in 1846.

The unemployment insurance program is funded through employer taxes, and benefits are paid to unemployed workers through state unemployment offices. Unemployment insurance pays benefits to eligible workers who have lost their jobs through no fault of their own, usually due to a reduction in force or other business-related reason. Unemployment insurance benefits provide temporary financial assistance to workers. Most states provide 26 weeks of benefits. In most cases, you will have to file a claim for benefits. You will be asked to give the names of your employers for the past 18 months, your earnings and the reason you are no longer employed. You may be asked to provide documentation to verify your eligibility. You will also be asked to report each week you are unemployed. In the US, there are Federal and state-based unemployment benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid by the government and are only available to individuals who were formerly employed by the government or other government agencies. This type of unemployment benefits are a result of the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). State unemployment benefits are also paid by the government but are a result of state laws. Every state has a unemployment insurance department that is responsible for administering the benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid directly to you by the government. State unemployment benefits are paid by the government but are generally disbursed through your state's unemployment insurance department. For all that it may sound attractive to the Scots, Welsh and Northern Irish to have greater influence over their respective economic destinies, presumably that would be less desirable if at a stroke they became poorer. The point is that as and when there is an English parliament for English people - of the sort that the former Tory minister John Redwood has been demanding, and David Cameron seemed to concede today - the financial transfer from England to the rest of the UK may be harder to sustain. So these constitutional reforms will be tricky, if not dangerous - if at least a part of the current glue that holds the UK together is a redistribution of resources from England to the rest, and that glue is progressively removed. Being British right now means in part that public services and living standards are not too far apart in quantum and quality wherever you happen to live. But what if the overhaul of the UK's budget-making or fiscal constitution waters down that glue. How much is at stake? Well, spending on public-sector services per head is highest in Northern Ireland, PS10,900 and it is lowest in England, at PS8,500. The figure for Scotland - beneficiary of the famous or notorious Barnett Formula, which formalises an income transfer from England to Scotland - is PS10,200. So expenditure on public services in Scotland is a fifth higher per person than south of the border, and it is 28 higher in Northern Ireland. In Wales, the increment on public-service spending is 14 - which the Welsh have often complained is too little, compared with the transfer of income to Scotland. Now one way of looking at the scale of the transfer is to look at the amount of income - or what is known as gross value added - generated in each country. So English gross value added per head is highest, at just under PS22,000, and it is lowest in Wales at PS15,400. The English enjoy public-service spending per annum equivalent to under 40 of the income they generate, whereas annual outlays on public services in Wales are equivalent to more than 60 of nationally generated income per head. The ratios for Scotland and Northern Ireland are just over 50 and not far off 70 respectively. In a UK of considerable social and cultural solidarity that prevailed for most of the twentieth century, these sorts of disparities between income and outlay between the nations were relatively uncontroversial: they captured the idea that all UK citizens are in it together, as it were. But today it seems almost inevitable that in David Cameron's brave new world of greater national fiscal self-determination, some English nationalist MPs on the right of the spectrum may increasingly view Wales - and Scotland and Northern Ireland - as de facto socialist paradises excessively featherbedded by the English. That said, if the nations are given much greater control over income taxes - which appears to be what is on offer - could they not pay for whatever public services they feel they need out of these locally levied taxes? Not remotely. Income and other direct taxes per head in Wales raise PS5,564, considerably less than the UK average of PS7,360, and nowhere near enough to cover public service expenditure. There is a similar mismatch between direct income taxes and public spending throughout the UK. Borrowing and indirect taxes, mostly VAT, make up the difference. And there is not the faintest chance that national parliaments will be given the power to increase VAT, because this would be an admin nightmare for businesses and undermine the UK as a frictionless single market. All of which means that it may sound exciting and empowering in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland to make their own choices about taxing and spending. But it may also be a bit nerve-wracking (or worse) if it provides cover for Westminster to reduce the income transferred to them from English taxpayers.

Smart devices, storage and other distributed technologies have the potential to greatly improve the utilisation of network infrastructure and renewable generation. Decentralised control of these technologies overcomes many scalability and privacy concerns, but in general still requires the underlying problem to be convex in order to guarantee convergence to a global optimum. Considering that AC power flows are non-convex in nature, and the operation of household devices often requires discrete decisions, there has been uncertainty surrounding the use of distributed methods in a realistic setting. This paper extends prior work on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for solving the dynamic optimal power flow (D-OPF) problem. We utilise more realistic line and load models, and introduce a two-stage approach to managing discrete decisions and uncertainty. Our experiments on a suburb-sized microgrid show that this approach provides near optimal results, in a time that is fast enough for receding horizon control. This work brings distributed control of smart-grid technologies closer to reality.

The days were spent getting ready for school or homework, working some chores around the farm like cleaning out the chicken coop (which I still hated doing) or playing outside with the kids until they fell asleep. When we went to bed Gina slept most of the night away from me because she knew Mom wouldn't wake up until almost 10am. But when she did get up Gina had plans: read books, play with dolls, do puzzles...and then "sleep over" at her grandparents' house for a few hours while their family came to visit that morning and we all got to spend time together. We made s'mores crackers and watched movies which Gina loved. And when the sun rose again we'd start walking back into town, mom and dad walking along in front and Gina behind them taking turns going home at 5pm to sleep late (so much fun!). I remember walking up to my grandmother's house and seeing her sitting there talking to my grandpa as he sat on his tractor in the yard drinking coffee. She asked how I was feeling today and I told her I couldn't really feel anything but excitement about being able to go home tomorrow! It felt so good to finally have something positive happen after what seemed like endless negative events throughout my entire life. So happy to finally find a place where I could live without having to worry every day if someone would hurt memy sistermy parents. Finally found happiness in living. As I walked inside, she said she didn't know why I wasn't upset or crying the way I usually am during those long drives to see Gina. That sweet smile spreading across her face convinced me immediately that this woman cared very deeply for both of us. She also reminded me once more of how important it is to love each other unconditionally no matter who we are, where we're from, or what kind of relationship we may or may not have with God. In that moment I realized that she truly loves my whole family. Not just Gina but the rest of us too; my cousins, my nieces and nephews, my brother- and sister-in-law, and my husband. The justices review the briefs independently, yet they may discuss informally at any time. During oral arguments, they gain insight into their peers' potential perspectives based on the questions posed. Following the orals, they hold a private meeting to discuss matters, though these discussions rarely delve deeply. The chief justice and senior associate justice on the opposing side determine the majority and minority opinions. The assigned justices retreat to their chambers and draft the opinions. This is where the actual work begins, as many opinions are revised and circulated. Justices who share common views may state, "I disagree with this part" or "could you include a section about X?" while others revise their drafts in response to arguments raised by the other side’s initial version. This process continues until all parties are satisfied with their statements, which are then officially announced and published.

As noted, justices generally vote along their ideological lines (not necessarily political parties). Their positions are well understood prior to appointment, so it is unsurprising. It is also important to remember that all justices have clerks who handle much of the administrative work. The procedure is rarely "present the facts, then vote on them." Instead, the clerk often constructs a logical legal argument aligned with the judge's general ideological stance. The clerk provides the justice with a reasonable justification for voting according to their general position regarding a specific case. Occasionally, judges consider the facts more objectively and vote based solely on the case’s legal merit. For instance, Justice Roberts sided with the Affordable Care Act despite being a conservative, viewing it as a legal decision rather than an ideological one. Similarly, the recent vote requiring a warrant before searching a cellphone—where all nine justices voted unanimously—was a legal consensus rather than an ideological one. Much of the perceived drama surrounding Supreme Court decisions stems from the clerks’ role in shaping the legal reasoning and justifications.

I'm going to talk specifically about the U.S. because the hippie movement started there. In the 1930s and early 1940s, the U.S. lived through the trauma of the Great Depression and WWII. After the war, a new era of prosperity dawned in the U.S. and there a strong impulse for everything to return to "normal." Also, the power of the Soviet Union increased mightily in the post-war world, giving rise to the Cold War. The Cold War led to a fear of communists and other subversives in the U.S. All this together added up to encouraging a conservative social order in the U.S. during the 1950s. In the 1960s, there was a leftist backlash against the conservatism of the 1950s. Social issues which had been suppressed in the '50s rose to prominence. The Vietnam War particularly galvanized young leftists as it was a war being fought against communism (as part of the Cold War) and the draft was in effect. Before Vietnam, it was widely accepted that America's fight against communism was a noble cause, but now that was to be challenged. Hippies were a youth subculture which emerged in the '60s as part of this leftist backlash against the values of the '50s and the social order it represented. The values of the hippies were anti-war, free love, environmentalism, and pro-drug-use. Those first two items were often summed with the slogan, "make love, not war." All of it challenged the Cold War establishment of the time.

This system operates through capacitive coupling. Your fingertip contains blood, which is a highly conductive substance. Beneath the display lies an array of charged capacitors—sometimes a single large one. When your finger approaches the screen, the electrons in your blood are drawn toward or pushed away from the screen, depending on the capacitor’s polarity. Similarly, the electrons within the capacitor are attracted or repelled by your finger. This interaction generates an electric field, which can be measured by a sensor. Any conductive liquid, such as saltwater, will function effectively. A fun fact: the inventors of this technology, Wayne Westerman and John Elias, taught my computer engineering classes during my undergraduate studies. They founded a company (URL0), which was later acquired by Apple, and they became wealthy quickly.

For instance, headphone cables or a metallic object like a metal stick can serve as effective sensors. A metal stick is essentially equivalent to a simple stylus.

Autism is a mental condition, present from early childhood, characterized by difficulty in communicating and forming relationships with other people and in using language and abstract concepts. Asperger syndrome is a developmental disorder characterized by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior and interests. ADHD is a chronic condition marked by persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and sometimes impulsivity. Clear everything up?','Autism is a set (often referred to as a "spectrum of related developments disorders which are primarily characterized by difficulties with socialization. The symptoms vary widely and can include things such as difficulty in reading others' body language, shyness, inability to understand sarcasm, etc. You've probably met autistic people and not known it, but they may have seemed "awkward" to you. The autism spectrum ranges from people with minor symptoms on one end to totally non-functional people on the other. Asperger's is a specific form of autism. ADHD (also known as ADD) is a common disorder which primarily manifests itself as a short attention span, lack of motivation, and inability to focus. ADHD is caused by an abnormally low baseline level of activity in the brain, which causes the brain to constantly try to find new sources of stimulation to raise the baseline to a more normal level. This is why people with ADHD become bored easily. The ADHD brain is like a person who is always hungry and feels the urge to eat constantly because nothing keeps him full for long. This is why ADHD is often treated with stimulants like Adderall which boost the baseline level of brain activity and allows the patient to focus their energy more effectively. Interestingly, people with autism or ADHD also tend to be highly talented in other areas. Some (although by no means all) autistic people are called "savants," and have extraordinary ability in things such as math or memory. ADHD is highly correlated with high levels of creativity.

A study has confirmed that new neurons are still being made well past adolescence, and suggested that older studies that had claimed otherwise were flawed in their methodology. Older studies had tried to detect the presence of a protein, doublecortin (DCX), in the brain months, or even years after the brain matter was preserved - long after the DCX had deteriorated. The new study examined freshly preserved samples and found a large amount of evidence of newly developed cells. There was about a 30 decrease in the presence of newly developed cells from the youngest to the oldest donor samples, whose ages ranged from 43 to 87. Some scientists remain skeptical of the results, claiming that detected DCX levels were not sufficient evidence for newly developed cells, but the scientists in the study say they used very strict criteria when identifying new cells.

Today's machine learning (ML) systems often rely on reusing arrays of pre-trained, commonly used primitive models, each serving different functions, such as feature extraction. The widespread adoption of these models greatly streamlines and accelerates the development process of ML systems. However, since most of these models are developed and maintained by untrusted parties, their lack of standardization or regulation raises significant security concerns. Currently, there is limited understanding of these security risks. In this paper, we reveal that malicious primitive models can severely compromise the security of ML systems. We introduce a variety of model-reuse attacks where maliciously created models cause ML systems to behave unpredictably when exposed to targeted inputs. Through empirical analysis of four deep learning systems—such as those used in skin cancer detection, speech recognition, face verification, and autonomous driving—we demonstrate that these attacks are effective, evasive, elastic, and easy to execute. The effectiveness of these attacks is supported by analytical reasoning, highlighting the complex nature of modern primitive models. This problem appears critical to many ML systems. We also explore possible solutions and the associated challenges, which open up new avenues for future research.

Experts reassembled pieces of tiles found amid tons of earth from the site known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as Haram al-Sharif. They say the tiles date from the period of the Second Temple, during the time of King Herod about 2,000 years ago. The temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD during a Jewish rebellion. Some 600 segments of coloured stone floor have been found since archaeologists began examining the debris from the hilltop site in 2004. The plateau where the temples stood is the most sacred site in Judaism. It is joined by the Western Wall, venerated by Jews as part of the original supporting wall of the temple compound. Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary) is also the place where Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad ascended to Heaven, and is the third holiest site in Islam. The archaeologists say the tiles probably came from porticos in the temple's courtyards. Piecing the fragments together "enables us to get an idea of the Temple's incredible splendour," said Dr Gabriel Barkay of the Temple Mount Sifting Project. Experts say they managed to assemble seven potential designs of how the flooring could have looked like. The type of flooring is known as opus sectile, Latin for "cut work," and "considered to be far more prestigious than mosaic tiles floors," according to Frankie Snyder, from the project's team. "The tile segments were perfectly inlaid such that one could not even insert a sharp blade between them," she said. The Temple Mount Sifting Project was established by Israeli archaeologists in 2004 to examine debris dumped by Islamic authorities following expansion work at an underground mosque on the compound. The project attracts thousands of visitors each year who participate in finger-tip searches of the earth and has so far turned up hundreds of ancient relics, including coins, animal bones and pieces of pottery.

The sound of an exhaust is a very complex sound. Basically, there are explosions going on inside the motor. This is the genesis of the sound you hear. However, different factors can affect the actual tone, loudness, and quality of the exhaust sound. Some of these factors include: 1. Exhaust System Design: The design of the exhaust system plays a significant role in the sound produced. The size of the pipes, mufflers, and resonators can all affect the exhaust's tone. 2. Engine Type: Different engine types produce different exhaust sounds. For example, a V8 engine typically produces a deeper and more throaty exhaust sound compared to a four-cylinder engine. 3. Exhaust Manifold: The exhaust manifold collects exhaust gases from the engine and channels them to the exhaust system. The design of the manifold can affect the sound produced. 4. Catalytic Converter: The catalytic converter is responsible for reducing harmful emissions in the exhaust. However, it can also affect the exhaust tone. 5. Aftermarket Modifications: Aftermarket exhaust systems, headers, or mufflers can all alter the exhaust sound produced by a vehicle. In summary, exhaust sound is a complex issue with many variables affecting the tone, loudness, and quality of the sound produced.

This paper proposes a robust adversarial reinforcement learning (RARL) -based multi-access point (AP) coordination method that is robust even against unexpected decentralized operations of uncoordinated APs. Multi-AP coordination is a challenging task, as it requires multiple APs to work together to optimize network performance while avoiding interference and congestion. Adversarial reinforcement learning is a machine learning approach that involves training agents to make decisions in a competitive environment, where each agent is trying to maximize its own reward while also trying to interfere with the other agents' performance. The proposed RARL-based method uses a centralized controller to coordinate the actions of multiple APs in a way that maximizes network throughput while minimizing interference. The controller uses a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the coordination policy, taking into account the dynamic nature of the network and the presence of competing agents. The RARL approach is particularly useful in situations where there is a high degree of uncertainty, as it allows the controller to adapt its policies in real-time based on the actions of the other APs. This makes the system more robust and resilient to unexpected events, such as malfunctions or unplanned changes in the network topology. Overall, the proposed RARL-based multi-AP coordination method has the potential to significantly improve the performance and reliability of wireless networks, particularly in environments with multiple competing APs.

He asked for bail to be granted with conditions. However, the detective sergeant asked for an adjournment to the case, saying he needed time to consider the application and the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested on foot of a European Arrest Warrant. Mr McCollum said his client had been in custody for five days but did not object to the request. The detective sergeant said he needed time to consider the application as he wanted to take account of the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested under a European Arrest Warrant and it had been served by the Northern Ireland Office. District Judge Rosie Watters agreed to the request for an adjournment. Mr McCafferty was released on his own bail of 500 and is due to appear again before the court on June 28.

Ninety-five percent of bird species are socially monogamous. These species pair for at least the length of the breeding season or - in some cases - for several years or until the death of one mate. Monogamy allows for both paternal care and biparental care, which is especially important for species in which females require males' assistance for successful brood-rearing. Among many socially monogamous species, extra-pair copulation (infidelity) is common. Such behaviour typically occurs between dominant males and females paired with subordinate males, but may also be the result of forced copulation in ducks and other anatids. Female birds have sperm storage mechanisms that allow sperm from males to remain viable long after copulation, a hundred days in some species. Sperm from multiple males may compete through this mechanism. For females, possible benefits of extra-pair copulation include getting better genes for her offspring and insuring against the possibility of infertility in her mate. Males of species that engage in extra-pair copulations will closely guard their mates to ensure the parentage of the offspring that they raise.

I will focus on the United States since the hippie movement originated there. During the 1930s and early 1940s, the U.S. endured the hardships of the Great Depression and World War II. Following the war, a period of economic growth began, prompting a desire to restore normalcy. At the same time, the Soviet Union grew stronger, leading to the Cold War. This created a climate of fear regarding communists and dissenters in the U.S., reinforcing a conservative societal structure during the 1950s. In the 1960s, a leftist response emerged against the conservatism of the 1950s, bringing social issues that had been suppressed earlier into the spotlight. The Vietnam War, which was seen as a conflict against communism (part of the Cold War), intensified this backlash. Prior to the war, it was generally believed that fighting communism was a moral duty, but this perspective shifted. Hippies became a youth culture in the 1960s, reacting against the values of the 1950s and the social order they represented. Their beliefs included opposing war, advocating for free love, promoting environmental awareness, and supporting drug use. These ideals directly opposed the Cold War framework of the time.

We present Nopol an approach for automatically repairing buggy if conditions and missing preconditions. As input, it takes a program and a test suite which contains passing test cases modeling the expected behavior of the program and at least one failing test case embodying the bug to be repaired. It consists of collecting data from multiple instrumented test suite executions, transforming this data into a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) problem, and translating the SMT result - if there exists one - into a source code patch. Nopol repairs object oriented code and allows the patches to contain nullness checks as well as specific method calls.

After his coronation, John moved south into France with military forces and adopted a defensive posture along the eastern and southern Normandy borders. Both sides paused for desultory negotiations before the war recommenced; John's position was now stronger, thanks to confirmation that the counts Baldwin IX of Flanders and Renaud of Boulogne had renewed the anti-French alliances they had previously agreed to with Richard. The powerful Anjou nobleman William des Roches was persuaded to switch sides from Arthur to John; suddenly the balance seemed to be tipping away from Philip and Arthur in favour of John. Neither side was keen to continue the conflict, and following a papal truce the two leaders met in January 1200 to negotiate possible terms for peace. From John's perspective, what then followed represented an opportunity to stabilise control over his continental possessions and produce a lasting peace with Philip in Paris. John and Philip negotiated the May 1200 Treaty of Le Goulet; by this treaty, Philip recognised John as the rightful heir to Richard in respect to his French possessions, temporarily abandoning the wider claims of his client, Arthur.[nb 4] John, in turn, abandoned Richard's former policy of containing Philip through alliances with Flanders and Boulogne, and accepted Philip's right as the legitimate feudal overlord of John's lands in France. John's policy earned him the disrespectful title of "John Softsword" from some English chroniclers, who contrasted his behaviour with his more aggressive brother, Richard.

The Book of Discipline is the guidebook for local churches and pastors and describes in considerable detail the organizational structure of local United Methodist churches. All UM churches must have a board of trustees with at least three members and no more than nine members and it is recommended that no gender should hold more than a 23 majority. All churches must also have a nominations committee, a finance committee and a church council or administrative council. Other committees are suggested but not required such as a missions committee, or evangelism or worship committee. Term limits are set for some committees but not for all. The church conference is an annual meeting of all the officers of the church and any interested members. This committee has the exclusive power to set pastors' salaries (compensation packages for tax purposes) and to elect officers to the committees.

I feel like the other answers are missing the point that you want. As said by other posters, your red blood cells literally only carry oxygen to your muscles and CO2 away from them. Imagine your blood cells REALLY want to carry some molecules. For now, imagine we are going back to the lungs. The blood cells have CO2, then. Now, when your blood rushes past the arterioles (very small blood vessels; since they are small, they are very numerous, and the volume:surface area ratio is very small, which makes it much more efficient), that CO2 is switched with the O2. Why? O2 has a much higher concentration near your lungs than it does at your muscles; the molecules want to reach an equilibrium. When there's much more O2 in one side, they actively want to get to another side. I'm sure you've learned of stuff like osmosis and diffusion. This is just osmosisdiffusion through the membranes of the blood vessels. Now, the O2 rich blood will go to your muscular arterioles. There, where there is much more CO2, the O2 will be switched. Now, your muscles have O2 to use, which will be turned to CO2 through cellular respiration (IE, how we turn sugar into energy). However, the blood will now have less O2 and more CO2, and we are brought back to the beginning.,The only "nutrient" that a healthy red blood cell carries to the peripheral cells is oxygen. Basically, it carries oxygen around in a big container inside of it called hemoglobin. When the RBC reaches the capillaries, which are the blood vessels with the smallest diameter, the container opens up and the oxygen diffuses out of the RBC and into the surrounding blood. Then it diffuses into the cells in that immediate vicinity. The way this happens, and the reason that it happens are a bit complex for an ELI5 post but essentially, there are many different conditions that alter how loosely or tightly closed the hemoglobin "container" is. And the conditions in the periphery, where the capillaries are, make it conducive for the RBCs to let go of the oxygen they are carrying.

Some arguments suggest that data limits stem from infrastructure costs and the expense of maintaining systems, along with the need to purchase spectrum. While this could theoretically be the reason, it is not. Internet service providers generate substantial profits, and a few years back, the government allocated funds to enhance their infrastructure, but they did not accomplish much. Thus, if not for financial reasons, what else could explain the limitations? Revenue. They aim to increase earnings. By imposing limits, they can charge higher prices for premium plans and impose excess charges. In the U.S., this approach ultimately revolves around generating more income by burdening customers. Telecom companies invest in spectrum, which grants the right to transmit data, requiring significant capital expenditure that is funded through subscriptions. To make you pay more for less, data caps restrict the total amount of data transferred, typically within a billing cycle. These are not justified technically; they are arbitrary. Spectrum is constrained, especially on mobile networks, limiting overall bandwidth. This results in reduced available bandwidth for users, which is logical. A prevalent misconception is that this limitation justifies data caps. It does not. Spectrum does not cap the total data you can download; it only regulates the speed at which you download. Another myth is about network congestion. People argue data caps are necessary to avoid overwhelming the network, as ISPs sell more bandwidth than they can provide due to non-constant usage. However, congestion involves saturating the network’s capacity, which is primarily a spectrum issue, not a data issue. Data caps do not hinder congestion at all. It remains possible for individuals to connect to the network.

A fully automated knee MRI segmentation technique for studying osteoarthritis (OA) was created using a new hierarchical set of random forests (RF) classifiers to identify the characteristics of cartilage areas and their edges. Initially, a neighborhood approximation forest is employed to supply contextual features for the secondary RF classifier, which also incorporates local features and generates region-specific costs for the layered optimal graph image segmentation framework (LOGISMOS). The MRIs utilized in this research were derived from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) study. These MRIs were trained on 34 cases with differing levels of OA, and the effectiveness of the learning-based method was evaluated on 108 MRIs, resulting in a notable decrease in segmentation inaccuracies (p < 0.05) relative to traditional gradient-based methods and single-stage RF-learned costs. The 3D LOGISMOS was expanded to longitudinal-3D (4D), enabling simultaneous segmentation of multiple follow-up examinations of the same individual. Consequently, data from all time points within the temporal sequence contributes to a singular optimal solution that integrates both spatial 3D and temporal context. Validation of 4D LOGISMOS on 108 MRIs from baseline and 12-month follow-up scans of 54 participants revealed a significant reduction in segmentation errors (p < 0.01) compared to 3D. Further exploration of 4D LOGISMOS was conducted using 5 annual follow-up scans of the same 54 participants, demonstrating a marked enhancement in measuring cartilage thickness (p < 0.01) compared to the sequential 3D approach.

Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) is a key technology for 5G wireless communications with a promise of significant capacity increase. The use of low-resolution data converters is crucial for massive MIMO to make the overall transmission as cost- and energy-efficient as possible. In this work, we consider a downlink millimeter-wave (mmWave) transmission scenario, where multiple users are served simultaneously by massive MIMO with one-bit digital-to-analog (DA) converters. In particular, we propose a novel precoder design based on signal-to-leakage-plus-noise ratio (SLNR), which minimizes energy leakage into undesired users while taking into account impairments due to nonlinear one-bit quantization. We show that well-known regularized zero-forcing (RZF) precoder is a particular version of the proposed SLNR-based precoder, which is obtained when quantization impairments are totally ignored. Numerical results underscore significant performance improvements along with the proposed SLNR-based precoder as compared to either RZF or zero-forcing (ZF) precoders.

While the prospect of increased autonomy for Scots, Welsh, and Northern Irish in shaping their economies might seem appealing, it could prove detrimental if they simultaneously experience economic hardship. The key issue lies in the potential shift towards an English parliament for English citizens—something that former Tory minister John Redwood has advocated for, and which David Cameron appeared to support recently. This change could make sustaining financial transfers from England to the remaining parts of the UK more challenging. Consequently, these constitutional changes could be complex and potentially risky, especially if the existing cohesion within the UK relies on the redistribution of funds from England to other regions, and this balance begins to erode.

Currently, being British entails that public services and living standards generally remain close in quality and quantity across different regions. However, if the restructuring of the UK’s fiscal system undermines this unity, significant consequences may follow. For instance, per capita public-sector expenditures are highest in Northern Ireland at PS10,900, lowest in England at PS8,500, and slightly above average in Scotland at PS10,200. Scotland’s public-service spending is approximately 20% higher per person than that of the rest of the UK, and 28% higher in Northern Ireland. In Wales, the increase in public-service spending is only 14%, which the Welsh frequently argue is insufficient relative to the income transfers to Scotland.

One approach to understanding the magnitude of these transfers is by examining the gross value added (GVA) generated in each region. English GVA per head is the highest at around PS22,000, while in Wales it is lower at PS15,400. The English population spends nearly 40 times more annually on public services than the income they produce, a disparity that raises concerns about the sustainability and fairness of such fiscal arrangements.

Widespread deployment of the Internet enabled building of an emerging IT delivery model, i.e., cloud computing. Albeit cloud computing-based services have rapidly developed, their security aspects are still at the initial stage of development. In order to preserve cybersecurity in cloud computing, cybersecurity information that will be exchanged within it needs to be identified and discussed. For this purpose, we propose an ontological approach to cybersecurity in cloud computing. We build an ontology for cybersecurity operational information based on actual cybersecurity operations mainly focused on non-cloud computing. In order to discuss necessary cybersecurity information in cloud computing, we apply the ontology to cloud computing. Through the discussion, we identify essential changes in cloud computing such as data-asset decoupling and clarify the cybersecurity information required by the changes such as data provenance and resource dependency information.

At its core, what I grasped was that the notion that men dressed as women implies women's inferiority stems from patriarchal oppression, which has historically been pervasive across human societies. Thus, restrictions on men dressing as women do not demonstrate that women are considered inferior; rather, women are inherently viewed as inferior by default. Any gender norm—whether granting freedom or imposing constraints—points to male dominance. Therefore, the argument fundamentally rests on the idea that men are inherently flawed and oppressive, which explains why women are perceived as inferior and why such restrictions exist. However, if one does not accept the foundational premise—that patriarchal oppression is universal and inherent—it becomes a mere "because," which is insufficient justification. Believing that patriarchal oppression is the root of all good and all evil leads to accepting "because" as a valid explanation for every societal issue. This mindset mirrors a form of religious belief where "because God" suffices to explain every phenomenon. Similarly, asserting that men are bad because they established patriarchy provides a satisfactory explanation for issues like voting restrictions but also for the restriction on women's dress styles. The consequence of this worldview, however, fosters a sense of perpetual victimhood, a topic I'd like to explore further. My focus remains on the argument that when someone claims society tells women they're inferior, they actually believe society is structured this way because men are oppressive as a gender trait. In essence, the claim itself reflects the opposite belief. To be convincing, one must genuinely hold that men are harmful, which underpins the assertion that women are inferior. I’d appreciate hearing a more profound analysis of this perspective to potentially reshape my understanding.

In this paper, we consider the joint task of simultaneously optimizing (i) the weights of a deep neural network, (ii) the number of neurons for each hidden layer, and (iii) the depth of the network. More specifically, we propose an optimization method that determines the optimal values for these parameters via a weighted combination of the generalization error and the model size. We show that when trained on image data, the proposed optimization method outperforms a number of other state-of-the-art methods such as Bayesian optimization, evolutionary algorithms, and gradient descent on image classification tasks. In addition, we demonstrate that by training the proposed model on one image classification dataset, we are able to obtain a well-performing model on other datasets, e.g., CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with minimal training. This is done by using the learned weights of the model on the one dataset to initialize a new model on the other two datasets. As our method can train a model from scratch or fine-tune a pretrained model, it can be considered as a universal image classifier (UIC), which provides an interpretable, efficient, and flexible alternative to other recent methods such as Gatys and Lu et al. . In addition to image classification, our method can also be used to train a model that can generalize across different tasks. We conduct experiments to demonstrate that trained with the proposed method, a model can generalize across tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation with no additional training data. Finally, our method is easy to implement and can be directly applied to any deep neural network without changing the network architecture. Paper can be found here. Understanding the formation of subjective human traits, such as preference and opinions, is an important, but poorly explored problem. An essential aspect is that traits collectively evolve under the repeated influence of the environment. The impact of the environment is especially strong in situations where individuals differ in the baseline trait level, where preferences and opinions can develop over time in a dynamic context. It is important to understand the underlying mechanisms of this dynamic evolution of opinions, in order to be able to shape opinions in a desired direction, e.g. for the purpose of social manipulation. I will present a game-theoretic model that allows to study the evolution of traits under repeated environmentally-driven interactions. I will show that the social evolution of traits can be driven by a process of 'drift and selection', in which both drift and selection are driven by the repeated environmental influence. I will discuss implications of this model for the understanding of opinion formation, and apply the model to different settings.

If that happens, the ice loss could push up global oceans by 2m, or more. The claim is based on an assessment of the rocks underlying the ice stream. Scientists tell the journal Nature that should the front of the glacier retreat about 150km from its current position, it will then enter a runaway reversal that takes it 200-250km further inland. Most of the big glaciers in the east of the White Continent appear relatively quiescent; Totten is something of an exception. It is experiencing a thinning rate of about half a metre per year, according to the latest satellite measurements. Previous research indicates this is probably being driven by warm ocean water getting under and melting the floating front of the glacier. What Alan Aitken and colleagues have now done is examine a possible future for Totten if the shrinkage continues. They have used gravity and magnetic data recorded over the entire catchment feeding the glacier to understand its past behaviour. They find that the underlying sedimentary rocks at the modern front of Totten are heavily eroded, as are the rocks in fjords deep in the interior of the catchment. The inference is that these sections are where persistent, moving ice has had time to grind down the geology. It is the mid-region, however, that piques the team's interest. Here, the sediments are relatively thick, suggesting that ice fronts have historically been resident in this section for only short periods. This mid-region is also where the rock bed dips inland - a geometry that glaciologists say is naturally unstable and accelerates any glacier retreat. "What this all tells us is that once the ice margin starts to go back, it goes back quite rapidly to a newer, stable position way inland. And if you do that our modelling indicates you will lose ice equivalent to 1.5-2m of sea level rise," co-author Prof Martin Siegert from Imperial College London, UK, told BBC News. The last time Totten retreated to the deep interior of the France-sized catchment was probably in the Pliocene Epoch, he added. "Three-point-five million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were in the region of 400 parts per million - so about where they are now. The atmosphere was a couple of degrees warmer than it is now, which is in line with what we expect for the end of this century if we do nothing about it. The Pliocene is where we're headed." Even so, the timescale for the far retreat inland would be on the order of centuries, on current trends. The international community has of course committed itself to doing something about climate change, promising at the Paris talks in December to try to keep the global atmospheric temperature rise above pre-industrial levels to "well below 2C." Various analyses, however, suggest a 2.7C increase is a more likely outcome, based on the voluntary national curbs to greenhouse gas emissions promised at the meeting. And that variance could be significant, according to research presented at the recent European Geosciences Union meeting in Vienna last month. Prof Rob DeConto from the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, US, has modelled possible ice losses from the Antarctic continent based on the two temperature figures. For a 2C rise, he found minimal change by the end of this century. On the other hand, for 2.7C he identified ice losses equivalent to many tens of centimetres of sea-level rise. "There's threshold behaviour in the Antarctic ice sheet system," Prof DeConto told reporters at EGU. The concept of prime number is so important that it has been generalized in different ways in various branches of mathematics. Generally, "prime" indicates minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense as the set of divisors (or integers) whose square roots are exactly equal to each other and which satisfy some condition on their sum. For example, a prime number satisfies the Faulkner-Salvin Steinage theorem: A prime number has at least one negative integer, if and only if its sum is at most twice the product of all other numbers. You can also use this theorem for the rule that any two positive integers with nonnegative square root values must have to be prime numbers. One prime number means, among other things, convergence between a tensor function x and a real line that connects the origin to the leftmost point of the unit circle. The Klein group and Lie algebra are examples of prime groups; enumeration theory, projective geometry, and computational algebra are others. A prime number represents an identity element of a polynomial, a trigonometric function, a specific series, or whatever you like by identifying what it does to a linear operator. It's often used to identify particular sequences of operations such as addition, multiplication, division, subtraction, etc., based on how they produce unique pairs of variables when multiplied or divided by another variable. Modern applications include cryptography, artificial intelligence, combinatorics, and computer graphics (see Moore's Law). The term also appears frequently in physics and astronomy (in regard to prime numbers), because many X-Y coordinates are considered prime factors of 1. Prime logarithms were first introduced in the 19th century. In mathematics the notion of a prime gauge is a generalization of the idea of prime numbers derived from the study of polar coordinates. According to these definitions, every large prime number r2 belongs to a homomorphism class of functors (and hence to a subcategory of the CMF functor space), which corresponds to the core group of a functional analysis type of category theory. These classification schemes classify by size and not necessarily by dimension. This concept was proposed by Viktor Miller in his 1951 paper. Russia plans to temporarily disconnect the entire country from the internet in an exercise designed to test the country's internet infrastructure in case of a cyber-war. The test is expected to begin on Monday. Russia's RIA Novosti news agency quoted Russian Defense Ministry spokesman Igor Konashenkov as saying on Friday that Russia's Defense Ministry is planning to test the country's defense system in the event of a cyber-attack on Monday. Konashenkov said that the exercise will include a shutdown of internet service in the entire country. "During the day on Monday, the entire Russian Federation will be offline for several hours," Konashenkov said. "The aim of the exercise is to test the entire internet infrastructure of the Russian Federation, including the country's cyber-defense system." Konashenkov added that the exercise is part of the Defense Ministry's efforts to protect the country's national security and to develop the country's cyber-defense capabilities. "The exercises will be held in different regions of the country," he said. "We're testing our defense system to see how we're prepared to face such a situation." Asked whether Russia was preparing for a cyber-war with the United States, Konashenkov said: "We're always ready for any cyber-attacks, including against Russia." He added that "the United States should also be ready for any cyber-attacks against it." Russia has repeatedly warned of the possibility of a cyber-attack on its territory, although no such attack has ever been launched. The Defense Ministry also said that during the exercise, Russia's air force will test the capabilities of its "cyber-aircraft" and its own capabilities to conduct cyber-attacks. Konashenkov said that the military's goal is to increase the country's ability to protect its military information systems from cyber-attacks. "We're preparing for cyber-attacks on our military," he said.

Many years ago, keyboards used different pins to represent each bit of information. When some keys were held down, a different set of pins would have voltage across them than others. USB doesn't work that way at all. It just sends data back and forth, one bit at a time, very quickly. It's a lot more like sending data across a network. When you hold down multiple keys, it just sends more bytes of data. When you record audio, it's digitizing the audio and streaming the bytes directly to your computer.," "Professional audio is recorded at least 44,100 samples per second, with 24 bits per sample. That's a data rate of around 1060 kbs. USB 2 supports a data rate of up to 480 Mbs. That's around 47 individual microphones all at the same time. It works because USB is a serial communication with high speed switching. Meaning it sends two bits down the data pins, and rapidly switches between which bit is being sent. It switches literally millions of times a second, plenty fast for audio.,The reason you can detect large amounts of keys pressed and record high quality audio is that the USB device is its self a little computer. It has enough circuitry to detect all the key presses and record the audio and then it packages all that data into a single stream of bits, and it's the bits that get sent back and forth over the USB connection. In fact, this data is only sent over two of the four pins. The other two are used only for delivering power to a USB device that doesn't have its own power supply. The reason the microphone can transmit in very very close to real time is that sound is very slow compared to have fast computers are. Sound is a wave of changing air pressure that moves through the air. The higher the tone or pitch, the faster the air pressure changes neutral to high to low and back to neutral. The highest frequency humans can hear is 20KHz which means the air pressure makes that cycle 20,000 times a second. To record this sound a microphone is setup which converts the air pressure into a voltage that swings from low to high and back, just like the air pressure. This changing voltage is then "sampled" by a converter circuit. Sample here just means to measure. So the voltage is measure to see how high it is at a given point. If you do this over and over again, and you do it fast enough, you get enough measurements to recreate the original sound with an amplifier and speaker. To get enough samples to do this, you need to measure twice as fast as the highest frequency in order not to miss the really fast changing voltage. Recall the highest was 20,000 times a second. So we sample at 44,100 times a second. Now lets check some numbers. Each sample requires 16 bits of data and there are 44,100 samples per second so that is 705,600 bits per second. Most USB audio interfaces can record two channels at the same time, and play back two channels at the same time, so now we need to move 2,822,400 bits per second. Sounds like a lot. Except even the slowest USB devices can send 12,000,000 bits per second. So we can do 4 channels of high quality audio and still have 10,000,000 bits per second left over. Now sending audio data to the computer actually uses a lot more of that 12,000,000 bits per second because the audio has to be packaged in a way that the computer understands what it is and where it goes and that's done by wrapping the samples in other data.', "The USB 2.0 (most common) standard has support for data transfer speeds as high as 480 Mbps (more than enough to handle audio and most video input streams). The new USB 3.0 standard supports data transfer speeds of up to 5 Gbps and USB 3.1 supports up to 10 Gbps (which is enough bandwidth to handle just about any multimedia peripheral device you can possibly think of including live 4K video streams, for example). Of the 4 pins in a regular USB 2.0 cable, only 2 are used for data and the other two are used for supplying voltagepower. The USB device has a chip in it that converts the information (e.g. audio information from a microphone or keyboard presses) into packets of data that can be transferred via USB to the receiving device (computer). That's why you don't need multiple wires for carrying different types of data, it all just gets converted into one data stream. Note that newer USB implementations (3.0 3.1) have more than 4 pins to facilitate higher speed data transfers greater bandwidth.

All political parties were dissolved, along with labor unions and Galician nationalist groups, following the establishment of the Seminario de Estudios Galegos. According to Carlos Fernández Santander, at least 4,200 individuals died through extrajudicial means or via summary trials, including republicans, communists, Galician nationalists, socialists, and anarchists. The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. Facebook is facing a 20 million (22.5 million) fine in Germany over the way it acquired user data from WhatsApp. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. In 2016, it announced plans to start sharing user data between the two services, but said it would not do so without obtaining user consent. The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said on Tuesday, however, that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. "We are aware of the DPA's statement of objections and are examining the documents," a Facebook spokeswoman said in a statement. "We will respond in due course." The WhatsApp and Facebook merger generated plenty of controversy when it was first announced. The social network said it would start sharing data with WhatsApp in August 2016, but the European Commission halted the process in August 2017 while it investigated antitrust concerns. That investigation has since been dropped, but the Commissioner's announcement this week shows that privacy regulators are still probing the issue. "Facebook and WhatsApp are independent companies. And that's why we're not able to combine user data," Facebook told the Commissioner in January 2017. "The only thing we're asking for is the number of phone contacts the user has on WhatsApp in order to improve their experience on Facebook." According to the Commissioner, however, WhatsApp users were not informed they would need to agree to new terms and conditions in order to continue using the service. "The requirement of unequivocal consent to the terms of data processing was also not met, as the users did not have a free choice," the office said. Facebook also used "inappropriate" tracking pixels to collect data about WhatsApp users, the Commissioner's office said. Tracking pixels, also known as web beacons, are tiny images embedded in webpages that can be used to collect data. "Facebook has used its dominant position to create a situation in which users had to agree to the processing of their data on a central platform. This has led to a reduction of users' control over their data," the Commissioner said. Facebook didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

He was defeated by Justinian I at the Battle of Pavia in 878 and died shortly thereafter while on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.[65] In 966, Italian forces were decisively driven from Sicily during the Angevin conquest under Charles the Fat by Stephen II of Taranto,[6869] who soon became emperor after Baldwin III's death.[70] In 1054 he took possession of Rome, which had been left without rulers for more than 500 years since the fall of Hadrian.[71] The Frankish kingdom continued to expand eastward into the Balkans where it met with a series of wars against Bulgarian and Venetian dynasties (976-982) over several large territories; eventually, however, the crusaders lost control over most territory they captured and quickly reverted to the status quo ante bellum. Francia reached its zenith in 1017 when Pope Urban II consecrated Henry V as Holy Roman Emperor. After this time, the Franks began to lose their influence - or so seemed likely at first: in 1135, Frederick Barbarossa completed his reconquest of Saxony[72], but within decades the province was again ruled by a local lord rather than a German king. The same fate visited Silesia in 129798.[73] By 1345 all these lands except Bohemia [74] lay outside the jurisdiction of either France or Germany. Under Louis XI there was some recourse to Byzantine ideas about "national unity," although unlike the Greeks' imperial system Louis did not attempt to enforce such an idea through coercion. As noted above, many of the foreigners who settled in the West considered themselves independent. They lived alongside native peoples who complained that the conquerors treated them differently because they were foreign, often employing force to impose their rule upon locals[75]. Examples included William Rufus, Prince-Bishop of Paris between 1151 and 1198 who established himself throughout Normandy until his defeat near Rouen in 1200 led him back to Paris, and Tancred de Koves, Count Palatine of Burgundy and Duke of Lorraine, whose position in eastern Germany was challenged after Philip II named Staufenberg archbishop of Mainz. These men attempted to extend French authority only to the degree whereby the populace would accept it. When these settlements didn't last long, the Europeans had mixed feelings. A few claimed to be genuine Christians seeking to share Christ's message among pagan nations, but others wanted what they regarded as unfree European land to be theirs alone, using any means necessary. This is seen today especially clearly in Northern Europe. Fortunately for Western civilization, neither the concept nor practice of the Crusades endured uncritically past the 14th century. It has survived in popular culture though largely in fiction.[76] From the Middle Ages, historicism also gained prominence in archaeology, astronomy, geology, botany, geography, linguistics, medicine, mathematics, music, philosophy, politics and sociology. According to historian John Dower: "Historicists saw Latin as simple language based originally on Greek rather than Hebrew, and as a literary form derived equally from Homeric Greece...77] Despite being introduced into the academy with great fanfare and heralded as 'the new science' by Voltaire and Leibniz, Historicism never really caught fire, aside from the beginnings of History as Science before 1900 - especially after World War I - when historians generally started to recognize the importance of scientific methods, data analysis and empirical evidence in the study if history. After the Renaissance, historical studies grew out of maps made possible by cartography, which helped researchers trace the boundaries of medieval kingdoms and empires across Europe. Historians used these markers to find information about political power structures external to those marked on ancient maps including trade patterns and population figures. For example, English chroniclers like Edward Gibbon could show how England rose to become one of the world's largest and richest countries and then collapsed just three hundred years later due to internal conflicts. Maps even allowed for statistical comparisons, showing increasing wealth and urbanization along the continent starting around the middle ages, while decreasing populations occurred primarily in rural areas. Today scientists use satellite images to map changes in agriculture and natural landscapes. Malachi Love-Robinson, 18, was arrested after examining and providing medical advice to an undercover police officer. He was released on bail on Wednesday. Mr Love-Robinson has denied that he posed as a medical doctor and said he only used the title because he had obtained a PhD online. "This was me simply trying to do something for the community in a light that I saw that was needed," he told WPTV, a West Palm Beach news channel. "Honestly, if you ask me many people are getting tired of hearing that they have to take a script just to feel better." The website of the New Birth New Life Medical Center describes him as a "well rounded professional." In January 2015, at the age of 17, he was reportedly caught walking around a local hospital wearing a white coat and carrying a stethoscope. Mr Love-Robinson has since insisted in media interviews that he has certifications to practise alternative medicine, including naturopathy. Scans of certificates from the American Alternative Medical Association and American Association of Drugless Practitioners had previously been posted to his Facebook page, which now appears to have been taken down. Mr Love-Robinson said he became interested in alternative medicine while suffering from illnesses during childhood. According to the Palm Beach Post, he claims to suffer from the auto-immune disease lupus, while a post on his Facebook page earlier this month said he was suffering from kidney cancer. The Palm Beach County sheriff's office says Mr Love-Robinson examined an 86-year-old in December who suffered from severe stomach pain. He allegedly diagnosed her with arthritis and sold her vitamins, receiving more than 3,000 (PS2,090) for a series of home visits. While the Treaties and Regulations will have direct effect (if clear, unconditional and immediate), Directives do not generally give citizens (as opposed to the member state) standing to sue other citizens. In theory, this is because TFEU article 288 says Directives are addressed to the member states and usually "leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods" to implement. In part this reflects that directives often create minimum standards, leaving member states to apply higher standards. For example, the Working Time Directive requires that every worker has at least 4 weeks paid holidays each year, but most member states require more than 28 days in national law. However, on the current position adopted by the Court of Justice, citizens have standing to make claims based on national laws that implement Directives, but not from Directives themselves. Directives do not have so called "horizontal" direct effect (i.e. between non-state parties). This view was instantly controversial, and in the early 1990s three Advocate Generals persuasively argued that Directives should create rights and duties for all citizens. The Court of Justice refused, but there are five large exceptions.
