It's more cost-effective to manufacture engines with greater displacement. The relationship between horsepower and RPM is direct; smaller engines require higher RPMs to generate more power. Higher RPMs necessitate lightweight yet robust components. Automotive manufacturers must optimize intake and exhaust systems and invest significant time in designing chambers for enhanced efficiency and performance. Developing smaller engines demands more time and research compared to creating a larger engine.

Most responses here are incorrect. Some are more so than others. Internal combustion engines are highly intricate, and providing a simplistic explanation does them injustice. Recall that when a manufacturer states horsepower, it refers to peak horsepower, which is the maximum power produced within the engine's operating range. Avoiding overly technical language, consider this: try accelerating your vehicle at 1500 RPM and then again at 4000 RPM. Since your car typically has a power curve that delivers more power at higher RPMs, flooring it at 4000 RPM will result in quicker acceleration. This is because the engine produces less power at 1500 RPM. Claiming two vehicles have "300 hp" isn't informative if one produces 300 hp across all RPMs, whereas the other generates 300 hp at high RPMs but lacks power at lower RPMs. Several factors contribute to manufacturers opting for large-displacement engines. A key reason is achieving a more uniform power delivery curve. While this isn't universally true, larger engines are easier to design with balanced power characteristics. This is beneficial for various driving scenarios as it allows smooth acceleration from low RPMs, advantageous for both road use and racing. Another reason is simplicity and weight. Weight? What? I had assumed bigger displacement equaled heavier engines. Actually, smaller displacement engines frequently employ turbochargers to enhance power and efficiency. While this is beneficial, turbochargers add weight and occupy space.

Quantum annealing (QA) is a quantum computing algorithm that works on the principle of Adiabatic Quantum Computation (AQC), and it has shown significant computational advantages in solving combinatorial optimization problems . QA has recently been extended to general matrix operations by introducing a multipoint thresholding technique called Multi-Objective Quantum Annealing, which allows for the calculation of more than one objective at once using an ensemble of measurement outcomes while preserving the original state before any measurements were performed. This approach has become known as Multimodal QA because multiple objectives can be simultaneously optimized with very different error rates; however, its performance cannot yet match those obtained from QA alone owing to limitations intrinsic to the process itself, such as decoherence with respect to the environment. Although there are several techniques available to reduce this effect, not all have proven effective enough to allow real-time implementation of multimodality. Furthermore, the development of new devices capable of performing multitudinous object analyses may take decades or longer, resulting in unacceptable delay times between problem formulation and solution execution. The goal of our project was therefore to develop novel methods to accelerate the algorithms used in Multi-objective QA so they can be implemented within milliseconds rather than minutes. To accomplish this, we developed two new approaches: 1) A method where solutions are found concurrently across all objectives instead of sequentially, thus obviating the need for global environmental control during multi-objective analysis 2) Methods to reduce coherence noise inherent to the AQC procedure itself through the use of tailored engineered environments

Overly parameterized pre-trained language models may exhibit significant miscalibration across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) data. To counteract this problem, we introduce a regularized fine-tuning approach. This method incorporates two types of regularization to enhance calibration: (1) On-manifold regularization, which creates pseudo on-manifold samples by interpolating within the data manifold. Scientists from the University of California San Diego have developed a method to create neurons. The technique is able to convert astrocytes, the supporting cells in the brain, into neurons, including three types of neurons with distinct functions - for example, excitatory, inhibitory and neurological. The researchers say that their work provides an alternative to current methods used by neuroscientists who use stem cells in developing new neurons which might otherwise be lost when those cells are destroyed during this process. "Neuroshima," discovered 60 years ago, was one of the first tools scientists employed to create nerve cells containing neurons but it could not produce enough neurons because it lacked sufficient support cells. This problem means that most attempts at making neurons using pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) end up as either 'osteoblasts' - like embryonic fibres - or smooth muscle cells, which do not possess sufficient neuron-producing ability to develop into new neurons. Researchers had previously failed to create neurons using these techniques because they contained insufficient astrocyte survival factors (ASF). In 2001, Dr Liisa Talvi and her team at UCSD identified ASFs in astrocytes and demonstrated they were capable of generating neurons in animal studies. They also discovered that astrocytes provided the necessary nutrients needed to promote neural cell growth. Now, after a series of experiments on human brains, they have found that adding these ASMs can help them generate neurons with particular properties such as excitability, strength and electrical conductivity. These characteristics make astrocytes suitable candidates as targets for controlling neuronal activity through stimulation and inhibition. Professor Talvi said: "We showed that we can direct the development of astroglia when stimulating the vascularization of their parenchyma, the fluid surrounding them. We also discovered that inhibiting the formation of astroglial vesicles via a small molecule antagonist completely changes the shape of the organelles so that they form a different type of neuron. Our research has helped us achieve our goal and advance our knowledge about how astrocytes affect neuronal function and how this affects the development of neurons. This provides us with exciting possibilities where we may use these astrocytes to speed up neuroscientific discoveries and ultimately improve human health."

It's taken me a long time to decide. There are still 5 days for me to change my mind, but as it stands I want to leave the UK's economic injustice, its shoddy governance, and its establishment. I'm going to go through each issue and give a brief overview of the arguments. Then I'll state why I'm choosing Yes, and why I'm not choosing No. Democracy - Nobody from either side argues that Westminster is without fault. On the Yes side they pretend that Westminster is bad because it projects Tory government into Scotland. On the No side they believe that Westminster can be changed for the better from within. They're both wrong. Westminster is anti-democratic in other ways. Not just with the problems of the Lords, Cash for Honours and Expenses: the voting system means that even when Labour gets into power, it is not because Scotland voted for it. First-past-the-post means that there is [bias towards a two-party system] , and the main parties become inevitably more alike as they appeal to centrist, swing voters. And there is no swing in Scotland. It is mainly in the South of England. So it is no surprise that in 69 years of Westminster rule, Scottish votes changed which party received power only once, in 1974. In addition, Westminster steals our best politicians and leaves only numpties like Johann Lamont to hold the Scottish Government to account. If you think those Scottish MPs are doing a good job, over 30 of the 59 voted for benefit caps, and are straying from the ideology of their voter base. Why would we agree to that arrangement? Why, when we have the Additional Member System in Holyrood that is (by voting standards) pure sex, creates representative parliaments, and where coalitions force parties to adopt common-sense policies everyone can agree on rather than top-down ideological reorganisations? Politics - The SNP have created a myth that they are the party of progressiveness, and that independence is the stepping stone to social justice. Many no voters I've spoken to just can't see past Alex Salmond, don't like "nationalism," (the word is used in the same ignorant way socialism is in the USA) and have not thought about the long term consequences of independence on the political discourse. I think the argument that I've heard that Scotland has more in common with the London dockworker than the Scottish baron is absolute nonsense. It ignores the fact Scottish and English politics is diverging. Holyrood does not draw on ethnic identity politics. It draws on Scotland's collectivism. The anti-bedroom tax payment, removing charges and private investment from the NHS, community buying of privately owned land, and free university education stand in stark contrast to austerity and corporate welfare. Meanwhile, UKIP's rise guarantees that Westminster will resemble the worse kind of nationalism more than Holyrood ever could. They stress benefit thievery, not tax-dodging. Immigration, not job creation. That we need to protect ourselves from Putin with Trident and from Islamists with military force. Moreover, the system entrenches establishment, widens the wealth gap and shrinks social mobility. Rather than uniting so the system can disenfranchise as it has done, Scotland is far better off walking away from the corporate agenda, not incrementally coaxing it to what it wants. Defence Foreign Policy - The SNP want rid of trident but want to join NATO, Better Together cry doom at Scotland's defence and lack of influence at the top. Jobs at Faslane could be threatened but the SNP have pledged to re-employ them. We got dragged into an illegal war, and the UK's foreign policy has been nothing but bad news when it comes to the middle east. Having a smaller voice that says good things is better than a large, infinitely belligerent one. Leaving the UK is not going to change what the UK says, so if you like UK foreign policy, don't worry, it's still going to be there. In addition, it will give us a seat on the EU council where the Cabinet secretary stopped the Scottish Fisheries minister from attending , when he is the person with the most influence. EU - This is an shitstorm equal to the economic arguments. Vast quantities of legal opinions on both sides. At the end of the day, given that Scotland holds 25 of the EU's renewable energy potential, 20 of the fishery stocks, and only 1 of the population of Europe, a deal will be struck. The EU can't risk looking anti-democratic and it certainly won't risk those fishery stocks. It will probably take longer than the SNP claim though. Duncan wasn't really convinced that the plan was going to work. Two days ago he was awaiting transfer to a more secure location, which sounded like they were going to "suicide" him if one believed the word around the holding cells, and suddenly yesterday a guard he had seen on duty for the past three weeks handed him a most surprising note written on a napkin during the usual weekly search of his "apartment" as the guards referred to them. The note read: "Tomorrow. Midnight. Be ready. Get rid of the note" After reading it 10 times or more Duncan flushed the note down the poor excuse of a toilet his "apartment" contained and sat on his bed considering the significance of it. It could be a cruel joke or an attempt to find excuses to make his stay even more unpleasant. He had managed to hold his mouth shut as far as the most important information went and that didn't sit well with his hosts. The interrogations had been long and tiresome and they had started to get painful in the last 2 weeks, the scars on his back a testimony to the latter. And yet there he was staring at the guard that handed him the note with something far more dangerous in hand. Another explosion drove him from his thoughts and into action, grabbing the gun and saying "Lead on then." The air was filled with the shouting and running of the other guardsmen who went back and forth above them on the platforms. Taking a moment to let them pass Mr Bond, as Duncan decided to call his rescuer, started leading him through the maze of corridors and staircases that filled the facility and in no rare occasion they had to pause and wait before they could continue until they made their way to the main gate. It was a wide corridor leading to a security checkpoint with always two guards present and the door could only be opened by the key card one of them carried although he didn't know who. There was no way they could approach without being spotted "I hope you have something good planned because I can't think of any way to get through this without getting spotted by your ex-colleagues" whispered Duncan turning to Mr Bond. "Don't worry I have this covered. We will approach quickly but don't run. I will be escorting you to a different cell because the Warden fears for your safety due to the explosions. Say nothing and hide the gun. Do not stop walking before we reach the gate whatever happens. We don't want to give them any doubts." Duncan nodded in agreement, hid his gun and after taking a deep breath to pick up some courage followed Mr Bond. The moment they turned the corner Mr Bond hailed the two guards who looked at him with startled faces. "The Warden wants this one moved. Open the gate quickly." They were at the middle of the way to the gate. "They told us nothing of this change Eddie. We have to check with Taylor upstairs." They were almost upon them. "We don't have time for you to check! Haven't you heard the explosions? Open this gate NOW." Before the guard could give voice to his answer Mr Bond thrust his right hand downwards expanding a baton not even Duncan noticed he was holding and with one swift stroke hit the guard in the head making him topple over. The other one went for his gun but it only took that one moment of surprise for Mr Bond to reach him and take him out as well. In thirty seconds they were running towards a 4x4 with all their might hearing the alarm go off as they reached it. They wasted no time in getting away with Mr Bond at the wheel making for the nearby hills. When they reached the nearest woods they left the car. "A helicopter is supposed to meet us two kilometers north of here in three hours" said Mr Bond and motioned Duncan to follow. "So how much did you tell them?" asked Mr Bond as they were making their path through the trees. "Well they know the movements of the rest of my platoon for the past weeks but I managed to withhold the real purpose behind them. Which was? What day is it? Thursday the 15th. Well then tomorrow those guys are going to have the surprise of their lives. We have gathered our forces in secret with my platoon running interference to attack the underground base of operations they maintain to the west part of the valley. Really? How did we learn of it existence in the first place? We captured some key personnel during another mission near the borders of that area. Pure luck. You're right. Pure damn luck" The next thing Duncan saw was Mr Bond pulling out his own gun and pointing it at him with a smile. He heard a loud noise and he knew no more.

A study conducted by The Local Data Company (LDC) and the University of Stirling revealed that the average retail vacancy rate in Scotland decreased from 14.5 to 13.7. East Kilbride holds the highest vacancy rate among Scottish towns at 33%, whereas Inverurie has the lowest at 1%. The research indicated that 40 of Scotland's empty shops have remained unoccupied for over three years. It further noted that town vacancy rates have improved at twice the pace of Scotland's urban areas. The most notable improvements were observed in Anstruther, Clydebank, Dumfries, Inverkeithing, Lochgelly, Peterhead, and Pitlochry. Five towns have maintained vacancy rates below 6% for the past three years—Inverurie, Ellon, North Berwick, Dunbar, and Biggar. Conversely, five towns have retained vacancy rates exceeding 22% for the same period—Banff, Dumbarton, Cumbernauld, East Kilbride, and Ardrossan. Dundee recorded the highest percentage of persistent vacancies at 11%. Anstruther reported the highest proportion of independent shops (86%), while Gretna had the lowest (5%). Leisure activities are becoming increasingly vital in cities and towns, contributing 39% of total shop stocks in Edinburgh and Glasgow. Leisure businesses also account for over 30% of shops in Renfrew, St Andrews, Lochgelly, and Fort William. Aberdeen leads with the highest proportion of charity shops for a city at 4.2%, while Penicuik in Midlothian has the highest proportion of charity shops for a town at 8.9%. Matthew Hopkinson, director at LDC, stated: "The report highlights key trends and challenges misconceptions about deprived towns failing to thrive. A critical finding is that nearly 40% of vacant units in many Scottish towns have been unoccupied for more than three years. This figure underscores obsolescence and presents a significant obstacle to creating healthy and sustainable communities." The study examined the vitality of high streets across more than 100 cities and towns in Scotland.

As the muscles holding the spine straight begin to relax, the spine naturally curves, causing slouching. This problem occurs more often than you think, and it is extremely common for people who have back problems in general to experience this problem. The most common symptoms include: The slouched posture can be caused by any number of factors including body mass index (BMI), weight gain or loss, muscle strength or weakness, low blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol levels, and certain medications such as gastric bypass surgery. Another cause of a slouchy posture has actually been identified, which means that it will not go away unless addressed from an early age. It's called "postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome" (POTS). Though POTS isn't life-threatening, if left untreated it can lead to serious health issues later on in life. If you suspect your posture may be affecting your sleep because you are slouched over all night long then getting some help might be necessary. If you are tired during the day but still find yourself falling asleep with a slumped forward position at night then having a change in attitude towards how you sleep could make a big difference. Here are four tips to consider when trying to solve this issue: Try sleeping on your side instead of your back, though it may take a little time to get used to. Have one pillow under each arm so that you don't have to try too hard to adjust your body to place itself across either side of the pillow. Put a blanket over both sides of the bed so that if you do need to decide where you want to sleep it would be easy enough to lean into the blankets without worrying about hurting your head due to length. Finally, put pillows between your knees - putting them slightly off center will allow you to raise your legs up higher while keeping them below your chest. Doing this should keep you from slumping sideways on your mattress. In order to maintain proper alignment and balance throughout your day, you must also make sure that your back is in good shape. A perfectly healthy spine helps to support the rest of your body, and can even prevent you from suffering debilitating conditions like arthritis down the road. Unfortunately, many people aren't aware of these benefits until their backs start acting up after years upon years of poor posture. Along with better mobility comes improved flexibility, and those who suffer from bad posture tend to spend far less time working out. In fact, studies show that just 15 minutes per week of yoga can affect your posture by improving your flexibility, mood, and overall physical fitness. In this paper, we proposed T-Net containing a small encoder-decoder inside the encoder-decoder structure (EDiED). T-Net overcomes the limitation that U-Net can only have a single set of the concatenate layer between encoder and decoder block. To be more precise, the U-Net symmetrically forms the concatenate layers, so the low-level feature of the encoder is connected to the latter part of the decoder, and the high-level feature is connected to the beginning of the decoder. T-Net arranges the pooling and up-sampling appropriately during the encoder process, and likewise during the decoding process so that feature-maps of various sizes are obtained in a single block. As a result, all features from the low-level to the high-level extracted from the encoder are delivered from the beginning of the decoder to predict a more accurate mask. We evaluated T-Net for the problem of segmenting three main vessels in coronary angiography images. The experiment consisted of a comparison of U-Net and T-Nets under the same conditions, and an optimized T-Net for the main vessel segmentation. As a result, T-Net recorded a Dice Similarity Coefficient score (DSC) of 0.815, 0.095 higher than that of U-Net, and the optimized T-Net recorded a DSC of 0.890 which was 0.170 higher than that of U-Net. In addition, we visualized the weight activation of the convolutional layer of T-Net and U-Net to show that T-Net actually predicts the mask from earlier decoders. Therefore, we expect that T-Net can be effectively applied to other similar medical image segmentation problems.

They now had a thriving colony on Mars, with its own culture and way of life. They had to figure out what to do next. Some wanted to stay on Mars, to continue their venture and explore the vast unknown. Others longed to come home, to be reunited with their loved ones and the life they had left behind. As the pioneers contemplated their future, they had a profound sense of humility. They had been given a second chance, and they had taken it. Lets Start with some basics of American Utilities companies and procedures. Television Television is broken up into several subcategories. You have Broadcast Networks and Cable Television Networks. Note: These are not analogous to Antenna vs. Cable Television. Broadcast Networks, are your standard American Broadcast Company (ABC), Columbia Broadcasting Service (CBS), FOX, and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC). These are your network television providers, or are most often associated with the local news networks. These 4 (sometimes more) are by law established as free to access networks that utilize primarily Antenna based transmissions. As these networks grow, or gain competition, they are required to remain free-to-broadcast, meaning you don't have to pay any monthly subscription fees or access fees to get things like local news. However, these are still public entities, and rely on advertising, viewership and other sales in order to continue operations, and have become very wealthy as a result. Cable networks, are not analogous with "Cable TV," though their roots do stem from the invention of Community Access Television, CATV. Cable networks first started appearing in local networks where CATV systems were designed with local content and programming. After the first CATV system was built, local municipalities and other organizations had lots of free space, not dependent on radio waves through the air, and so began to produce their own local content. These eventually started being shared and rebroadcasted as producers and things grew. Stations like CNN, FXX, USA, TNT, TBS etc. all started as local or regional stations, and did not fall under government jurisdiction like the Broadcast Networks above. CATV networks began charging for the services that the Community Antenna networks began providing, and also sharing information back and forth. As they got larger, small, regional companies like Alert Cable, Adelphia and Carolina Cable were bought up by multi-state conglomerates to become the likes of Comcast, Time Warner, Charter, Brighthouse and the other Major Service Providers (MSOs). Cable companies quickly stopped and diverged from producing content, and the two became separate. So, Cable Networks started to divide the space between Broadcasters and Cable networks, as you can only recieve Cable Channels by using a Cable Network. CATV eventually morphed into being known as a "Cable Provider" because of the transmission medium, similar to Satellite or Fiber Optics. Essentially though, Satellite and Fiber are still just CATV systems, just using different transmission means than before. Broadcasters on the other hand, are still able to be recieved with just an antenna with no subscription, and are limited to only a few local providers and your major 4-5 networks. Currently as of 2017, you have still ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC and The CW (formerly UPN and The WB before the merger). And before anyone says it no, PBS is not a broadcast network, they are more a local station that has many affiliates but is the only large scale non-profit and goverment funded educational television source. They are a public broadcaster, and considered Public Televison, but are not included in the Major Networks of most cities. CATV networks you do have to pay a subscription service for, and monthly base rates for just your local stations are around 15-40monthly depending on your location. That only covers your subscription fee and taxes for local stations, and doesn't include any of the aformentioned "cable networks." Currently the list includes in most areas some variation of the following: ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC, The CW PBS (3-5 stations depending on where you are) El-Ray C-Span other local government and local broadcast stations Your "Cable" channels start after that, and depending on the provider, can be cut up in a multitude of ways. This is where negotiations with the Production Companies come into play. Discovery Networks, Viacom and the like, the companis like mentioned before that split off and started producing content, well now they sell it to various cable and satellite companies for redistrobution instead of making and producing locally for one service provider. Your baseline cable packages vary in price, between 12-80month on top of the broadcast rate. Then you have your "Cable Premiums." These are going to be HBO (gotta have your thrones), Showtime (gotta have your Longmire), Cinemax (gotta have your.... skin-e-max), Epix, Starz, Encore and TMCSundance. These "Premiums" are basically your Adult Programming, and do not have to be purchased in addition with the Cable channels, but again you MUST subscibe to at least your broadcasters to have access. In recent years, HBO and Showtime have begun offering their own streaming services like HBO Go, and bypass the Provider level and become an Internet based provider like Netflix and Hulu, where now an Internet connection is required. If you get Antenna only stations, you will normally only get around 5-15 channels, depending on your local area. Some have more, and some have less, but the Majors will normally always be present, though quality is an issue. This quality issue was the direct reason leading to the development in CATV in the first place, to bring antennas down into the areas where radio was having difficulty reaching. Thus the name, Community Antenna Television, and not "CAble TeleVision" like it is colloquially known. Internet Internet, is of course a more modern phenomenon, spanning only the past 40 or so years. Originally what we now consider "Internet" was actually a government project for Universities and Government entities to communicate and share information privately using Dial-up modems and analog telephone networks. Up until around 1997, you only had one choice in service. Dial-upDSLT-1 through the local telephone company. Internet networks were completely dependent and intertwined with public telephone. Since by law, every house had to have access to 911 service, it made for a convenient way to distribute internet by means of additional, already accessible, twisted-pair copper wires. In 1997, CableLabs, in conjunction with around 30 other corporations, developed DOCSIS, the Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification. With this new development, CATV networks superseded their original intended function of being a television service, and were able to add Internet to their arsenal as well. Cable networks were able to provide services without using additional coax lines to the house unlike dialup, which required you use either phone or internet, or have separate numbers dedicated to each service. Cable Internet was able to utilize technology in the network to do TV and Internet at the same time without interference. Satellite providers like Hughes-net or Gen5, Fiber-optic Providers like Google or Verizon FiOS and even Mobile Data providers like Verizon or T-Mobile began their own versions of offerings, however still cannot compete to the scale and size of CATV or Telephone networks due to many years of both saturation and technological investment. Satellite has great download capability, but lacks in upload capability and is for very obvious reasons prohibitively expensive. Fiber-optic is amazing bi-directional capability but is prohibitively expensive and is running into alot of roadblocks due to federal regulation and local government push back to increasing construction costs and size. Finally Mobile data is extremely portable and scale-able, however is beginning to feel MASSIVE strains from over-utilization and restrictive bandwidth requirements that make it prohibitively expensive as well, although has been fairly well adapted in comparison to the Fiber and Satellite. Internet Services generally range between 10-500month or more, depending on your requirement, limitations of provider, service tier choice and any overages you may see based on usage. Consider the problem of sampling sequentially from a finite number of N 2 populations, specified by random variables X I k, I 1, ..., N, and k 1, 2, ...; where n is some integer. The functions f1 0...,fN are continuous, i.e., they do not have an expiration time either stored in their form or as a real-valued function on n, but rather behave like discrete functions (see point 5). Furthermore, to compute the values for each population we must also know how many samples we can use per sample: if it is zero then we start with the first one, otherwise we begin with the last one. For example, if two samples are taken at different times, we always choose a sample at least twice equal in size to the number of samples taken together. In this case we only need to count the true samples in each population when making a choice about which sample fits best into our model. But what happens if a single sample cannot be chosen? We could consider stopping all calculations after one sample was selected since there will be no more samples available until that sample gets picked up. The same procedure would apply here except that instead of waiting for all samples to get collected before moving forward, then using them to select among multiple choices, we continue picking out samples based upon their uniqueness (the probability density function) and their "luckiness" (their power). If this method of selecting randomly works well for small numbers of cases, we may want to expand its scope so that we specify how many samples are needed per case. However, this strategy becomes very complex when the number of cases increases rapidly. It turns out that once we achieve the maximum size of our population, we should stop counting samples altogether unless one were to pick out those species that are larger than the others. This holds true even though we might want to proceed onward via other selection methods. The way we solve this dilemma is to perform a search or clustering algorithm involving a statistical technique such as nonparametric statistics [34]. A first step involves identifying the most logical clusters to group, as shown in Fig. 3. Next, we ask the user to assign probabilities to each cluster according to a set of predefined criteria, hopefully under constraints sufficient to ensure that we select the closest possible cluster to whatever design objective we intend to reach. It should be apparent that the inference will tend towards being biased toward the nearest cluster, because it is easier to determine whether something belongs to a given cluster compared to its neighbors. We typically add additional parameters, usually latent variables, to position models closer to some desired state; these parameters provide information about the causal relationships between factors and allow us to make better predictions about future states. As discussed earlier in this paper, these latent variables include latent prognostic traits such as likelihood that animals in the same population will exhibit certain characteristics during life: for example, individual cats having an identical disposition will likely live in the same area, breed, and not mate together. Various approaches employing latent variables andor cluster analysis techniques can be used to obtain meaningful conclusions regarding natural systems. One common approach requires that a user define a set of attributes associated with a variable that represent its characteristic trait and ask him or her to rate that attribute's significance relative to another such value (for instance, "strongly agree" means that the characteristic has a relatively high effect on the outcome while "disagree" means that the characteristic has a relatively low influence on the outcome). This approach allows users to estimate the strength of the association between a factor and a feature in a given data set using exactly the same set of parameters as was employed in finding the original relationship between the factor and the feature. However, another alternative based on latent variables is to base recurrent decision trees [35] on aggregate estimates of predicted outcomes obtained from a sample of data as described above. Using this technique, the user defines a new set of predefined attributes called "features," assigns probabilities to each of these features independently, and asks for further attribute values assigned to each of these features. These feature weights are structured around a set of predictors defined by the attributes themselves; the general idea is to weight some attributes higher more significant than others. Experiments show that statistically robust regression results, including strong correlations, are achieved through such classification algorithms. Moreover, modeling behavior of any animal inevitably introduces error depending solely on the representation taken. To overcome this drawback, a more sophisticated type of approach is proposed in [36], termed "model predictive control." That is, instead of asking the user to give his own preferences for the number of traits he wishes to account for, the system itself decides the values that the user should assign to each element of the model by incorporating various prediction algorithms designed to monitor the current state of affairs using currently available data sets. While this approach offers statistical stability due to its use of reinforcement learning, we note that there still remains a risk that the system may fail to properly handle uncertainty or drift in the environment, especially with respect to unknown situations. Denoising techniques rely on certain assumptions regarding the desired signal and the noise. Most conventional approaches necessitate knowledge of the noise level, which might not always be feasible in practical scenarios. In this work, we assume that the signal representation within a specific dictionary follows a heavier-tailed distribution compared to the noise. This assumption enables us to derive a stopping condition for greedy search algorithms that is independent of the noise level. Drawing inspiration from the effectiveness of ensemble methods in machine learning, we introduce a method to decrease the variability of greedy estimators by averaging results from multiple sub-sampled dictionaries. We name this denoising technique Blind Random Pursuit Denoising (BIRD). We extend this approach to multi-dimensional signals using a structured sparse model (S-BIRD). The significance of this methodology is illustrated through synthetic and real-world MEG data, where BIRD achieves superior performance over established algorithms even without parameter adjustment, regardless of whether they incorporate noise information. Source code is provided to replicate all experiments.

By decentralizing control, these technologies address many scalability and privacy challenges, yet they typically require the underlying issue to be convex to ensure convergence to a global solution. Given that AC power flows are inherently non-convex and household device operations often involve discrete choices, there remains uncertainty about the practical application of distributed methods. This study builds upon previous research on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve the dynamic optimal power flow (D-OPF) problem. We incorporate more accurate line and load models and propose a two-step strategy for handling discrete decisions and uncertainty. Experiments on a small-scale microgrid demonstrate that this approach yields nearly optimal results within acceptable computational limits, making it suitable for receding horizon control applications. This work advances the feasibility of distributed control strategies for smart grid technologies.

Previously, sublinear bounds were known only for restricted "semi-online" settings [Chan, SODA 2002]. 2. item 2 2 item 2 We slightly improve previous fully dynamic data structures for answering extreme point queries for the convex hull of a 3D point set and nearest neighbor search for a 2D point set. The query time is O (log 2 n), and the amortized update time is O (log 4 n) instead of O (log 5 n) [Chan, SODA 2006; Kaplan et al., SODA 2017]. 3. item 3 3 item 3 We also improve previous fully dynamic data structures for maintaining the bichromatic closest pair between two 2D point sets and the diameter of a 2D point set. The amortized update time is O (log 4 n) instead of O (log 7 n) [Eppstein 1995; Chan, SODA 2006; Kaplan et al., SODA 2017].

" Yes, I can hear you, " came a soft voice much like my own. I looked around but found no one there. I brushed it off as hearing things. But as I took a few more steps I heard it again. nbsp; " I said I can hear you. " Came the voice, louder this time, but still retaining it's gentle nature. I looked around once more. There was no one near me. The house was empty. I spoke into my own head, feeling slightly silly as I did. nbsp; " Hi? " I thought. I wondered what could be causing this? Had I finally gone off the deep end or was I about to find out I had an new allergy I never even knew about. nbsp; " Hi, " replied the voice a few moments later. I couldn't deny it, it was coming from my head. I shook a little at the thought. nbsp; " Who are you? " I asked, before instantly feeling silly. Why I am asking myself who I am? nbsp; " I don't know, " the voice responded. I paused for a few moments, unsure of my next move. How do you react when you are talking to yourself but don't seem to know the answers to the questions you are posing? nbsp; " Well this has never happened before, " I thought to myself, only to be interrupted by the voice once more. nbsp; " Well I haven't been around before. I just started. " It replied. I was confused, to talk to yourself is one thing, but to interrupt yourself during the conversation is a whole new level of madness. After a few moments of silence, the voice spoke up again. nbsp; " I'm a part! " It exclaimed. It's voice showing a solid emotion for the first time since it started talking. nbsp; " A part? " I asked, slightly confused by what it meant and slightly distracted by trying to remember the number of my doctor. nbsp; " Remember? We learned about it in psychology class, " continued the voice, talking over my attempts to find the number. I thought about it for a moment and suddenly it flooded back into my head, like it was almost fresh. The boring classes on Richard Schwartz and his idea that people were made up of little bits. My train of thought was cut off by the voice speaking once more. nbsp; " But if I am a part, what part am I? " It mused, leaving me unsure if it was asking a rhetorical question or not. " Could I be an exile? Running away from something we didn't like? " It rambled. I found myself trying not to think so as not to interrupt. nbsp; " No, I don't feel like an exile, anyhow exiles don't just walk back in. That never happens in any story, apart from that game we played that time. But that is because Alice forgot she was playing an exile. " It finished. It was weird hearing this new voice talking about memories from years ago. But as it did, I felt the memory come to the forefront of my mind, like I was remembering it myself. I smiled at the memory, I had forgotten those silly games we used to play. I had forgotten Alice, work had gotten on top of me since I moved and I never found the time to call her. nbsp; " Well, I doubt I can be a firefighter. I never really had the looks for it, " the voice started again. " I mean being a firefighter suggests I am good in a crisis. But, I would think a part that was good in a crisis wouldn't pop up and scare you half to death. " nbsp; " You didn't. Don't worry. " I thought, trying to reassure whatever this voice was. nbsp; " I can hear your thoughts you know. I heard you mentally rehearsing the call to the doctor. " The voice replied. I shuffled awkwardly, realizing my thoughts about it had not been dramatically positive. " It's okay, I would do the same if I was in your position. Because I am you, so I can't pretend like I would think differently. " It said, a slight touch of humour coming into it's voice. I smiled and nodded. nbsp; " Well I can't think what part you are, " I thought. nbsp; " Maybe we don't need to know yet? Maybe I just popped out at random? " The part replied. I nodded to myself and the self inside myself. It had a point, I mean psychology was never exact. I smiled, I remembered my professor saying that. I smiled some more as I remembered another friend dropping psych the second they could, they couldn't handle the non-exact sciences. nbsp; " Yeah. That could be it. " nbsp; " Well then. I guess I should follow the model right? " It said. And I quickly remembered the model. I hadn't thought about it for years, but it felt like yesterday. I could almost smell the classroom, the memory was that fresh. nbsp; " Become part of the whole again, " I recited, " Until reality and your role clash once more. " I sat down and smiled as I remembered a few more of my school buddies. nbsp; " That is exactly it. " replied the voice. " So I guess I'll be seeing you? Or hearing you at least. " It said. I laughed a little and nodded. nbsp; " See you around, " I thought. I sat there in silence for a little bit. My head quiet once more. I got up from the chair and smiled, still basking in the glow of the memories that had resurfaced. I moved to my computer, I had a few people I needed to catch up with.

The ongoing commercial deployment of millimeter wave systems brings into focus a number of practical issues in form factor user equipment (UE) design. With wavelengths becoming smaller, antenna gain patterns becoming directional, and link budgets critically dependent on beamforming, it becomes imperative to use a number of antenna modules at different locations of the UE for good performance. While more antennasmodules can enhance beamforming array gains, it comes with the tradeoff of higher component cost, power consumption of the associated radio frequency circuitry, and a beam management overhead in learning the appropriate beam weights. Thus, the goal of a good UE design is to provide robust spherical coverage corresponding to good array gains over the entire sphere around the UE with a low beam management overhead, complexity, and cost. The scope of this paper is to study the implications of two popular commercial millimeter wave UE designs (a face and an edge design) on spherical coverage. We show that analog beam codebooks can result in good performance for both the designs, and the edge design provides a better tradeoff in terms of robust performance (with hand blockage), beam management overhead, implementation complexity from an antenna placement standpoint and cost.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) is an active research area of the visual domain. One of its fundamental sub-tasks is semi-supervised one-shot learning: given only the segmentation mask for the first image and the remaining parts of the video, a VOS mode is used to make it possible to identify the segments that are missing from the original scene. Using this technique, students can see which part of the body has been copied in the previous scene. However, while some aspects of learning are still being studied, there are several methods available to overcome the problems associated with such a high level immersion experience. One method involves the use of techniques known as "virtual objects"; these are virtual images of previously-missing or expanded portions of the image. This technology relies on the fact that if all of the portions of the scene have been referenced by camera movement, then the video will be rendered by using a captured portion of the computer animation. However, these techniques require expert decision making to accomplish their task. Thus, there exists a need for a system that allows for a student to re-enact the scene and the scene itself in real time without having to select footage from the previous scene.

The deluge of date rate in today's networks imposes a cost burden on the backhaul network design. Developing cost efficient backhaul solutions becomes an exciting, yet challenging, problem. Traditional technologies for backhaul networks include either radio-frequency backhauls (RF) or optical fibers (OF). While RF is a cost-effective solution as compared to OF, it supports lower data rate requirements. Another promising backhaul solution is the free-space optics (FSO) as it offers both a high data rate and a relatively low cost. FSO, however, is sensitive to nature conditions, e.g., rain, fog, line-of-sight. This paper combines both RF and FSO advantages and proposes a hybrid RFFSO backhaul solution. It considers the problem of minimizing the cost of the backhaul network by choosing either OF or hybrid RFFSO backhaul links between the base-stations (BS) so as to satisfy data rate, connectivity, and reliability constraints. It shows that under a specified realistic assumption about the cost of OF and hybrid RFFSO links, the problem is equivalent to a maximum weight clique problem, which can be solved with moderate complexity. Simulation results show that the proposed solution shows a close-to-optimal performance, especially for practical prices of the hybrid RFFSO links.

Several years later, in 88 BC, a Roman army was sent to put down an emerging Asian power, king Mithridates of Pontus. The army, however, was defeated. One of Marius' old quaestors, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, had been elected consul for the year, and was ordered by the senate to assume command of the war against Mithridates. Marius, a member of the "populares" party, had a tribune revoke Sulla's command of the war against Mithridates. Sulla, a member of the aristocratic optimates party, brought his army back to Italy and marched on Rome. Sulla was so angry at Marius' tribune that he passed a law intended to permanently weaken the tribunate. He then returned to his war against Mithridates. With Sulla gone, the populares under Marius and Lucius Cornelius Cinna soon took control of the city.

During the Hellenistic era, various philosophical schools emerged. Athens, known for its diverse intellectual traditions, remained a hub of philosophical activity. Yet, Athens had relinquished its political autonomy, and Hellenistic philosophy reflects the challenges of this transformative period. In this context, philosophers sought ideals like tranquility, self-reliance, and freedom from hardship, aiming to attain well-being or eudaimonia amidst adversity. The focus on inner peace, personal liberty, and the pursuit of eudaimonia became a shared characteristic among all Hellenistic philosophical traditions.

More recently, women's football soared in popularity after the nation's female team won the World Cup in 2011 and Olympic Games silver in 2012. Now rugby union is looking for a similar breakthrough into the national consciousness, when its World Cup is hosted by Japan in 2019. With the Olympic Games being held in Tokyo a year afterwards, the end of the decade is shaping up to be a major sporting time for Japan. "These two events coming together means the Japanese citizens' interest in sport has already gone up, and should increase rapidly nearer the events," Koji Tokumasu, general manager of the Japan 2019 Rugby World Cup Organising Committee, tells BBC News. He was recently in the UK for his nation's friendlies against Scotland and Gloucester, where Japan played with tenacity but lost both matches. Japan - known as the Cherry Blossoms or Brave Blossoms - are traditionally the strongest rugby union power in Asia. But Mr Tokumasu says in Japan, where baseball is the most popular sport and football second, rugby union lags behind in about 10th spot. "This is something we have to work on over the next six years," he says. "We want to approach our existing fans - we do already have some rugby fans in Japan, and activate them to spread the World Cup message." He says this hardcore fan-base can use digital media to publicise the rugby experience and the excitement surrounding the sport, including the thrill of match day. They will also be able to explain the intricacies of the sport, including the scoring system. "We want to raise interest and passion in the sport by bringing quality teams like New Zealand to our fans, who can then pass on the message to their family, friends and colleagues," says Mr Tokumasu. When Japan hosted world champions the All Blacks earlier in November, the 25,000 tickets were sold out after half an hour. The host nation, not surprisingly, lost that encounter, but there has been playing success this year. Japan won this year's HSBC Asian Five Nations tournament, and also beat a Wales second string team in the summer. That victory was their first win over a major rugby nation in eight decades of trying. To show it was no fluke, they have also beaten the US and Canada this year. In addition, this month Japan beat Russia, thrashed Spain, and also won the 2013 HSBC Asian Rugby Sevens. The first stage of 2019 preparation is already under way, with the release of the criteria for would-be World Cup host cities and stadiums. Organisers want to select between 10 and 12 match venues before March 2015, for the 48-game tournament. "The reason we have chosen that date is because we want the successful host venues to then be able to attend that year's World Cup in England to see and experience how the event is staged," says Mr Tokumasu. "At present we are visiting cities and telling them how exciting hosting the 2019 World Cup can be for them." In Tokyo, a showpiece 80,000-capacity Olympic Stadium is being built in time for the 2019 rugby event, and in other match venue centres local government will pay for stadiums. In many cities stadiums have remained underused since the 2002 World Cup. Mr Tokumasu says: "We would like it if we could use some of the those stadiums, but we cannot force those cities to take part - they have to express an interest." As well as increasing awareness, another major pre-2019 aim is to increase playing participation. "This is a major aim, and our government supports this, they think that sport is good for health," he says. "We are going to take rugby into primary schools, first going into 5,000 schools, and by 2019 hoping to have spread the word in all 22,000 primary schools. "Boys and girls can learn together and we will be introducing tag [touch] rugby, so that teachers won't be worried about children getting hurt. So by 2019 a lot of young people will know all about rugby." That work among the young should widen the base of the next generation of rugby players in a country where 95 of participants are university graduates. Rugby playing is also very intertwined at present with the top end of the corporate workplace, In the premier domestic competition, the Top League, the clubs are owned by large Japanese corporations such as Toshiba or Panasonic, and when a player's career comes to an end, they then usually take up a management role with the parent company. The government also wants to see people taking part as event volunteers, following a successful programme at the 2002 global football event, and ahead of Tokyo 2020. But he stresses again that the 2019 organisers want to bring rugby to a wider audience. "In Japan people tend to stay at home to watch the very best of global or national sports on TV or the internet, rather than actually attending live events - we want to overcome this and attract people to rugby games," he says. "We are going to produce more opportunities for people to attend a match - we really want to make the best use of the next six years "

There is experimental evidence that supports the concept that mitosis-specific phosphorylation of amyloid precursor protein (APP) at threonine 668 (T668) influences its processing and association with centrosomes. Studies have shown that phosphorylation of APP at T668 occurs during mitosis and is highly restricted to dividing cells. This phosphorylation event seems to play a role in the observed altered processing of APP and generation of amyloid-beta (A) peptides, which are involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease. Phosphorylated APP at T668 (pT668-APP) has been found to accumulate in centrosomes during mitosis. Centrosomes play a key role in cell division, as they are involved in the formation of mitotic spindles that ensure proper chromosome segregation. The localization of pT668-APP at centrosomes suggests that it may participate in the regulation of cell division. Moreover, it has been reported that the altered processing of APP, associated with the generation of A peptides, is regulated by cell cycle-dependent kinases that control the phosphorylation of APP at T668. Inhibition of these kinases affects the generation of A, highlighting the importance of this phosphorylation event in APP processing. Overall, APP phosphorylation at T668 during mitosis may affect its processing and lead to its association with centrosomes. Further research is needed to fully understand the relevance of this phosphorylation event, its role in cell cycle regulation, and implications for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's.

Physician assisted suicide (PAS) is a rational and empathetic form of end of life care for terminally ill individuals. Autonomy over ones life is something that should be preserved even at the end of one's life. PAS allows an individual to die with the dignity that he deserves, not under conditions of pain, suffering, or humiliation. There are certainly risks that could arise from legalizing this form of palliative care, however, I believe that they can all be mitigated under a certain set of criteria. In order to commit PAS, a person must, first, be terminally ill and have no option for cure. Second, he must be able to rationally and voluntarily make the decision to end his life. Third, the patient must self administer the lethal dose of medication. Fourth, if a PAS goes against a doctor's values, he must afford his patient with an alternative doctor who is willing to comply with the patient's wishes. If you are not in favor of PAS from a moral standpoint please explain why. If you are not in favor of PAS because you think it is impossible to legalize, please explain why decriminalizing the act does not solve that issue. It's a beautiful sunny day. There are plenty of kids playing around in the park. The parents are standing around, talking amongst themselves. Everyday was like that: everyday would be another boring life where nothing ever changed or got better; it felt empty and pointless. Cynical? Yep! A group from church who had come over on a mission trip some weeks before. They spoke about their work trying to help villagers in need rebuild their lives after the tsunami disaster; rebuilding schools, homes and other buildings destroyed by the devastating natural disasters. These missionaries also invited me to join them in doing something meaningful - working together toward serving others. After all, Christianity wasn't new news to me anymore. My dad did talk to me a little bit about this stuff when we went over things in Sunday school lessons growing up during youth meetings once every month or two. Still, back then, I never really took any interest until now. And honestly speaking, it would take more than someone telling me what I already know to change my heart completely. That takes conviction already burning inside you. You have to feel inspired by your own desire to serve Christ and not because of someone else's ideas to make you do so. This journey was bound to happen someday, but the question was whether or not I would go "all-out" and pursue a life dedicated solely to following Christ regardless of consequences. At least, I thought so initially. Then came reality.... We'll get to that later in the story. The world today may seem saturated with religious leaders claiming godly authority and preaching about salvation or whatever spiritual topic comes up nowadays. But that's not necessarily true everywhere. In many places throughout Asia, Africa, South America and Europe, churches struggle to keep members coming out regularly due to financial trouble, lack of awareness of what real faith looks like according to scripture, or simply because young guysgals don't want to attend those type of services to begin with. Many Christians are looking forward to seeing a revival in their local congregations. One reason why I'm glad to say that the situation here isn't that extreme in Australia yet. So far, we've built houses for individuals receiving care and support from these clinics; we've provided toolsequipment needed for workshops involving livestock breeding techniques that can earn money to put food on the table; plus educational materials which will help spread knowledge regarding AIDS prevention and ways of coping with the disease within communities. Child sponsorship provides children from poor families with clothing, health checks, school supplies, bicycles and extra tuition fees for high school university entrance exams. Right now, we're supporting 200 students in primary schooling classes. Some of these students have dropped out long ago due to poverty and economic hardships brought upon them by having too many siblings to look after in addition to wanting to finish off their studies. Also specially selected for enrollment is a small number of underprivileged female students to encourage a bright future for women - especially single mothers struggling to raise their children alone without dependable male figures in their lives. Some kids drop out early from school altogether because they aren't able to cope well with hard study material. For example, maths and science subjects don't click with certain pupils. Thus, although not very popular among some teachers, alternative learning methods become necessary for both boys and girls aged 9-16. During recent times, we've been busy conducting Bible studies with prisoners held in three prisons across the country. More recently, we started teaching English language courses (not as a requirement) to teenagers interested in becoming teachers. The most extreme form of chimerism, known as tetragametic chimerism, occurs when a woman becomes pregnant with twins. Two of her eggs are fertilized by two of her partner's sperm, resulting in zygotes. Typically, these zygotes would develop into separate individuals, but instead, they fuse to form a single embryo. This phenomenon involves four gametes—two sperm and two eggs—and can also occur during the blastocyst stage, when the embryo is approximately 100 cells large. The resulting embryo contains cells with DNA from both twins, leading to genetic tests revealing that a single individual has two origins. Such cases are extremely rare in humans, but they might go undetected unless a person undergoes genetic testing. Even then, whole organs may carry DNA from one twin while the other's DNA resides elsewhere in the body.

A less extreme variant is microchimerism, where some cells possess DNA from another individual. Many people have cells with their mother's DNA during childhood, which migrated through the placenta and integrated into the developing infant. Marmosets, for instance, are typically born as fraternal twins, and each tends to have some organ tissue or blood cells with the DNA of their twin due to shared blood supply. Stem cells can easily migrate between them.

Detecting chimerism in cases where identical twins are fused is challenging, making the majority of documented cases focus on fraternal twins, as their genetic differences are more pronounced and easier to identify.

As we walked in, three or four people were waiting around a table - but which one, I wondered, was the father of Bitcoin? Then I realised that one man was staring intensely at a very chunky laptop - this was Dr Craig Wright. He carried on working, apparently unaware that we had entered the room. Once we had been introduced he gradually warmed up - especially when it came to performing the demonstration that showed that he did have access to the cryptographic keys used by Satoshi when he made the first Bitcoin transaction in 2009. We had arrived wondering just how convincing a case would be made that the almost mythical creator of Bitcoin was at last stepping out of the shadows. What we saw seemed impressive - though it would need a far higher level of expertise than we possess to be certain. But Jon Matonis, a senior figure in the Bitcoin world, was in the room watching, having had his own demonstration some time before. And the news that Gavin Andresen, chief scientist at the Bitcoin Foundation, was also convinced provided more reassurance. Now Craig Wright has published his evidence on his blog, it will be examined in minute detail for any chink in his case. But put aside the question of whether you believe him or not - and he told me he didn't care either way - there were still plenty of questions we wanted to put to the fascinating, if somewhat prickly Dr Wright. Why keep his secret so long? Why come out now? What about that run-in with the Australian tax authorities? And is he fabulously rich, with a huge stock of Bitcoin? At our first meeting - without a television camera - we roamed freely over all sorts of territory. We learned that he ran a substantial business in London, employing quite a few people here in what seemed to be some kind of Bitcoin trading and consultancy operation. We challenged him about that tax investigation - he conceded that there was what he called an "audit" underway in Australia but insisted that this was mainly due to the tax authorities there not really understanding Bitcoin. We asked where the pseudonym had come from - he mentioned a 17th century libertarian philosopher called Nakamoto but said he'd keep the Satoshi bit to himself. He talked of the French writer and philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, whose statement refusing the Nobel Prize is used in the Satoshi-signed file given as evidence in the blog published today. His politics were very far from the "lefty" Sartre, he explained, but like him he did not want his identity to be defined by one thing - he refused to be Craig "Satoshi" just as Sartre did not want to be Jean-Paul Nobel. What he wouldn't say is how many Bitcoins he has - "that would be telling" - though he indicated that he would not be spending any of them in a hurry. He told us that he had a "nice big house and a nice fast car" in London, went on holidays to Paris, and didn't feel the need to acquire vast riches. The second time we met, to film a television interview, the mood changed. It was immediately clear that he hated the whole process, refusing to move from behind his laptop to a more spacious room where the shot would have been much better. At first, he insisted that he would give an answer to just one question - why he had decided to go public after all these years. Once we started filming he opened up a little, but mainly because he wanted to express his anger at, as he sees it, being forced into the public eye. "I don't want money, I don't want fame, I don't want adoration, I just want to be left alone," he said with some venom. He accused journalists of threatening to make up stories about him if he did not cooperate and said lies had been told that would affect his family and his staff. It seems his main grievance surrounds the stories that spread last December when he was first identified as a potential Satoshi, then dismissed by some as a hoaxer. At that time, questions were asked about his academic and business career, and there were some who said he just did not have the intellectual capacity to be the man behind Bitcoin. Throughout the demonstrations he showed us he kept on stressing the complexity of the process - "obviously everyone said I have no idea about this stuff so I'm going to do it in the most convoluted way possible." We were then supplied with a series of documents providing evidence that Dr Craig Stephen Wright was a Master of Statistics, IT Management, and Law, and a long list of peer-reviewed articles. Now he says he intends to continue his research into improving the technology behind Bitcoin, and plans to publish several papers over the coming months. With the community around the currency in some turmoil right now over how it develops, you might think that Craig Wright could provide some leadership. After all, he could be said to be to Bitcoin what Tim Berners-Lee is to the web. But he bridled at my suggestion that he could be a figurehead for the currency, making clear that this was the first and last television interview he would do. Having emerged from the shadows, Craig Satoshi Wright now wants to return to them as quickly as possible.

Question-answering (QA) is certainly the best known and probably also one of the most complex problem within Natural Language Processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI). Since the complete solution to QA is an unreachable goal, many researchers have investigated different approaches for its subtasks. In particular, supervised learning methods such as statistical machine translation [Durrani et al., 2006], neural network architectures [Lee et al., 2005b] or case-based reasoning [Klementiev and Roth, 2012; Simoes et al., 2015a] are widely used in order to produce a system that can be trained from available annotated data. In this work we propose an informative approach for Question Answering based on two main ideas: 1) using knowledge about possible answers provided by users for querying purposes when training systems, 2) combining multiple sources of information including user feedback for improving performance. We apply our model to three well-known datasets. The experimental results show improved accuracy compared with state-of-the-art algorithms without relying on external resources like web search engines. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 overviews related works. Sections 3, 4 and 5 describe the proposed framework, dataset preparation and experiments performed, respectively. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 6 along with future research directions. Related Works Traditional models for text classification divide the set of documents into disjoint categories according to predefined rules. Over time, however, better performing techniques emerged since they were able to learn the features defining each category through large amounts of labeled examples [Shenker et al., 2008]. This paradigm has been applied successfully to various areas such as Spotlight Search [Agarwal et al., 2007 ], sentiment analysis [Baroni and Lenci, 2002], authorship identification [Cui et al., 2011] and question answering [Liu and Barzilay, 2015]. Supervised Learning Methods These methodologies use classifiers whose parameters are optimized by minimizing the error between predicted label values and ground-truth labels [Geman and Geman, 1984]. They usually assume some form of distributional hypothesis and exploit linguistic properties to define features [Rosenfeld et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2003]. Among these last ones, named entity recognition (NER), which aims at identifying words denoting persons, locations, organizations etc., is particularly relevant for QA tasks in languages where proper names occur frequently. As shown by Liu [2015], NER is one of the major factors affecting answer quality in automatic QA systems. Unsupervised Methods Non-supervised clustering methods aim at grouping similar instances together while allowing them to belong to distinct clusters. Many distinct unsupervised learning paradigms exist but agglomerative hierarchical clustering seems promising for task-specific applications [Vlachos et al., 1991; Jain and Dubey, 2004; Chen and Lin, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2008; Karypis et al., 1997; Haghighi and Kleinberg, 2004]. However, cluster discovery remains challenging due to noise inherent to free-text document representation, mostly caused by homonyms, synonymy, spelling mistakes, repetitions etc. To overcome this issue, several heuristics have been devised to filter out noisy units following diverse criteria e.g. edit distance [Manning et al., 2003a [Manning et al.,,b, 2009 Widdows et al., 2005; Coecke and Manning, 2009; Suardari et al., 2010]. These methods are easily integrated into existing frameworks for unsupervised learning such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Recently, deep learning became quite popular in computer vision, speech processing and natural language understanding because it allows designing more expressive models than traditional methods [Lin et al., 2014; LeCun et al., 1998 ]. For example, convolutional networks allow capturing local patterns rather than global characteristics, leading to higher generalization capacity [Lin et al., 2014]. On another hand, recurrent attention mechanisms provide end-to-end trainability thanks to multi-layered structures that capture sequential dependencies among elements [Huang et al., 2016; Luong et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017]. Combining Multiple Sources of Information Several studies showed how incorporating additional knowledge sources improves performances in linguistic tasks both in monolingual [Mehmood and Dagan, 2011; Snir and Schiele, 2010; Caffarel et al., 2009; Maezawa et al., 2002; Blei and Lafferty, 2006; Ng et al., 2003; McCallum et al., 2000] and cross-lingual scenarios [Klein et al., 2011; Zoph and Knight, 2001; Fung et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Headden and Callan, 2013]. Although allance approaches are not suitable for every application domain, they seem particularly well suited for combination problems in QA settings, given their flexibility and ability to leverage complementary forms of information. For example, Zhang et al. [2012] combine word embeddings derived from Wikipedia corpora and lexical similarity calculated from WordNet to improve query expansion for fast retrieval methods. "Indeed, Dr. Fish," he replied, sitting back in the chair opposite me. "I am Jesus." I continued writing a few more lines in my psychiatric journal. This was my first patient since being transferred to the hospital, and I had yet to interview anyone. If they were all like him, well. His file indicated megalomania, delusions of grandeur, and the case suggested it wasn’t schizophrenia, as he had only one identity. I should confirm this. "No, doctor, this is the only role I play. I am myself. Yes, I am that I am." He casually reached over, took a pen, and started spinning it between his fingers. He was quite proficient, and I might have taken more notes to avoid speaking aloud while writing. Did I say anything? But truly, did he expect me to believe Jesus was adept at pen spinning? He was skilled at it, but such a talent didn’t align with his persona. "Doctor," he said, leaning forward and passing the pen back and forth as it spun around each finger, "I am the son of God. The sole begotten in flesh. I created this world. Do you think spinning a pen is difficult for me?" He made one final spin and placed it neatly into my cup. He was very good, and I could see why others had reservations about his file. However, I had arrived late, and it was nearly time for lunch. I was about to speak when he interrupted. "It’s almost time for lunch, Doctor. Would you like to join me?" He rose and walked toward the door, which wasn’t locked. It rarely was when I was with a patient, so an orderly wouldn’t have difficulty entering if the patient became agitated or acted irrationally. I quickly stood and followed him; I didn’t want to provoke him or make him angry, as the next destination would be lunch anyway.

Some berries have adaptations that select for preferential eaters. For instance, many of the fruits we consider'hot peppers' or chili peppers, are primarily dispersed by birds. Where a large mammal may eat the fruit, it will often eat it from a standing position, often at a higher level than the other animals. A bird, on the other hand, will fly to the fruit and eat it while airborne, or drop it from a high perch. This requires that the bird have strong talons and can fly, and also that the fruit be large enough to sustain this activity. Most berries are therefore dispersed by birds. Other species of fruit are dispersed by rodents, which may also have a preference for certain species of berries. The fruits of many plant species have specialized or modified structures to aid in dispersal. One example is the orange-red fruit of the passionfruit. The fruit is large and has numerous seeds. It is also very fleshy and somewhat succulent. Birds that eat the fruit are often severely dehydrated. As a result, they are unable to transport the fruit to the nest, and it usually perishes in the bird's crop. In addition, the bird must eat the fruit from a standing position, which is unlikely for most birds. In this case, the fruit has evolved a structure that prevents the bird from being able to eat it while standing, and is so fleshy and succulent that the bird cannot transport it to the nest. It has evolved a structure that is nearly inedible by birds. A large volume of digital video content is generated and distributed daily, resulting in extensive media archives. To ensure accessibility of this information, effective methods are required to process such data. Automatic metadata tagging of broadcast media plays a crucial role in multimedia indexing, typically involving multimodal inputs. This study presents a new approach for automatically identifying media genres and show identities by leveraging acoustic and textual features. Incorporating existing metadata, like broadcast times, significantly enhances performance. Latent Dirichlet Allocation is applied to model both audio and text, producing fixed-dimensional representations that facilitate classification using Support Vector Machines. Experiments were carried out on over 1200 hours of BBC TV broadcasts, aiming to classify them into 8 genres or 133 shows. On a 200-hour test dataset, accuracy rates of 98.6% and 85.7% were achieved for genre and show recognition, respectively, when combining acoustic, textual, and metadata features.

Acid-base reactions are ubiquitous in nature. Understanding their mechanisms is crucial in many fields, from biochemistry to industrial catalysis. Unfortunately, experiments only give limited information without much insight into the molecular behaviour. Atomistic simulations could complement experiments and shed precious light on microscopic mechanisms. The large free energy barriers connected to proton dissociation however make the use of enhanced sampling methods mandatory. Here we perform an ab initio molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and enhance sampling with the help of methadynamics. This has been made possible by the introduction of novel descriptors or collective variables (CVs) that are based on a conceptually new outlook on acid-base equilibria. We test successfully our approach on three different aqueous solutions of acetic acid, ammonia, and bicarbonate. These are representative of acid, basic, and amphoteric behaviour.

The main response of the immune system to tumors is to destroy the abnormal cells using killer T cells, sometimes with the assistance of helper T cells. Tumor antigens are presented by cells such as macrophages, which are phagocytic cells that engulf and digest cellular debris and pathogens. When activated, T cells recognize a processed form of the tumor antigen, which is presented to them by an antigen-presenting cell (APC). This causes the T cells to proliferate and produce cytokines such as IFN- and TNF, as well as cell surface molecules that enable them to kill tumor cells. For example, CD8 T cells will produce perforin and granzymes, which are used to kill tumor cells. In addition to T cells, Natural Killer (NK) cells are also involved in the destruction of tumor cells. NK cells are innate immune cells that are stimulated to kill tumor cells in a manner that is similar to CD8 T cells. However, in most cases, the tumor is not destroyed by the immune system. There are several possible explanations for this: Antigen presentation: The tumor may not be recognised as foreign. Evasion: The tumor may evade the immune system by a variety of mechanisms including suppression of immune cells, antigen loss and the ability to avoid the immune system. Immunosuppression: The immune system may be suppressed, for example, by the tumor. Defective immune system: The immune system may be defective. Failure of immune response: The immune system may fail to respond. The normal immune response to tumors is discussed in more detail in the immune system, cancer and immunotherapy notes.
