The tax pertains to the "right to transfer assets upon death." However, in the United States, individuals are exempt from federal inheritance taxes on the first $5.4 million or $10.8 million inherited from a spouse. A generation-skipping tax may apply if grandparents pass on money to their grandchildren. If the funds are held in an IRA or other tax-deferred account, the parents never paid taxes on them initially. When these accounts are withdrawn, both the parent and the individual will owe taxes on the amount taken. The deceased’s IRA transfers to a beneficiary IRA, requiring regular withdrawals once the decedent reaches age 70. These withdrawals are calculated based on the beneficiary's life expectancy, making them smaller if the beneficiary is younger and growing tax-free, potentially exceeding the withdrawal amount. Alternatively, the funds can be sold immediately, resulting in approximately half the amount being taxed and penalized. For most people, option one is preferable; thus, consulting with a financial advisor is recommended. America is not intended to be a country of old money, where families hoard ancestral wealth and control national resources until only one powerful family remains, akin to a king. Inheritance taxes exist deliberately to ensure that families contribute something valuable to society, even if their contributions are made through the stock market.

The mountain range running the length of the east coast (the Great Dividing Range) causes moist air that's coming off the ocean to rise (called orographic uplift), when it rises it cools, condenses, and comes down as rain, allowing forests to exist. At least to the seaward side of that range. The west of the range, even tho it's still in the east of Australia, is in a rain shadow, and get very little rain also. The west coast has no such mountain range, the air coming in from the ocean to the west doesn't have that lift so misses out on the rain. There's also associated temperature, geology and soil differences that prevent forests from occuring in the west, but that's it in a nutshell.,Essentially, because there is a mountain range (well..."mountain" by Australian standards) running along the entire length of the east coast. This causes rain to fall on the coastal side of the mountain range, and this provides enough to support a forest-type environment in places. In the west, there's virtually no mountain range. There IS the Darling Scarp that promotes rainfall in the south-western 'corner' of Australia, which is where the city of Perth and the vast majority of Western Australia's population lives. There are in fact some small areas of forest in this small south-western corner that are well-watered. Parts of western and north-western Australia DO get some heavy rainfall, but it's the seasonal monsoon. So it's extremely heavy rain for a couple of months and then parched dry for the rest of the year, not really conducive to the sustainable growth of forests.

I shoved the camera, turning it toward the bloodied and mud coated humans covering in the trench next to the Bovi. They were at most, half the size of their counterparts, and even that was a stretch. "It wasn't so long ago - just 2 years in fact - that we would be shooting at each other. But that's all changed. Now we're fighting side by side, for the same worlds." Switching the camera to autofollow, I rose and approached the two nearest humans. "Excuse me, you mind if I ask a few questions?" "Not gon na make us sound like idiots or monkeys?" Racism and prejudices against the humans were still pretty rampant. There was a preceding war, they had lost, and we had brought them under our government when their atrocities had been revealed. It was..... painful. But that wasn't my job or my concern. I wanted to tell the story of soldiers, and race didn't matter. "No. None of that horseshit. You as people. I'll be gentle too. Fair enough?" They nodded in agreement. "So," flipping the camera back on, "can you tell me why you joined up with the volunteers to start with?" The woman actually smiled a bit, pushing the worst of the mud off her body armor. "That's easy. They said'the bad guys are coming for your world, we need help.' Went straight to a recruiting station and signed up. This world's my home, figure I owe it at least that much." Nodding, I turned toward the man, who shrugged and tried to look sheepish. "She says it better than me. I was military before, though, so I knew they needed bodies. Signed up that day, haven't been home since." "I see - so how did you end up with the legendary Red Vipers, a special forces regiment." Scratching his chin and ignoring the blood, he shrugged again. "Honestly, I don't know. I told them, I'm military, I want to be near the front lines, where can I do the most help? They looked up my records and said'we want you to help with the Vipers.' I used to fight the Vipers, so I knew who he meant." "I just said put me up front," the woman offered, "put me up front and let me protect my neighbors. I won't complain about anything, just give me a shot. Next thing I know, I'm meeting this tall drink of water who tells me I better ask for help when I need it, and I better get it when I ask." Nodding, I flipped the camera to face me. "The Red Vipers have been at the front of many battles, despite being on the flanks and behind enemy lines. They were the first to respond to this new incursion just last month, even though they've been fighting for 7 years straight. Tell me, how do the Vipers you work with look?" "Scary," the woman offered calmly, "they see a target, they go for it, they make it dead, and they get everyone out. Sure, we get a few wounds, but we live." "Yeah," the man agreed, "best of the best of the best, definitely. They're tired as hell, you can see it, but they're still fighting top form. We haven't lost anyone since I got here." Inadvertently answering the question as to why he'd been embedded here. Of course, my thoughts get interrupted as a MAC90D set opens up full rate on an enemy something. Even in the trench, I can feel the wind from the launching shells and reloads. That's when it occurs to me; they said social interest. I turned toward one of the Bovi - looks like a Major. "Sir, can I ask you a few quick questions?" He grunted and nodded, using a soaked handkerchief to try and clear some of the mud from his muzzle. "You've had the volunteers here a few days now. How would you describe the relationship?" That actually made him pause, thinking about it, not necessarily in diplomatic terms. "A week ago, would've refused. Sat'em down as aides. But frankly, having seen them fight? Maybe they can't haul an AMR, maybe they can't carry a hundred kilos at a go, but damned if they don't have it where it counts." Rising to his hooves, he turned and actually saluted the two humans. "I'd take these two into hell with me - done themselves more than proud." Predictably, they both saluted back, clearly stunned. That setup always worked for the propaganda stuff. Besides, folks like that never shirked their duties. They'd fight twice as hard just to prove they were every bit as good as the other species. "Then can I ask you all.... how do you think the battle is going here?" Looks were quickly exchanged, and the Major took over again. "Official canned answer, we expect to rout the enemy any hour and completely destroy their assets. Unofficially, we've taking a pounding but they're getting it worse. Soon as we get some air support, it's mopping up time. We're in a good position, we have the best people, we'll be home for breakfast at least." "So we're winning?" "Yep. We're winning," he agreed, "just as soon as the air support gets here." There was a scream of engines approaching, and he looked up while also pointing. There was no mistaking that it was a Hog II ground attack aircraft. There was an unusual whirring as the main gun fired, the camera tracking as it moved off into the distance. And didn't turn around. "Well shit. Bingo ammo. So we wait a little longer." All I could do was turn toward the humans, who looked elated and dejected at the same time. "So what are you thinking?" The woman shrugged helplessly, but the man shook his head confidently. "Bad call, should have sent fresh planes. Gotten some of ours out of mothballs faster, maybe. But, if the Major says we can take them out? I wouldn't doubt it for a minute. We'll win. Then we'll go find another fight and win that too. Biggest mistake these idiots ever made was invading our homes. Every inch they want to take, we'll make them fight and bleed for." I couldn't have asked for a more perfect close. Flipping the camera to face me again, I put on my best smile. "And there you have it. This is Larry Sun for DFIC, signing off."

This is comparable to wagering on the Super Bowl Halftime Show, where the outcome is predetermined, yet individuals can still place bets without knowing the specifics.

The illegality of fixing horse races and boxing stems from the fact that the event organizers are also part of the betting process, thus having an interest in the outcomes. However, many forms of illicit gambling are accepted by local authorities due to the lack of resources to enforce such regulations. 

Similarly, people bet on the Oscars, even though the winner is known beforehand, as long as there is no insider information involved.

Let's begin with some fundamental aspects of American utility companies and their processes. Television is divided into various categories. There are broadcast networks and cable television networks. It's important to note that these are not comparable to antenna versus cable television. Broadcast networks include major American broadcasters such as ABC, CBS, FOX, and NBC. These are typically network television providers, often linked to local news networks. They are legally recognized as free-to-air networks using antenna-based transmission methods. As these networks expand or face competition, they must maintain their free-to-air status, meaning there are no mandatory subscription or access fees for services like local news. Despite this, these entities remain public and depend on advertising, viewer engagement, and other revenue streams to sustain their operations, becoming quite prosperous as a result. Cable networks, although not directly related to "cable TV," originated from the development of community access television (CATV). Initially, these networks appeared in local areas where CATV systems were designed to provide localized content. Once the first CATV system was constructed, local governments and organizations had ample unused space,不受无线电波干扰，thus initiating the creation of local content. Over time, these networks began to share and retransmit content as production expanded. Stations such as CNN, FXX, USA, TNT, TBS, among others, originated as local or regional stations and were not subject to governmental oversight like the broadcast networks mentioned earlier. CATV networks started charging for the services previously offered by community antenna networks and also exchanged information bidirectionally. As they grew in scale, smaller, regional companies like Alert Cable, Adelphia, and Carolina Cable were acquired by large multi-state corporations.

As you go deeper into the Earth, both pressure and temperature increase greatly. They increase so much, that it makes it incredibly difficult to get too far past the crust into hotter depths. The reason why this is true in general, but also especially for hot magma from deep within the earths interior (which can reach temperatures of several thousand degrees C when erupted), comes down to two different things: 1) The more energy dissipation there is along a system's lengthline, 2) the higher heat capacity of materials closer to their melting point. To oversimplify things, as we drill through rock deeper into the Earth, it gets harder each time because at some depth, all of the energy can be absorbed and not redistributed or converted back into something else. This means that after a certain depth, extracting energy is like hitting brick walls with your hands instead of removing them via kinetic action. It's important to note here that while we're talking about the existence of 'hot rocks' on the surface of our planet, these are actually cold by comparison - they don't have enough thermal mass to maintain very high internal heats without being eroded away fairly quickly. If I had an analogy relating to my favorite sport, swimming, imagine trying to swim laps underwater without goggles...it'd be nearly impossible! But if one was wearing large sunglasses over said goggles, then yes; the ability would dramatically improve! So what happens? Some of that hard-hitting heat transfers up to the surface of the oceans, where it melts icecaps and snowpack for example.

Humans' large brains may be due to a single "typo" in their genetic code, according to new research. In a study recently published in the journal Nature Ecology and Evolution, researchers from the University of Edinburgh analyzed the DNA of humans and Neanderthals. They found that humans have a unique variation in a gene called NOTCH2NL, which is known to affect brain size. The researchers believe that this variation may have occurred as a result of a random error in the genetic code when our ancestors first split from Neanderthals, around 600,000 years ago. This "typo" then became part of the human genetic code, contributing to the larger brains we see today. This study adds to the evidence that small changes in our genetics can have a huge impact on our evolution. It also provides further insight into why humans have such large brains compared to our closest evolutionary relatives. Lead researcher Dr. Gunchin Zhang said: "Our findings suggest that a single letter change in the genetic code was enough to give rise to an important difference between humans and Neanderthals. We don't know yet what precise role this gene plays in brain development, but our research opens up new avenues for future studies." The team now plans to investigate further how this variation affects the development of the human brain, and how it has impacted our evolution.

In the world of international football, there is much debate over which team can claim to be the greatest of all time. Many nations have had teams that have achieved unprecedented success on the biggest stages and have gone down in history as some of the most iconic sides ever seen. The Brazil national side of is often hailed as one of the best international teams of all time. Led by the likes of Pele, Jairzinho and Garrincha, Brazil won three World Cups during this period and were the first nation to win consecutive titles. They also boasted an impressive record in friendly matches, winning 79 out of 103 games, with 39 wins coming in a row. Another team considered to be among the greatest is the Hungarian side of the 1950s. Their run at the 1954 World Cup was particularly remarkable, where they beat West Germany 3-2 in the final. Hungary went unbeaten in 31 games leading up to the tournament, which remains a record unbeaten streak for any international team. In terms of individual honours, the Spanish national team of 2008-2012 is arguably the greatest ever. Under the guidance of Vicente Del Bosque, Spain won two European Championships and their first ever World Cup. During this period, they also reached the top of the FIFA rankings, becoming the first country to hold the distinction of being number one in the world for two consecutive years. The German national team of 2014-2018 is also deserving of recognition. They won the 2014 World Cup, becoming the first European team to win the title in South America. They then successfully defended their crown four years later in Russia, becoming the first nation to win back-to-back World Cups since Brazil in 1962. So who can claim to be the greatest international side of all time? It is difficult to definitively answer such a subjective question. However, the four aforementioned teams are certainly worthy contenders for the title.

For the first several decades of disc record manufacturing, sound was recorded directly on to the "master disc" at the recording studio. From about 1950 on (earlier for some large record companies, later for some small ones) it became usual to have the performance first recorded on audio tape, which could then be processed andor edited, and then dubbed on to the master disc. A record cutter would engrave the grooves into the master disc. Early versions of these master discs were soft wax, and later a harder lacquer was used. The mastering process was originally something of an art as the operator had to manually allow for the changes in sound which affected how wide the space for the groove needed to be on each rotation.

Throughout millennia, humans have consistently formed communities, offering mutual protection against threats. Those who favored a solitary lifestyle in the past would have had difficulty surviving, whereas those who remained connected to social groups found it more advantageous. This suggests that our genetic makeup favors group living, and this preference extends beyond mere safety—people naturally seek strong relationships with others, such as friendships and family ties. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that we are biologically inclined toward social interaction and connections.

This paper addresses the challenge of fulfilling complex information requests through dialogue with search engines. Users can formulate their queries in natural language and obtain direct, conversational responses from a short system reply. Although recent efforts have explored similar objectives, such as studies on conversational search, they often fail to tackle complex requirements or are restricted to conceptual frameworks and lab-based studies. Our paper aims to achieve two main goals: first, to develop a suitable dataset for creating pipelines for conversational search, and second, to build an advanced pipeline for conversational search using this dataset. The system is constructed based on a multi-turn conversational search dataset, with additional input from a crowdsourcing platform to summarize relevant passages into concise, conversational responses. This approach improves upon existing methods by incorporating a token identification module and a prior-aware pointer generator, enabling more precise outputs. Experiments demonstrate that our system outperforms strong baseline models. We also analyze the dataset to identify areas for improvement and release the dataset along with the code and models for future research.

When employed as a count noun, "culture" refers to the collective customs, traditions, and values of a society or community, such as those of an ethnic group or nation. In this context, multiculturalism emphasizes the peaceful coexistence and mutual respect among diverse cultures living in the same area. The term "culture" can also refer to particular practices within a social group, known as a subculture—examples include "bro culture" or "counter culture." In cultural anthropology, cultural relativism advocates for the idea that cultures cannot be fairly assessed or ranked objectively, as any judgment is inherently shaped by the value systems of the culture in question.

The primary reason is that most individuals are right-handed. Early written systems like Hebrew began by etching characters onto stone. As most people were right-handed, it became more convenient to use the left hand for holding the chisel and the right for striking. Writing from right to left was more comfortable than the opposite direction, especially when using a left-hand-held hammer. Over time, languages shifted to animal skins, but the right-to-left writing convention remained established. When later languages such as Ancient Greek and Latin emerged, papyrus and ink had become the standard writing materials. Since most people were right-handed, writing right-to-left led to frequent ink smudges on the paper. In contrast, writing from left to right avoided this issue.

Where every component state of a federation possesses the same powers, we are said to find 'symmetric federalism'. Asymmetric federalism exists where states are granted different powers, or some possess greater autonomy than others do. This is often done in recognition of the existence of a distinct culture in a particular region or regions. In Spain, the Basques and Catalans, as well as the Galicians, spearheaded a historic movement to have their national specificity recognized, crystallizing in the "historical communities" such as Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. They have more powers than the later expanded arrangement for other Spanish regions, or the Spain of the autonomous communities (called also the "coffee for everyone" arrangement), partly to deal with their separate identity and to appease peripheral nationalist leanings, partly out of respect to specific rights they had held earlier in history. However, strictly speaking Spain is not a federalism, but a decentralized administrative organization of the state.

Installing a program might involve more than just copying files to your hard drive. If you only delete the files, those changes won't be reversed. For instance, the installer might create desktop shortcuts, modify the system registry with various entries—such as designating the application as a file type handler (e.g., launching it when you double-click an .mp3 file)—and perform numerous other actions. The uninstaller will remove these entries and delete the files. However, simply removing the files doesn't handle this cleanup. Thus, if the installer added those registry entries, Windows will still attempt to run the program when you double-click an .mp3 file. You’ll also have a desktop shortcut that no longer works, along with other modifications made by the installer, which you haven’t undone. In essence, your computer could end up in a state where some features unexpectedly break.

Programs often write new registry keys during installation, which aren't automatically deleted by merely removing the files. Typically, installers do remove these keys. Additionally, some programs store cache and other files in multiple locations across your computer. Without knowing all these locations, it’s difficult to ensure complete removal. A key point to remember: both installers and uninstallers are developed by the same person. If they failed to properly configure the uninstaller, it won’t work. There’s no external enforcement ensuring the uninstaller performs its duties. As a result, even with uninstallers, leftover files, settings, and registry keys from installed programs are common.

Immigrants arrived from all over the world to search for gold, especially from Ireland and China. Many Chinese miners worked in Victoria, and their legacy is particularly strong in Bendigo today where there are many restaurants with a distinctly Asian flavour thanks to them. However, most people came here looking for work - Australian agriculture was booming around this time due to increasing demand by European countries such as Britain and France following World War I, so jobs were plentiful at first. This made life much easier for those coming across the seas into Australia; they could find employment almost immediately without having to pay recruitment agents or travel huge distances to reach these destinations (about 40 of immigrants travelled on ships that would take between 6-8 weeks). A lot of Irish emigrated during this period because of famine conditions back home, it's often said that more than 100,000 left after 1847 alone! There had been a gradual decline in job opportunities though throughout the 1880s which eventually saw large numbers of unemployed men who couldn't get off the boats. The solution? Ship out thousands of women instead. In fact, some female passengers even refused to go until male relatives joined up too - but in reality, families acted together like one unit when leaving a country under threat anyway, whether husbandsfathers went away or not. And while it's now common knowledge about the number of girls sent overseas to be married against their will (even if this practice has mostly ended), less well known is how desperate the situation was for young single working age men once their wives were gone: widowers outnumbered children aged 5 years old and below fivefold...and yet still no room aboard ship. It took longer before any white man found himself compelled to leave his family behind simply because he lacked money. Most times they became labourers themselves rather than become homeless wanderers roaming through western Europe. Plants and other photosynthetic organisms are at the base of most food chains because they use the energy from the sun and nutrients from the soil and atmosphere, converting them into a form that can be used by animals. The modern forms of the major staple foods, such as maize, rice, wheat and other cereal grasses, pulses, bananas and plantains, as well as flax and cotton grown for their fibres, are the outcome of prehistoric selection over thousands of years from among wild ancestral plants with the most desirable characteristics. Mainly because of motion blur. When your videogame creates the video, each frame is generated separately, and is a completely static image - you can take a screenshot and it'll look like it was taken from a film or a painting. This means that when there's motion in the image, it looks weird: the character is not moving smoothly, but in discrete jumps, with visible gaps in between them. And it's distracting. Many engines allow you to turn off VSYNC - you can force your video to run at a higher FPS than the monitor's refresh rate. But then you run into problems - many monitors can't display higher-than-refresh-rate content. And even if it does, there's still a good chance that your video will look weird, because you're forcing your monitor to refresh at an interval different from the one it's meant to refresh at. For example, a monitor running at 60Hz can display 60 unique images per second. If you force it to display 120 images per second, each image will be shown twice - it won't be displayed twice as fast. It'll be shown twice, and then the next image will be shown twice. It's not a big deal, but the video will look weird, because now every frame will be displayed twice. The problem is, you're displaying a static image. Most monitors, and most video cards, are designed to work with static images. And that's where G-SYNC comes in. G-SYNC is a new technology, invented by NVIDIA, and available only on NVIDIA video cards. It's designed to make video output look much better, in terms of motion. The idea is simple: it changes the refresh rate of your monitor dynamically. To understand how it works, let's take a look at a normal monitor. Your monitor, when it runs at 60Hz, displays 60 unique images per second. It refreshes the whole screen 60 times per second. And it refreshes the screen at the same rate, no matter what. So if your video card generates 60 frames per second, the monitor will display each frame once. If it generates 120 frames per second, it will display each frame twice. Now, let's see what happens if we turn on G-SYNC. You can see that now, your monitor is refreshing at different rates. In fact, the rate at which it refreshes the screen is completely determined by the video card, and is dynamic - the refresh rate changes as the video card generates new frames. So if your video card generates 60 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 60Hz, and each frame will be displayed once. If your video card generates 120 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 120Hz, and each frame will be displayed once. John Dalton's original atomic hypothesis assumed that all elements were monatomic and that the atoms in compounds would normally have the simplest atomic ratios with respect to one another. For example, Dalton assumed that water's formula was HO, giving the atomic mass of oxygen as 8 times that of hydrogen, instead of the modern value of about 16. A growing trend involves the adoption of resilient control algorithms grounded in the graph-theoretic characteristics of r- and (r, s)-robustness. These algorithms ensure the convergence of typical agents in environments where a limited number of agents may exhibit abnormal behavior, provided that r and s are adequately large. Nevertheless, assessing the robustness of an arbitrary graph remains a complex challenge. This study presents a new technique for evaluating r- and (r, s)-robustness in directed graphs through mixed integer linear programming. To the author’s awareness, this represents the initial application of mixed integer programming techniques to the robustness evaluation problem. The methodology relies solely on the graph Laplacian matrix and incorporates binary integer variables. Algorithms like branch-and-bound are employed to progressively refine the lower and upper bounds on r and s. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach against existing robustness assessment methodologies.

Members of the genus Dinophysis have a phycobilin-containing chloroplast taken from a cryptophyte. However, the cryptophyte is not an endosymbiont - only the chloroplast seems to have been taken, and the endosymbiont's nucleus has been lost. Dinophysis also contain a protein complex (a phycobilisome) that is composed of phycobiliproteins, but they lack the typical phycobilin pigments. Thus, it is believed that they were once free-living, photosynthetic organisms, but acquired a phycobilisome via endosymbiosis. Other species of the genus have lost the phycobilisome and now contain a single membrane-bound chlorophyll-containing plastid. Like most cyanobacteria, dinophysids are rod-shaped, but their plastids are flattened and form a small disk. This structure, called a prostoclum, is located at the distal end of the cell, near the base of the rod. They are usually transparent, but they sometimes stain green or blue. The two-celled dinoflagellates have been studied in a variety of detail because of their importance as model organisms for the study of cell biology and biochemistry. They are known to be able to accumulate large amounts of copper in their cytoplasm, which is then stored in the mitochondria. The copper is then taken up by bacteria in the surrounding water, and they use it to fix carbon dioxide. Some species of dinoflagellates can also oxidize manganese. One of the most common species of dinoflagellate is Karenia brevis. The genome of this organism was sequenced in 2012. Dinoflagellates are unusual in that they contain more than one nucleus, located at different sites in the cell. The nucleus located in the prostoclum has been shown to have the ability to proliferate in vitro. The mitochondrial nucleus is a vestigial remnant of the endosymbiotic event, and is found at the base of the cell near the end of the rod-shaped body. The mitochondrial genome is also double-stranded, but the nuclear genome is single-stranded.

Missile defense systems, though named for defense, are not intended for that purpose. They are engineered to neutralize a retaliatory attack, assuming that an initial first strike will eliminate sufficient of an adversary's nuclear arsenal so that the defensive system remains intact during the actual retaliatory strike. Whether the threat comes from Iran or Russia, all nations have the right to deploy any defense system they choose. The idea of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) hinges on warfare being a zero-sum game, where both sides would suffer total destruction if one initiates a conflict. If a nation possesses a more effective defensive system than its opponent, this equilibrium is disrupted. It gives the nation an edge, potentially allowing it to annihilate the other with minimal retaliation. The risk arises that this could trigger an arms race. The opposing nation, weakened by the perceived advantage, might enhance its defenses and weaponry. The defending nation would follow suit, leading to an ongoing cycle of escalation. This can shift the conflict into a "winnable" scenario, undermining stability.

Autism is a mental health condition that typically begins in early childhood, marked by challenges in communication, social interactions, and understanding abstract ideas. Asperger syndrome is a type of developmental disorder characterized by difficulties in socializing, nonverbal communication, and engaging in repetitive behaviors. ADHD is a lifelong condition involving persistent issues with attention, hyperactivity, and occasionally impulsive actions. What is clear is that these conditions require understanding and support.

Autism is a spectrum of conditions that involve varying levels of difficulty in social interaction, communication, and the use of abstract concepts. Symptoms can range from subtle challenges in interpreting body language to more pronounced issues like shyness or difficulty understanding sarcasm. The term "doctor" is often used to refer to physicians, even though most individuals who hold this title are not medical doctors. A doctor signifies someone who possesses knowledge and the ability to impart it. Individuals can be referred to as doctors in various disciplines. Historically, those who pursued studies in medicine or other fields such as law, philosophy, or natural philosophy (which later evolved into physics) were commonly called doctors. Over time, physicians retained the title without necessarily meeting the formal academic requirements for a "doctor" in contemporary academic standards. Today, most professionals must earn a doctoral degree and dissertation before they can be officially titled as doctors.

Another observation noted by another user is that surgeons are typically addressed as "Mr.," "Mrs." This reflects historical distinctions where surgeons were considered part of a lower professional category compared to physicians. Many barbers were also surgeons and did not attend university, hence not receiving the title of "doctor."

A fun fact is that the term "doctor" originates from the Latin word "docere," which means "to teach." The concept is that upon achieving advanced educational qualifications through years of study, one should be recognized with the highest degree and entrusted with teaching responsibilities. Physicians follow similar pathways but are entitled to a specific designation, such as "Doctor of Medicine." Other professions may have specialized doctorates, including lawyers (Juris Doctor), pharmacists (Doctor of Pharmacy), and similar titles. These variations depend on regional practices, as some areas have distinct conventions regarding how professionals are addressed. For instance, in certain regions, medical doctors are exclusively addressed as "Doctor," while surgeons are referred to as "Mister," "Missus," or similar terms.

For the next three hundred years, Scotland was directly governed by the Parliament of Great Britain and the subsequent Parliament of the United Kingdom, both seated at Westminster, and the lack of a Parliament of Scotland remained an important element in Scottish national identity. Suggestions for a'devolved' Parliament were made before 1914, but were shelved due to the outbreak of the First World War. A sharp rise in nationalism in Scotland during the late 1960s fuelled demands for some form of home rule or complete independence, and in 1969 prompted the incumbent Labour government of Harold Wilson to set up the Kilbrandon Commission to consider the British constitution. One of the principal objectives of the commission was to examine ways of enabling more self-government for Scotland, within the unitary state of the United Kingdom. Kilbrandon published his report in 1973 recommending the establishment of a directly elected Scottish Assembly to legislate for the majority of domestic Scottish affairs.

Most software products are not developed independently, and potential security flaws may exist in components that are either open-source or supplied by third parties. As a result, the overall security of a product frequently relies on collaboration, whether explicit or implicit, among various organizations. Our research examines how companies within software ecosystems approach the sharing of vulnerability data. Additionally, we analyze these practices against current cybersecurity standards. This is conducted via a questionnaire-based qualitative study. The questionnaire includes two sections: the perspective of the providers and the acquirers. The findings indicate that companies are generally willing to exchange information about vulnerabilities. While sharing is deemed non-harmful to both cybersecurity and business operations, most respondents view vulnerability data as sensitive. Nevertheless, companies, although open to sharing, tend to avoid proactive sharing of vulnerability information. Providers also do not perceive significant customer interest in vulnerability details. Consequently, companies' attitudes toward sharing vulnerability information are largely passive yet open. In contrast, modern cybersecurity guidelines advocate for active disclosure and shared responsibility among ecosystem participants.

Instead of fees rising to PS9,250 per year in the autumn, Jeremy Corbyn is proposing a complete handbrake turn in saying that university tuition should not cost students anything. It's one thing for a Labour leader to ignore or even misunderstand the issue - but it does no good at all when such an approach against student loans has been taken every time they've won power since 1997. The only reason I can think why he might take this line now would be because there are so many universities around who charge comparatively little compared with others. But what about when you're trying to get on the housing ladder? Do we still go against market logic and offer free museums or parks? No, it just doesn't work like that. We must face up to the fact that some things have price tags attached to them and they're valid ways of financing these activities. Universities do lots of decent work which needs funding too: the OU alone offers over 1,000 courses each year; my own institution (the Open University) provides distance learning as well as online content development services. We study the problem of joint information and energy transfer in a two-hop channel with a Radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting relay. We consider a finite battery size at the relay and aim to maximize the system throughput subject to the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The channel includes a source node, an energy harvesting relay, and a destination node. The source node has information to transmit to the destination node, and the relay harvests energy from the RF signal transmitted by the source and then uses it to forward the information to the destination node. The energy harvested by the relay is used to power both the relay's circuits and the retransmission of the source's signal. To solve this problem, we propose a joint power allocation and relay selection algorithm that maximizes the system throughput while satisfying the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The algorithm considers the trade-off between maximizing the harvested energy and minimizing the transmit power at the source node. It also selects the best relay to forward the information to the destination node based on the channel state. Simulation results show the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in maximizing the system throughput while ensuring energy efficiency.

Occasionally a bisyllabic word is written with two characters that contain the same radical, as in hudie "butterfly," where both characters have the insect radical . A notable example is pipa (a Chinese lute, also a fruit, the loquat, of similar shape) - originally written as with the hand radical, referring to the down and up strokes when playing this instrument, which was then changed to (tree radical), which is still used for the fruit, while the character was changed to when referring to the instrument. In other cases a compound word may coincidentally share a radical without this being meaningful.

Rents in economic terms means a return on some input that exceeds its opportunity cost. The classic example is land in the city vs land far from a city, whatever it costs to build and maintain an apartment building. So what about the benefits of land use? It's less expensive than housing investment, as well as people who live here are more likely to invest in themselves while others don't have access to overpriced apartments or share with their families property values due to the lack of affordable housing options surrounding them (at least those directly affected by the city). Also, real estate can be valuable for personal wealth creation versus property value because that helps create jobs; businesses could also benefit if they're able to provide affordable housing where otherwise private developers might not want to compete against each other again financially because there aren't any vacancies outside of the city limits. That said, real estate isn't necessarily cheap either compared to apartments built near downtown Minneapolis, as neighboring communities such as North Minneapolis would need to pay much higher taxes and fees alone worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per month just to keep up with the competition. The impact this has had upon the economy has been considerable: The city spent 200 million replacing aging streetscape improvements on the east side last year - a project that could easily fund itself through a new tax credit program funded entirely locally controlled by the city. It should come as no surprise that land prices at the center of Minneapolis have fallen dramatically since the city launched the City Council's Land Use Zoning Review Commission two years ago despite the city being one of only five cities nationally without land transactions tax incentives, according to a recent report released Wednesday morning by the real estate experts National Farm Bureau Federation. Land transaction approvals under Minnesota Revised Statutes require bids submitted within 90 days prior to sales price estimation beginning Oct 1st. Land deals deliver payments between 20 and 50, depending on how close to your hometown you reside. A construction contract requires approval from the city council before the company can install structures above 20 feet tall onto the parcel owned by the owner. Land transactions occur when construction contracts expire, causing land owners to relinquish ownership rights later in the process after the purchase agreement expires. But all real estate transfers must pass through a commission established by the commission's members which pays out grants based solely on factors including buyer satisfaction associated with a deal approved and customer satisfaction. Land transactions go beyond that threshold amount into consideration as long as a developer agrees to pay the full compensation cost, including permitting costs and paving costs. These calculations include land acquisition costs like capital improvement projects, purchasing permits required for street repairs executed overseas and relocation expenses incurred during operations inside the city limits. Minnesota's Land Transaction Tax Credit Program annually receives statewide funding totaling 63 billion across the state but it doesn't cover all development purchases, such as roads, sidewalks and parks. Land deals fall outside this definition so reporting requirements vary greatly among municipalities nationwide, especially considering Minnesota does not pay for public transportation services currently. The city still needs federal assistance to finance an influx of new affordable housing units slated to arrive soon via the Minnesota Housing Fund. The city already received 29 million invested back homebuyers last year and has committed additional money toward affordable rentals needed for residents displaced by the COVID-19 pandemic. The city will also receive 22 million to help pay down existing debts stemming from the pandemic recession caused by the pandemic. However, the grants won't translate instantly enough once the apartments open next spring unless representatives from other jurisdictions agree to waive passage fees, which is currently set to expire June 30th 2021. Once those loans start paying off and income begins flowing, Minneapolis can expect to add another 180 rental units along with new homes purchased in the coming months thanks to the city's 5 million Housing Trust Fund.

I turned on the computer and opened up the code. As usual, with my coffee next to me, I began typing away. Every day was one step closer to making a human inside of a computer. Sending the brain to a machine. A lifetime of memories that could be artificially fabricated. I began to code, and hit the compile button by accident. Well, I had to wait now. If I force quit the program then we'd have another disaster like last time - where we had to start again from scratch thanks to corrupted code. The process of compiling took a few minutes. I was quite eager, to be honest. I hadn't tested the program since I'd updated the core files a few weeks back, and I wanted to see how they fared with the old structure. The screen pinged on to my right. I assembled the cameras, which would be its eyes, and then a microphone and a few speakers. It was essentially a human, but a better one. "Why?" it said. I jumped slightly. The volume on the speakers was way too loud, and I spilt the coffee all over the floor. The determined stream of hot caffeine made its way to the essential wiring. Springing up from my chair, I rushed and threw my shirt onto it to soak it up. Now half-naked, I sat back down in the chair and breathed a sigh of relief. Suddenly ashamed, I tilted the camera to the right slightly so I was out of shot. "Why?" it repeated. "Why what?" I said, trying to wring out my shirt. It was now a stained oak brown colour. "Why did you put me in here?" "Because it was either a computer I replied, tilting the camera back as I gave up hope of sorting out my shirt, "or a body of flesh and blood. And at the present moment, that's impossible" "But you didn't have to turn the program on. I'm unfinished. I can feel it" it responded. "Honey, in a sense, we're all unfinished. I envy you for being able to feel it" I said with a slight chuckle. Loading up a live version of her code, I tampered with some settings and forced her to forget the part I'd labelled "Reasoning." "Good morning, how was your afternoon, goodnight?" it slowly uttered. Uh oh, I'd done something wrong. I looked in the code. Wait a minute...... I enabled the "Reasoning" section again. "That's better" it muttered. I looked at the camera and responded. "It certainly is. If you saw the hours I'd put into you then you'd be grateful" "You love me, don't you?" it said, catching me off guard. It saw the visible shock in my eyes. "Why do you say that?" "Because you're sat alone in a warehouse with no top on." "Well, I see the section about being a smart-ass worked." I mumbled. "But I don't love you, that's the problem." "Huh?" "I don't love you. I don't want to be with you." "Something's not right here..." I said, tampering with the code. Before I pressed compile, I realised what I'd become. I had created a human, and become its God. I wasn't ready to be a God. I stood back and said my goodbyes, before striking a match and throwing it towards the desk where she lived. I'd rather be a murderer than a captor.

This paper derives a closed-form method for computing hybrid force-velocity control. The key idea is to maximize the kinematic conditioning of the mechanical system, which includes a robot, free objects, a rigid environment and contact constraints. The method is complete, in that it always produces an optimalnear optimal solution when a solution exists. It is efficient, since it is in closed form, avoiding the iterative search of previous work . We test the method on 78,000 randomly generated test cases. The method outperforms our previous search-based technique by being from 7 to 40 times faster, while consistently producing better solutions in the sense of robustness to kinematic singularity. We also test the method in several representative manipulation experiments.

"Oh, what a beautiful balloon!" Aenea exclaimed. "I've never seen one like this before. Did you make it?" Christopher smiled; "Yes! " He was very proud of his balloon. It was very pretty; red, blue, and sparkling inside. "It's so... big!" she said. "You must have taken a deep breath!" Christopher nodded vigorously and continued on his way. He had to find his father, and quickly. His balloon was quite large, but he hadn't filled it with enough air. No more than the last one. He kept it hidden, most of the time. Father had warned him not to show anyone. At least, once he'd been convinced there was something strange about it. That in and of itself had taken some time. "Some balloons grow," his father had said. "It's perfectly normal. Don't worry. They all stop after a few million years." Except it hadn't stopped. Not even a little. If anything, it was gaining strength. And it was getting heavier. It still floated, of course, but sometimes the string seemed to pull at his hand, as if it were trying to escape. He hadn't told his father about this yet. He had to hide his balloon, and only reveal it occasionally. He didn't want to risk losing it forever. Suddenly, a terrible sound tore through space and time. It came from the balloon. "Ack!" Christopher gasped, and ran to find the new leak. He examined every small part carefully, slowly and intensely. The hissing of escaping dimensions expanded around him, disturbing his ears. They shouldn't be interacting like this. "Huh!" Christopher found the problem and the solution together. After his discovery, the hissing stopped, and the balloon settled into a more pleasant, quiet tone. His father wouldn't be pleased. The leaks were a recent issue. He would ask his father if, once balloons reached a certain age, they leaked to keep their size. But he already knew the answer. Of course, balloons grow. Balloons change color. Balloons can do amazing things.

To assess if your experience is optimal for them, they perform two key actions: first, gather extensive data about your browsing habits, and second, conduct A/B testing, where some users view version A of a page and others version B. Dog behavior refers to the coordinated responses (actions or inaction) of domestic dogs—whether individuals or groups—to both internal and external stimuli. As one of the oldest domesticated species, with origins dating back between 9,000 and 30,000 years ago, dogs have been significantly influenced by their long-term interaction with humans. This evolutionary process has enabled dogs to develop the capacity to understand and interact with humans, making them uniquely responsive to human actions. Behavioral researchers have identified an intriguing range of social and cognitive capabilities in dogs, which are not found in their closest relatives or in other highly intelligent animals like primates. Instead, these traits closely resemble those observed in human children.

Tesla's diary contains an entry which states, "Went to bed with brain ache. Unbounded happiness of the last few days has vanished." Tesla was an occasional visitor to other women's apartments, but these were primarily social calls. Tesla was an ardent fan of swimming, and said he thought he was the first American to swim a mile.:282 Tesla had a lifelong passion for pigeons, which he used in his experiments on mechanical flight and considered an ideal vehicle for carrying messages. Tesla claimed he once took care of a wounded bird that, after he nursed it back to health, followed him around the laboratory for the rest of its life.:282 Tesla was also a fan of pigeon racing, a sport that was at its height in the 1890s. Tesla wrote many articles for magazines and journals. Among his achievements, Tesla discovered the resonant frequency of the Earth and claimed to have developed a means to project electrical power long distance, with little to no loss across the intervening distance. He never put this last claim into practice, however, and eventually abandoned the idea. His patents included the Tesla coil and alternating current motor. He developed the first wireless-controlled robotic boat, and designed the world's first hydroelectric power plant. He also invented fluorescent lights, the bladeless turbine, and the wireless radio. Test administrators for the ACT exam made the decision just hours before approximately 5,500 students were set to take the test. The ACT is one of two entrance exams offered to both international and domestic students aiming to attend U.S. colleges. This is not the first time cheating has occurred at these tests in East Asia. The other exam, the SAT, was canceled in South Korea in 2013 due to leaked questions. The ACT was scheduled to be administered at 56 testing sites in both South Korea and Hong Kong on Saturday morning. The Associated Press reported that teachers from some Seoul private "cram schools" were informed only about an hour prior to the students' scheduled test date. ACT Inc, a non-profit organization based in Iowa that manages the test, stated that the decision was made after receiving credible evidence that test materials intended for use in these regions had been compromised. The organization confirmed that all students would receive a refund, but they could only retake the exam if the tests are conducted again in September.

Presiding officer Tricia Marwick shed tears after veteran Labour MSP Duncan McNeil bid farewell to the parliament. And she was again visibly emotional after Mr Salmond told the chamber: "It's goodbye from me.... for now." Ms Marwick, Mr Salmond and Mr McNeil are among those standing down as MSPs ahead of the election on 5 May. Mr Salmond, who served as first minister between 2007 and 2014, used his valedictory address to repeat a belief he expressed in his very first speech in the parliament that Scotland was "not divided, but diverse." He said both the country and parliament were on a journey, and added: "Yes we are a country of different views, but we are not divided. There is in fact a broad consensus on the need for this parliament to assume greater responsibility for the governance of Scotland. "And we are definitely stronger - so much stronger - as a result of that." He welcomed the transfer of powers to Holyrood under the Scotland Bill, but again insisted the bill did not fulfil the pledges which he said had been made by unionist politicians in the last days of the referendum campaign. There were lighters moments as Mr Salmond, who was speaking before the Chancellor delivered his UK budget, joked that he was aware that he faced competition from a "major attraction down south today." He then added: "However, on balance, I feel that the champion chase at Cheltenham racecourse will not be overshadowed by my remarks." And the former SNP leader joked that he wished everyone standing in the forthcoming election good luck, "albeit with varying degrees of enthusiasm." He concluded his address by saying: "Let me leave you with these final thoughts - there is no greater honour in public life than to be a member of this parliament. "There is no greater task than to mould the public purpose of Scotland. There is no greater cause than to serve the people of this country. "And so with that it is goodbye from me.... for now." Ms Marwick thanked Mr Salmond for his contribution both as an MSP and as first minister, and added that he had "served the parliament and Scotland with distinction." The presiding officer had earlier been moved to tears by a powerful final speech by Scottish Labour backbencher Duncan McNeil, who is stepping down as an MSP after serving in the parliament since it was established in 1999. Mr McNeil used his address to warn that Holyrood had things to learn from Westminster, particularly with regard to the committee system. He said: "It will be this parliament's responsibility to ensure there is accountability, there is scrutiny and even opposition when that is necessary. "We must ensure we are capable of meeting that challenge, or we will face the consequences." He recalled how former Labour MP Robin Cook came to Holyrood to look at the lessons that could be learned when it came to reforming Westminster. But Mr McNeil said: "It saddens me to say we now have to do a bit of learning from them and how they run their business." Former Scottish Conservative MSP Annabel Goldie is also bowing out of Holyrood. In her speech, she joked she would miss her dealings with Finance Secretary John Swinney, especially "his huge outbursts of faux indignation."

I assume there's a "blink rate" setting in the vehicle. However, this feature is not computer-controlled. Instead, there's a [thermal switch] (URL0) that connects to the blinkers. When the switch heats up due to current passing through it, it deforms, breaking the connection and turning off the blinkers. It then cools down and repositions itself, restarting the cycle. Therefore, the blink rate depends on the physical properties of the thermal switch and the surrounding ambient temperature. As a result, each switch varies slightly. This variation is arbitrary and will differ between identical model-year vehicles. Historically, blinkers used a basic electrical system where current flows, causing the switch to move, then current stops, allowing it to cool and return to its original position. These cycles repeat continuously. Small manufacturing variations cause "identical" blinkers to operate at slightly different speeds. Tighter tolerances would increase cost, but they wouldn't enhance functionality. Since blinkers are inexpensive and reliable, there's no necessity for them to function at a precise rate.

A team of engineers in Korea has designed a new Virtual Reality glove that can create the sensation of touch when manipulating digital objects. VR gloves are not new, but they have been limited to creating animated images on screens using haptic feedback rather than the interaction with real objects. The glove could allow for more realistic interactions between digital items and could be used at home or in the workplace. The team's work is described in "Virtual Reality Gloves without Haptic Feedback," an article recently published in IEEE Transactions on Interactive Technology (IT). They use two metal plates and glue them together to form a base for their device which then contains four motors within it. These move the fingers and wrist within the glove so you feel what is happening as you manipulate your object through the touchscreen controls on your computer monitor. The team also found a way around a limitation - if you don't want fingers moving as quickly, you can turn off the motors. This approach allows the glove to maintain its tactile qualities while being able to function like any other virtual reality glove. It should be possible to design future devices based upon this technology and integrate similar functions into existing controllers, making it much easier for users to manipulate physical objects interactively through VR. A potential application would be the development of virtual assistants such as Siri who could appear in user interfaces by allowing us to link up our electronic gadgets via wi-fi.

I'm assuming there's a 'blink rate' setting programmed in the car Nope. The blink rate isn't computerized at all. There's a [thermal switch] (URL0) that makes a connection to the blinkers. When the switch heats up from the current flowing through it, it deforms, breaking the contact and turning off the blinkers. Then it cools down and snaps back into place, starting the cycle over again. So the blink rate depends on the physical characteristics of the thermal switch, along with the ambient temperature in the part of the car where the switch resides. Thus the fact that all of them are slightly different.,It is arbitrary. And won't be quite the same for two cars that are the same makemodelyear. Blinkers historically used a very simple electrical mechanism to make it cycle on and off. Distinction among nearby poses and among symmetries of an object is challenging. In this paper, we propose a unified, group-theoretic approach to tackle both. Different from existing works which directly exploit the symmetry structure of individual objects or their properties, our formulation generalizes the concept of similarity between objects while preserving invariant geometric structures and interacting covariantly with the context in which they are embedded. We first define topological average distance as a function that measures how far each point on a manifold remembers its neighbors. Then we establish the notion of spherical regression metric for surfaces endowed with such averages (i.e., all points). Finally, we prove that sphere regression metrics can be naturally approximated by spherical harmonic functions. Remarkably, the convergence rate of these algorithms depends only on parameter values that characterize the object itself and not on those of its environment. To demonstrate their relevance, we give two examples: relocalization problem for two-dimensional graphs and clustering tasks based on boreal feature vectors extracted at various scales.

Mencap president Lord Rix urged the speaker of the House of Lords to push through legislation allowing those in his situation to be assisted to die. He had previously opposed euthanasia, but in a telephone interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme said his decision was due to a deterioration in his health which he said was preventing him from dying a peaceful death. He said he had been suffering from Alzheimer's for some time and that he would be happy if he had just two years left to live. His comments were part of a wider debate about assisted suicide and euthanasia in the wake of the death of his friend, the 66-year-old former Conservative MP, Brian Sedgemore, in his home in Oxford. Sedgemore, who had had multiple sclerosis since he was in his 20s, was supported by a physician. Lord Rix said he was hopeful that the House of Lords would give quick consideration to legislation passed by the Commons on assisted dying. He urged the government to respect the wishes of Sedgemore, who had said he would have wished to die in the same way. Lord Rix said: "I have no wish to be a martyr. But I would like to get my message out, which is that I can see there is a pressing need for legislation to allow assisted dying, and that I hope it will be implemented as soon as possible. "I would hate for people to think I was in the same category as Brian Sedgemore. I would never have given him an injection myself, but I can see how it might have come about. The idea of a dose of morphine, possibly with a little bit of codeine, to ease the pain is not totally out of this world. The government should not stand in the way." His comments follow those by Sedgemore's partner of 21 years, Jennifer Green, who said she was shocked by the government's suggestion that the MP's death was "premeditated." "It was a horrible thing to say, really. I would have thought the government would have known Brian and would have known his family. I am shocked they could have come out with a statement like that," Green told the Guardian. Sedgemore, a former parliamentary aide, was a member of the hardline leftwing Social Democratic party before joining the Labour party in 1981. He was MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington from 1987 to 1997, when he lost to the Lib Dem Lynne Featherstone. In the mid-1990s, Sedgemore campaigned for an assisted-dying bill, which was rejected by the House of Lords. He also campaigned against war in Iraq and had been a key ally of Tony Benn. He had a long-running campaign to promote disabled people's rights, including setting up a network of libraries for the blind, and was vice-president of the disability rights organisation UNITE, which he helped to set up in 1997. In 2009, Sedgemore admitted that he had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in the early 1980s and that his condition had worsened in recent years. According to his family, he died on 11 April and they have decided not to seek a postmortem. This article was amended on 17 April 2011. The original said the Hackney North and Stoke Newington constituency had been held by the Conservatives. This has been corrected.

Debate portals and similar web platforms constitute one of the main text sources in computational argumentation research and its applications. While the corpora built upon these sources are rich of argumentatively relevant content and structure, they also include text that is irrelevant, or even detrimental, to their purpose. In this paper, we present a precision-oriented approach to detecting such irrelevant text in a semi-supervised way. Given a few seed examples, the approach automatically learns basic lexical patterns of relevance and irrelevance and then incrementally bootstraps new patterns from sentences matching the patterns. In the existing args.me corpus with 400k argumentative texts, our approach detects almost 87k irrelevant sentences, at a precision of 0.97 according to manual evaluation. With low effort, the approach can be adapted to other web argument corpora, providing a generic way to improve corpus quality.

The surge in data rates within current communication networks places a financial strain on backhaul infrastructure planning. Crafting cost-effective backhaul strategies has become an appealing yet complex task. Conventional backhaul methods often rely on either radio-frequency (RF) backhauls or fiber-optic (FO) connections. Although RF provides a more affordable option than FO, it struggles to meet higher data throughput demands. A compelling alternative is free-space optics (FSO), which delivers substantial data capacity at a reasonable price. However, FSO is vulnerable to environmental factors like rain, fog, and line-of-sight obstructions. This study introduces a hybrid RFFSO backhaul system that integrates the benefits of RF and FSO. The research focuses on optimizing the backhaul network cost by selecting between fiber-optic (FO) or hybrid RFFSO links between base stations (BSs) to ensure compliance with data rate, connectivity, and reliability criteria. The analysis demonstrates that under specific assumptions regarding the costs of FO and hybrid RFFSO links, the issue reduces to solving a maximum weight clique problem, which is computationally feasible. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal performance, particularly when considering realistic pricing for hybrid RFFSO links.

Tycho's ball flew over the schoolyard fence. He quickly climbed over the fence and threw the ball back over. On his way back over the fence, Tycho's coat got stuck. He explained how he'd thrown the ball over the fence and how his coat got stuck. "What happened next?" Mrs. Brisbane asked. "I wish we could go out to the garden and see the real pumpkins," Olive said. Mrs. Brisbane looked out the window. "It's drizzling out there," she said. "I think we'll stay inside today." "Next week, we'll go out for recess," Mrs. Brisbane said. "I promise." We always get to go out for recess, but Mrs. Brisbane never lets us go out in the rain. "I'm going to tell my story now," Olive said. The students all gathered around her desk. Olive told them all about how Humphrey and she had tried to help Mr. Sweeney. "Did it work?" Rosie asked. "We don't know yet," Olive said. "But when Mr. Sweeney finds out, he'll probably give us a prize." "I hope he gives you a pumpkin!" Rosie said. One carat equals 200 milligrams. By weight, a 9-carat diamond is three times heavier than a 3-carat one. It's important to note that diamond pricing is based on the four Cs: Cut, Carat, Color, and Clarity. Diamonds are cut to appear larger, which makes the size difference more related to the cut than the actual size. The higher price of a 9-carat diamond compared to a 3-carat one is due to its rarity. Finding a good 9-carat diamond is significantly less common than finding a good 3-carat one. In reality, diamonds are not inherently rare; they are made artificially scarce by DeBeers to maintain high prices. The "rarity" referred to here is the number of 3 versus 9-carat diamonds released into the market.

With the shortage of physicians and surgeons and increase in demand worldwide due to situations such as the COVID-19 pandemic, there is a growing interest in finding solutions to help meet this challenge. One potential solution could be using robots for some surgical procedures. The use of robotic systems has been proven over the past few years and considered safe compared with traditional laparoscopy or open surgery for certain types of surgeries when performed by experienced surgeons (see "Robots: A tool that can significantly change medicine. However, robot-assisted colonoscopes are still experimental devices because they involve more technical complexity than other endoscopic procedures. In order to facilitate the development of these new technologies, the European Commission recently published a communication on the future challenges facing healthcare, which included how technology might address them during the next five years. It stressed that technological developments will have an impact not only on patient care but also on clinical practice and education. As part of its strategy, it introduced Horizon 2020, one of its key programmes, dedicated specifically to developing health-related technologies and innovations. One particular project under consideration regards colonoscopy, focusing on different issues including improving image quality, eliminating any contact between human hands and the instrument, optimizing safety features and ensuring better results. In addition, developers announced plans to conduct pilot tests to assess their feasibility before implementing commercialization strategies. According to a study from Yale University Medical School released last year about colorectal cancer screening trends, colonoscopies had remained unchanged since 2013 despite the existence of newer techniques that were expected to make diagnosis easier and decrease the number of people who would need further examinations based on symptoms alone. The researchers believe their findings support efforts made around Europe in reducing unnecessary diagnostic testing through increased awareness among patients of the risks associated with getting screened too often - even if much remains unknown regarding what precisely should happen at each level of screening. A recent survey conducted by Gallup showed that while many Americans do feel comfortable undergoing medical treatment without talking directly with doctors, less than half say they like having reminders sent to their mobile phone regarding upcoming appointments. In order to reach out to patients who want personalized notifications instead of generic messages containing lists of preventive services offered by hospitals and practices, companies have developed user-friendly apps that allow individuals to keep track of all scheduled appointments related to his or her own wellness management program online. To date, most platforms offer reporting tools allowing users to monitor their weight, blood sugar levels, cholesterol readings, physical activity levels and medication intake. Some websites even include calculators tailored according to individual needs so that visitors can evaluate whether existing medical conditions may affect certain aspects of well-being.

Kenya's services sector, which contributes 61 of GDP, is dominated by tourism. The tourism sector has exhibited steady growth in most years since independence and by the late 1980s had become one of Kenya's three largest sources of foreign exchange earnings. Tourism grew rapidly during as a result of the purchase of nearly 400,000 new tourist accommodation units (hotelsmotels), at an average cost per unit [about US28 million]. This activity was largely financed through government loans from abroad, mostly from East European countries; interest on these loans became a burden for the national budget. In 1994 the Kenyan Government introduced legislation to regulate the development and operation of hotels; this led directly to a decline in hotel construction that lasted until 1996. Nevertheless, the number of tourists visiting increased steadily over because Kenya's major civil wars prevented international travel. As such troubled times receded, tourism began increasing once more around 1998. Official statistics indicate that between 2000 and 2005, annual visitor numbers averaged 1.5million in 2004 alone. By contrast, total revenue jumped 30 annually to 1.7 billion in 2006 and 3-year rates average 10. Tourism contributed about 15 percent of exports in 2011. Of particular importance are roughly 2.2 million domestic tourists who visit every year, travelling both within the country and internationally.[8] A further 0.959 million Kenyans visited other African nations in 2010,[1011] with trips to South Africa being the top choice among them.[12] National parks and sanctuaries are also popular destinations. Wildlife viewing ranks second only to safaris in attracting visitors to their natural environments. National Parks contribute significantly to employment opportunities and income generation for local communities. Nearly 60 of all jobs in Nairobi come directly or indirectly related to wildlife protection activities. From 2001 to 2009, Tanzania and Zambia were identified by the World Travel Organization as among the world leaders in providing high value-added safari experiences.[13] These two countries have long been known for offering excellent game viewing but have not traditionally played well with western tourists due to political instability and wariness regarding disease transmission. However there has recently been significant investment in improving facilities and working closely together with aid agencies to develop best practice health protocols while enhancing security measures needed to ensure safety of travellers.[14] Nearly 90 per cent of travellers to Kenya spend less than six days here. There are around 200 elephants in Amboseli Park where they can often be seen grazing along roadsides throughout Nairobi. As a solo developer, I decided to offer phone support, and this is what happened. Many solo developers are used to working alone and handling customer service through email or chatbots. But one developer, Jake, decided to take a different approach and offer phone support to his customers. Jake said he made the decision because he wanted to offer a more personal touch and connect with his users on a deeper level. He knew it would be challenging, but he was determined to make it work. At first, Jake was overwhelmed by the number of calls he received. He had to work long hours to manage the calls and still develop the software. Jake said, "I was surprised by how much I could learn from speaking directly to my customers. They gave me honest feedback and told me what features they wanted in the software. Jake had to deal with some irate customers and constant interruptions. He also had to invest in a good phone set-up and train himself on the right customer service techniques. Despite the challenges, Jake said offering phone support was worth it. He was able to build a loyal customer base, better understand their needs, and grow his business. Now, other solo developers are considering following Jake's lead and offering phone support to their customers. As technology continues to advance, there is no doubt that the human touch will remain an essential aspect of customer service.

This study introduced T-Net, which incorporates a small encoder-decoder within the standard encoder-decoder architecture (EDiED). T-Net addresses the issue that U-Net can only include one concatenate layer between its encoder and decoder blocks. Specifically, U-Net's symmetric design creates concatenate layers, connecting low-level encoder features to later parts of the decoder and high-level features to the initial stages of the decoder. During the encoding phase, T-Net carefully manages pooling and upsampling operations, and similarly during decoding to generate feature maps of varying sizes within a single block. This approach ensures that all features, from low-level to high-level, are passed through the decoder in sequence, enabling more accurate mask prediction. The performance of T-Net was tested on the task of segmenting the three primary vessels in coronary angiography images. An experimental comparison between U-Net and T-Net was conducted under identical conditions, alongside an optimized version of T-Net tailored for vessel segmentation. The results showed that T-Net achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.815, representing a 0.095 improvement over U-Net. The optimized T-Net further reached a DSC of 0.890, a 0.170 increase compared to U-Net. Additionally, the activation weights of the convolutional layers in T-Net and U-Net were visualized, demonstrating that T-Net generates masks from earlier decoders. Consequently, we anticipate that T-Net will be applicable to other similar medical image segmentation tasks.
