Charon gently paddled the long oar across the dark waters, silence his only companion in the foggy waters of Styx. He craned his bony neck as he stared off into the mist and rain, listening for any sound that would indicate the presence of a soul. He knew it would not be easy. The grief-stricken, the weeping, the tortured, the angry and confused all came to the river, but none were always ready to step off the bank into the boat and on to the next life. No one knew this better than Charon, who had been ferrying the dead to the underworld for countless centuries. Some souls were stubborn, preferring to cling to the belief that there was something else waiting for them when they reached the end of the journey. There was no explanation for their disbelief, no reason for their fear. Charon did not judge them, simply did his duty, waiting patiently, determined to carry out the task until the last breath had been exhaled. For a thousand years, he had been waiting. He had ferried souls from every corner of the Earth, from the great cities of Rome and Paris, from the vast expanses of the plains of Russia and the steaming jungles of the Far East, from the icy tundras of the Arctic to the steamy jungles of the Amazon. He had ferried souls from the battlefields of the American Civil War and the trenches of World War I. From the beaches of Normandy, the shores of Guadalcanal, the fields of Vietnam and the deserts of the Gulf War. He had ferried souls from the World Trade Center on 911. He had seen many wars, many natural disasters, and the death of millions of souls. It was hard for him to believe he was still waiting. The long oar dipped into the water with a barely perceptible splash. Charon's ears twitched, and he stared through the misty fog. He heard it again, a little louder this time. There was nothing he could do but wait. He had a boat full of souls, and while he would not force them to leave the comfort of the world they knew, he would have to wait for the boat to empty before he could go in search of the one who called to him. He waited, listening to the gentle lapping of the waters against the sides of the boat. He had been waiting for more than a thousand years. He waited for what seemed like an eternity. He looked up at the dark clouds hanging low over the waters. Rain began to fall, and Charon cowered slightly in the bottom of the boat, letting the water run down his face and neck. He closed his eyes, and felt the dampness seeping into his bones. When he opened them again, the darkness was gone. The clouds had cleared and the fog had lifted, and the waters of Styx were clear and bright in the morning sun. Charon looked down into the bottom of the boat. They were all gone. He looked over at the bank, and saw a lone figure standing there. He could barely make him out, but he recognized him. He had waited so long for this moment. Charon stood up and began to walk toward the bank. He reached the edge of the boat and extended a bony hand to help the soul step out of the boat. It had been such a long time since he had carried a soul. He would not make that mistake again. The man looked back at Charon and gave him a small smile, then began to walk up the bank. Charon nodded and smiled. He had waited so long. He had finally ferried a soul. Attention mechanisms that connect encoders and decoders have been extensively used in tasks such as object recognition, image captioning, visual question answering, and neural machine translation, leading to improved performance. In this study, we introduce a bottom-up gated hierarchical attention (GHA) framework tailored for image captioning. The proposed model utilizes a CNN as the decoder, enabling it to capture diverse concepts across various layers of the network. These concepts are associated with specific regions within an image, allowing us to integrate lower-level attention weights into higher-level representations and propagate these features upward for prediction. Our GHA enhances the performance of models that rely solely on single-level attention, such as the CIDEr score, which rises from 0.923 to 0.999, matching the performance of advanced models employing attribute boosting and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate both the CNN decoder and the GHA, revealing that deeper decoders do not yield superior results, and as the convolutional decoder becomes more complex, the model tends to collapse during training. A recent study by the National Institute of Dairy and Frozen Treats (NIDFT) has uncovered the key to keeping ice cream creamy, not crunchy. The scientists at NIDFT conducted a series of tests to determine what factors contributed to ice cream becoming crunchy. After months of experimentation and analysis, they concluded that it was the presence of air bubbles in the mixture that caused the ice cream to lose its creaminess. The team discovered that the best way to prevent ice cream from becoming crunchy was to reduce the amount of air bubbles in the mixture. This could be done by stirring the ice cream slowly while it is being churned. The slower the stirring, the less air bubbles would be incorporated into the mixture and the creamier the end result. The researchers also determined that the temperature at which the ice cream was stored also had an effect on its texture. Ice cream should be stored at -17C in order to keep it creamy for longer. The findings from this study will help people everywhere enjoy their favorite frozen treats for longer. With the right techniques and storage conditions, you can enjoy scoop after scoop of creamy, delicious ice cream without having to worry about it going stale or turning crunchy.

Environmental determinism functioned as a moral rationale for exerting dominance over specific regions and populations. It posited that an individual's actions were shaped by their surroundings, thereby legitimizing their authority. For instance, those residing in tropical climates were regarded as less civilized, thereby justifying colonial rule as a form of cultural uplift. During the three phases of European colonization—initial in the Americas, subsequent in Asia, and finally in Africa—environmental determinism was employed to assign indigenous peoples a racial order. This approach manifested in two ways: orientalism and tropicality.

I don't respond.  
There's a low, buzzing, whistling noise.  
The hairs in my ears, on the back of my neck, prickle and I know his finger, moistened by his lips, is one head-jerk away from being buried in my ear canal.  
"Noodle, noodle, big boy."  
"For the love of Christ," I say.  
He whips the finger back.  
"Aren't you done?"  
The only thing separating us is a small hole, about five feet off the ground, no more than half the size of my palm, maybe, knocked into the wall.  
Son of a bitch has been here eight years and spent the last three wearing away this hole. Or so he told me.  
Several times.  
Whether or not it's true, who cares. It's a pain in the ass.  
"I'm not done 'til you are, sweetie."  
I turn my head and meet his eyes, of course staring through the hole.  
His eyes are downturned. Yellow at the edges.  
I'm sure they would have been a lovely shade of green without the veneer of batshit insanity whirling in their depths.  
"You're going to stare at me now, right?"  
I say.  
The eyes crinkle at the edges and the hole is once again filled with darkness and his finger emerges.  
"Come on, don't you want me to touch you?"  
I turn my head away in response.  
The finger whips back.  
"Ever think about the type of person who's in here?"  
he continues, his voice little more than a gurgle with consonants.  
"What they've done with their hands?"  
"Keep talking," I say.  
"Please. You're not going to get to me, but you seem bored."  
"Damn right I am," he says.  
"Bored and lonely and what I would love to do to you, big boy. I miss the smell of skin, that soft, baby powder smell. But you know what I miss most?"  
I don't respond.  
"The screams," he says.  
"The cries for me to stop. The muffled screams of pain, the tongue on my hand when I try and shut 'em up. And it would be easy with you, you're so small and skinny."

To leave Earth, you must attain escape velocity, which decreases as you move farther away. This means that to enter orbit, you need to descend below this velocity. However, the key point is that the lower the altitude, the less escape velocity is required. A slow rocket might still surpass escape velocity once it descends sufficiently, but if it doesn’t, it will either return or enter orbit. The reason we don’t do this is due to several factors. One major issue is that each unit of fuel adds to the overall mass, requiring more fuel to lift it higher. By burning fuel early, you reduce the amount needed later. While many rockets initially accelerate slowly to minimize drag, their "slowness" is far greater than what humans experience, making it feel very rapid.

From a physics perspective, there’s no obstacle to escaping Earth gradually. Escape velocity varies with altitude, so higher altitudes allow for lower speeds. You can escape Earth’s gravity without exerting additional force, as long as your speed matches the required velocity. Imagine throwing a ball upward from the Moon—gravity weakens as it ascends, but it also slows down. If thrown fast enough, gravity will decrease faster than the ball’s speed, ensuring it never returns. The exact direction doesn’t matter, as long as it’s not hitting the ground. Throwing it faster than the escape velocity means it won’t return. From a high tower, the required speed is significantly lower. It’s important to note that this refers to escape velocity. Anything reaching space (typically around 62 miles or 100 kilometers) follows similar principles, though the specifics differ.

These proxies encounter challenges in scaling to serve more clients while ensuring they meet the complex user profiles of those clients. In this study, we employ an abstraction of complex execution intervals (CEIs), built upon simple execution intervals (EIs), to represent user profiles and utilize existing offline approximations as a foundation for enhancing the accuracy of capturing CEIs. The first approach focuses solely on characteristics of individual EIs, whereas the other two leverage features of all EIs within the CEI. Fast Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is highly in demand for many clinical applications in order to reduce the scanning cost and improve the patient experience. This can also potentially increase patient throughput and reduce the need for repeat scans. In the context of this project, the problem of accelerating MRI is treated as an image reconstruction problem, i.e., the main goal is to reconstruct a high-quality image from under-sampled k-space data. This project is a joint collaboration between Dr. Hanjoong Jo and Dr. Haris Vikalo. Dr. Hanjoong Jo is a professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois at Chicago (UIC), and the leader of the Medical Imaging Research Laboratory (MIR Lab). Dr. Haris Vikalo is an assistant professor at the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) at the University of Iowa (UI). This collaboration brings together the complementary expertise of the two groups in order to address the problem of accelerating MRI. In this project, we propose a novel image reconstruction algorithm for MRI based on the following premise: in order to accelerate MRI, we should capture the sparsity of the image in the spatial domain, and the sparsity of the image in the Fourier domain. Our algorithm is a regularized image reconstruction algorithm. We use the 1-norm of the image to capture the spatial sparsity, and the 1-norm of the Fourier transform of the image to capture the Fourier sparsity. This idea of enforcing sparsity of the Fourier transform of an image is novel. To the best of our knowledge, it has never been employed for the purpose of accelerating MRI. The algorithm is computationally efficient, because it does not require the computation of the Fourier transform of the image. This project is currently funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) through the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB).

In 1881, Tesla moved to Budapest to work under Ferenc Puskas at a telegraph company, the Budapest Telephone Exchange. Upon arrival, Tesla realized that the company, then under construction, was in terrible disrepair and needed immediate repairs. He also began working on a new electrical system for both the Budapest Telegraph Exchange and the Central Telegraph Company of Hungary (the latter company would later become Trans-Siberian Electric Power Ltd.). After learning about electricity from Edison's patents in 1882, he decided to pursue his own invention based upon them instead. Tesla focused mainly on electric current measurements using electromagnets and inductive coils; these were used as an alternative means of measuring alternating currents without sampling the signal. During this period, Tesla first coined the term "electronic phase" or "phase shift" to refer to a measure of voltage, rather than frequency due to a capacitance effect. It is usually a crypto currency like Bitcoin. The ransomware then gives a link that can be used to make the payment. I paid the hacker, and he sent me a decryption key. This enabled me to decrypt my files. I was very happy that I had gotten back my files. I had no other choice but to pay the ransom. Telehealth services may increase efficiency but may also improve access to care because of their capacity for geographic reach. Quebec, for example, recently announced plans to expand its telecheck program beyond cancer screening to more complex chronic conditions like diabetes, heart disease and hypertension. Here too, technology offers solutions: phones and tablets can easily connect patients to clinicians who live outside their home community. Similarly, telemedicine platforms can enable physicians to provide care wherever they happen to be located. Technologies like these will require investment, particularly given the scale involved. But even before the pandemic struck, many experts were calling for increased investments to support innovation in digital health technologies. We propose LETO, a new hybrid Lagrangian-Eulerian method for topology optimization. At the heart of LETO lies in a hybrid particle-grid Material Point Method (MPM) to solve for elastic force equilibrium. LETO transfers density information from freely movable Lagrangian carrier particles to a fixed set of Eulerian quadrature points. The quadrature points act as MPM particles embedded in a lower-resolution grid and enable sub-cell resolution of intricate structures with a reduced computational cost. By treating both densities and positions of the carrier particles as optimization variables, LETO reparameterizes the Eulerian solution space of topology optimization in a Lagrangian view. LETO also unifies the treatment for both linear and non-linear elastic materials. In the non-linear deformation regime, the resulting scheme naturally permits large deformation and buckling behaviors. Additionally, LETO explores contact-awareness during optimization by incorporating a fictitious domain-based contact model into the static equilibrium solver, resulting in the discovery of novel structures. We conduct an extensive set of experiments. By comparing against a representative Eulerian scheme, LETO's objective achieves an average quantitative improvement of 20 (up to 40) in 3D and 2 in 2D (up to 12). Qualitatively, LETO also discovers novel non-linear functional structures and conducts self-contact-aware structural explorations.

I am not a counselor, I'm not a teacher, and I'm not your mom. I am an advice columnist, which means that people write to me with their problems and I give them my opinion. That's it. I'm not a professional, I'm not qualified, and I'm not getting paid for this. I'm just some girl who likes to give advice. So please, don't write to me expecting me to fix your life. I can't. [header] How to deal with difficult in-laws [title] Respect your in-law's attachment to your spouse [step] Your spouse is their little boy or girl, and always will be, no matter how grown up. Especially if you have your own young children, think about how difficult it will be to "let them go" as adults someday. This attachment can often lead to difficult behaviors from your in-laws. Therefore, try to be understanding of their perspective and show empathy towards them. Reinforce your in-laws' connection to your spouse by encouraging them to spend time together, even if it doesn't include you. [step] Establish clear boundaries with your in-laws. If certain behaviors or topics of discussion make you uncomfortable, politely let them know. Remember to use "I" statements and avoid placing blame on your in-laws. Respect their boundaries as well, and try to find common ground on what is acceptable for both parties. [step] Keep communication open with your spouse about any issues that arise with their parents. It is important to work together as a team to find solutions and maintain a healthy relationship with your in-laws. Remember, you both have a shared interest in maintaining a positive relationship with them. [step] Lastly, don't be afraid to seek outside help if needed. This can include couples therapy or family counseling. A neutral party can help to provide strategies for managing difficult behaviors and conflicts within the family dynamic.

I am uncertain about vaccinations. While I do not believe autism can be directly caused by vaccines, I do consider there are valid reasons to oppose them. One reason is that, aside from the manufacturers, nobody knows exactly what substances are present in the vaccines. It's possible that some unknown ingredient might intentionally affect our immune system, keeping us dependent on pharmaceuticals. Another concern is that the pharmaceutical industry has no incentive to promote public health; instead, they focus on maintaining profitability by keeping people sick. These points are often seen as paranoid, but they resemble the oil industry, which also profits from maintaining the status quo. These arguments aren't mine, but I present them because I find them more reasonable than the autism controversy. My conclusion is that I don't strongly support or oppose vaccines; I simply don't have a clear opinion.
